## operator/src/lib.rs (2 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (maintainability)

`#![allow(warnings)]` globally suppresses every compiler warning for the entire operator library. In a production codebase this hides real defects: unused imports/variables, dead code, unreachable patterns, deprecated API usage, and ignored `#[must_use]` results all compile silently, so regressions are easy to introduce and hard to spot in review. This is especially risky here because many modules are large and continuously evolving. Prefer removing the attribute entirely (and fixing warnings), or at most gate it behind `#[cfg(feature = "dev")]` / narrow it to specific lints that are genuinely noise (e.g. `#![allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]`).

---

### [high] (maintainability)

`pub use db_abstraction::*;` is a broad glob re-export that silently collides with the explicit re-exports in this file. `db_abstraction` publicly defines its own `Trade` (db_abstraction/mod.rs) and `CircuitBreakerState`, while `pub use models::{..., Trade, ...}` and `pub use circuit_breaker::{CircuitBreaker, CircuitBreakerState, TripReason}` re-export differently-defined types with the same names. Rust resolves the collision by preferring the explicit imports and silently dropping the glob's `Trade`/`CircuitBreakerState`, so downstream users can never reach `db_abstraction::Trade` or `db_abstraction::CircuitBreakerState` from the crate root — and the two types are easy to confuse. It also pulls in the entire db_abstraction surface (trait `Database`, `timed_query`, conversion helpers, submodules `export`/`postgres`/`types`) into the root namespace without an explicit interface. Replace the glob with an explicit re-export list of only the types this crate's public API should expose.

## ops/grafana/dashboards/trading/signal-pipeline.json (4 findings, 0 critical, 4 high)

### [high] (bug)

The `value` field is placed as a sibling of `options` inside each mapping object. In Grafana's value-mapping schema, the numeric value must be a key inside `options` (e.g. `options: {"0": {...}}`); a top-level `value` property next to `options` is not recognized, so both UNHEALTHY/HEALTHY mappings will be ignored and the panel will show raw numeric values. Merge both value cases into a single mapping object with the values inside `options`.

```suggestion
            {"type": "value", "options": {"0": {"text": "UNHEALTHY", "color": "red"}, "1": {"text": "HEALTHY", "color": "green"}}}
```

---

### [high] (bug)

This raw SQL has no `$__timeFilter(created_at)`, so the table always returns the same 30 most-recent rows regardless of the dashboard time range, which can show stale data that falls outside the selected window. Add a `WHERE $__timeFilter(created_at)` clause so the table respects the dashboard's time range.

```suggestion
          "rawSql": "SELECT wallet_address, token_address, signal_type, consensus_score, signal_count, created_at FROM signal_aggregation WHERE $__timeFilter(created_at) ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 30",
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`histogram_quantile` requires its input vector to have exactly one `le` label per series. If `chimera_signal_quality_score_bucket` carries any extra label (e.g. signal_type), `rate(...)` will produce multiple series sharing the same `le`, causing the query to error or return wrong quantiles. Aggregate with `sum by (le)` before applying `histogram_quantile`. The same fix applies to the p95 panel.

```suggestion
          "expr": "histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le) (rate(chimera_signal_quality_score_bucket[5m])))
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The heatmap consumes raw `rate(..._bucket[5m])` series without collapsing the non-`le` labels. If the metric has additional labels, Grafana will see multiple bucket series for the same `le` value, breaking the heatmap's bucket construction. Aggregate with `sum by (le)`; also consider adding `"format": "heatmap"` so the datasource returns proper heatmap bucket data.

```suggestion
          "expr": "sum by (le) (rate(chimera_signal_quality_score_bucket[5m]))",
          "legendFormat": "{{le}}",
```

## scout/core/decimal_utils.py (1 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

`Decimal('invalid')` (bad external string) and `Decimal(str(True))` (a JSON boolean, since `bool` is a subclass of `int` and reaches this branch) raise `decimal.InvalidOperation`, which is a subclass of `ArithmeticError`, not `ValueError`/`TypeError`. So invalid external strings or JSON booleans will propagate the exception and crash instead of returning `Decimal('0')`, contradicting the documented contract of this boundary helper. Catch `decimal.InvalidOperation` as well (import `decimal`), e.g. `except (ValueError, TypeError, decimal.InvalidOperation)` — or more broadly `decimal.DecimalException` — in both try blocks.

```suggestion
    if isinstance(value, str):
        try:
            return Decimal(value)
        except (ValueError, TypeError, decimal.InvalidOperation):
            return Decimal('0')
```

## add-admin-wallet.sh (3 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (security)

WALLET_ADDRESS is interpolated directly into the Python source via an unquoted heredoc, and the address is never validated. An address containing a single quote (e.g. `x'); import os; os.system('id') #`) breaks out of the `wallet_address = '...'` string literal and injects arbitrary Python code that runs with the invoking user's privileges. The unquoted `<< PYTHON_SCRIPT` delimiter also makes the heredoc body subject to shell expansion, compounding the risk. Fix: validate the address format up front (non-empty, expected charset/length), and pass values into Python via environment variables or argv with a quoted heredoc delimiter (`<< 'PYTHON_SCRIPT'`) so no shell/Python interpretation of the input occurs.

```suggestion
WALLET_ADDRESS="$WALLET_ADDRESS" ROLE="$ROLE" python3 << 'PYTHON_SCRIPT'
import sqlite3
import sys
import os

db_path = 'data/chimera.db'
wallet_address = os.environ['WALLET_ADDRESS']
role = os.environ['ROLE']
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

With `set -e` at the top of the script, a nonzero exit from the `python3` heredoc command terminates the whole script immediately. The `else` branch below is therefore dead code: the "✗ Failed to add admin wallet" message can never be printed, and the intended exit path is bypassed (the script exits with python3's raw status instead). Restructure so the python3 invocation is the `if` condition itself, or wrap it with `set +e`/`set -e`, so the failure branch is actually reachable.

```suggestion
if python3 << PYTHON_SCRIPT
...
PYTHON_SCRIPT
then
    echo ""
    echo "✓ Admin wallet added successfully!"
    echo ""
    echo "You can now authenticate with this wallet using:"
    echo "  ./authenticate-and-merge.sh $WALLET_ADDRESS /path/to/keypair.json"
else
    echo ""
    echo "✗ Failed to add admin wallet"
    exit 1
fi
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`INSERT OR REPLACE` deletes the existing row and inserts a fresh one, silently wiping `added_at` and `notes` whenever a wallet that already exists is re-added. Since this script is intended as an upsert (add a wallet or update its role), use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(wallet_address) DO UPDATE SET role = excluded.role` so pre-existing metadata is preserved.

```suggestion
    cursor.execute("""
        INSERT INTO admin_wallets (wallet_address, role, added_by, added_at)
        VALUES (?, ?, 'SCRIPT', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)
        ON CONFLICT(wallet_address) DO UPDATE SET
            role = excluded.role,
            added_by = 'SCRIPT'
    """, (wallet_address, role))
```

---

## audit.toml (3 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

The cargo-audit `[advisories]` key is `ignore`, not `ignored`. cargo-audit deserializes its config with unknown-field rejection, so this unrecognized key either makes `cargo audit` fail to parse `audit.toml` or is silently dropped — in both cases RUSTSEC-2023-0071 is not actually exempted and the audit will still report/fail on it. Rename the key to `ignore`.

```suggestion
ignore = ["RUSTSEC-2023-0071"]
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`[informational]` is not a section recognized by cargo-audit (valid top-level sections are `advisories`, `database`, `output`, `report`, `yanked`), and `warn-unmaintained` is not a valid key either. Because cargo-audit's config deserializer rejects unknown fields, this section will cause a hard parse error (breaking `cargo audit` entirely); at best it is silently ignored. The intended behavior belongs under `[advisories]` as `informational_warnings = []` (an empty list suppresses all informational warnings, including "unmaintained"). Note also that `quiet = true` only reduces output verbosity — it does not suppress warnings, so the current file does not achieve its stated goal.

---

### [medium] (security)

This rationale is stale and the ignore is overly broad. RUSTSEC-2023-0071 (rsa < 0.9.11, Marvin Attack) was fixed upstream in rsa 0.9.11, and later sqlx releases have moved past the vulnerable rsa version, so the "no fixed upgrade available" claim (from 2023 issue #2951) is very likely no longer true in 2026. The ignore is also global: it hides the advisory project-wide regardless of features, so if a MySQL feature is ever enabled the vulnerable code path becomes reachable with no audit signal. Re-check the lockfile (e.g. `cargo tree -i rsa`) to see whether sqlx can be upgraded to a patched rsa, and remove the ignore once the fix is in place.

---

## check_profitability.sh (6 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

The "PnL" metric here is computed from `amount_sol` (trade size in SOL: cost on BUY, proceeds on SELL), not from the actual PnL columns. Per the schema (`trades.pnl_sol` / `net_pnl_sol`) and the rest of the codebase, `amount_sol` is trade size, so `SUM(CASE WHEN action='BUY' THEN amount_sol ELSE -amount_sol END)` is really net SOL flow (cost − proceeds), which is the *negative* of round-trip profit (a profitable buy 2.0 / sell 2.6 round trip yields 2.0 − 2.6 = −0.6 here). This same wrong formula is used in sections 3, 5, 7, and 8 and drives the final PROFITABLE/LOSING verdict, making the entire report materially wrong. Use the `pnl_sol`/`net_pnl_sol` columns as section 6 already does (e.g., `SUM(pnl_sol)` for realized PnL).

```suggestion
    COALESCE(SUM(pnl_sol), 0) as net_pnl_sol,
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`TOTAL_PNL` is a SUM of NUMERIC(30,18) values and will almost always be fractional (e.g. "0.5" or "-1.25"). POSIX `[ ... -gt 0 ]` only handles integers, so for any fractional value it fails with `integer expression expected` and falls through to the `else` branch — meaning a profitable or losing run is reported as BREAK-EVEN. Compare with `bc`/`awk` instead (and note the `-lt 0` branch has the same problem).

```suggestion
if [ "$(echo "$TOTAL_PNL > 0" | bc)" -eq 1 ]; then
    echo "✅ PROFITABLE - System is generating positive returns"
elif [ "$(echo "$TOTAL_PNL < 0" | bc)" -eq 1 ]; then
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

This AVG() is computed over all trade rows, so it is the average PnL *per trade*, not per wallet — the printed label "Average PnL per wallet" is misleading. Divide the total by `COUNT(DISTINCT wallet_address)` (or average a per-wallet subquery) to get a true per-wallet figure. It also inherits the `amount_sol`-as-PnL bug from the other sections.

```suggestion
    AVG_PER_WALLET=$(docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose-haproxy.yml exec -T postgres psql -U chimera -d chimera_db -t -c "SELECT COALESCE(SUM(pnl_sol) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT wallet_address), 0), 0) FROM trade_history WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '12 hours';" 2>&1 | tr -d ' ')
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The WHERE clause filters on the right-hand table (`th.created_at`), which nullifies the LEFT JOIN and turns it into an INNER JOIN: any `wallet_roster` entry without trades in the window is dropped, defeating the purpose of the LEFT JOIN and making `COUNT(th.trade_uuid)`/`COALESCE(...)` useless. If the intent is to show all roster wallets (including 0-trade ones), move the time predicate into the ON clause.

```suggestion
LEFT JOIN trade_history th ON wr.address = th.wallet_address
  AND th.created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '12 hours'
WHERE true
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`AVG(CASE WHEN exit_reason = 'PROFIT_TARGET' THEN pnl_sol ELSE 0 END)` treats every non-matching row as a zero-PnL observation, diluting the per-strategy average; when a strategy has no matching exits it reports 0 instead of NULL, which is misleading. Use `AVG(pnl_sol) FILTER (WHERE ...)` or drop the `ELSE 0` so non-matching rows are excluded as NULL.

```suggestion
    ROUND(AVG(pnl_sol) FILTER (WHERE exit_reason = 'PROFIT_TARGET'), 4) as avg_profit_target_pnl,
    ROUND(AVG(pnl_sol) FILTER (WHERE exit_reason = 'STOP_LOSS'), 4) as avg_stop_loss_pnl
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Capturing `2>&1 | tr -d ' '` without `set -o pipefail` swallows psql failures (the pipeline's exit status is `tr`'s, so `set -e` never fires). On a DB/connection error, the error text (spaces stripped) or an empty string is stored into TOTAL_PNL/TOTAL_TRADES/WALLET_COUNT, which later breaks the numeric comparisons and division (and can silently print a bogus BREAK-EVEN verdict). Add `set -o pipefail` and validate that captured values are numeric before using them.

```suggestion
set -o pipefail
TOTAL_PNL=$(docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose-haproxy.yml exec -T postgres psql -U chimera -d chimera_db -t -c "SELECT COALESCE(SUM(pnl_sol), 0) FROM trade_history WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '12 hours';" 2>&1 | tr -d ' ')
```

## database/migrations/001_add_arb_detection_tracking.sql (3 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

`TIMESTAMP` (without time zone) deviates from the project-wide convention — every other migration/schema uses `TIMESTAMPTZ` (e.g. `0010_inactivity_rotation.sql` adds `last_speculative_signal_at TIMESTAMPTZ`, which serves the same purpose). For the 24-hour cooldown comparison against `now()` (a timestamptz), PostgreSQL coerces this column's values using the session's `TimeZone` setting, so rows written under different client timezones can be off by hours, causing premature or missed re-analysis. Use `TIMESTAMPTZ` storing UTC; the type choice is hard to change later on a populated table.

```suggestion
ALTER TABLE wallets ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS last_arb_check_at TIMESTAMPTZ;
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

Most `wallets` rows will have NULL `last_arb_check_at` (only wallets that have already been checked get a value), so a full B-tree index stores a NULL entry per row, wasting storage and adding write amplification on every wallet update. A partial index is smaller and equally effective for the `last_arb_check_at < now() - interval '24 hours'` cooldown query, and matches the project's existing style (e.g. `idx_trades_net_pnl ... WHERE net_pnl_sol IS NOT NULL`).

```suggestion
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_wallets_last_arb_check_at ON wallets(last_arb_check_at) WHERE last_arb_check_at IS NOT NULL;
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

Plain `CREATE INDEX` takes a SHARE lock on `wallets`, blocking all writes (and DDL) for the duration of the table scan — a real risk if this migration runs against a large live wallets table. Consider `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` to avoid blocking writes. Note that CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block and leaves an invalid index behind on failure, so confirm the migration runner supports non-transactional DDL before switching.

```suggestion
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS idx_wallets_last_arb_check_at ON wallets(last_arb_check_at);
```

---

## database/migrations_sqlite/001_add_cost_tracking.sql (3 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

This migration is not wrapped in a transaction and the `schema_migrations` bookkeeping INSERT is the last statement. Since the sqlite3 CLI (used by ops/deploy.sh) auto-commits each statement, a failure or interruption between the ALTERs and the final INSERT leaves the schema partially migrated (columns added) while version '001' is not recorded. Worse, SQLite's `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` does not support `IF NOT EXISTS`, so re-running the migration then fails with "duplicate column name" and cannot self-heal. Recommend executing the whole script inside a single transaction (BEGIN IMMEDIATE / COMMIT) or having the migration runner wrap each file and record the version atomically; at minimum add an idempotency guard (e.g., check `PRAGMA table_info(trades)` for the column before ALTERing).

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

`total_cost_sol` (and `net_pnl_sol`) are stored as TEXT, but the partial-index predicates compare them with the numeric literal `0` (`total_cost_sol > 0`). SQLite will apply numeric affinity to the stored text at comparison time, so behavior depends entirely on every value being a canonical decimal string: values like `''` or any non-numeric string silently coerce to 0 and those rows are quietly excluded from the index (and from queries that rely on it), which can make cost analysis silently incomplete. Consider declaring these columns with NUMERIC/REAL affinity, or enforcing canonical formatting at write time, so conversions and index selection are predictable.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

`total_cost_sol` and `net_pnl_sol` are plain stored columns with no generation expression or trigger, so nothing in the schema guarantees they stay consistent with `jito_tip_sol`, `dex_fee_sol`, and `slippage_cost_sol`. If application code forgets to update them, or updates them in a separate write from the cost components, cost/PnL analysis queries silently return stale or wrong numbers. Consider defining `total_cost_sol` as a STORED generated column (SQLite ≥ 3.31) or adding a trigger to recompute it, and ensure `net_pnl_sol` is written in the same transaction as its input columns.

---

## database/migrations_sqlite/004_signal_aggregation_fk.sql (3 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

These unique indexes are created on the copied table after the old table has already been dropped. The upfront DELETE only removes orphaned wallet_addresses — it does nothing about duplicate rows. If the pre-existing table ever accumulated data violating these constraints (e.g., duplicate (token_address, wallet_address, signature), or duplicate (token_address, wallet_address, direction, created_at) with NULL signature), `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` fails at this point: the migration is stuck half-applied (old table gone, new table without the indexes) if the runner is not transactional, or the whole migration fails and blocks startup until the data is cleaned manually. Add a pre-flight duplicate check / dedupe step on the source data before the destructive table rebuild, and make sure the entire migration runs inside one transaction so a failure rolls back atomically.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Destructive cleanup with no guard: this DELETE permanently removes every row whose wallet_address is not currently in wallets, with no affected-row check, backup, or rollback protection. A mistake in the subquery (or a momentarily empty/truncated wallets table) silently wipes data that the FK migration was meant to validate rather than destroy. Also note that `NOT IN` evaluates to UNKNOWN (deletes nothing) if the subquery ever contains a NULL — today `wallets.address` is NOT NULL per the shared schema so it works, but `NOT EXISTS` is immune to that and reads more clearly. Recommend wrapping the migration in an explicit transaction, checking the deleted-row count before proceeding, and using NOT EXISTS.

```suggestion
DELETE FROM signal_aggregation
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM wallets WHERE wallets.address = signal_aggregation.wallet_address);
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`INSERT ... SELECT *` maps columns by ordinal position, so it silently depends on the source table having exactly the same column layout as `signal_aggregation_new`. If the original table's columns are in a different order (or an extra column was added over time), values can be copied into the wrong columns with no error; a count mismatch would fail, but a reordering would not. Use an explicit column list to make the mapping self-documenting and robust against schema drift.

```suggestion
INSERT INTO signal_aggregation_new (id, token_address, wallet_address, direction, amount_sol, signature, is_consensus, consensus_wallet_count, created_at)
SELECT id, token_address, wallet_address, direction, amount_sol, signature, is_consensus, consensus_wallet_count, created_at
FROM signal_aggregation;
```

---

## database/migrations_sqlite/005_webhook_lifecycle.sql (4 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

When SQLite executes `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` with a non-NULL DEFAULT, every pre-existing `wallet_monitoring` row is backfilled with that default. This marks ALL existing rows (including rows with `monitoring_enabled = 0`, no `helius_webhook_id`, or never-registered webhooks) as `webhook_status = 'active'`. Application code such as `get_webhook_statistics` (`webhook_health_task.rs`) counts every row with `webhook_status == "active"` as an active webhook, and the webhook-lifecycle dashboard does the same, so these rows will be reported as healthy/active before any registration or reconcile actually confirms them. Use no DEFAULT (leave NULL until a reconcile sets it) or backfill explicitly based on `helius_webhook_id IS NOT NULL`.

```suggestion
ALTER TABLE wallet_monitoring ADD COLUMN webhook_status TEXT CHECK(webhook_status IN ('active', 'paused', 'failed', 'orphaned'));
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`ON DELETE CASCADE` on an audit/log table means that deleting a wallet permanently erases its entire webhook lifecycle history — the exact record this table exists to preserve. This makes the audit trail non-auditable after a wallet purge and also cascades deletes from `wallets` that application code may not expect. Unless wiping webhook history on wallet deletion is an explicit requirement, drop the CASCADE (RESTRICT/NO ACTION) so audit rows survive.

```suggestion
    FOREIGN KEY (wallet_address) REFERENCES wallets(address)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

This INSERT depends on a `config` table, but no `config` table is defined anywhere in the repo's SQLite schema or migrations (only `config_audit` exists, e.g. `database/schema_yaml/config_audit.yaml` / `database/schema.sql.deprecated`). If the target SQLite DB lacks `config`, this statement fails with "no such table: config" — the `WHERE EXISTS` subquery does not protect against that, and it aborts the whole migration after the earlier ALTERs have already run. Guard the statement with a `sqlite_master` check (or confirm a prior migration guarantees the table) so the seed is best-effort like the comment suggests.

```suggestion
INSERT OR IGNORE INTO webhook_configuration (config_key, config_value, updated_by)
SELECT 'current_webhook_url', value, 'migration'
FROM config
WHERE key = 'helius_webhook_url'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table' AND name = 'config');
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

This file is a sequence of standalone DDL statements with no transaction wrapper, and SQLite's `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` cannot be guarded with `IF NOT EXISTS`. If the migration runner applies the file statement-by-statement (not as one transaction) and anything fails partway — e.g. the `config` INSERT above, or a duplicate column from a previously interrupted run — the database is left partially migrated and any retry aborts with "duplicate column name". Since SQLite DDL is transactional, wrap the whole file in BEGIN/COMMIT so it applies atomically and can be safely retried from a clean rollback.

```suggestion
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

ALTER TABLE wallet_monitoring ADD COLUMN webhook_status TEXT DEFAULT 'active' CHECK(webhook_status IN ('active', 'paused', 'failed', 'orphaned'));
ALTER TABLE wallet_monitoring ADD COLUMN webhook_registered_at TIMESTAMP;
```

---

## database/postgres_optimizations/functional_indexes.sql (8 findings, 0 critical, 6 high)

### [high] (bug)

`DATE(created_at)` on a TIMESTAMPTZ column (`created_at TIMESTAMPTZ` per 0001_full_schema.sql) resolves to the STABLE function `date(timestamptz)`, whose result depends on the session TimeZone setting. PostgreSQL requires index expressions to be IMMUTABLE, so this CREATE INDEX will fail with `ERROR: functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE` — and even if it were allowed, buckets would be inconsistent across sessions with different timezones. Fix: index `created_at` directly (already covered by `idx_trades_created`), or convert to a fixed zone deterministically (e.g. `DATE(created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')`) and verify immutability before relying on it.

---

### [high] (bug)

Same non-immutability issue as `idx_trades_daily_pnl`: `DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamptz)` is STABLE (timezone-dependent). `created_at` is TIMESTAMPTZ, so this functional index cannot be created and would produce timezone-dependent hourly buckets. Also, the hourly bucket is rarely selective enough to justify its own index — consider a plain index on `created_at` plus bucketing in the query instead.

---

### [high] (bug)

Same non-immutability issue: `DATE_TRUNC('week', created_at)` on a TIMESTAMPTZ column is STABLE/timezone-sensitive — index creation will fail with `functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE`, and week boundaries would shift with the session timezone even if it succeeded. Use a fixed-zone deterministic expression or drop the functional index and rely on `idx_trades_created` for the time-range scan.

---

### [high] (bug)

Partial-index predicate uses `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` (STABLE, not IMMUTABLE). PostgreSQL requires partial index predicates to be immutable, so this CREATE INDEX fails with `ERROR: functions in index predicate must be marked IMMUTABLE`. Even if creation were allowed, a partial index predicate is only evaluated when rows are written: rows would never be evicted once they fall outside the 24-hour window, so the index would return stale/incorrect result sets. Remove this index; a regular `(status, created_at DESC)` index plus the `created_at >= now() - interval '24 hours'` filter in the query is the correct approach.

---

### [high] (bug)

Both the index expression `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP - last_updated))` and the partial predicate `last_updated < CURRENT_TIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '5 minutes'` use `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, which is STABLE. Index expressions and predicates must be IMMUTABLE, so this CREATE INDEX fails. Conceptually it is also wrong: the index stores the age at write time only, so a position can never become "stuck" or "unstuck" in the index as time passes. Drop this index and query with a normal `(state, last_updated)` index (already covered by `idx_positions_state_updated`) plus a `now()` filter.

---

### [high] (bug)

The index expression `COALESCE(closed_at, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)` uses `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` (STABLE), so this functional index fails to create (must be IMMUTABLE). Additionally, even if it built, the epoch value would be computed once at insert/update time and never refreshed, so "position age" in the index would be permanently stale for open positions. Prefer a plain `(wallet_address, opened_at, realized_pnl_sol)` index and compute age in the query.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Semantically incorrect expression: `realized_pnl_30d_sol + avg_trade_size_sol` mixes a PnL amount with an average trade size, so the indexed value has no financial meaning as a "total PnL". Any query that orders/filters on this index for wallet total-PnL rankings will get meaningless results. If the intent is total PnL, index `realized_pnl_30d_sol` (or the correct PnL metric) alone; if it was meant to be a score combining PnL and size, the columns should be weighted/separated deliberately, not summed.

```suggestion
    ON wallets ((COALESCE(realized_pnl_30d_sol, 0)))
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

Index bloat / overlapping coverage: this migration adds ~17 new indexes on hot write tables (`trades`, `positions`), each imposing per-row write amplification and maintenance cost. The same expression appears repeatedly (e.g. `net_pnl_sol - COALESCE(total_cost_sol,0)` in 4 indexes; `COALESCE(total_cost_sol,0) + COALESCE(network_fee_sol,0)` in 2), and several overlap with existing indexes already defined in 0001_full_schema.sql (`idx_trades_status`, `idx_trades_created`, `idx_trades_net_pnl`, `idx_positions_state_updated`, `idx_positions_closed_at`, `idx_wallets_status`, `idx_wallets_wqs`). On a high-volume trading table, 15+ indexes on `trades` will measurably slow INSERT/UPDATE throughput. Also `idx_trades_failed_analysis` puts the unbounded `error_message` TEXT column into the index, which can greatly inflate index size. Recommend consolidating/removing unused or redundant indexes and validating each against an actual EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan before shipping.

## deploy-production.sh (8 findings, 1 critical, 3 high)

### [critical] (security)

Live production credentials (Helius RPC API key, `CHIMERA_SECURITY__WEBHOOK_SECRET`, Jito API key) are hardcoded in this committed script. Anyone with repo read access gets working credentials for the production trading system (RPC access, webhook spoofing, Jito tip authority). Inject these at deploy time from a secret store / CI secrets instead of committing them, e.g. reference `$HELIUS_API_KEY` and require it to be set.

---

### [high] (security)

The heredoc delimiter `'ENV_EOF'` is quoted, so shell expansion is disabled. The generated `.env` will literally contain `$(openssl rand -hex 32)` for POSTGRES_PASSWORD / HAPROXY_STATS_PASSWORD / GRAFANA_PASSWORD and the raw `${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}` inside DATABASE_URL. Every deployment therefore uses the same static, publicly readable "random" password, and `DATABASE_URL` is also broken unless the app performs its own interpolation. Generate values before the heredoc (e.g. `DB_PW=$(openssl rand -hex 32)`), then reference `$DB_PW` in an unquoted heredoc (escaping literal `$`), or write the file with printf.

---

### [high] (bug)

Two problems: (1) due to the quoted heredoc, `$(openssl rand -hex 32)` is written literally, so every environment shares the same static credential string; (2) the emitted lines are not valid HAProxy userlist syntax — HAProxy requires `user <name> password <value>` (or `insecure-password`), so bare `admin $(...)` entries will be rejected/misparsed and monitoring auth will not be enforced. Emit valid `user` entries with real generated secrets.

---

### [high] (bug)

Images built locally in build_images() (haproxy, operator, web, security services) are never transferred to the server — only compose/env/haproxy/ssl files are scp'd, and `tools/` is not copied either. This remote `docker build -f tools/Dockerfile.geoip` will fail because `tools/Dockerfile.geoip` does not exist on the remote, and `docker compose up -d` will similarly fail for services with `build:` directives (operator/web/scout) whose Dockerfiles/contexts are missing. Ship images with `docker save ... | ssh <server> docker load` (as the other deploy scripts in this repo do) or copy `tools/` and build entirely on the remote.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`docker/haproxy/monitoring-auth.cfg.template` is never created anywhere, so this envsubst (and start-monitoring.sh as a whole) will fail. Moreover start-monitoring.sh is never executed during deployment, so the auth file actually shipped is the invalid one from prepare_environment(). Remove this script or create the template and wire it into the deploy flow.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`set -e` does not propagate into the remote ssh shell, and `|| true` / `2>/dev/null` swallow errors. Remote `docker build` / `docker compose up -d` failures will not abort the deployment, so after `sleep 30` + `docker compose ps` the script reports "Production Deployment Complete!" even if containers never started. Run the remote body with `set -e`, check the `up -d` exit code, and verify container health before continuing.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

All build output is discarded, so if a build fails under `set -e` you get no diagnostic about which image/step failed. Preserve logs on failure (drop `> /dev/null 2>&1`, or tee to a log and exit non-zero with a clear message).

---

### [medium] (bug)

The production Helius webhook URL points at a transient ngrok tunnel (`captivity-grunge-curtsy.ngrok-free.dev`) whose address changes on every ngrok restart, so Helius monitoring webhooks will silently stop being delivered. Use the production domain, e.g. `https://${PRODUCTION_DOMAIN}/api/v1/monitoring/helius-webhook`.

---

## diagnose-degraded.sh (7 findings, 0 critical, 4 high)

### [high] (bug)

With `set -e` active, this unguarded pipeline is fatal: if no `chimera*` container is running (exactly the degraded scenario this script is meant to diagnose) or `docker ps` itself fails, `grep` returns 1 and the entire script aborts before any later diagnostic runs. The same hazard exists at the `grep chimera` after `docker stats` (section 5). Guard the command with a fallback.

```suggestion
docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}" | grep chimera || log_warning "No chimera containers found"
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Same `set -e` hazard as the `docker ps` check: when no chimera container matches (or `docker stats` fails), `grep` exits non-zero and aborts the remaining diagnostics and the summary. Add a `|| log_warning ...` fallback so the script always completes.

```suggestion
docker stats --no-stream --format "table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}" | grep chimera || log_warning "No chimera containers found"
```

---

### [high] (bug)

False positive: `grep -q '"health".*"up"'` succeeds as long as *any one* target reports `up`, so a fleet with 9 of 10 targets down still prints "Prometheus targets are up". Parse the JSON and count targets whose health is not `up`, reporting success only when the down count is 0.

```suggestion
UP=$(echo "$TARGETS" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(sum(1 for t in json.load(sys.stdin)["data"]["activeTargets"] if t["health"]=="up"))' 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
DOWN=$(echo "$TARGETS" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(sum(1 for t in json.load(sys.stdin)["data"]["activeTargets"] if t["health"]!="up"))' 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
if [ "$DOWN" -eq 0 ]; then
    log_success "Prometheus targets are up"
else
    log_warning "Some Prometheus targets may be down ($DOWN down, $UP up)"
fi
```

---

### [high] (bug)

This summary is hardcoded: it always reports Alertmanager restarting, Jupiter API failures, and a dashboard health issue regardless of what the earlier checks actually found — even on a fully healthy system it claims problems. It also references a `mainnet-paper` service that never appears anywhere in the checks. Collect the results into variables during the checks and print the summary from those real values.

```suggestion
log_section "Diagnosis Summary"
echo "Issues found:"
[ "$ALERTMANAGER_STATUS" = "restarting" ] && echo "  1. Alertmanager is restarting"
[ -n "$ERRORS" ] && echo "  2. Errors found in operator logs"
[ "$WEB_STATUS" != "200" ] && echo "  3. Web dashboard returned: $WEB_STATUS"
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

This `curl` has no timeout, so if the health endpoint hangs the script blocks indefinitely. In addition, when the endpoint is unreachable (connection refused) `curl` returns non-zero and — because of `set -e` — the command substitution aborts the whole script instead of reporting the failure. Add `--connect-timeout`/`--max-time` and guard with `|| true`.

```suggestion
HEALTH=$(curl -s --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 5 http://localhost:8080/api/v1/health 2>&1 || true)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Same issues as the health check: no timeout (a wedged Prometheus hangs the diagnostic forever) and a non-zero `curl` exit aborts the script via `set -e` before the check can report that targets are down. Add timeouts and guard the assignment.

```suggestion
TARGETS=$(curl -s --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 5 http://localhost:9090/api/v1/targets 2>&1 || true)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

No timeout on this `curl` either — a hanging dashboard request stalls the whole script. Also, if `curl` fails (e.g., connection refused) it returns non-zero and `set -e` aborts before the summary is printed. The `000`/non-200 case is already handled correctly once the assignment succeeds; just add timeouts and `|| true`.

```suggestion
WEB_STATUS=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 5 http://localhost:3000 2>&1 || true)
```

## docker/haproxy/geoip.lua (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (performance)

This is a synchronous, blocking `socket.http` call executed inline in an `http-req` action on the HAProxy worker thread. Every request performs a full round trip (plus DNS resolution of `geoip-lookup`) on the data path; if the service is slow or down, all traffic handled by that worker stalls. LuaSocket's default timeout is ~60s, so a hung connection can freeze the proxy for up to a minute per request, and even the DNS lookup can block indefinitely. Use HAProxy's non-blocking/yield-friendly I/O or offload the lookup, and always bound the call with an explicit short timeout.

```suggestion
    local response, status, headers = http.request{
        url = geoip_url,
        timeout = 0.5, -- bound per-op time; set a connect timeout as well
        headers = { ["Connection"] = "close" }
    }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

For IPv6 clients, `txn.f:src()` returns an unbracketed address (e.g. `2001:db8::1`), producing the path `/geoip/2001:db8::1`. The embedded colons make the address ambiguous in the URL, and the downstream service is likely to reject or mis-parse it, so the lookup silently fails for all IPv6 traffic. Bracket the address whenever it contains a colon (and consider percent-encoding zone identifiers).

```suggestion
    if src_ip:find(":") then
        src_ip = "[" .. src_ip .. "]"
    end
    local geoip_url = "http://geoip-lookup:8001/geoip/" .. src_ip
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Parsing JSON with Lua string patterns is brittle. In particular the ASN pattern `'"asn"%s*:%s*"?([^",]*)"'` requires a closing quote after the captured group, so a numeric ASN (e.g. `"asn": 15169,`) never matches and the ASN is silently dropped; whitespace variants, escaped characters, `null` values and field ordering can likewise break both patterns. Prefer a real JSON parser (`cjson`/`cjson.safe` if available) or explicitly handle numeric/null values.

```suggestion
        local cjson = require("cjson.safe")
        local ok, data = pcall(cjson.decode, response)
        if ok and type(data) == "table" then
            txn:set_var("txn.geo_country", data.country_code or "")
            if data.asn and data.asn ~= cjson.null then
                txn:set_var("txn.geo_asn", tostring(data.asn))
            end
        end
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Every failure mode — connection refused, DNS failure, timeout, or any non-200 response — is swallowed silently: the geo variables are left empty with no diagnostic, which masks upstream geoip-service outages and makes production issues very hard to debug. Add logging on the failure path (e.g. `core.Warning(...)`) and consider falling back to a cached last-known value.

```suggestion
    if status == 200 and response then
        -- ...
    else
        core.Warning("geoip lookup failed for " .. src_ip .. ": " .. tostring(status or "no response"))
    end
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

This action runs on every HTTP request (including repeated requests on the same keep-alive connection), and each run issues a fresh HTTP call for the same source IP. Under normal load this produces a storm of redundant lookups and adds latency to every request. Cache results per IP at module scope (per worker) with a TTL, and only call the service on a cache miss.

```suggestion
local geo_cache = {} -- src_ip -> {country, asn, expire}
local TTL = 3600
-- check geo_cache before issuing http.request; store the result on success
```

---

## docker/init-db.sh (3 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Under `set -e`, when stdin is not a TTY (common with `docker compose` without `-i`/`-t`, Kubernetes, or CI), `read` returns immediately with a non-zero exit status, causing the script to abort with an error instead of safely skipping or recreating the database. Guard the prompt with a TTY check and fall back to a non-interactive default.

```suggestion
    if [ -t 0 ]; then
        read -p "Do you want to recreate it? (y/N): " -n 1 -r
        echo
    else
        REPLY="n"  # Non-interactive: keep the existing database
    fi
    if [[ ! $REPLY =~ ^[Yy]$ ]]; then
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Defaulting to `./data` and `./database/schema.sql` makes the script behavior depend on the caller's current working directory. When invoked from a different directory (e.g., from a Docker entrypoint that changes CWD), it may silently write the database to the wrong location or fail to find the schema. Resolve these relative to the script's own directory (e.g., `SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"`) or explicitly require running from the repo root.

---

### [medium] (bug)

When recreating the database, only `.db`, `.db-shm`, and `.db-wal` are removed. A leftover `.db-journal` from a crashed or interrupted previous process is not cleaned up; on opening the freshly created database SQLite may attempt hot-journal rollback against the stale journal, leading to errors or a corrupted/newly-created DB being rolled back. Add `chimera.db-journal` to the removal list.

```suggestion
    rm -f "$DATA_DIR/chimera.db" "$DATA_DIR/chimera.db-shm" "$DATA_DIR/chimera.db-wal" "$DATA_DIR/chimera.db-journal"
```

---

## examples/tests/test_weighted_rate_limiting.rs (3 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (test)

This demo prints unconditional success markers — there are no assertions anywhere in the file. Even if the rate limiter were broken (e.g., TransactionFetch weighted as 1, or credits never counted), the run would still print all ✅ lines and exit with status 0, so it cannot detect regressions. Since this is a manual test, replace the unconditional prints with real checks (e.g., `assert_eq!(metrics.current_credits, ...)` / `assert_eq!(metrics.credits_by_category...)`) and only print the success banner after all checks pass.

---

### [medium] (test)

The Entry-priority claim is never actually exercised: at this point only 8 of 10 credits are in use and there are no waiters, so `acquire()` returns immediately and the priority-based wait-time adjustment (Entry waits `wait_time * 3/4`, Polling waits the full `wait_time`) is never triggered. The later claim "Priority system reduces wait times for important calls" is therefore unsupported by this test. To exercise priority, first fill the limiter to capacity (e.g., 10 credits worth of calls), then concurrently spawn Polling and Entry requests and verify the Entry request completes first.

---

### [medium] (test)

`current_credits` is the weighted credit count in the *current 1-second sliding window* (the limiter is created with `window_secs = 1`) and it decays as requests age out of the window; it is not a cumulative counter. So the "expected: 3" / "expected: 8" labels are only valid if the entire run finishes in under one second, and they are never compared against the actual value anyway — a wrong weight implementation would still look fine. Use the cumulative `total_credits_used` field for expected-count checks and assert the values instead of just printing them (the final StatusCheck should bring the cumulative total to 9, which is never checked either).

---

## operator/benches/worker_pool.rs (3 findings, 2 critical, 0 high)

### [critical] (bug)

This import does not resolve: the crate has no `worker::pool` module (`lib.rs` declares `pub mod engine;` only). The type is defined at `crate::engine::worker_pool::WorkerPool`. As written, the benchmark fails to compile. Use the correct path.

```suggestion
use chimera_operator::engine::worker_pool::WorkerPool;
```

---

### [critical] (bug)

`WorkerPool::new` does not accept a `usize` worker count. The real signature is `new(queue: Arc<PriorityQueue>, signal_processor: SignalProcessor, config: WorkerPoolConfig, cancel_token: CancellationToken) -> Self` — the worker count lives inside `WorkerPoolConfig.num_workers`, and workers are actually spawned by the async `start()` method. This call cannot compile against the current API; construct the required dependencies instead.

---

### [medium] (performance)

Even after fixing the API mismatch, this benchmark measures only `WorkerPool::new`, which is a trivial synchronous constructor (a `Semaphore` and a few atomics) — it spawns no threads (that happens in the async `start()`) and the pool is dropped at the end of each iteration. The measurement is dominated by constructor/drop overhead and says nothing about worker-pool behavior. Consider benchmarking the async processing path (e.g., on a tokio runtime: `start()`, push signals through the `PriorityQueue`, then `shutdown()`) or remove the benchmark if only lifecycle cost is intended.

---

## operator/benches/write_queue.rs (2 findings, 1 critical, 0 high)

### [critical] (bug)

The import path `chimera_operator::queue::write::WriteQueue` does not exist in this crate. The write-queue type is `AsyncWriteQueue` defined in `state::write_queue.rs` and re-exported as `chimera_operator::state::AsyncWriteQueue`; there is no `queue` module (lib.rs declares `state`, `engine`, etc., but no `queue`). Furthermore, the real constructor is `AsyncWriteQueue::new(db: Arc<dyn Database>, retry_config: RetryConfig, batch_config: BatchConfig)` — it takes three arguments, not a single `usize`. As written, this benchmark file will fail to compile. Fix by importing the real type and constructing it with a database mock and configs, e.g. `use chimera_operator::state::{AsyncWriteQueue, BatchConfig, RetryConfig};` and `AsyncWriteQueue::new(mock_db, RetryConfig::default(), BatchConfig::default())`.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

This benchmark only times `WriteQueue::new(100)` (i.e. object construction) and never exercises enqueue, worker start, batch flush, or write-retry behavior. The queue's actual value is its asynchronous batching/retry/backpressure path, so performance regressions there would go entirely undetected. Consider adding benchmarks for `enqueue`, batched throughput, and flush/backoff behavior, and note that construction is infallible in the real API so no error is being dropped here — the primary problem is the nonexistent API path (see the import comment above).

---

## operator/build.rs (3 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

The rebuild triggers only watch `../.git/HEAD` and `../.git/refs/heads`, so commit/checkout updates that land in `.git/packed-refs` (which happens once refs are packed by `git gc`/`git pack-refs`) are never detected, and in a git worktree checkout `.git` is a file pointing at the real gitdir (HEAD lives under `.git/worktrees/<name>/HEAD`), so this path won't even resolve. In both cases the stamped `GIT_HASH` can silently go stale after a commit. Consider also watching `../.git/packed-refs` and the worktree HEAD location, or use a robust trigger such as comparing the resolved `git rev-parse HEAD` output.

```suggestion
    println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed=../.git/HEAD");
    println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed=../.git/packed-refs");
    println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed=../.git/refs/heads");
    println!("cargo:rerun-if-env-changed=GIT_HASH");
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The doc comment states the stamp is meant to be "the exact code revision that produced it" (C1 run-scoped evidence), but the working tree is never checked for uncommitted modifications. A dirty tree will be stamped with a commit hash it does not correspond to, producing misleading evidence. Consider running `git status --porcelain` (or a diff against HEAD) alongside `rev-parse` and appending a `-dirty` marker (or a worktree hash) when there are local changes.

```suggestion
            Command::new("git")
                .args(["rev-parse", "HEAD"])
                .output()
                .ok()
                .filter(|o| o.status.success())
                .map(|o| String::from_utf8_lossy(&o.stdout).trim().to_string())
                .filter(|s| !s.is_empty())
                .map(|hash| {
                    let dirty = Command::new("git")
                        .args(["status", "--porcelain"])
                        .output()
                        .map(|o| !o.stdout.is_empty())
                        .unwrap_or(false);
                    if dirty { format!("{hash}-dirty") } else { hash }
                })
```

---

### [medium] (security)

A `GIT_HASH` env value is interpolated verbatim into the `cargo:rustc-env=` line. Cargo parses build-script output line by line, so a value containing a newline (or other control characters) can inject additional directives into the build output (e.g. `cargo:rustc-flags`, `cargo:warning`, or a second `cargo:rustc-env=`) and thereby alter the build of the crate, and `cargo:rustc-env` values are themselves required to be escaped for `\n`/`\t`/`\r`. Since this env var may come from an external/untrusted build system, validate it (e.g. restrict to a hex hash `[0-9a-fA-F]+` or at minimum reject all control characters) before printing it.

```suggestion
    let hash = hash.replace(['\n', '\r', '\t'], "");
    println!("cargo:rustc-env=GIT_HASH={}", hash);
```

---

## operator/migrations_postgres/0001_full_schema.sql (7 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

PostgreSQL treats `NUMERIC(30)` as `NUMERIC(30, 0)` — the scale defaults to 0, so fractional values are rounded to integers on insert. Columns like amount_sol, price_at_signal, pnl_sol, jito_tip_sol, entry_price, current_price, exit_price, liquidity_usd, etc. (used throughout this schema) will silently corrupt sub-SOL / sub-dollar amounts (e.g., 0.5 SOL stored as 1). Specify an explicit scale, e.g. NUMERIC(30, 9), for monetary columns.

```suggestion
    amount_sol NUMERIC(30, 9) NOT NULL,
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`remaining_fraction NUMERIC(5)` also has implicit scale 0, so fractional exit sizes like 0.5 are rounded to 1 (or 0), making partial-exit position-sizing wrong. There is also no CHECK constraint bounding the value to (0, 1]. Use a scaled type plus a range constraint, e.g. NUMERIC(5,4) CHECK (remaining_fraction > 0 AND remaining_fraction <= 1).

```suggestion
    remaining_fraction NUMERIC(5,4) NOT NULL DEFAULT '1.0' CHECK (remaining_fraction > 0 AND remaining_fraction <= 1),
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`signal_success_rate NUMERIC(5)` has implicit scale 0 (a 0.75 success rate is rounded to 1) and no range CHECK, so values outside [0,1] (or 0-100) can corrupt per-wallet performance metrics. Add explicit scale and a range constraint.

```suggestion
    signal_success_rate NUMERIC(5,4) DEFAULT '0.0' CHECK (signal_success_rate >= 0 AND signal_success_rate <= 1),
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Unlike `kill_switch_state` (which has `CHECK(id = 1)`), this single-row restore table has no such guard, so additional rows can be inserted and the startup restore logic can read an unexpected state. Enforce the single-row invariant explicitly.

```suggestion
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK(id = 1),
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

`positions` (and `exit_targets` below) use `ON DELETE CASCADE` from `trades`, so deleting a trade — e.g., cleanup of FAILED/DEAD_LETTER entries — silently destroys position history and exit-target/stop-loss records that reconciliation and audit depend on. Financial records should be preserved: use ON DELETE RESTRICT/NO ACTION or soft-delete trades.

```suggestion
    closed_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    FOREIGN KEY (trade_uuid) REFERENCES trades(trade_uuid) ON DELETE RESTRICT
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Tables and indexes are guarded with IF NOT EXISTS (and functions with CREATE OR REPLACE), but the five CREATE TRIGGER statements are not idempotent — re-running this migration fails with 'trigger already exists', contradicting the file's idempotent-guard intent. Guard each trigger with a DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS first.

```suggestion
DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trades_updated_at ON trades;
CREATE TRIGGER trades_updated_at
    BEFORE UPDATE ON trades
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

created_at defaults to CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, which is constant for the whole transaction. Two signature-less signals for the same wallet/token/direction inserted in one transaction get identical created_at, so the second insert fails with a unique-violation, while near-identical rows inserted a microsecond apart (in separate transactions) are both accepted. The dedupe key is not stable — use an application-generated event id/hash (e.g., a dedupe_key column) instead of the timestamp.

---

## operator/migrations_postgres/0002_seed_circuit_breaker_state.sql (2 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

State value case mismatch with the rest of the codebase. The schema default and the 0001 seed use 'Active' (mixed case), and operator/src/circuit_breaker.rs persists the canonical value "Active" and compares it case-sensitively at startup (restore_from_db checks `state_str != "Active"`). Seeding 'ACTIVE' here means that if the singleton row was deleted and this migration re-inserts it, startup will see 'ACTIVE' != "Active" and treat the breaker as having been in a non-Active (tripped) state, triggering a spurious trip/re-evaluation. Use 'Active' to match the existing convention.

```suggestion
VALUES (1, 'Active', NOW())
ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING;
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING only covers the "row missing" case. If the singleton row already exists with a stale or non-Active state (e.g. left over from a prior crash or manual edit), this seed will not restore it, so the migration's stated purpose of 'fixing' the singleton may be ineffective. If the intent is to guarantee the row is in a known-good state, consider ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET state = EXCLUDED.state, ... or a targeted UPDATE. Note: blindly overwriting state would also clobber a legitimately tripped record on a live DB, so scope any update to clearly-stale rows if that matters.

---

## operator/migrations_postgres/0003_fix_numeric_precision.sql (3 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

NUMERIC(30,18) reserves 18 digits for the fractional part, leaving only 12 integer digits (max 999,999,999,999.99...). The original NUMERIC(30) allowed 30 integer digits, so this change actually *narrows* the integer range — it is not purely a "widening change" as the comment claims. The ALTER will fail with a numeric field overflow on any existing row whose value has 13+ integer digits, e.g. token_amount stored in raw token units for high-supply/high-decimal tokens, or liquidity_usd/volume_24h_usd above $1T on large pools. Future writes with such values will be rejected/rounded as well. Consider NUMERIC(38,18) or NUMERIC(40,18) to keep ample integer capacity (26/22 integer digits), or at minimum audit the max current value of each column before running this migration.

---

### [medium] (performance)

Each ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE rewrites the entire table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock because the on-disk representation of NUMERIC(30) differs from NUMERIC(30,18). Issuing 10 separate statements for `trades` (11 for `positions`, 6 for `exit_targets`, etc.) rewrites and locks each table that many times, multiplying downtime and blocking all production reads/writes on large tables. PostgreSQL performs a single rewrite when multiple column type changes are batched into one ALTER TABLE statement, e.g.:
ALTER TABLE trades
  ALTER COLUMN amount_sol TYPE NUMERIC(30,18),
  ALTER COLUMN price_at_signal TYPE NUMERIC(30,18),
  ...;
Consider batching all columns of each table into a single statement (and/or running with a lock_timeout + retry strategy).

---

### [medium] (bug)

Changing the column type only prevents future truncation; rows already written as 0 (amount_sol=0.02 → 0, entry_price=0.0000028 → 0, etc.) remain 0 after this migration. Historical trades/positions and any profitability/sizing reporting built on them stay wrong even after the fix is deployed. If the lost fractional values can be recovered from a source of truth (chain data, event logs, or the trading engine), add an explicit backfill/UPDATE step as part of this migration; otherwise the affected historical rows should be flagged for reprocessing so downstream consumers don't silently rely on zeroed data.

---

## operator/migrations_postgres/0011_cleanup_stale_pending_seed_trades.sql (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

`trades.status` has a CHECK constraint (`trades_status_check`) defined in 0001 and redefined in 0006_trade_statuses.sql, and it does NOT include 'CANCELLED' (allowed values: PENDING, QUEUED, EXECUTING, ACTIVE, EXITING, CLOSED, FAILED, RETRY, DEAD_LETTER, REJECTED, PENDING_CONFIRMATION). This UPDATE will therefore fail at runtime with a check-constraint violation and abort the migration. Either extend the constraint to include 'CANCELLED' first, or use an existing status such as 'REJECTED' (documented in 0006 as the status for trades rejected before execution, which matches this never-executed seed-trade-init case).

```suggestion
ALTER TABLE trades DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS trades_status_check;
ALTER TABLE trades ADD CONSTRAINT trades_status_check
    CHECK (status IN ('PENDING', 'QUEUED', 'EXECUTING', 'ACTIVE', 'EXITING', 'CLOSED', 'FAILED', 'RETRY', 'DEAD_LETTER', 'REJECTED', 'PENDING_CONFIRMATION', 'CANCELLED'));

UPDATE trades
SET status = 'CANCELLED',
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The precondition documented in the header (no ACTIVE positions referencing these trades) is only a commented-out SELECT — it is not enforced by this statement. If any ACTIVE position still references a seed-trade-init trade (positions.trade_uuid is an FK to trades.trade_uuid), the trade will be cancelled anyway, silently breaking position/trade integrity. Embed the guard in the UPDATE so the precondition cannot be skipped.

```suggestion
WHERE status = 'PENDING'
  AND tx_signature = 'seed-trade-init'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM positions
      WHERE positions.trade_uuid = trades.trade_uuid
        AND positions.state = 'ACTIVE'
  );
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The verification SELECT and this UPDATE are not atomic (TOCTOU race). Because the check exists only as a manual comment, an operator can skip it, and a position can become ACTIVE referencing one of these trades between the check and the UPDATE. Make the migration fail loudly instead of relying on manual discipline: verify inside the migration and RAISE EXCEPTION if any ACTIVE position references these trades.

```suggestion
DO $$
DECLARE
    active_refs INTEGER;
BEGIN
    SELECT COUNT(*) INTO active_refs
    FROM positions p
    JOIN trades t ON t.trade_uuid = p.trade_uuid
    WHERE p.state = 'ACTIVE'
      AND t.tx_signature = 'seed-trade-init';
    IF active_refs > 0 THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'Cannot cancel seed-trade-init trades: % ACTIVE position(s) reference them', active_refs;
    END IF;
END $$;

UPDATE trades
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

No staleness/age guard: every PENDING trade with the 'seed-trade-init' sentinel is cancelled regardless of when it was created. tx_signature is a plain nullable TEXT with no UNIQUE constraint (0001_full_schema.sql), so a recent, legitimate trade that still uses this sentinel and is still PENDING would be silently cancelled. Add a created_at bound (e.g., older than 30 days) so only genuinely stale rows are cleaned up.

```suggestion
  AND tx_signature = 'seed-trade-init'
  AND created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days';
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

This migration is destructive and non-reversible: after it runs, the original PENDING state and the set of affected rows are not preserved anywhere, so an accidental or premature run cannot be rolled back cleanly. Persist the affected rows to a backup/audit table first (or at minimum log the affected trade_uuids) before performing the UPDATE.

```suggestion
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS stale_seed_trade_backup AS
SELECT trade_uuid, wallet_address, token_address, amount_sol, created_at
FROM trades
WHERE status = 'PENDING'
  AND tx_signature = 'seed-trade-init';

UPDATE trades
SET status = 'CANCELLED',
    updated_at = NOW()
```

---

## operator/src/constants.rs (3 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

These mint/program addresses are exposed as unvalidated `&str` constants. A typo in any base58 address (wrong length, wrong characters) would silently produce incorrect transactions/routes in both Operator and Scout, since nothing verifies these values at compile time or in tests. Consider adding a `#[cfg(test)]` module that parses every constant as a `solana_program::pubkey::Pubkey` (checks 32-byte length and base58 validity), or store them as validated `Pubkey` values / `LazyLock<Pubkey>` so they are checked once at startup.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

The `verified_majors` allowlist intentionally bypasses the Liq/FDV liquidity heuristic in `slow_check`, but the documented safety requirements (deep multi-pool/CEX liquidity, revoked mint/freeze authority) are only stated in comments and are not enforced by any code or test. Any token appended here will silently disable the liquidity safety check for what may be a high-value copy target. Consider adding a CI/test check that at least validates each entry parses as a `Pubkey` and verifies mint/freeze authority status on-chain, or tracking the manual review gate somewhere enforceable.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

The `@deprecated` tags are plain doc-comment text and produce no compiler warnings, so downstream users receive no signal to migrate to the namespaced constants. Use the `#[deprecated]` attribute instead so that any usage triggers a compiler warning (and can be denied in CI).

```suggestion
/// Use `mints::SOL` instead
#[deprecated = "Use mints::SOL instead"]
pub const SOL_MINT: &str = mints::SOL;
```
