## operator/src/db_abstraction/mod.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

The fallback is not atomic: `insert_trade` and `insert_position` are two independent writes with no transaction, so a failure in the position insert leaves an orphaned trade row. Worse, the comment admits the position is never linked to the trade (missing `trade_id` FK), so even a successful run creates a position that cannot be associated with its trade. This default must not be used for real entry paths — implement `insert_trade_and_create_position` with a genuine transaction (and set the FK), or return an error here instead of pretending the operation succeeded.

---

### [high] (bug)

This fallback silently swallows the position-state update: when `position_state` is `Some`, it only emits a debug log and returns `Ok(())`. Callers of `update_trade_status_and_position` will believe the position was transitioned (e.g., to ACTIVE/EXITING) when in fact nothing was written, leading to divergent trade/position state. Either call the real `update_position_state` here or return an error/`unimplemented` style failure so the caller knows the operation was not performed.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`text_to_dec` silently converts any non-empty malformed Decimal string to `0` with only a warning. Since this helper is public and used for reading financial values, DB corruption (truncated/NaN/garbage values in price/amount columns) is masked as a zero value and can flow into PnL, position sizing, or risk calculations undetected. Prefer `text_to_dec_res` in critical paths, or make this helper return a `Result` so corruption surfaces rather than defaulting to zero.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The doc comment contradicts itself: "idempotent" means repeated calls yield the same result, but "adds to existing values" means each retry accumulates `jito_tip_sol`/`dex_fee_sol`/`slippage_cost_sol`, double-counting costs when a call is retried after a network/DB failure. Clarify the intended contract — if the operation truly adds, drop the word "idempotent" and document the accumulation semantics (or make it truly idempotent by overwriting).

---

### [medium] (bug)

`pool.size()` is the *current* number of connections in the pool (idle + in-use), not the configured maximum. Using it as `max_connections` understates the real pool limit whenever the pool hasn't grown to capacity, and it varies over time — misleading capacity monitoring. For `Pool<Postgres>`, use `pool.options().get_max_connections()` for the true cap; note also the sqlx methods return `usize` while `PoolStats` fields are `u32`, so the conversion should be explicit.

---

## operator/src/engine/position_sizer.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Performance and quality penalties are silently dropped by the hybrid averaging. `performance_mult` can be 0.8 (success rate < 0.4) and `quality_mult` can be 0.7 (quality < 0.7), but in the boost average `.max(Decimal::ONE)` normalizes them back to 1.0, and neither is included in the penalty average. So underperforming wallets and low-quality signals are never de-sized, contradicting the documented ranges (performance 0.8×–1.1×, quality 0.7×–1.3×) and the header claim that penalties 'still reduce size significantly'. Include `performance_mult` and `quality_mult` in the penalty set via `.min(Decimal::ONE)` and adjust the divisor accordingly.

```suggestion
        let penalty_multiplier = (
            token_age_mult.min(Decimal::ONE) +       // age penalty: 0.5x - 1.0x
            slippage_mult.min(Decimal::ONE) +       // slippage penalty: 0.5x - 1.0x
            volatility_mult.min(Decimal::ONE) +      // volatility penalty: 0.5x - 1.0x
            performance_mult.min(Decimal::ONE) +     // performance penalty: 0.8x - 1.0x
            quality_mult.min(Decimal::ONE)           // quality penalty: 0.7x - 1.0x
        ) / dec!(5.0);  // Average penalties (0.5x - 1.0x range)
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The WQS micro-position cap is applied after `size.max(min_size_sol)`, so a cap below `min_size_sol` (typical for low-WQS wallets) can push the final size under the configured minimum — producing exactly the dust trade this method rejects above when `strategy_max < min_size_sol`. Floor the cap at `min_size_sol` (or skip it / reject the trade when the cap is below the minimum) so the invariant `min_size_sol <= final size` holds.

```suggestion
        if let Some(wqs_cap) = factors.wqs_capped_max_size {
            if wqs_cap < self.config.min_size_sol {
                tracing::warn!(
                    wqs_cap = %wqs_cap,
                    min_size_sol = %self.config.min_size_sol,
                    "WQS cap below min_size_sol — skipping cap to avoid dust trade"
                );
            } else if size > wqs_cap {
                tracing::debug!(
                    wallet_wqs = %factors.wallet_wqs,
                    original_size = %size,
                    capped_size = %wqs_cap,
                    "Applying WQS-based micro-position cap"
                );
                size = wqs_cap;
            }
        }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

DB failures are silently collapsed to neutral defaults here (`get_wallet_copy_performance` error → 0.4), in `get_wallet` (error/None → wqs 0), and in `get_closed_trade_count_for_wallet` (`.unwrap_or(0)` inside `calculate_size`). When WQS falls back to 0 the base size computes to 0, and the later `size.max(min_size_sol)` raises it back up to `min_size_sol`, so a DB outage results in a minimum-size order being placed on stale/absent data — the opposite of the fail-safe rejection used in `can_open_position`. Prefer propagating the error (make `get_sizing_factors`/`calculate_size` fallible, or return a reject marker) instead of trading on defaults derived from a failed query.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The intended neutral WQS default of 50 is unreachable for a wallet with no score: `w.wqs_score.unwrap_or(Default::default())` yields `Decimal::ZERO` when the score is `None`, and `to_f64()` then succeeds, so the outer `unwrap_or(50.0)` only guards f64-conversion failure. An unrated wallet therefore gets `wqs = 0.0` (wqs_factor = 0), collapsing the base size to 0, which combined with the `min_size_sol` clamp mints a minimum-size order for an unproven wallet rather than the intended neutral 50 scaling. Default the missing score to `dec!(50)` before conversion (or default the f64 to 50.0 directly).

```suggestion
        let wqs = match &wallet_opt {
            Ok(Some(w)) => w.wqs_score.unwrap_or(dec!(50)).to_f64().unwrap_or(50.0),
            _ => 50.0,
        };
```

---

## operator/src/engine/profit_targets.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Zero/low `vol_scale` collapses the trailing stop distance to 0. `scaled_base_distance = base_trailing_distance * vol_scale` has no floor, and `vol_scale` can be exactly 0 whenever `calculate_volatility` returns `Some(0.0)` (a flat/stable price history produces zero variance, which `price_cache.calculate_volatility` returns as `Some(0.0)`). The stop then becomes `raw_stop = peak_price * (1 - 0) = peak_price`, so `current_price <= trailing_stop_price` is true the very tick the stop activates — even at the peak — causing an immediate `FullExit` and defeating the trailing-stop mechanism entirely. Add a minimum distance floor (e.g. `.max(Decimal::from(...))` after scaling) or clamp `vol_scale` away from 0 for the stop-distance computation.

```suggestion
        // Scale trailing distance by vol_scale so low-vol tokens get tighter stops,
        // but keep a floor so the stop can never collapse to the peak and instantly fire.
        let scaled_base_distance = (base_trailing_distance * vol_scale)
            .max(Decimal::from(1)); // at least 1% trailing distance
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The catch-all `_` arm treats a `load_exit_target` failure (`Err`) exactly like "no row" (`Ok(None)`). On a transient DB error, this builds a fresh `ProfitTargetState` (peak = current price, targets_hit = [], trailing stop inactive, remaining_fraction = 1.0) and then calls `upsert_exit_target`, overwriting the persisted peak/targets/trailing-stop state on disk. After a restart-recovery or an in-flight DB hiccup, saved tier progress and the trailing stop are silently wiped, which can re-trigger already-sold tiers or remove stop protection. Match `Ok(None)` separately from `Err`: on error, log it and keep the fresh in-memory state without upserting over the DB row.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Tiered partial exits are returned before the trailing-stop / time-exit `FullExit`. If a tier target and a trailing-stop breach (or time exit) occur in the same tick, `ExitAmount` (a partial sell) is returned first and the position is left open past its protective stop for at least one more full tick — during a fast downward move the stop is a capital-protection mechanism and should win. Reorder so `trailing_hit`/`time_exit` (or at least `trailing_hit`) short-circuit to `FullExit` before the tiered `ExitAmount` is returned, consistent with how momentum exit already takes priority over the tiered exit.

---

### [medium] (performance)

The write lock on `active_targets` is acquired at the top of `register_position` and held across both `load_exit_target(...).await` and the initial `upsert_exit_target(...).await`, only being released at `targets.insert(...)`. A slow DB round-trip therefore blocks every other tracking operation (check_targets, sweep_hwm_stale_entries, remove_position) for all positions — unlike `check_targets`, which deliberately drops the guard before DB I/O. Load/restore state before taking the lock, or perform the initial upsert after releasing it, so DB latency doesn't stall the whole tracking loop.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`format!("{:.4}", vol)` produces "NaN"/"inf" for non-finite readings, `Decimal::from_str` then fails, and `unwrap_or(Decimal::ZERO)` maps that to a zero scale rather than a safe full-scale default — compounding the zero-distance trailing-stop problem and flooring all targets to min_target_pct. Prefer `Decimal::from_f64(vol)` with a `Decimal::ONE` (full-scale) fallback. Note the same fragile pattern is duplicated in `register_position` for `initial_vol_scale`, where the result is also not clamped at zero (a negative volatility reading would produce a negative scale that `compute_vol_scale` returns unclamped from the `None`-volatility path).

```suggestion
            let vol_dec = Decimal::from_f64(*vol).unwrap_or(Decimal::ONE);
```

---

## operator/src/engine/signal_pipeline.rs (6 findings, 1 critical, 1 high)

### [critical] (bug)

Brace imbalance / compile error: the `if` block opened for the portfolio-heat/strategy re-check (`if signal.payload.action == Action::Buy && signal.payload.strategy != Strategy::Exit {` before "1. Portfolio Heat Check") is never closed before the duplicate-token guard, and this trailing `}` (after the guard's own closing brace) is an extra closing brace. It will prematurely close `process_signal` (the rest of the function then sits at module/impl level), so this file fails to compile. Fix by closing the re-check `if` at the correct nesting level (right after the strategy-allocation `match`) and removing the stray `}` — the duplicate-token guard should be a sibling `if` (its condition is identical, so nesting it inside the re-check block is harmless, but the current brace count is wrong either way).

---

### [high] (bug)

Admission pre-check is blind to PENDING_CONFIRMATION: `get_active_position_by_wallet_token` only matches positions with state `ACTIVE`/`EXITING` (postgres.rs:558), and an unconfirmed BUY never inserts a position row. So when the first BUY for a wallet/token ends in PENDING_CONFIRMATION, a second concurrent BUY passes this pre-check and submits another on-chain order. The write-time backstop `activate_trade_and_open_position` won't catch it either — its duplicate/heat checks also only see `ACTIVE`/`EXITING` rows (postgres.rs:1333, 1353), so no conflict exists yet and both buys execute; one is then DEAD_LETTERed after the fact, stranding funds. The per-token admission lock only serializes the two pipelines and cannot close this window because the first pipeline has already returned. Consider rejecting when any unresolved (PENDING/PENDING_CONFIRMATION/EXECUTING) trade or position exists for the same wallet/token, or have the atomic open refuse while an unresolved trade is present.

---

### [medium] (bug)

In-memory registry not rolled back on executor errors: the pipeline set the registry to `TradeStatus::Executing` at the top, but this deferral arm (as well as the generic `Err(e)` arm that marks the trade FAILED and the ExecutionCostTooHigh arm that dead-letters) only updates the DB — the registry keeps EXECUTING while the DB moves to PENDING/FAILED/DEAD_LETTER. Fast-path consumers (`get_portfolio_heat`, `has_active_position_for_token`, etc.) then see stale state, e.g. a deferred trade counted as in-flight or a dead-lettred token treated as live. Call `registry.update_trade_status` with the matching status in every terminal/error arm before returning.

---

### [medium] (performance)

Unbounded growth of `admission_locks`: entries are inserted per token address and never removed, so over a long-running process every traded token permanently leaks an `Arc<Mutex<()>>` in the DashMap (memory grows with the number of distinct tokens ever traded). The entry can safely be removed after the admission guard is dropped (the guard already holds its own Arc clone, so a worker queued on the old lock is unaffected), or bound the map with an LRU/eviction policy.

---

### [medium] (bug)

This arm dead-letters the trade regardless of side. For a SELL the on-chain exit was never submitted, so dead-lettering abandons the exit and the position row stays ACTIVE — potentially stuck open with no retry. The MarketConditionsUnfavorable arm already distinguishes SELL (marking it FAILED so the position monitor re-attempts the exit); do the same here: dead-letter only BUYs, and for SELLs mark the trade FAILED (leaving the position for the exit system) so the position isn't orphaned.

---

### [medium] (bug)

When `outcome.confirmed == true` but `atomic_portfolio_heat_check_and_open_position` fails (e.g. heat limit or duplicate detected at write time by another path), the trade is DEAD_LETTERed even though the BUY already executed on-chain: funds are spent with no tracked position and no recovery/refund path is engaged. The same happens when `entry_price` is zero, since `activate_trade_and_open_position` rejects `entry_price <= 0`. Consider routing these confirmed-BUY failures into the recovery/reconciliation flow (like the PENDING_CONFIRMATION path) rather than dead-lettering a confirmed on-chain BUY.

---

## operator/src/engine/tip_inlining.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Round-trip is not exact for signer accounts that appear in `account_keys` but are not referenced by any instruction. `decompile_legacy_message` only emits `AccountMeta`s for accounts actually used by instructions, so when the message is rebuilt via `Transaction::new_with_payer` in `inline_jito_tip`, header-only signers (e.g., a multisig cosigner, or any signer not listed in an instruction) are dropped from the new `account_keys` and `num_required_signatures` shrinks. The original swap could therefore land with a smaller (or different) authorization set than the signed swap transaction. Since the decompiled instruction list is what gets recompiled, the doc's "round-trip exact" claim only holds for the instruction list, not the full message. Validate after recompilation that the signer set matches the original message (e.g., every signer in the original header is still a signer in the rebuilt message, and no new signer was introduced) and return a typed `TipInlineError` on mismatch.

---

### [high] (bug)

`swap_tx.signatures` is silently ignored: any pre-existing signature on the swap transaction (e.g., from a cosigner) is discarded and the returned transaction carries default (empty) signatures. The caller (`executor.rs::inline_and_serialize_tip`) only re-signs with the wallet keypair, so if the original swap required additional signatures they are lost without any error — and combined with the header-only-signer issue, the rebuilt message may even no longer require them, letting the swap land without the cosigner's approval. Guard this contract explicitly: return a typed error if any of `swap_tx.signatures` is non-default (or if the original message's `num_required_signatures` differs from the rebuilt message's), rather than silently dropping approvals.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The message header is trusted without validation: `saturating_sub` silently clamps, so a malformed/inconsistent `MessageHeader` (e.g., `num_readonly_signed_accounts > num_required_signatures`, or `num_readonly_unsigned_accounts > num_accounts - num_signers`) yields `AccountMeta` signer/writable flags that do not correspond to the actual message layout, and `inline_jito_tip` will happily recompile and return a transaction with wrong account semantics. The module claims determinism/safety for legacy messages, so a header that violates Solana's layout invariants should produce a typed `TipInlineError` rather than silently wrong flags. Validate the header against `account_keys.len()` before deriving metas.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Recompiling with `Transaction::new_with_payer` recomputes account writability globally (per-account flags are merged/OR-ed across all instructions). If an account shared with the tip transfer already exists in the swap message with a different writable flag — e.g., `tip_account` (or `payer`) appears as read-only in a swap instruction but the tip transfer marks it writable — that account becomes writable for the entire rebuilt message, so the original swap instructions execute with a different `is_writable` view than the signed swap transaction. Programs that branch on account writability would see changed semantics. Compare each account's writable flag in the original message against the rebuilt message (for the accounts shared between the swap and the tip transfer) and reject with a typed error if any flag would change, or at minimum document this deviation explicitly.

---

## operator/src/handlers/auth.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (security)

This endpoint re-issues a fresh 24h JWT from any valid, unexpired JWT without re-checking that the wallet (`sub`) is still authorized in the DB, without any token revocation mechanism, and without rotating a separate refresh token — `refresh_token` is literally the same string as `access_token` and carries the same 24h expiry. Consequences: a stolen JWT becomes an effectively indefinite rolling session (each refresh starts a new 24h window forever), and a demoted/removed admin keeps their stale `role` claim indefinitely because refresh never re-validates against the DB. Consider short-lived access tokens paired with a revocable, single-use refresh token, and re-validate `sub`/`role` against the DB on every refresh.

---

### [high] (security)

Replay protection is incomplete for future-dated messages. Nonces are evicted 300s after first receipt (`seen_at`), but a message whose timestamp is up to 300s in the *future* at receipt remains inside the ±300s validity window for up to 600s after receipt. After the nonce is evicted (seen_at+300s), the same signed message can be replayed for another ~300s and will still pass both the drift check and the (now empty) nonce check. Evict based on the message's own validity window (e.g. drop entries when `now - timestamp > 300`, or key/evict by `timestamp + 300`). Also note the store is process-local and resets on restart, reopening the replay window after any restart.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`now - timestamp` can overflow: `timestamp` is parsed directly from the attacker-controlled message and may be as extreme as `i64::MIN`/`i64::MAX`. The subtraction (and `.abs()` on the wrapped result) will panic in debug builds — a trivial request-level DoS — or wrap with undefined semantics in release builds. Compute the drift with checked/saturating arithmetic, e.g. promote to `i128` and use `unsigned_abs()`, or reject timestamps far outside a sane range before the subtraction.

```suggestion
    let now = Utc::now().timestamp();
    let drift = (now as i128 - timestamp as i128).unsigned_abs();
```

---

### [medium] (security)

The nonce map is keyed by attacker-controlled wallet addresses and pruned only lazily: `retain` runs on every request (O(n) each time) and only removes entries after 300s. A flood of unique requests grows memory up to 300 seconds' worth of entries and makes every subsequent request O(n), enabling a cheap memory/CPU DoS. Bound the map size (e.g. cap entry count and evict the oldest) or move replay state into short-lived storage with TTL-based eviction.

---

## operator/src/handlers/market.rs (6 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

Snapshot inconsistency: `detect_regime()` internally acquires and releases the price-history read lock (see `MarketRegimeDetector::detect_regime`), and then this handler re-acquires the lock to compute volatility/trend. If a price update lands in between, the reported regime and the metrics come from different snapshots and can contradict each other (e.g., a "bull" regime with negative trend strength). Detect the regime from the same locked snapshot used for the metrics, e.g. read the guard once and derive both from it, or expose a variant of `detect_regime` that takes the guard.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Same snapshot-consistency issue as in `get_market_regime`: the regime is detected before the price-history lock is acquired, so `market_sentiment`/`recommended_allocation` can be derived from a different data snapshot than `volatility_index`/`trend_strength`. Compute the regime from the same guard used for the metrics.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Placeholder analytics are returned to API consumers as if they were real: `confidence` is hardcoded 0.75, `last_regime_change` is fabricated as "now" (changes on every request and does not reflect an actual regime change), and `regime_history`/`performance_by_regime` are always empty. Callers cannot distinguish fabricated from computed data and may act on wrong confidence/change timestamps. Either implement these or expose them as `Option`/"unavailable" markers and document the endpoint as placeholder.

---

### [medium] (bug)

A fixed liquidity index of 50.0 is returned as a real market measurement. Since this is a public endpoint, consumers will treat it as aggregated DEX liquidity rather than a constant. Return `Option<f64>`/"unavailable" until real DEX aggregation exists, or clearly mark the field as provisional.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Returning 0.0 both for insufficient data (`len() < 2`) and for `Decimal -> f64` conversion failures silently reports "zero volatility", which callers will misread as a calm market. Worse, when there is no data this 0.0 propagates into `get_market_conditions` as `risk_level = "low"` — a dangerously reassuring verdict with no data at all. Return `Option<f64>`/`Result` and surface "insufficient data" distinctly, and propagate conversion failures instead of defaulting to 0.0.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Same silent-zero problem as `calculate_volatility`: fewer than two price points or a failed `Decimal -> f64` conversion yields 0.0%, which is indistinguishable from a genuinely flat market with no trend. Return `Option<f64>`/`Result` and let the handler report data unavailability rather than emitting a fabricated "no trend" value.

---

## operator/src/handlers/monitoring.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (security)

When no ACTIVE wallet matches — including when get_wallets_by_status("ACTIVE") fails and falls back to an empty set — this fallback promotes an arbitrary entry from account_data (often a mint, program, or authority account rather than a trader wallet) to wallet_address. That address is then passed to record_speculative_activity and upsert_wallet below, so unauthenticated webhook data can create garbage rows in the wallets table and speculative-activity records. Skip the event when tracked_wallet is None instead of guessing a wallet from account_data.

---

### [high] (bug)

An Err from get_wallet falls into the same branch as Ok(None), so a transient DB failure is treated as "wallet not found". The code then calls upsert_wallet with auto-enrollment defaults; the ON CONFLICT upsert overwrites trade_count_30d (=1), notes, and updated_at on the existing row (wqs_score/roi are COALESCE-preserved, but trade_count_30d/notes are not). A DB hiccup can therefore silently mutate a real wallet's metrics. Match on the Result explicitly: on Err log and `continue`, only auto-enroll on Ok(None).

---

### [medium] (security)

No authorization check on this endpoint, unlike every other handler in this file (enable/disable require Operator, get_wallet_monitoring_states requires Readonly). It exposes monitoring enabled state, rate-limiter rate/credit usage, and the active wallet count to unauthenticated callers, which also lets an attacker probe rate-limit headroom. Add AuthExtension and enforce at least Role::Readonly, matching get_wallet_monitoring_states.

---

### [medium] (performance)

Rate limiting is not actually enforced: current_rate() is called per event and its result discarded, with no acquire or threshold rejection. A flood of webhook events still reaches RPC verification, per-event DB queries, and the signal pipeline, defeating the purpose of the limiter. If the blocking acquire has Send-bound issues, gate on a non-blocking check (e.g., reject when current_rate exceeds the configured limit) instead of discarding the value.

---

### [medium] (bug)

When Helius delete_webhook fails, the code deliberately continues and marks monitoring as disabled in the DB. However, the webhook handler never checks monitoring_enabled — it only checks wallet.status == "ACTIVE" — so the still-live webhook keeps delivering events and trades keep being generated after the operator disabled monitoring. Prefer returning an error (INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR) when deletion fails, or add a monitoring_enabled check in helius_webhook_handler.

---

### [medium] (bug)

enable_wallet_monitoring does not check whether monitoring is already enabled before registering a new Helius webhook. Calling enable twice for the same wallet creates two live webhooks; disable only stores/clears the latest webhook_id, leaking an orphaned webhook that continues delivering events (and is still processed by the handler because it only checks wallet ACTIVE status). Check the existing wallet_monitoring record and short-circuit or reuse the existing webhook_id when already enabled.

---

## operator/src/handlers/operations.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (performance)

Blocking synchronous system calls (`System::new_all()`/`refresh_all()` and `Networks::new_with_refreshed_list()` read /proc and /sys) run directly inside an async handler. On a busy Tokio runtime this stalls the worker thread for the duration of the scan, and it is repeated on every request to this endpoint. Wrap the sysinfo collection in `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` (or collect metrics in a background task and cache the result). Also note `networks.refresh(false)` is redundant since `new_with_refreshed_list()` already refreshes.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The "disk" metric is fabricated from memory counters (`total_memory`/`available_memory`), so the reported disk usage/status is identical to memory and can mislead operators into acting on a wrong resource. Likewise `error_rate` is hardcoded to 0.0, and `bytes/packets` sums include loopback interfaces. Use `sysinfo::Disks` to measure actual filesystem usage, compute the error rate from real counters (or omit the field), and exclude loopback if the intent is external traffic.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Rotation history is fetched as the 10 most recent config-audit entries and then filtered for `secret_rotation` keys. If more than 10 non-rotation audit entries have been written since the last rotation (or if several distinct rotation keys push older entries out), the rotation events will be silently dropped — `last_rotation_at` becomes None and the endpoint reports `NeverRotated` for a deployment that has rotated. The key-prefix filter should be applied at the query level (or a much larger/complete history fetched) so the true last rotation is found.

---

### [medium] (bug)

An invalid/corrupted `changed_at` timestamp is silently replaced with `Utc::now()`, which then yields a next-rotation date ~90 days in the future and a status of `Active`/`DueSoon` — masking the data error instead of surfacing it. The same silent fallback occurs again when re-parsing `next_rotation_at` in `days_until_due`. Propagate the parse error (e.g., return an `AppError`/`Unknown` status) so bad audit data is visible rather than reported as a healthy rotation schedule.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Rotation events are reported with hardcoded placeholder values: `duration_seconds: None`, `keys_rotated: 1`, `failed_keys: 0`, regardless of what actually happened during rotation. Combined with the fragile substring check on `item.new_value` (`contains("success")`/`contains("failed")` — e.g. a value containing both words, or a different field matching the substring, misclassifies the event), the rotation reporting corrupts the data returned to operators. Parse the real values from `new_value` (or store structured rotation metrics) and surface parse failures instead of defaulting.

---

### [medium] (bug)

This endpoint fabricates its entire payload: `current_rate` is hardcoded to 30% of the configured limit, `window_seconds` (1) contradicts the fixed 60-second `reset_at`, and none of it reflects actual rate limiter state. Operators querying `GET /api/v1/operations/rate-limit` receive data that is always "Healthy/Ok" and never changes, which can mask real throttling. Either query the real limiter state (e.g., per-endpoint counters/backoff from the engine) or remove this endpoint until it reports genuine data.

---

## operator/src/jupiter.rs (3 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

First-wins semantics silently swallow conflicting later calls with no diagnostic: `let _ = API_KEY.set(key)` discards both the later value and the `Err(old_value)` that carries it. Since this is a public library API (consumed by `main.rs` and integration tests), an accidental early `set_api_key(None)` — e.g. from a test harness or a misordered startup path — permanently installs `None` and every subsequent Jupiter request silently goes out without the `x-api-key` header, which can be a hard-to-diagnose production auth failure. Consider returning `bool` (or logging a warning when a second call is rejected) so conflicting installation can be detected.

```suggestion
pub fn set_api_key(key: Option<String>) -> bool {
    API_KEY.set(key).is_ok()
}
```

---

### [medium] (test)

This test asserts `api_key().is_none()` against the process-global `OnceLock`, but `set_api_key` is a public API that any other test (in this crate's test modules, or in any downstream crate linking this library) may invoke — and the `OnceLock` can never be reset. Under parallel test execution such a test can install a key concurrently, making this assertion order- and parallelism-dependent and flaky. Prefer not asserting on the global state in a unit test; instead factor the header-attachment logic (or inject the key) so it can be exercised deterministically without touching the process-global.

---

### [medium] (test)

The only test covers the unauthenticated path (no key installed → no-op). The primary production behavior — a configured key being attached as the `x-api-key` header on every `*.jup.ag` request — is never verified, so a regression in `with_api_key` (e.g. wrong header name or dropped key) would go unnoticed. Add a test that installs a known key and asserts the resulting request carries the correct `x-api-key` value (or refactor to a key-injected helper so the global `OnceLock` doesn't have to be mutated in tests).

---

## operator/src/middleware/auth.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (security)

SECURITY: The full request URI and query string — which contains the bearer token (?token=...) — are logged verbatim at info level. The following lines also log the raw token: "Parsing query string", "Processing pair" + "Key/Value", and "Extracted query token". This directly defeats the mitigation strategy documented in this same module ("Configure log sanitization to redact query parameters") and leaks long-lived credentials into application/aggregation logs. Remove every log line that emits the query string, parsed pairs, or the extracted token; at most log a boolean indicating query-auth was attempted.

```suggestion
        let uri = request.uri();
        // Do NOT log the URI/query string: it contains the bearer token (?token=...)
        let _ = uri;
```

---

### [high] (security)

SECURITY: For API-key authentication the full API key is stored as `AuthenticatedUser.identifier`, which is then logged unredacted at: (1) the debug success log, (2) the warn log when authenticated via query parameter, and (3) `require_role`'s "Authorization failed - insufficient permissions" warning. API keys are long-lived high-entropy credentials, so logging them turns logs into a credential store. Store a non-secret alias (e.g., a truncated/hashed form or a separate key ID) for the identifier used in logs.

---

### [high] (bug)

BUG/DoS: `token_str[..token_str.len().min(8)]` slices at a raw byte index that may fall inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character, panicking with "byte index N is not a char boundary". A crafted token such as "€€€" (9 bytes) supplied by any unauthenticated client turns a recoverable 401 into a request-handler panic. Truncate on a char boundary (or better, log a hash of the token instead of any prefix).

```suggestion
            tracing::warn!(
                token_prefix = %token_str.get(..token_str.len().min(8)).unwrap_or(token_str),
                "Authentication failed - invalid token"
            );
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

BUG: The manual `split('&')`/`split_once('=')` query parsing never URL-decodes the token value. Percent-encoded characters stay encoded and '+' is not converted to space, so tokens containing such characters will fail to authenticate or be misparsed; additionally an encoded `&` (`%26`) inside a token would wrongly split the value. Use a proper query-string parser (`url::form_urlencoded` or `serde_urlencoded`) instead of hand-rolled splitting. (Also note this loop logs every key/value pair — see the token-leak finding above.)

---

### [medium] (bug)

BUG: The auth-scheme comparison `s.strip_prefix("Bearer ")` is case-sensitive, but RFC 7235 defines auth-scheme as a case-insensitive token, so a standards-compliant `bearer <token>` header is rejected with a 400. Compare the scheme case-insensitively (e.g., split on whitespace and use `eq_ignore_ascii_case`), and consider trimming the rest of the value.

```suggestion
                match s.split_once(' ') {
                    Some((scheme, t)) if scheme.eq_ignore_ascii_case("bearer") => Some(t.to_string()),
                    Some(_) => {
                        return auth_error(
                            StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST,
                            "Authorization header must use Bearer scheme",
                        )
                    }
                    None => {
                        return auth_error(
                            StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST,
                            "Authorization header must use Bearer scheme",
                        )
                    }
                }
```

---

## operator/src/middleware/mod.rs (1 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

These glob re-exports expose the entire public surface of all three modules without explicit curation. Any `pub` helper added for intra-crate use (or any future `pub` item) silently becomes part of the crate's public API, and as the modules evolve, name collisions (e.g. another `Role` or `SIGNATURE_HEADER`) would produce confusing ambiguous-import errors. This is already observable: `VerifiedTimestamp` from `hmac.rs` is re-exported here even though the `hmac_verify` middleware never inserts it into request extensions, making it dead public API. Prefer explicit re-exports of only the intended middleware API, e.g. `pub use auth::{AuthState, AuthenticatedUser, Role, bearer_auth, require_role, get_auth_user};` etc., and keep module-internal helpers private.

## operator/src/models/signal.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

Missing webhook fields silently default to `Strategy::Shield`, `Action::Buy`, and token `"UNKNOWN"`, and `validate()` never rejects these sentinel values: token `"UNKNOWN"` is non-empty (passes the empty check) and strategy/action are never inspected. A malformed or partial webhook that omits strategy/action/token is therefore accepted and executed as a legitimate Shield/Buy trade with the "UNKNOWN" token — dangerous for an external-facing endpoint. Fix: make `strategy` and `action` required fields (drop `#[serde(default)]` so deserialization fails on omission) and reject `"UNKNOWN"` in `validate()` (or drop the token default too).

```suggestion
    /// Trading strategy
    pub strategy: Strategy,
    /// Token symbol (e.g., "BONK")
    pub token: String,
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The dedup key omits `strategy`, `exit_fraction`, and `token_address`. Distinct legitimate intents — e.g. a Shield SELL of 0.5 SOL vs an Exit SELL of 0.5 SOL, or a full exit vs a partial 0.5 exit on the same wallet/token/amount — hash to the same `trade_uuid`. Since this UUID is the dedup key used by the webhook and monitoring pipelines, the DB dedup check will silently drop one of the distinct signals. Include all intent-defining fields in the hash.

```suggestion
        hasher.update(self.wallet_address.as_bytes());
        hasher.update(b"|");
        hasher.update(self.token.as_bytes());
        hasher.update(b"|");
        hasher.update(self.action.to_string().as_bytes());
        hasher.update(b"|");
        hasher.update(self.amount_sol.to_string().as_bytes());
        hasher.update(b"|");
        hasher.update(self.strategy.to_string().as_bytes());
        hasher.update(b"|");
        hasher.update(self.token_address.as_deref().unwrap_or("").as_bytes());
        hasher.update(b"|");
        hasher.update(self.exit_fraction.map(|f| f.to_string()).unwrap_or_default().as_bytes());
```

---

### [high] (bug)

When `token_address` is absent this method returns the token *symbol* (e.g. "BONK") as if it were an address. Downstream callers pass the result to `Pubkey::from_str` (transaction_builder.rs) and use it as a cache/registry key (signal_pipeline.rs, executor.rs), so a symbol-only signal either fails with a misleading parse error or collides with entries keyed by real mint addresses. Return `Option<&str>` (or resolve the mint before constructing `Signal`) instead of silently substituting the symbol.

```suggestion
    pub fn token_address(&self) -> Option<&str> {
        self.payload.token_address.as_deref()
    }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`exit_fraction` is never validated: a zero, negative, or >1 value passes `validate()` and flows into downstream position math, which can produce invalid partial-exit sizes (e.g. exiting more than the entire position). Add a range check in `validate()` (fraction must be in (0, 1]).

```suggestion
        // Exit fraction must be in (0, 1]
        if let Some(f) = self.exit_fraction {
            if f <= Decimal::ZERO || f > Decimal::ONE {
                return Err("exit_fraction must be greater than 0 and at most 1".to_string());
            }
        }

        // Exit signals must be SELL
        if self.strategy == Strategy::Exit && self.action != Action::Sell {
            return Err("Exit strategy must have SELL action".to_string());
        }
```

---

## operator/src/monitoring/exit_detector.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Each sell is compared against the original entry position (`est_tokens = entry_amount_sol / entry_price`), so prior partial sells are never accounted for. After a wallet partially sells (e.g. 50%), the remaining position is less than 90% of the original size, so the final sell that actually closes the position will also be below the 90% threshold and be misclassified as `Partial` instead of `Full`. Track the cumulative amount already sold (or the remaining position size) per wallet/token and compare `amount_in` against that remaining size.

---

### [high] (bug)

`should_generate_exit` (read lock) and `mark_exit_processed` (write lock) are separate lock acquisitions, creating a check-then-act race: concurrent consumers can all observe the entry as ready and emit duplicate EXIT signals before one of them removes it. Make the readiness check and removal atomic under a single write-lock acquisition (e.g. a `take_ready_exit` that removes the entry when `elapsed >= delay_secs`) so only one consumer wins.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Both a missing DB and a DB query failure fall back to `ExitType::Full`, so a transient infrastructure failure silently produces a confident "full exit" signal even when the wallet only partially sold. Errors should not be conflated with a definite classification; consider returning `Partial` (a less damaging default), propagating the error to the caller, or introducing an `Unknown`/retry state instead of emitting a potentially wrong full-exit signal.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The pending map is keyed only by wallet+token and stores a single `SystemTime`; a second sell of the same token before the first pending exit is processed overwrites the timestamp, resetting the delay timer and effectively discarding the earlier exit event. Store a queue of timestamps (or refuse to overwrite an unprocessed pending exit) so multiple exits on the same token are tracked independently.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Pending exits are only removed via `mark_exit_processed`; if a signal is never processed (consumer drops it, shutdown, or `SystemTime::elapsed()` returns `Err` due to clock skew — which currently makes `should_generate_exit` return false forever), the entry leaks in the map for the lifetime of the process. Add TTL/periodic cleanup for stale entries and handle the `elapsed()` error path so a clock adjustment does not permanently block or leak a pending exit.

---

## operator/src/monitoring/helius_wss.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

The health-check task can never actually trigger a reconnection: it only logs a warning and breaks its own loop, and it has no handle to `ws_stream` or any way to make `connection_loop` (blocked on `ws_stream.next().await`) return. If the server silently stalls (no messages, no pings), the client will stay 'Connected' forever and monitoring silently stops. Additionally, this `cancel_token` is never cancelled anywhere, so when `connection_loop` exits for any other reason, the spawned task keeps polling `is_healthy()` indefinitely — a leaked task per connection (compounded during reconnect churn).

Suggestion: race the message loop against a cancellation token that the health task cancels when unhealthy (so `connection_loop` returns and `start()` reconnects), and cancel the token when the loop exits to stop the health task.

---

### [high] (security)

The token-safety fast-path result is computed and only logged (`fast_check_safe = ...`); when `safe == false` the signal is still queued to the engine. The RPC polling path (`polling_task.rs`) rejects such signals (`Ok(result) if !result.safe => return Ok(())`), so this is an inconsistent bypass of a fail-closed safety gate — freeze/mint-authority or TransferHook/PermanentDelegate tokens can be traded here. Add a guard that returns early when `result.safe` is false (and log the rejection reason).

```suggestion
                Ok(result) if !result.safe => {
                    let reason = result
                        .rejection_reason
                        .unwrap_or_else(|| "Token failed safety check".to_string());
                    tracing::warn!(
                        token = %token_address,
                        wallet = %wallet_address,
                        signature = %tx.signature,
                        reason = %reason,
                        "wss: signal rejected by token safety check"
                    );
                    return Ok(());
                }
                Ok(result) => Some(result),
                Err(e) => {
                    tracing::warn!(
                        error = %e,
                        token = %token_address,
                        wallet = %wallet_address,
                        signature = %tx.signature,
                        "Token safety check failed"
                    );
                    return Ok(());
                }
```

---

### [high] (bug)

For `SwapDirection::Sell` (Token -> SOL), `token_out` is the received SOL and `amount_in` is the sold token amount — yet the payload unconditionally uses `token_out` as the token/token_address and `amount_in` as `amount_sol`. Exit signals therefore reference SOL as the monitored token (and `fast_check` would then validate the SOL mint instead of the token) and misstate the SOL amount. Map fields per direction: Buy -> `token_out`/`amount_in`; Sell -> `token_in` (sold token) with `amount_sol` from the received `amount_out`.

```suggestion
            token: match parsed_swap.direction {
                super::SwapDirection::Buy => parsed_swap.token_out.clone(),
                super::SwapDirection::Sell => parsed_swap.token_in.clone(),
            },
            token_address: match parsed_swap.direction {
                super::SwapDirection::Buy => Some(parsed_swap.token_out.clone()),
                super::SwapDirection::Sell => Some(parsed_swap.token_in.clone()),
            },
            action,
            amount_sol: match parsed_swap.direction {
                super::SwapDirection::Buy => parsed_swap.amount_in,
                super::SwapDirection::Sell => parsed_swap.amount_out,
            },
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`tokio::time::sleep` inside this select arm is not raced against `cancel_token` — while sleeping, the `cancel_token.cancelled()` branch is not polled, so shutdown is delayed by the full backoff (up to `max_backoff_secs` = 60s by default). Wrap the sleep in a `tokio::select!` against `cancel_token.cancelled()` (returning `Ok(())`) to make the retry loop cancellation-safe.

```suggestion
                            // Wait before reconnecting, but stay responsive to shutdown
                            tokio::select! {
                                _ = cancel_token.cancelled() => return Ok(()),
                                _ = tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_secs(backoff_secs)) => {}
                            }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

A graceful close (`Ok(_)`) resets `retry_count` to 0 and immediately reconnects with zero backoff. If the server accepts the connection and closes it right away (e.g., invalid API key, unsupported commitment, auth rejection), this produces a hot reconnect loop with no delay — and with `max_attempts = 0` (infinite retries) it never gives up. A graceful close is not proof the connection is healthy; consider applying at least the initial backoff (or a short fixed delay) and counting consecutive immediate closes instead of unconditionally resetting.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The wallet address is derived from `accountKeys[0]`, which is only the fee payer/signer. For transactions routed through relayers/aggregators (or bundles where the monitored wallet is not the first signer), this attributes the transaction to the wrong wallet: `db.get_wallet()` returns None and the signal is silently dropped, or worse, processed under an unrelated wallet. Since subscriptions are per-wallet, the transaction should be attributed to the subscribed wallet (e.g., verify the extracted address against the subscribed/ACTIVE wallet set, or use the subscription mapping) rather than trusting the first account key.

## operator/src/monitoring/helius_wss_subscription.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

subscribe_wallet builds a SubscriptionRequest, binds it to `_request` (which is never read after construction and is dropped immediately), then logs "Successfully subscribed" and returns Ok(()) without ever sending anything over the WebSocket. The success return does not reflect real remote subscription state. Note that `websocket_url` is stored in the struct but never used, so no connection is ever established. Either wire this up to an actual WebSocket send with response correlation, or return an explicit error (e.g. NotConnected/NotImplemented) instead of reporting success.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Check-then-act race on `subscribed_wallets`: the "already subscribed" check is done under a read guard, the guard is dropped, and the insertion happens later under a write guard. Two concurrent callers can both pass the check and both proceed to subscribe, which would issue duplicate remote subscriptions once real WebSocket delivery is added. Perform the check and the insert atomically under the same write lock (e.g. use the return value of `HashSet::insert`), or otherwise serialize this path.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Every request hardcodes `id: 1`, and the `subscription_ids` field is never written or read anywhere in this file. Once a real WebSocket connection is added, JSON-RPC responses cannot be correlated to the originating request, and unsubscribe/resubscribe cannot reference the remote subscription IDs returned by Helius. Maintain a monotonically increasing request id and store the remote subscription id returned by the server, keyed by wallet.

---

### [medium] (performance)

`active_wallets.contains(wallet)` inside the loop over `current_subscriptions` makes the reconciliation O(n²) (Vec linear scan per subscription). Convert `active_wallets` to a `HashSet<String>` once and reuse it for both the subscribe and unsubscribe membership tests to make reconciliation linear.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`resubscribe_all` snapshots the set under a read lock, then clears it under a separate write lock before re-adding. A wallet added concurrently in that window is wiped from the set and never restored. Also, since `subscribe_wallet` only updates local state (no remote send), clearing and re-inserting is effectively a no-op that cannot restore any real remote subscriptions. Serialize the snapshot+clear+resubscribe under one lock (or atomically swap the set) and implement the actual remote re-subscription before relying on this for reconnection handling.

## operator/src/monitoring/rate_limiter.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Concurrency hazard: `now`/`window_start` are captured *before* `requests` is locked. If thread A captures an earlier timestamp but acquires the lock after thread B has pushed a later timestamp, `push_back` inserts an out-of-order (older) entry behind newer ones. The cleanup loop only pops from the front and breaks on the first non-expired entry, so an expired entry behind a live one is never evicted — its weight keeps counting toward `current_credits`, inflating the measured rate and causing false rejections. The same pattern exists in `try_acquire_weighted`. Capture `Instant::now()` inside the lock (after acquiring `requests`) so pushed timestamps are monotonically non-decreasing and front-popping cleanup is correct.

```suggestion
        loop {
            let weight_value = weight.value();
            let (can_proceed, wait_time) = {
                let mut requests = self.requests.lock();
                let mut current_credits = self.current_credits.lock();
                // Capture `now` after acquiring the lock so pushed timestamps
                // are monotonic w.r.t. deque order.
                let now = Instant::now();
                let window_start = now - Duration::from_secs(self.window_secs);
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Documented preemption ('higher priority requests can preempt') is not implemented — `acquire` is a spin-wait where priority only scales the sleep duration (Exit/2, Entry*3/4). Under contention, an Exit waiter's remaining-wait sequence halves each retry (1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ...) and converges to the full window, so its total wait approaches that of a Polling request; there is no priority queue and no guarantee an Exit request overtakes queued lower-priority requests. Either implement a real priority-aware admission/scheduling mechanism, or align the docs and the timing-based test with the actual halving behavior.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`RateLimiter::new` accepts unvalidated configuration. `max_requests = 0` makes `acquire` loop forever with 10 ms sleeps (no weight >= 1 can ever satisfy `0 + w <= 0`), and `window_secs = 0` makes `current_rate`/`get_metrics` compute `len / 0.0` (inf/NaN metrics) while effectively disabling the window. The public constructor should reject these configurations — e.g., assert with a documented invariant or return `Result`.

```suggestion

        assert!(max_requests > 0, "max_requests must be > 0");
        assert!(window_secs > 0, "window_secs must be > 0");

```

---

`*current_credits + weight_value` can overflow: `RequestWeight::new` accepts any `u32`, so a large custom weight wraps in release (and panics in debug). On wrap, e.g. current_credits=1, weight=u32::MAX → sum=0 ≤ max_credits, so the request is admitted and `current_credits` wraps to 0 while the deque still holds a huge weight — corrupting accounting and admission. Additionally, `RequestWeight::new(0)` is allowed, letting weight-0 requests bypass the limiter entirely. Use `saturating_add`/`checked_add` (or u64 arithmetic) in the admission check and validate `weight > 0` in `RequestWeight::new`.

```suggestion

                let proposed = current_credits.saturating_add(weight_value);
                if proposed <= self.max_credits {
```

### [medium] (bug)

`RpcMethodCategory::Simulation` is documented as weight 10 ('Simulation calls (weight 10)') but `category_to_weight` maps it to `RequestWeight::SIMULATION`, which is defined as 5. Simulation requests are therefore admitted at half their documented cost and may exceed the intended plan limit. Reconcile the two: set `RequestWeight::SIMULATION` to 10 (and update its users) or map Simulation to `RequestWeight::new(10)`.

## operator/src/monitoring/wallet_performance.rs (5 findings, 1 critical, 1 high)

### [critical] (bug)

Self-deadlock: `record_trade_result` holds the `metrics_cache` write guard (`cache`) for the whole function body, including across the `update_wqs_from_copy_performance(...).await` call. Inside that call, `should_demote()` invokes `get_metrics()`, which tries to acquire `self.metrics_cache.read().await`. `tokio::sync::RwLock` is not reentrant, so the read can never be granted while the same task still holds the write guard — every call with `auto_demote_enabled = true` (and a wallet present in the DB) deadlocks. Note the guard also stays held across the `get_trades_filtered` DB query, blocking all `get_metrics` readers for the duration of the query. Fix: compute the updated metrics, drop the write guard, then call `update_wqs_from_copy_performance` (or pass the already-computed metrics into `should_demote` instead of re-reading the cache).

---

### [high] (bug)

Logic bug: `should_demote()` returns `true` for BOTH copy-PnL and inactivity demotion. So when `auto_demote_enabled` is on, an inactivity-triggered demotion enters this auto-demote branch and the wallet is demoted to `CANDIDATE` with a misleading "Copy PnL" reason, while the inactivity branch in the `else` (oscillation-count increment, `REJECTED` at max cycles) is skipped entirely. As a result the inactivity `REJECTED`/escalation path never runs whenever `auto_demote_enabled` is enabled. Make the two modes mutually exclusive (e.g., have `should_demote` report which criterion triggered the demotion) and route each trigger to its own handler.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The breach-timer condition here (`copy_pnl_7d < 0`) does not match the demotion condition used in `should_demote()` (`copy_pnl_7d < original_roi_7d * 0.01 * 0.7`). When the expected threshold is positive but small, the timer starts late (demotion delayed); when the original ROI is negative the threshold is negative, so the timer starts as soon as PnL goes slightly negative even though the wallet is still above its expected threshold — leading to a premature 7-day demotion. Compute the same threshold used by `should_demote()` (the wallet's `roi_7d` is available via `db.get_wallet`) so the timer and the demotion decision use identical conditions.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Cache is mutated before the fallible DB work: `total_trades`/`winning_trades`/`signal_success_rate` are updated here, then `get_trades_filtered` can fail and the `?` returns early, leaving `copy_pnl_7d`, `avg_return_per_trade`, and `last_updated` stale while `total_trades`/`signal_success_rate` already reflect the new trade. The cached metrics are then inconsistent for subsequent WQS/weighting decisions. Move the in-place mutations to after the DB query succeeds (or restore the previous values on error).

---

### [medium] (bug)

DB errors are swallowed here and at `let _ = self.db.increment_inactivity_demotion_count(...)` below. If `get_inactivity_demotion_count` fails, `unwrap_or(0)` can reset the oscillation counter to zero and pick `CANDIDATE` instead of `REJECTED`; if the increment fails, oscillation cycles are undercounted so the `REJECTED` escalation is never reached. Propagate or at least log these errors instead of ignoring them.

---


## operator/src/monitoring/webhook_lifecycle.rs (8 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

`cleanup_wallet_webhook` is also called from `health_check_webhooks` to remove an *unhealthy* webhook for a wallet that is still ACTIVE and eligible. `upsert_wallet_monitoring(wallet, None, false)` flips `monitoring_enabled`/`rpc_polling_active` to false, and since `reconcile_webhooks` recovery only re-registers rows with `monitoring_enabled == 1`, the wallet is never re-registered — monitoring is permanently lost for an active wallet. Cleanup should distinguish "webhook removed but wallet still monitored" (keep `monitoring_enabled=true` with `helius_webhook_id=None` so reconcile recovery can re-register) from a full demotion.

---

### [high] (bug)

Any non-404 error (network, 5xx, timeout) while verifying an existing webhook ID falls through to a fresh `register_webhook` call even though the existing webhook may still exist in Helius. This creates a duplicate Helius webhook; the subsequent DB upsert overwrites the old ID, orphaning the old webhook until the next reconcile deletes it. Additionally, 404 detection via `err_str.contains("404")` / `"Not Found"` is brittle against error-message changes. Return an `Err` (or retry) on non-404 verification failures instead of re-registering, and classify 404 via a structured error type from the Helius client.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`if let Ok(Some(...))` silently discards the DB error from `get_wallet_monitoring`. On a transient DB failure the function proceeds to register a brand-new webhook even though one may already exist, producing a duplicate Helius webhook. Match the `Err` branch explicitly (return/retry) instead of continuing.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`register_wallet_webhook` returns `Ok(WebhookRegistrationResult { success: false, .. })` for invalid addresses and Helius rejections, but the `_ => {}` arm swallows these — they are neither counted in `failed` nor logged, so reconciliation can report success while webhooks are silently missing. Add an explicit arm for `Ok(result)` with `success == false` that increments `failed` and logs the error.

```suggestion

                    failed += 1;
                    warn!(
                        wallet = %wallet,
                        error = ?result.error_message,
                        "Failed to register missing webhook"

```

---

### [medium] (bug)

In non-dry-run mode, any Helius webhook whose ID is not present in the DB is classified as orphaned and deleted. `register_wallet_webhook` writes the DB only after Helius returns the ID, and a DB-write failure is only logged as a warning — so a just-created webhook (or one whose DB write failed) can be deleted as "orphaned" by a concurrent or subsequent reconcile, silently dropping monitoring. Consider excluding very recently-created webhooks from the orphan scan and retrying/failing hard on the DB write instead of only warning.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`update_wallet_webhook` persists the new URL under the key `webhook_url:<wallet>`, but `reconcile_webhooks` only reads `current_webhook_url`. Per-wallet URL changes are therefore invisible to reconciliation; when the global URL differs, reconcile bulk-reverts every webhook (including deliberately updated ones) back to `config.webhook_url`. Persist per-wallet URL updates to a key/column that reconcile actually reads (e.g., update `current_webhook_url` or read `last_updated_url` from the monitoring row).

---

### [medium] (bug)

In the recovery loop, if deleting the stale Helius webhook fails — including the case where it was already deleted externally (404) — `continue` skips re-registration entirely, so an ACTIVE wallet with an unhealthy/paused/error webhook never gets a fresh one. Deletion failure should not abort recovery: clear the DB webhook ID and still attempt registration.

### [medium] (performance)

The existing-webhook verification call `get_webhook_typed`, the auth-header sync `update_webhook`, and `check_webhook_health`'s `get_webhook` all bypass `rate_limiter` (as do the orphan/recovery deletions inside `reconcile_webhooks`), so registration and health-check loops can exceed Helius API rate limits even though the create/delete calls are throttled. Acquire a rate-limit permit before these Helius calls as well.

## operator/src/state/registry.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

`token_position_counts` is incremented for every inserted position regardless of its `state`, while `update_position_state` only decrements when a position *leaves* ACTIVE and never increments when one *enters* ACTIVE. As a result `has_active_position_for_token` reports false positives (non-ACTIVE positions counted) and false negatives (e.g. an ACTIVE position that round-tripped through a non-ACTIVE state leaves the count at 0). Re-inserting the same `trade_uuid` with a different token also double-counts the new token while leaving the old token's count stale. Since this drives duplicate-position checks, derive the count from ACTIVE positions directly or maintain it atomically in both transition directions.

---

### [high] (bug)

`insert_trade` unconditionally overwrites any existing entry for the same `trade_uuid` without checking the `version` field or rejecting a conflict, and `trade_uuid_exists` + `insert_trade` is a non-atomic check-then-act sequence. Concurrent duplicate submissions can race and silently lose prior state (including a higher version). Use `DashMap::entry`/insert-if-absent semantics or optimistic version checking so an existing record is rejected rather than clobbered.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Every unrecognized status string is silently mapped to `TradeStatus::Failed`, so a new or unexpected database status will corrupt in-memory trade state (e.g. flipping a live trade to Failed, or permanently mislabeling a dead-letter) with no way to distinguish it from a genuine failure. Prefer `TryFrom<&str>` returning a typed error, or preserve the unknown raw string, so unexpected states surface instead of being silently misclassified.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`hit_rate` is not a valid ratio: batch reads like `get_active_positions`/`get_positions_by_token` increment `hits_total` by the number of returned entries but `reads_total` by only 1, and filtered reads never record misses, so the ratio can exceed 1.0 and misses are undercounted. Count one read per logical lookup (or per entry) consistently and compute hit rate as hits/(hits+misses), or drop the derived ratio from the snapshot.

---

### [medium] (performance)

There is no eviction/removal path in this registry: closed/failed trades, closed positions, and wallets accumulate forever, and `token_position_counts` entries are never deleted once they reach 0. For a long-running trading system this grows memory without bound and makes the O(n) scans in `get_all_trades`/`get_all_positions`/`calculate_portfolio_heat_fast` progressively slower. Add removal on terminal states or a TTL/retention policy.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`calculate_portfolio_heat_fast` folds Pending/Queued/Executing BUY trades into `total_exposure_sol`/`shield_exposure_sol`/`spear_exposure_sol`, yet always returns `pending_heat_sol: Decimal::ZERO`. If `pending_heat_sol` is meant to represent in-flight/pending exposure, it should be populated from those trades (consistently, without double-counting); otherwise the field is misleading. Clarify the intended semantics or compute it.

### [high] (bug)

Compile error with the `redis-cache` feature: the parameter is named `_ttl_secs`, but this branch references `ttl_secs`, which does not exist in scope (this code path is excluded from compilation when the feature is off, so it won't be caught until the feature is enabled). ### [high] (performance)

`KEYS metadata:*` performs an O(N) scan that blocks the Redis event loop; on a production cache with a large key space this can stall the entire Redis instance and all clients. Use `SCAN` in batches (or maintain an explicit set of inserted keys) instead. Note also that this deletes every key matching `metadata:*` in the instance, which can clobber keys owned by other applications if the Redis server is shared.

`.ok().flatten()` silently converts every Redis failure (network error, timeout, deserialization failure) into a cache miss with no logging. During a Redis outage this makes the failure invisible — every request silently falls through to upstream safety checks and the cache appears merely cold. Log the error before returning `None`, or propagate a `Result` so callers can distinguish "miss" from "backend down".

```suggestion
                    }
                }
```

---

Redis clear errors are silently discarded with `let _ =`. If `clear_redis` fails (e.g., KEYS or DEL network error), stale metadata remains in the cache after a clear operation and nothing is logged, leaving the cache in an inconsistent state. Log or propagate the error.

```suggestion
                    tracing::error!(error = %e, "Redis metadata cache clear failed");
                }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

For the Redis backend, `len()` always returns 0 while `is_empty()` always returns false — the two are mutually inconsistent and mislead monitoring/metrics or any caller that checks emptiness (an empty cache reports as non-empty). Track an atomic counter updated on insert/clear, or return `Option<usize>`/`Result` to signal the size is unknown for Redis instead of fabricating values.

This hardcodes the literal `metadata:` prefix while `get_from_redis` builds keys from the `METADATA_KEY_PREFIX` constant. If the constant is ever changed, reads and writes will target different keys and the cache silently stops working. Reuse the constant here.


### [medium] (bug)

The public `insert` accepts `ttl_secs`, but the memory backend never enforces expiry and never evicts entries, so callers relying on this abstraction can read stale metadata indefinitely past the intended TTL while the HashMap grows unboundedly. Either store a timestamp and prune expired entries on read, or clearly document (and make the API reflect) that TTL is only enforced by the Redis backend.

## operator/src/vault.rs (9 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (security)

`save_secrets` writes to a predictable sibling path (`<name>.tmp`) using `create(true)`/`truncate(true)`, which follows symlinks and preserves the mode of a pre-existing temp file. A local attacker with write access to the directory can pre-create `secrets.tmp` as a symlink to any file the operator can write (it will be truncated and overwritten with ciphertext), or as a 0644 regular file so the final vault file stays world-readable despite the documented 0600 guarantee. Additionally, the temp file is not fsync'd before `rename`, and on write/rename failure the partially-written tmp file is left behind. Prefer `tempfile::NamedTempFile` (or `O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW` with a random suffix), fsync before rename, and clean up the temp file on error.

---

### [medium] (security)

On non-Unix platforms this branch uses `std::fs::write`, which applies the process-default permissions (often 0644), so the encrypted secrets file can be readable by other local users — defeating the 0600 guarantee documented above. Use `OpenOptions` with restrictive permissions (or `tempfile`) on all platforms instead of two diverging code paths.

---

### [medium] (security)

`key_bytes` (the decoded 32-byte key) remains on the heap and is never zeroized after being copied into `Vault`, and `Vault.key` itself is never zeroized on drop — only `VaultSecrets` is. For a secrets vault, add a `Drop` impl that zeroizes `self.key` and explicitly zeroize the temporary `key_bytes` Vec once copied.

---

### [medium] (security)

`encrypted_bytes` and the decrypted `plaintext` Vec remain in heap memory without zeroization, even though the code deliberately zeroizes `VaultSecrets` on drop. Explicitly zeroize these intermediate buffers after parsing so the plaintext doesn't linger in memory.

---

### [medium] (security)

The serialized JSON Vec (`plaintext`) holds all secrets in cleartext and is not zeroized after `encrypt` returns. Zeroize the buffer once the ciphertext has been produced.

---

### [medium] (security)

When `CHIMERA_VAULT_KEY` is set but the vault file at `CHIMERA_VAULT_PATH` does not exist, this code silently falls through to env-var secrets. Since setting the key is a strong signal that the vault is intended to be used, a missing file usually indicates a path typo or misconfiguration — and the decryption-failure branch above deliberately rejects silent fallback. Consider failing loudly (or at minimum emitting a `warn!`) when the key is set but the vault file is absent.

### [medium] (bug)

Optional secrets read from env vars are not filtered for empty values: an empty `CHIMERA_SECURITY__WEBHOOK_SECRET_PREVIOUS`, `CHIMERA_RPC__API_KEY`, or `CHIMERA_RPC__FALLBACK_API_KEY` becomes `Some("")`, which downstream code may treat as a configured credential. Apply the same `.filter(|s| !s.is_empty())` used for `webhook_secret` to all optional fields.

---

### [medium] (bug)

After decryption, only `webhook_secret` is validated: `webhook_secret_previous`, `wallet_private_key`, `rpc_api_key`, and `fallback_rpc_api_key` may be `Some("")`, turning an empty optional secret into a silently misconfigured credential. Normalize empty values to `None` (or reject) for all fields. Also, returning `VaultError::InvalidKey` for a data-validation failure in a decrypted bundle is misleading — prefer a dedicated variant such as `InvalidSecrets`/`CorruptVault`.

---

### [medium] (security)

This `windows(4)` check never actually detects the claimed 'highly repetitive 4-byte patterns': for all windows to equal `key[0..4]`, window 1 (`key[1..5]`) must equal `key[0..4]`, which forces `key[0]==key[1]==key[2]==key[3]`, and the equality then cascades to all 32 bytes. So only constant keys are caught (which the all-zeros check already handles), while a genuinely weak key like `01020304` repeated passes. Check periodicity explicitly (e.g., for `p in 1..16`, reject if `key[..32-p] == key[p..]`) or fix the misleading error message.

## operator/tests/integration.rs (2 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Inconsistent module path: unlike every other module in this file (which uses `integration/...`), this one points to `reconciliation_tests.rs` at the tests root (resolves to `tests/reconciliation_tests.rs`). Because that file sits directly in `tests/`, Cargo also auto-discovers it as its own standalone integration-test binary — so every test in it is compiled and executed twice (once standalone, once as a module of this crate), producing duplicated test runs in `cargo test` output. If the intent was to include `integration/reconciliation_tests.rs`, that file doesn't exist and the wrong file is being pulled in. Align the path with the other modules (`#[path = "integration/reconciliation_tests.rs"]`) or drop this duplicate registration entirely.

---

### [medium] (documentation)

This doc comment is misleading. Cargo's test runner auto-discovers only files directly under `tests/`; files in subdirectories such as `tests/integration/` are never compiled unless they are explicitly registered here via `mod`. The comment therefore invites maintainers to drop new test files into `tests/integration/` without registering them and silently lose coverage — this has already happened: `tests/integration/jito_integration_tests.rs` exists but is not listed in this file, so its tests are silently skipped. Reword the comment to state that every file in the integration subdirectory must be manually registered in this module list.

## operator/tests/integration/db_tests.rs (3 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING` does not reset an existing row. If a previous run failed before the DROP TABLE cleanup (or the table was left behind by an interrupted run), the row keeps its old value and the final `value == 10` assertion fails spuriously (e.g., a leftover value of 5 plus 10 increments yields 15). Reset the counter explicitly so the test starts from a known state regardless of leftovers.

```suggestion
    sqlx::query("INSERT INTO concurrency_counter (id, value) VALUES (1, 0) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET value = 0")
        .execute(&pool)
        .await
        .unwrap();
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The TempDir is created but never used to scope or name the database — every test connects to the same external TEST_DATABASE_URL. Since `#[tokio::test]` cases in the same binary run in parallel by default, the two tests here (and any other integration binary using the same URL) call `create_database`/`run_migrations` concurrently against one shared database, which can race on migrations or collide on table names. Consider deriving a uniquely named database/schema per test run from the temp dir (or the test name) so runs are isolated.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Cleanup only runs on the success path: if any spawned writer panics (`.unwrap()` on the query) or the `value == 10` assertion fails, the DROP TABLE is skipped and `concurrency_counter` remains with a stale value, making later runs order-dependent (see the INSERT ... DO NOTHING issue above). Prefer a cleanup guard (e.g., a struct whose `Drop` drops the table) or reset the table state at the start of the test so cleanup is guaranteed even on failure.

This test is NOT marked `#[ignore]`, so it runs in every default `cargo test`/CI invocation. ```

Additionally, asserting `v1 == v2` does not prove the second result came from the cache — two live API calls could return the same age. To meaningfully test caching, fail the test on API errors and/or verify the second call performs no network request (e.g., via a mock client with a request counter).

The purpose of this ignored test is to validate that token age is successfully fetched from Helius, but the `Err` branch only prints and lets the test pass, so a broken integration or auth failure would never be detected. ### [high] (bug)

`config.rpc.primary_provider` is a `String`, and `let _ = config.rpc.primary_provider;` moves it out of `config`. On the second loop iteration the field has already been moved, so this code fails to compile (E0382: use of moved value) and the entire test target will not build. ### [medium] (test)

These "concurrency" tests use the default `#[tokio::test]` runtime, which is the single-threaded current-thread runtime. The spawned tasks (`tokio::spawn`) are pure CPU-bound loops with no `.await` points, so they execute serially to completion and never actually overlap — the tests do not measure concurrent behavior at all. The same problem affects `test_atomic_counter_performance`, `test_concurrent_metric_updates`, `test_concurrent_health_checks`, and `test_notification_throughput`. Use `#[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = N)]` (or a real thread pool / barrier) so the code under test is genuinely exercised in parallel.

### [medium] (test)

The hot loops here only read locals (`health.healthy`, `health.latency_ms`, ...) and discard every result, with no observable side effect. In release builds the optimizer can eliminate the entire loop, so the test passes without exercising anything (and in debug builds the timing is meaningless). Wrap the reads in `std::hint::black_box(...)` to force evaluation. The same applies to `test_jito_health_clone_performance` (`health.clone()`), `test_error_classification_performance`, `test_concurrent_health_checks`, and `test_configuration_reading_overhead`.

```suggestion
    for _ in 0..iterations {
        // Simulate health check operations
        std::hint::black_box(health.healthy);
        std::hint::black_box(health.latency_ms);
```

---

### [medium] (test)

Absolute wall-clock thresholds (e.g. `< 10ms` / `< 1000ns` per update here, and similar `< 100ms`, `< 50ms`, `< 5ms`, `< 20ms` asserts throughout this file) are flaky in CI: results vary with machine load, scheduler behavior, debug vs release profile, and runtime noise, so these tests either spuriously fail on slow runners or mask real regressions on fast ones. Prefer relative/self-calibrating comparisons (e.g. compare against a baseline measurement or an un-instrumented control), much more generous budgets, or use performance counters/histograms rather than wall-clock time for pass/fail decisions.

---

### [medium] (test)

`test_concurrent_metric_updates` only asserts elapsed time; it never verifies the final counter values, so lost, duplicated, or mislabeled metric updates would go completely undetected — the test could pass while the counters are wrong. Add data-integrity assertions after joining the tasks. ## operator/tests/test_decimals_cache.rs (2 findings)

### [medium] (test)

This test does not actually exercise the RPC fallback path. `UnknownToken11111111111111111111111111111111` is not a valid Solana pubkey (it is a 44-char base58 string with a leading 'U', whose value exceeds 2^256, so it decodes to more than 32 bytes), which means `Pubkey::from_str` in `fetch_metadata_from_rpc` fails with a Validation error *before* any RPC call is made. The fallback branch is therefore never reached, and the test only asserts the `None` outcome — so a `get_decimals_only` implementation with no RPC fallback at all would pass just as easily. To genuinely cover the fallback, stand up a local mock RPC server (e.g. httpmock/wiremock) that returns a valid mint account and assert the RPC was actually hit (e.g. expect `Some(decimals)`), in addition to the cache-miss `None` case.
