### [medium] (test)

`mock_rpc_url` is not a valid URL and is not backed by any mock server (no mock-server infrastructure exists in this repo). Depending on the solana-client version, `RpcClient::new` may panic on the unparseable URL or silently treat it as an unknown cluster name and fall back to a live endpoint, and if the fallback path is ever reached (e.g. a future valid token address) the test would perform real network I/O against an uncontrolled host with a 10s timeout — making the test slow, flaky, and environment-dependent. Point the fetcher at a hermetic loopback mock server (e.g. `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`) or inject a stub RPC client so this test does not depend on external DNS/network behavior.

### [high] (bug)

Only `Some(Ok(...))` messages are handled; `Some(Err(_))` and `None` (stream closed/errored) fall through and the loop simply iterates again. Once the stream is closed/errored, `next().await` completes immediately, so the loop spins without ever yielding and the 30s `timeout` future is never polled — the test can hang indefinitely. Handle `Err`/`None` by breaking out of the loop.

```suggestion
        while message_count < max_messages {
            match ws_receiver.next().await {
                Some(Ok(message)) => { /* existing message handling */ }
                Some(Err(e)) => { println!("❌ WebSocket error: {}", e); break; }
                None => { println!("🔌 Stream closed"); break; }
            }
        }
```

The test returns `Ok(())` in every outcome, so it "passes" even when zero subscription notifications were observed — the WebSocket behavior is never actually verified. If the goal is verification, fail the test when `count == 0` (e.g. `anyhow::bail!`) instead of printing a warning.

```suggestion
            if count > 0 {
                println!("✅ WebSocket test PASSED");
            } else {
                anyhow::bail!("No transaction messages received within 30 seconds");
            }
```

The test returns `Ok(())` even when no pong was received, so the ping/pong test always passes regardless of the outcome. Assert that a pong was actually received to make the test meaningful.

```suggestion
    if pong_received == Ok(true) {
        println!("✅ Received pong - ping/pong working!");
    } else {
        anyhow::bail!("No pong received within 5 seconds");

```

Helius LaserStream `transactionSubscribe` uses Jito-compatible filter keys such as `accountInclude`/`accountExclude`; the `account` key used here may be unrecognized by the server, causing the filter to be ignored (the test would then either receive nothing or everything). Verify the parameter shape against the current LaserStream API docs.

## operator/tests/unit.rs (1 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

The `fix_verification_tests` module is documented in its own header (and in the comment above) as asserting CORRECT post-fix behavior — i.e. several of its tests (F3/F7 hard-stop, F4 trailing-stop ratchet, F6 silent status update) deliberately FAIL until the underlying bugs are fixed. However, the module is unconditionally included in this default test entry point and none of its tests are marked `#[ignore]` or gated behind a feature flag, so every plain `cargo test`/`cargo test --all-targets` run will stay red by design while any bug is open. That makes it impossible to tell apart "expected failure from a known bug" and "new regression", and it blocks CI for unrelated changes. Recommend marking these expected-fail tests `#[ignore]` (run them explicitly with `cargo test -- --ignored` when verifying a fix) or moving them into a separate opt-in test target so the default suite only contains tests that are expected to pass.

---

## operator/tests/unit/fix_verification_tests.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

This helper binds against a `Pool<Postgres>`, but sqlx's Postgres driver requires `$N` numbered placeholders (`?` is SQLite/MySQL syntax). Executing this query against Postgres will fail with a database syntax error at prepare/execute time, so every test that calls `insert_wallet` (the F3/F7 tests) fails during setup regardless of whether the bug under test is fixed. Use `$1`/`$2` as done elsewhere in this file (e.g. the `$1` in `should_succeed_on_status_update_for_existing_trade`).

```suggestion
    sqlx::query(
        "INSERT INTO wallets (address, status, wqs_score, created_at, updated_at) \
         VALUES ($1, 'ACTIVE', $2, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)",
    )
```

---

### [high] (test)

The two F3/F7 tests encode contradictory specs for the post-fix default `hard_stop_loss`. `should_not_fire_hard_stop_at_2pct_loss_with_default_config` documents the fixed default as -15.0, while this test assumes it is -25.0. If the actual fix sets the default to -15%, scenario A here (-16% loss) would trigger the hard stop and this test would fail; if it is -25%, the first test's comments are wrong. Additionally, scenario B's `StopLossAction::Exit` at -21% cannot distinguish a dynamic-stop exit from a hard-stop exit (a -15% hard stop would also fire), so the test does not actually prove the dynamic stop operates. Align both tests to a single documented default value.

---

### [medium] (test)

"00000000-0000-0000-0000-nonexistent00" is not a valid UUID (non-hex characters and wrong length for the last group). While the `trades.trade_uuid` column is TEXT so the bind will succeed, using a malformed value makes this test brittle and its failure mode ambiguous: if the schema/abstraction ever validates UUID format (or returns Err for any reason other than the intended missing-row path), the asserted `Err` would no longer prove the `rows_affected() == 0` check is what's being exercised. Use a well-formed but non-existent UUID (e.g. all-zero groups in proper 8-4-4-4-12 form).

```suggestion
            trade_uuid: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000".to_string(),
```

---

### [medium] (test)

This test mutates process-global environment variables with `std::env::set_var`/`remove_var` while other tests run concurrently in the same process (cargo runs tests in parallel by default), which can race with any test reading `CHIMERA_LOG_DIR`; it also never restores a previously set value. More importantly, it only reimplements the same `std::env::var(...)` lookup expression instead of invoking the actual log-pruning production code, so a regression in the real pruning path would pass this test unnoticed (false confidence). Prefer exercising the actual pruning function (ideally with an injectable directory parameter) and avoid global env mutation, or at least run it serially and restore the prior value.

## operator/tests/unit/helius_rpc_verify_tests.rs (2 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

Host validation via `starts_with` is not host validation. This prefix check also passes unintended hosts such as `https://mainnet.helius-rpc.com.evil.io/?api-key=...` (different registrable domain) and `https://mainnet.helius-rpc.com@evil.io/?api-key=...` (the string before `@` is parsed as userinfo, so the actual host is evil.io). Because `helius_rpc_url` takes `HELIUS_RPC_BASE_URL` from the environment, a wrong value would silently pass this test while the API key is sent to the wrong host. Parse the URL (e.g. `url::Url::parse`) and assert `host_str() == Some("mainnet.helius-rpc.com")` and `scheme() == "https"` instead of string prefix/contains checks.

```suggestion
    let url = url::Url::parse(&helius_rpc_url("test-key-123")).expect("valid URL");
    assert_eq!(url.scheme(), "https", "RPC URL must use https, got: {url}");
    assert_eq!(
        url.host_str(),
        Some("mainnet.helius-rpc.com"),
        "RPC URL must target mainnet.helius-rpc.com, got: {url}"
    );
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Asserting the RPC URL does not *start with* the DAS base URL does not verify that the two resolve to different hosts. It misses regressions where both URLs share the same host but differ in path or query (e.g. `das_base = https://mainnet.helius-rpc.com/v0` vs `rpc_url = https://mainnet.helius-rpc.com?api-key=key` — the hosts are identical yet the prefix check passes), and it can also false-fail on an incidental string prefix. Since the documented invariant is "different hosts", parse both URLs and compare `host_str()` directly.

```suggestion
    let rpc = url::Url::parse(&rpc_url).expect("valid RPC URL");
    let das = url::Url::parse(&das_base).expect("valid DAS base URL");
    assert_ne!(
        rpc.host_str(),
        das.host_str(),
        "RPC URL ({rpc_url}) must NOT share the DAS base host ({das_base}); \
         verify_signature_exists requires a different host than DAS endpoints"
    );
```

## operator/tests/unit/tip_manager_tests.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (test)

These test-local constants duplicate production constants in `operator/src/engine/tips.rs` (`cold_start_multiplier()` returning 2.0 and `MIN_SAMPLES_FOR_PERCENTILE = 10`), and none of the tests in this file invoke the production code (`TipManager::calculate_tip`, `cold_start_tip`, or `percentile_tip_from_history`). Every assertion recomputes the same local formula from the same local constants, so a regression in the real tip logic (e.g. multiplier changed to 1.5, or threshold changed to 5) would pass CI silently. Consider moving these cases into unit tests inside the `tips` module (where the private helpers are reachable) or driving the public `TipManager::calculate_tip` API with a mock `Database`, so the assertions exercise the code they claim to protect.

---

### [medium] (test)

Tautological assertion: `COLD_START_MULTIPLIER` is defined one line above as `2.0`, so this test only detects an edit to the test's own constant, not to the production cold-start multiplier. It provides no regression value and would not fail if `TipManager::cold_start_tip` changed.

---

### [medium] (test)

Tautological assertion: `MIN_SAMPLES_FOR_PERCENTILE` is the local copy of the production threshold (declared in `tips.rs`), and comparing it against the literal `10` only catches a local constant edit. The real cold-start transition logic (`count >= MIN_SAMPLES_FOR_PERCENTILE` in `TipManager::init`/`record_tip`) is never exercised.

---

### [medium] (test)

The percentile tests reimplement the index formula `(len * percentile / 100).min(len - 1)` locally rather than calling the production algorithm (`percentile_tip_from_history` in `tips.rs`), which is private and not reachable from an integration test. They also only test a raw percentile of a generic list, while production selects per-strategy percentiles (Shield=25, Spear=config, Exit=75) and then clamps with `tip_floor_sol` / the floor-ceiling midpoint for Exit — none of which is covered. If the production indexing convention changed (e.g. ceil, or percentile applied to a different window), these tests would keep passing.

---

### [medium] (test)

The cap/floor tests just call `f64::min`/`f64::max` on hand-written values, testing Rust primitives rather than the operator's Decimal-based capping in `calculate_tip`, which applies `base_tip.min(trade * tip_percent_max).min(tip_ceiling_sol).max(tip_floor_sol)`. The combined precedence (percent cap vs. ceiling vs. floor), Decimal rounding, and edge interactions (e.g. `max_by_percent < tip_floor_sol`) are untested, and converting to `f64` loses the Decimal precision the production path relies on.

---

## operator/tests/unit/webhook_restoration_tests.rs (8 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (security)

This test constructs the manager with `dry_run: false` (production mode). If a developer has a real `HELIUS_API_KEY` set in the environment (the code falls back to `test_key_123` only when unset), `reconcile_webhooks()` will hit the real Helius API in deletion mode and can delete real production webhooks that exist in Helius but not in the local DB. Note also that `orphaned_wallet` is never actually created here, so the scenario depends entirely on live external state. Tests should never be destructive against external services. Suggest forcing `helius_dry_run: true` here (and asserting `action_taken` contains "would delete"/"dry run"), or gating the destructive mode behind an explicit opt-in env var plus `#[ignore]` / early skip, with a mocked Helius client.

---

### [high] (test)

All tests share the same `test_chimera` PostgreSQL database: tables are created with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` and are never truncated or cleaned between tests. Since cargo test runs `#[tokio::test]` functions in parallel threads, rows inserted by one test persist and can leak into others. In particular, `webhook_registrations.wallet_address` is UNIQUE and several tests register/insert the same wallet addresses (e.g. `DakNYZdrGeFwF6BhD7ZhLU5qFPnGHXkAsLwq1w3SAJVc`), which can produce constraint conflicts and spurious failures. Suggest truncating all three tables at the start of each test, or isolating each test with its own schema/database or transactional rollback.

---

### [medium] (test)

Both assertions accept either outcome: `result.success || result.attempted_registrations > 0` and `!failed_registrations.is_empty() || successful_registrations > 0` pass whether restoration succeeded or failed. A broken `restore_webhooks_on_startup()` that reports failure for everything would still satisfy this test. Since the test inserted an ACTIVE wallet, it should assert a concrete expected result, e.g. that this wallet is present in successful registrations and `failed_registrations` is empty.

---

### [medium] (test)

`total_checked >= 0` is always true for an unsigned counter, making this assertion a tautology that passes even when reconciliation returned no results at all. The same pattern appears in `test_advisory_reconciliation_mode_no_deletion` (`orphaned_webhooks.contains(...) || !webhook_results.is_empty()`), which also passes on nearly any outcome. These should assert concrete expected counts/statuses rather than an OR of alternatives.

---

### [medium] (test)

`registration_result` is discarded without checking `success`. With the default fallback key `test_key_123` and `helius_dry_run: true`, registration can fail (no reachable Helius endpoint), in which case `check_webhook_health` likely returns None and the test fails on the unconditional `unwrap()` with no diagnostic about the root cause. Additionally, accepting `WebhookHealthStatus::Unknown` in the `matches!` means a completely broken health tracker could still pass. Suggest asserting `registration_result.success` first and unwrapping health only after confirming registration, with an informative message.

---

### [medium] (test)

The comment claims to verify SOL/WSOL handling, but the second mint `EPjFWdd5AufqSSqeM2qN1xzybapC8G4wEGGkZwyTDt1v` is USDC, not SOL/WSOL. The assertion therefore passes even if SOL/WSOL parsing is broken, as long as the USDC entry is aggregated. Check only the SOL/WSOL mints here and assert the USDC presence separately.

---

### [medium] (test)

`processed_count > 0` passes even if only one of the two payloads is parsed, so the test does not actually verify array/batch processing of multiple transactions. Assert `processed_count == 2` (both payloads should parse), or explicitly assert that each signature is present in the parsed results.

---

### [medium] (test)

`result.success || result.error_message.is_some()` accepts both success and failure, so a registration implementation that always fails still passes this test. Given the fake API key, the failure path is the likely outcome, meaning nothing is actually verified about retry behavior. Assert the specific expected outcome for the setup, or split this into separate success-path and failure-path tests.

## ops/collect-evaluation-data.sh (10 findings, 0 critical, 4 high)

### [high] (bug)

The PromQL query `{__name__=~".*"}` is embedded raw in the URL without percent-encoding (`{`, `}`, `"` are not valid unencoded URL query characters and can be rejected by Prometheus or an intermediary), and this `curl | jq` pipeline is NOT guarded — unlike the connectivity check on the previous line. Under `set -euo pipefail`, any failure (rejected query, Prometheus down, or jq not installed) aborts the whole collection before DB snapshots/logs/system data are gathered. Use `curl -G --data-urlencode` and guard the pipeline; also verify jq is present.

```suggestion
if curl -sfG "${PROMETHEUS_URL}/api/v1/query" \
    --data-urlencode 'query={__name__=~".*"}' | jq '.data.result' > "${EVAL_DIR}/day-${DAY_NUM}/metrics/prometheus-snapshot-${TIMESTAMP_FILE}.json" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "✓ Prometheus snapshot collected"
else
    echo "✗ Failed to collect Prometheus snapshot"
fi
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Under `set -e`, if `sqlite3 .backup` fails (DB locked, sqlite3 not installed, disk full), the script exits immediately — the `if [ $? -eq 0 ]` fallback is unreachable dead code, so the intended '✗ Failed to create Chimera database snapshot' path never runs and the rest of the collection is skipped. The same broken pattern exists on the evaluation-database backup below. Use `if sqlite3 ...; then` directly so the failure branch is actually reachable.

```suggestion
    if sqlite3 "${CHIMERA_DB_PATH}" ".backup ${EVAL_DIR}/day-${DAY_NUM}/database/chimera-snapshot-${TIMESTAMP_FILE}.db" 2>/dev/null; then
```

---

### [high] (bug)

These sqlite3 SELECT exports are unguarded. If the `trades`/`positions` tables don't exist or have a different schema (common during upgrades), the query fails and `set -e` terminates the entire run before system/log data, the summary, and the cleanup execute. Guard each export so a schema mismatch degrades gracefully instead of aborting the job.

```suggestion
    sqlite3 "${CHIMERA_DB_PATH}" "SELECT * FROM trades ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1000;" > "${EVAL_DIR}/day-${DAY_NUM}/database/recent-trades-${TIMESTAMP_FILE}.csv" 2>/dev/null || echo "✗ Failed to export recent trades"
    sqlite3 "${CHIMERA_DB_PATH}" "SELECT * FROM positions;" > "${EVAL_DIR}/day-${DAY_NUM}/database/active-positions-${TIMESTAMP_FILE}.csv" 2>/dev/null || echo "✗ Failed to export active positions"
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`top -l 1 -n 0 -b -o cpu` mixes macOS (`-l`) and Linux (`-b`, `-n 0`) flags and is invalid on both platforms; `vm_stat` is macOS-only and does not exist on typical Linux hosts. Under `set -euo pipefail` — compounded by the SIGPIPE from `head -20` — either failing command aborts the script, so no summary/cleanup is produced and the job reports failure. Detect the platform or guard each command with `|| true` and provide Linux equivalents (`top -bn1`, `free -h`).

```suggestion
if command -v vm_stat >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    vm_stat > "${EVAL_DIR}/day-${DAY_NUM}/system/memory-usage-${TIMESTAMP_FILE}.txt" 2>/dev/null || true
else
    free -h > "${EVAL_DIR}/day-${DAY_NUM}/system/memory-usage-${TIMESTAMP_FILE}.txt" 2>/dev/null || true
fi
top -bn1 | head -20 > "${EVAL_DIR}/day-${DAY_NUM}/system/cpu-usage-${TIMESTAMP_FILE}.txt" 2>/dev/null || true
```

---

### [medium] (security)

DAY_NUM/HOUR_NUM come straight from the environment and are interpolated unsanitized into filesystem paths (mkdir/find), the collection-summary JSON (`"day_number": ${DAY_NUM}`), and the Python CLI arguments. A value such as `../../etc` enables path traversal outside EVAL_DIR, and a non-numeric value (e.g. containing quotes/spaces) produces an invalid summary JSON and injects unexpected arguments into process-evaluation-metrics.py. Validate as integers before any use.

```suggestion
if ! [[ "${DAY_NUM}" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || ! [[ "${HOUR_NUM}" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then
    echo "ERROR: DAY_NUM and HOUR_NUM must be non-negative integers" >&2
    exit 1
fi
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

This script is designed to run hourly but has no inter-process locking. If a previous run is still executing (large DB backups, slow Prometheus/docker calls) when the next cron trigger fires, two processes write into the same day directory and can race on the same snapshot files and on evaluation.db (concurrent .backup and Python writes), producing corrupted/interleaved artifacts. Take an exclusive flock on a lockfile at startup and exit early if another run is in progress.

```suggestion
exec 9>"${EVAL_DIR}/.collection.lock"
flock -n 9 || { echo "Another collection run is in progress; exiting"; exit 0; }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Same unguarded-sqlite3 problem in the 'trade execution details' section: if the query references a missing column/table, `set -e` aborts the run here and the subsequent circuit-breaker/health/summary/cleanup steps never execute. Wrap in a conditional or append `|| true` so this optional metrics export cannot sink the whole collection.

```suggestion
    ORDER BY created_at DESC;" > "${EVAL_DIR}/day-${DAY_NUM}/metrics/recent-trades-${TIMESTAMP_FILE}.csv" 2>/dev/null || echo "✗ Failed to collect trade execution details"
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The `if command -v docker` guard only verifies the docker CLI is installed, not that the daemon is reachable. If the daemon is down, `docker stats` fails and, under `set -e`, aborts the entire run; likewise `docker inspect "$container" | jq` fails under pipefail if jq is missing or inspect errors (and container names with spaces also break the word-splitting loop). Guard these commands so docker unavailability degrades gracefully.

```suggestion
    docker stats --no-stream --format "table {{.Container}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}\t{{.MemPerc}}\t{{.NetIO}}\t{{.BlockIO}}" > "${EVAL_DIR}/day-${DAY_NUM}/system/docker-stats-${TIMESTAMP_FILE}.txt" 2>/dev/null || echo "✗ Docker daemon not available"
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

This cleanup deletes every file under EVAL_DIR older than 12 days, including the evaluation database itself (`DB_PATH="${EVAL_DIR}/evaluation.db"`). If the hourly run is suspended or the Python processor does not update the DB for more than 12 days, the entire accumulated evaluation history is silently deleted — contradicting the 'keep 2 extra days for safety' comment. Exclude database files (or store the DB outside the retention-scanned tree).

```suggestion
find "${EVAL_DIR}" -type f ! -name "*.db" ! -name "*.db.gz" -mtime +12 -delete 2>/dev/null || true
```

---

### [medium] (security)

The bot token is placed directly in the curl URL, so it is visible to any local user via `ps` while the command runs — load it from a permission-protected config file (e.g. `curl -K`) or another non-argv source. Additionally the command is unguarded: if Telegram is unreachable, curl's non-zero exit triggers `set -e` and the script exits with a failure status right before `exit 0`, so a purely cosmetic notification can mark an otherwise successful collection as failed. Add `|| true` and URL-encode both POST parameters (the message contains newlines/emoji).

```suggestion
    curl -s "https://api.telegram.org/bot${TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN}/sendMessage" \
        --data-urlencode "chat_id=${TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID}" \
        --data-urlencode "text=${MESSAGE}" > /dev/null 2>&1 || true
```

---

## ops/generate-reports.sh (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Invalid/unsupported PERIOD values silently fall through to 'all', generating a full-history report instead of the requested window. For example `--period=6d`, `--period=30D`, or an empty `--period=` will dump the entire `trades` table with no warning. For an audit tool this produces a much broader (and potentially expensive) report than intended, and the invalid value is also embedded directly into the output filenames. Validate the period against the allowlist and exit with an error.

```suggestion
        *)
            echo "Error: invalid period '$period' (expected 1d|7d|30d|90d|all)" >&2
            exit 1
            ;;
```

---

### [high] (bug)

All output filenames, the package directory, and the archive name are keyed on a second-resolution timestamp (%Y%m%d_%H%M%S). Two runs within the same second silently overwrite the previous compliance reports (both the sqlite3 `>` redirect and the later `mv`/`tar` overwrite existing files), destroying prior audit evidence. Use a higher-resolution timestamp plus PID, or refuse to overwrite existing outputs (e.g. `set -C` or fail if the target already exists).

```suggestion
    local timestamp
    timestamp=$(date -u '+%Y%m%d_%H%M%S')-$$
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

All reports are always written as CSV: FORMAT is parsed and logged but never used anywhere else. A user running `--format=pdf` (or any typo like `--format=xlsx`) silently receives CSV files with no error or warning, and the usage message advertises pdf as supported. Either implement the PDF output path or reject any format other than csv up front.

```suggestion
        --format=*)
            FORMAT="${1#*=}"
            if [[ "$FORMAT" != "csv" ]]; then
                echo "Error: format '$FORMAT' is not supported (only csv is implemented)" >&2
                exit 1
            fi
            shift
            ;;
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

An unknown --type value (e.g. `--type=pnl_daily`) silently falls through to the else branch and generates all five reports, which may be far more expensive/sensitive than the caller requested. Validate REPORT_TYPE as pnl|full before generating and error out on anything else.

```suggestion
    if [[ "$REPORT_TYPE" == "pnl" ]]; then
        # Daily PnL summary only
        generate_pnl_summary "${REPORTS_DIR}/pnl_summary_${PERIOD}_${timestamp}.csv" "$date_range"
        report_files+=("pnl_summary_${PERIOD}_${timestamp}.csv")
    elif [[ "$REPORT_TYPE" == "full" ]]; then
        # Full compliance report
```

---

### [medium] (security)

The reports contain sensitive compliance data (wallet addresses, tx signatures, PnL, configuration audit trail), but files are created with the process default umask (commonly 0644) and REPORTS_DIR with 0755. On a multi-user host (this tool defaults to /opt/chimera) that makes the data world-readable. Harden permissions by applying `umask 077` before creating the directory and files, and/or chmod 600/700 the outputs after generation.

```suggestion
    mkdir -p "$REPORTS_DIR"
    chmod 700 "$REPORTS_DIR"
```

---

## ops/grafana/dashboards/infrastructure/rpc-database.json (5 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

All 7 Prometheus panels hard-code datasource UID `PBFA97CFB590B2093` (and the slow-query table hard-codes Postgres UID `P4F7F8D3768E4C7A1`). If these UIDs do not exist in the target Grafana instance (different environment, or provisioned datasources with auto-generated UIDs), every panel fails to load. Consider binding the datasource via a dashboard variable (`$datasource`) or provisioning with stable UIDs so the dashboard is portable.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`histogram_quantile` is applied directly to `rate(chimera_rpc_latency_ms_bucket[5m])` without a `sum by (le)` aggregation. If the metric carries extra labels (instance, handler, status, etc.), Prometheus computes a separate quantile per label combination and the panel shows multiple identical 'p50' series, which is misleading. Wrap the rate with `sum ... by (le)`; the same fix applies to the p95/p99 queries here and to the DB p95 query in panel 3.

```suggestion
          "expr": "histogram_quantile(0.50, sum(rate(chimera_rpc_latency_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le))",
          "legendFormat": "p50",
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`sum(pg_stat_activity_count)` aggregates connections across all databases/instances, which is inconsistent with the `datname="chimera"` filter used by the PG Database Size panel. On a multi-database or multi-instance deployment this overstates the value shown for the 'chimera' service. Add the same `datname` filter to match the other PG panels.

```suggestion
          "expr": "sum(pg_stat_activity_count{datname=\"chimera\"})",
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`rate(chimera_rpc_errors_total[5m])` without any aggregation returns one series per label combination. With labels such as handler/method/instance, this panel will show many series instead of the single overall error rate implied by the panel title/legend. Use `sum(rate(...))` (or `max`) if a total error rate is intended.

```suggestion
          "expr": "sum(rate(chimera_rpc_errors_total[5m]))",
          "legendFormat": "RPC Errors/sec",
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

This raw SQL depends on the `pg_stat_statements` extension being loaded in the target database and on the Postgres datasource user having read access to it; otherwise the whole panel errors. Also note `mean_exec_time`/`total_exec_time` columns only exist since PostgreSQL 13 / pg_stat_statements 1.4 (older versions expose `mean_time`/`total_time`). Document the extension requirement or make the query version-aware.

## ops/grafana/dashboards/monitoring/real-time-events.json (2 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

Value mapping mixes the legacy top-level `value` key with the modern `options` schema. In Grafana's value-mapping format (schemaVersion 39) all value→config pairs belong inside a single mapping's `options` object; the stray top-level `"value": "0"` is legacy schema and is ignored (or may be interpreted instead of `options` depending on the Grafana version's migration logic), which can cause the UNHEALTHY/HEALTHY text/color labels not to render as intended. Merge both values into one mapping and drop the redundant `value` key.

```suggestion
          "mappings": [
            {"type": "value", "options": {"0": {"text": "UNHEALTHY", "color": "red"}, "1": {"text": "HEALTHY", "color": "green"}}}
          ]
```

### [medium] (bug)

Same mixed legacy/new value-mapping schema as in the RPC Health panel: each mapping object carries a legacy top-level `"value"` key alongside the modern `options` map, and the two values are split across two separate mapping entries. Consolidate into a single `type: "value"` mapping so the color/text labels for both HEALTHY and UNHEALTHY render reliably across Grafana versions.

```suggestion
          "mappings": [
            {"type": "value", "options": {"0": {"text": "UNHEALTHY", "color": "red"}, "1": {"text": "HEALTHY", "color": "green"}}}
          ]
```

## ops/grafana/dashboards/monitoring/webhook-lifecycle.json (4 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

The Postgres datasource UID `P4F7F8D3768E4C7A1` is hard-coded in every panel. If this dashboard is imported into a different Grafana instance (staging/prod) or the datasource is recreated with a new UID, all six panels will show 'datasource not found' and break. Recommend defining a datasource template variable (e.g. `DS_POSTGRES`) in the dashboard and referencing `"uid": "${DS_POSTGRES}"` in each panel instead.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The dashboard declares `"refresh": "10s"` and exposes a time-range picker, but none of the queries use `$__timeFilter`/`$__timeFrom()`/`$__timeTo()`. For the 'Recent Webhook Events' panel this means changing the dashboard time range has no effect — it always returns the newest 30 rows of the audit log, which is misleading. Add a time filter on `created_at` so this panel respects the selected range (the other panels are current-state snapshots, so they are less affected).

---

### [medium] (performance)

`ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 30` without a time-bound predicate forces the DB to scan and sort the entire `webhook_lifecycle_audit` table, and the cost grows linearly as the audit table accumulates. Combine this query with a `$__timeFilter(created_at)` predicate (which also makes the panel range-aware) and ensure an index on `created_at` exists to bound the scan.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The panel title is 'Active Wallets with Webhooks', but the query only filters `w.status = 'ACTIVE'` — it does not require `wm.helius_webhook_id IS NOT NULL`. Wallets that are active but have no Helius webhook registered will appear in this table with NULL webhook columns, contradicting the panel title and confusing operators. Add `AND wm.helius_webhook_id IS NOT NULL` to the WHERE clause.

## ops/grafana/dashboards/security/security-overview.json (4 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

Hardcoded datasource UIDs: all Prometheus panels use UID `PBFA97CFB590B2093` and both Postgres tables use `P4F7F8D3768E4C7A1`. These UIDs are environment-specific, so in any other Grafana instance the panels will render "datasource not found". Consider parameterizing with provisioning template variables (e.g. `${DS_PROMETHEUS}` / `${DS_POSTGRES}`) or substituting UIDs at deploy time.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Column name mismatch: the SQL orders by `created_at` and uses `SELECT *`, but the organize transformation renames `changed_at` / `changed_by`, which are never selected. If the actual column is `created_at`, the rename silently no-ops and the timestamp stays labeled `created_at`; `SELECT *` can also surface extra columns not covered by the rename map. Align the SQL column list with the rename mapping (and prefer explicit columns over `SELECT *`).

---

### [medium] (bug)

The value mappings key on strings `'0'`/`'1'`, but Grafana's Postgres data source returns boolean columns as `true`/`false`, so the NO/YES mapping will not apply to `acknowledged`. Additionally, the top-level `value` field is legacy Grafana syntax and is ignored under schemaVersion 39 (only `options` is read). Map `true`/`false` instead (or cast the column to int/text in SQL).

```suggestion
            {"type": "value", "options": {"false": {"text": "NO", "color": "red"}}},
            {"type": "value", "options": {"true": {"text": "YES", "color": "green"}}}
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Both `chimera_geoip_cache_hits` and `chimera_geoip_lookups_total` are cumulative counters, so this ratio shows the lifetime hit rate rather than the current cache hit rate, and it returns no data whenever `lookups_total` is 0. Wrap both sides in rate() to display an instantaneous hit ratio (e.g. over 5m).

```suggestion
          "expr": "rate(chimera_geoip_cache_hits[5m]) / rate(chimera_geoip_lookups_total[5m])",
```

## ops/grafana/dashboards/trading/chimera-overview.json (3 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Inconsistent circuit-breaker state mapping: this panel maps state 1 to ACTIVE and does not map state 2, but the metric's actual semantics are 2=ACTIVE, 1=COOLDOWN, 0=TRIPPED (see operator/src/metrics.rs: "2 = active, 1 = cooldown, 0 = tripped") and panel 9 of this same dashboard maps 1=COOLDOWN, 2=ACTIVE. As a result the same `chimera_circuit_breaker_state` value renders as "ACTIVE" here while "COOLDOWN" is shown in the Circuit Breaker panel, and state 2 appears as a raw unmapped number. Align this panel with the three-state mapping used by panel 9.

```suggestion
{"type": "value", "options": {"1": {"text": "COOLDOWN", "color": "yellow"}}, "value": "1"},
            {"type": "value", "options": {"2": {"text": "ACTIVE", "color": "green"}}, "value": "2"}
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Unusual value-mapping object shape: the top-level `"value"` key is not part of Grafana's current value-mapping schema, which expects `type: "value"` plus an `options` map (each option normally carrying an `index`). This looks like a leftover from the legacy mapping format (`{"type": 1, "value": "...", "text": "...", "color": "..."}`) and may be silently dropped when Grafana imports or re-serializes the dashboard, causing the mapping to be ignored. Remove the extraneous top-level `value` key and add `index` to each option entry. The same pattern is repeated in panels 1 and 9 of this file.

```suggestion
{"type": "value", "options": {"0": {"text": "UNHEALTHY", "color": "red", "index": 0}}},
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The legacy "Queue Backpressure" alert has an empty `notifications` list, so when the queue-depth condition fires it will only flip the in-dashboard alert state without notifying anyone — operators are never paged. Associate a notification channel/contact point with this alert (or migrate it to Grafana unified alerting / the prometheus alerts.yml rules where contacts are configured) so queue backpressure actually reaches operators.

## ops/grafana/dashboards/trading/trade-execution.json (6 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

This query does not apply $__timeFilter(created_at), so the table always returns the 20 most recent trades globally and ignores the dashboard's selected time range, making the panel misleading when viewing historical windows. Add a time filter to the WHERE clause.

```suggestion
"rawSql": "SELECT trade_uuid, wallet_address, side, amount_sol, status, created_at FROM trades WHERE $__timeFilter(created_at) ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20",
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The threshold steps are ineffective for risk display: the step at 50 uses green (same as the base step), so values from 50–75 render green with no warning, and the red step at 100 only triggers for values >100, which a heat percent capped at max 100 never reaches. Adjust the colors/values so the full range maps to distinct risk levels.

```suggestion
{"value": null, "color": "green"},
              {"value": 50, "color": "yellow"},
              {"value": 75, "color": "orange"},
              {"value": 90, "color": "red"}
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

histogram_quantile is applied directly to the rate() result without aggregating across labels. If chimera_trade_latency_ms_bucket carries any label besides le (e.g., venue, strategy, outcome), every label combination produces a separate quantile series and the stat becomes ambiguous/misleading. Aggregate first with sum(...) by (le). The same pattern is used in the 'Trade Latency p50/p95/p99' timeseries panel.

```suggestion
"expr": "histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(chimera_trade_latency_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le))",
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Same issue as the stat panel: each quantile expr applies histogram_quantile directly to rate() without aggregating across labels, so p50/p95/p99 will each render multiple series (one per label combination) if the histogram has any labels besides le, and legend collisions will make the panel unreadable.

```suggestion
"expr": "histogram_quantile(0.50, sum(rate(chimera_trade_latency_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le))",
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The mappings mix the legacy top-level 'value' key with the modern options-based format (schemaVersion 39 expects only type + options), which can be dropped or fail to render. More importantly, only 0/1 are mapped: if chimera_jito_health is absent (scraper/process down), the stat shows 'No data' instead of 'UNHEALTHY', hiding an outage. Use schema-valid mappings and treat missing data as UNHEALTHY.

```suggestion
{"type": "value", "options": {"0": {"text": "UNHEALTHY", "color": "red"}}},
            {"type": "value", "options": {"1": {"text": "HEALTHY", "color": "green"}}},
            {"type": "special", "options": {"match": "null", "result": {"text": "UNHEALTHY", "color": "red"}}}
```

---

### [medium] (security)

The query returns full wallet_address values and displays them under the 'Wallet' column, exposing sensitive trading wallet data to anyone with dashboard access. Consider masking the address in SQL (e.g., truncate to a short prefix) or restricting access to this dashboard.

```suggestion
"rawSql": "SELECT trade_uuid, LEFT(wallet_address, 6) || '...' AS wallet_address, side, amount_sol, status, created_at FROM trades ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20",
```

## ops/grafana/dashboards/wallet-intelligence/wqs-scoring.json (4 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

`scout_rugcheck_rejections_total` is a Prometheus Counter (see scout/core/metrics.py). A bare instant query in a stat panel displays the cumulative lifetime count, which resets whenever the scout process restarts and never reflects the dashboard time window — so the panel value is not "rejections" in any useful period. Use `increase(scout_rugcheck_rejections_total[$__range])` (or `rate(...)` with an appropriate stat calculation) so the panel shows rejections over the selected range.

```suggestion
          "expr": "increase(scout_rugcheck_rejections_total[$__range])",
          "refId": "A"
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`scout_wqs_distribution` is a Prometheus Histogram; `rate(scout_wqs_distribution_bucket[5m])` returns one series per `le` per exposing source. If more than one Prometheus target/instance exposes this histogram, the heatmap will not total the buckets correctly (le totals will be undercounted/duplicated). Aggregate across sources with `sum by (le) (rate(scout_wqs_distribution_bucket[5m]))` before the heatmap render.

```suggestion
          "expr": "sum by (le) (rate(scout_wqs_distribution_bucket[5m]))",
          "legendFormat": "{{le}}",
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

This query scans/orders the entire `wallets` table and is not constrained by the dashboard time range, even though the table has `created_at`/`updated_at` timestamps. With the dashboard refreshing every 30s, this repeatedly runs a full-table sort over all wallets regardless of the visible window. Constrain it to the dashboard window with `WHERE $__timeFilter(updated_at) AND wqs_score IS NOT NULL` (add an index on `updated_at`; the existing `idx_wallets_wqs` already covers the ORDER BY).

```suggestion
          "rawSql": "SELECT address, wqs_score, wqs_confidence, roi_30d, trade_count_30d, win_rate, archetype, status FROM wallets WHERE $__timeFilter(updated_at) AND wqs_score IS NOT NULL ORDER BY wqs_score DESC LIMIT 25",
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

This query aggregates over the entire `wallets` table on every 30s refresh and ignores the dashboard time range, so it does not represent status within the selected window and becomes progressively more expensive as the table grows. If the panel is meant to reflect the current window, add `WHERE $__timeFilter(updated_at)` (with an index on `updated_at`); otherwise, prefer a cached/summary aggregation or lower refresh frequency for a lifetime count.

```suggestion
          "rawSql": "SELECT status, count(*) FROM wallets WHERE $__timeFilter(updated_at) GROUP BY status",
```

## ops/grafana/experiment-dashboard.json (3 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

`profit_factor` is a ratio (gross profit / gross loss), typically ~1.0–3.0 (config/experiment.yaml sets `min_profit_factor: 1.2`, and the verdict code computes it as gross_profit/gross_loss). Displaying it with unit `percent` and thresholds at 10/20 is misleading: a healthy profit factor of ~1.5 renders as "1.5%" and the 10/20 thresholds are never meaningfully crossed by a ratio in the 1–3 range. Use a plain unit (e.g. `short`/none) with ratio-appropriate thresholds (e.g. 1.0/1.2) to match the metric's actual semantics.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The documented statuses for `chimera_experiment_status` are `running/paused/completed/aborted`, but this panel maps numeric values 0–3 to `Stopped/Running/Completed/Aborted`. "Stopped" does not appear in the documented status set, so if the exporter emits codes in the documented order the stat panel will mislabel live status (e.g. code 0 shown as "Stopped" while actually running, and "Paused" missing entirely). Verify the exporter's actual status codes and align the value mappings accordingly.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Several queries reference metric names that do not match the documented Prometheus metrics for this experiment (e.g. documented `chimera_experiment_total_pnl` vs `chimera_experiment_total_paper_pnl`/`total_tracer_pnl`; `chimera_experiment_max_drawdown` vs `max_drawdown_pct`; `chimera_experiment_toxic_wallet_count` vs `toxic_wallet_rate`; `chimera_experiment_credit_budget`/`credit_used` vs `credits_remaining`/`credits_projected_total`; plus the undocumented `abort_*` series). No code emitting any `chimera_experiment_*` series was found in the repository, so unless the exporter emits exactly these names, these panels will silently render empty. Align every `expr` with the exporter's actual metric registry.

## ops/install-crons.sh (5 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

No preflight validation is done before mutating system state. With `set -euo pipefail`, a single missing required file (chimera.service, logrotate.conf, backup.sh, reconcile.sh — all copied unconditionally) aborts the script after `create_user`/`create_directories` have already run, leaving a partially configured system (user/group/dirs created, systemd unit enabled but cron/logrotate never installed). Add a preflight check for all required files at the top of `install()` before any changes are made.

```suggestion
install() {
    local required_files=(
        "$OPS_DIR/chimera.service"
        "$OPS_DIR/logrotate.conf"
        "$OPS_DIR/backup.sh"
        "$OPS_DIR/reconcile.sh"
    )
    for f in "${required_files[@]}"; do
        if [[ ! -f "$f" ]]; then
            log_error "Required file missing: $f"
            exit 1
        fi
    done

    log_info "Installing Chimera operations..."
    
    create_user
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The optional helper scripts (rotate-secrets.sh, generate-reports.sh, update-metrics.sh) are copied only `[[ -f ... ]]`, yet their cron entries below are written unconditionally. If any of these files is absent, the install still succeeds but leaves permanent cron jobs that fail daily, writing errors to /var/log/chimera. Either validate these files in the preflight check too, or generate their cron entries conditionally (e.g. `if [[ -x ... ]]; then cat >>`).

---

### [medium] (bug)

These PostgreSQL-only prune jobs are installed unconditionally even though the installer's own 'Next steps' and the validation cron use SQLite (`sqlite3 $CHIMERA_HOME/data/chimera.db`). On a SQLite deployment (or when the chimera-postgres container/DB name differs), both jobs will run as root and fail every day forever. Install them only when PostgreSQL is actually in use (e.g. detect the container/db at install time or gate behind a flag), and/or parameterize the DB user/name instead of hardcoding `-U chimera -d chimera`.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`cd ... && flock ... || echo "skipped (already running)"` groups the whole chain under the `||`, so ANY failure (missing scout dir, python3 error, etc.) produces the same misleading 'already running' message as a genuine lock conflict. Since the weekly and daily jobs use different lock files, a real lock contention for the weekly job is practically impossible — meaning operational failures will be silently reported as skips. Wrap the job in a small runner script (or restructure with explicit `if cd ...; then` / distinct exit-code handling) so cd failures and command failures are logged separately from lock contention.

---

### [medium] (security)

Lock files in world-writable /tmp with predictable names (`/tmp/scout_daily.lock`) are vulnerable to local pre-creation/symlink attacks: another local user can create and hold the lock (or symlink it) to force every run to be silently skipped — a denial of service, with no visibility into the cause. Move the locks into a chimera-owned directory (e.g. `$CHIMERA_HOME/data/scout_daily.lock` or `/run/lock/chimera/`) and ensure the directory has restrictive permissions.

---

## ops/merge_roster.py (2 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

This INSERT ... SELECT copies only a subset of the columns defined in the shared `wallets` schema (see `scout/database/schema/wallets.sql` and `database/schema/wallets.sql`, both used by the scout roster writer). Columns `wqs_confidence`, `avg_win_sol`, `avg_loss_sol`, `profit_factor`, `realized_pnl_30d_sol`, `archetype`, and `avg_entry_delay_seconds` are silently dropped during the merge and become NULL in chimera.db, losing scout analysis data that the operator uses for archetype-aware WQS thresholds, position-sizing confidence, and profit-factor gates. Either copy all shared columns in the SELECT list, or at minimum validate the roster schema (e.g., `PRAGMA new_roster.table_info(wallets)`) against the expected columns before the destructive DELETE.

```suggestion
            main_cursor.execute("""
                INSERT INTO wallets (
                    address, status, wqs_score, wqs_confidence,
                    roi_7d, roi_30d, trade_count_30d, win_rate,
                    max_drawdown_30d, avg_trade_size_sol, avg_win_sol, avg_loss_sol,
                    profit_factor, realized_pnl_30d_sol, last_trade_at,
                    promoted_at, ttl_expires_at, notes, archetype,
                    avg_entry_delay_seconds, created_at, updated_at
                )
                SELECT 
                    address, status, wqs_score, wqs_confidence,
                    roi_7d, roi_30d, trade_count_30d, win_rate,
                    max_drawdown_30d, avg_trade_size_sol, avg_win_sol, avg_loss_sol,
                    profit_factor, realized_pnl_30d_sol, last_trade_at,
                    promoted_at, ttl_expires_at, notes, archetype,
                    avg_entry_delay_seconds, created_at, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
                FROM new_roster.wallets
            """)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The merge replaces the entire `wallets` table (`DELETE FROM wallets` then insert), but R4 only guards against an *empty* roster. If scout produces a truncated/partial roster (e.g., API failures mid-run that cause it to analyze only a subset of wallets), the merge silently deletes all production wallets not present in the roster, causing real data loss. Consider comparing `roster_count` against `before_count` and aborting (or requiring explicit confirmation) when the roster is dramatically smaller than the current database.

## ops/migrate-to-vector.sh (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Fluentd is stopped and removed in Step 3 before Vector is even started (Step 4) and health-verified (Step 5). If Vector fails to start, log aggregation is left down with no automatic rollback. In addition, `docker-compose.evaluation.yml` does not define a `fluentd` service (only a comment references Fluentd), so once a `chimera-fluentd` container is actually detected, `docker-compose stop fluentd` will fail and, under `set -euo pipefail`, abort the entire migration with an unhelpful error. Suggest starting and verifying Vector first, then removing the legacy container by name (e.g., `docker rm -f chimera-fluentd`), keeping Fluentd as fallback until Vector is confirmed healthy.

---

### [medium] (bug)

BACKUP_DATE only has day granularity (`date +%Y%m%d`), so running the migration twice on the same day silently overwrites the previous backups, destroying the only rollback artifacts. Also, the final summary prints `docker/env.evaluation.backup-...` unconditionally even when that file did not exist and no env backup was created. Include a time component (e.g., `%Y%m%d-%H%M%S`) or abort if the backup already exists, and only list backups that were actually made.

```suggestion
BACKUP_DATE=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`docker ps | grep -q "chimera-fluentd"` is a substring match, so it can match unrelated containers whose names merely contain the text. Worse, under `set -o pipefail`, `grep -q` exits as soon as it finds a match, `docker ps` can be killed by SIGPIPE and return non-zero, making the pipeline report a false negative even when the container exists. Use an exact name filter instead: `docker ps -q --filter "name=^/chimera-fluentd$"`. The same pattern is used for `chimera-vector` in the verification section and should be fixed there too.

```suggestion
if [ -n "$(docker ps -q --filter name=^/chimera-fluentd$)" ]; then
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

A hardcoded 10-second sleep is not a reliable readiness wait: on slower CI/host environments Vector may not have its API up yet, producing false health-check failures; on fast machines it wastes time. The compose healthcheck (interval 30s, retries 3) won't help within 10s either. Replace the sleep with a retry loop that polls `http://localhost:8383/health` until it succeeds or a timeout is reached.

```suggestion
for i in $(seq 1 30); do
    if curl -sf http://localhost:8383/health > /dev/null 2>&1; then
        break
    fi
    sleep 2
    if [ "$i" -eq 30 ]; then
        echo -e "${RED}✗ Vector did not become healthy in time${NC}"
        exit 1
    fi
done
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Under `set -euo pipefail`, a failed `docker-compose ... up -d vector` exits the script immediately, so the `if [ $? -eq 0 ]` test and its `else` branch (which prints the useful "Vector failed to start" message) are dead code. Put the command directly in the `if` condition, where failures are exempt from `set -e`, so the error path is actually reachable.

```suggestion
if docker-compose -f docker-compose.evaluation.yml --profile evaluation up -d vector; then
    echo -e "${GREEN}✓ Vector started${NC}"
else
    echo -e "${RED}✗ Vector failed to start${NC}"
    echo "Check logs with: docker-compose logs vector"
    exit 1
fi
```

---

## ops/monitor-evaluation.sh (6 findings, 0 critical, 4 high)

### [high] (bug)

`set -euo pipefail` is active and these calls are unguarded simple commands. `check_service_health` returns 1 for an unhealthy service, so the first failed health check terminates the entire monitoring script instead of reporting the outage — defeating the purpose of a 10-day continuous monitor. Guard each call (`|| true`) or capture the return code.

```suggestion
        check_service_health "Operator" "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/health" || true
        check_service_health "Scout" "http://localhost:8081/health" || true
        check_service_health "Prometheus Eval" "http://localhost:9091/-/healthy" || true
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Two problems here (applies to every metric parse in this block): (1) `grep "chimera_cpu_usage_percent"` also matches the `# HELP`/`# TYPE` lines of the Prometheus text format (their 2nd field is `#`), so `cpu_usage` becomes multi-line junk and all downstream comparisons fail. Anchor to actual samples, e.g. `^chimera_cpu_usage_percent `. (2) When a metric is missing, `|| echo "0"` silently fabricates a healthy zero, so an absent metric never triggers its threshold alert. Use `N/A` instead of `0`.

```suggestion
        local cpu_usage=$(awk '/^chimera_cpu_usage_percent /{print $2; exit}' /tmp/operator-metrics.txt)
        cpu_usage="${cpu_usage:-N/A}"
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Prometheus gauges are typically floats (e.g. `42.5`), but `-gt` is an integer-only test. On a float this fails with `integer expression expected` and the alert is silently skipped, so high CPU/memory/queue usage can go unreported. The same applies to the disk-percentage comparison at the bottom. Truncate to an integer (after validating it's numeric) or compare with `awk`.

```suggestion
            if [ "${cpu_usage}" != "N/A" ] && [ "${cpu_usage%%.*}" -gt "${ALERT_THRESHOLD_CPU}" ]; then
```

---

### [high] (bug)

None of the `curl` calls here (nor the `/metrics` fetch and Telegram/Discord alert sends) set `--max-time`, so one hung endpoint blocks the entire monitoring loop indefinitely — the script silently freezes instead of alerting. Add `--max-time` (e.g. 5–10s) to every curl invocation, and ideally `--connect-timeout` too.

```suggestion
    if curl -sf --max-time 5 "${health_url}" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`last_hour` is computed but never used: the SQL counts *all* unresolved anomalies regardless of age, so a single stale CRITICAL row re-fires a CRITICAL alert every 60s cycle for the rest of the 10-day run. Either remove the unused variable or add the time filter (adjust the column to the actual schema), e.g. `AND detected_at >= datetime('now','-1 hour')`.

```suggestion
        anomaly_count=$(sqlite3 "${EVAL_DIR}/evaluation.db" "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM evaluation_anomalies WHERE resolved = 0 AND detected_at >= datetime('now','-1 hour');" 2>/dev/null || echo "0")
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`get_system_metrics` uses an inverted convention (`return ${health_check}`, where 1 = metrics fetched), and the caller reads it via `$?` captured from a `local metrics_output=$(...)` assignment. `local` is a well-known bash gotcha: it can mask the command substitution's exit status, so `metrics_health` may always be 0 (failure) and the whole metric-alert block is skipped even when metrics were fetched. Returning non-zero on success is also fragile under `set -e`. Declare the variable first and capture `$?` from a plain assignment (or make the function return 0 on success).

```suggestion
        local metrics_output metrics_health
        metrics_output=$(get_system_metrics)
        metrics_health=$?
```

---

## ops/preflight-check.sh (7 findings, 1 critical, 2 high)

### [critical] (bug)

Under `set -euo pipefail`, `((PASSED++))` evaluates to the pre-increment value (0 on the first call), so the command returns exit status 1 and errexit terminates the script immediately. Since PASSED/FAILED/WARNINGS all start at 0, the very first `log_pass`/`log_fail`/`log_warn` call kills the whole script before any check completes (verified pattern applies to all three log functions). Use `PASSED=$((PASSED + 1))` or append `|| true` to each increment.

```suggestion
log_pass() {
    echo -e "${GREEN}✓${NC} $1"
    PASSED=$((PASSED + 1))
}
```

---

### [high] (bug)

This test writes a fake losing trade directly into the production `trades` table. If the script is killed, crashes, or the cleanup `DELETE` fails between the INSERT and the DELETE, the fake trade persists permanently and keeps the circuit breaker tripped in production. The fixed 30s sleep is also coupled to the breaker's evaluation cadence, so it can cause false failures (or false passes) if that cadence differs. Additionally, values are interpolated into SQL without validation (a non-numeric `max_loss` makes `bc` emit nothing and yields a malformed statement). Prefer a dedicated test table/transaction with `trap`-based cleanup, or a dry-run/simulated evaluation instead of mutating live data.

---

### [high] (bug)

Reset failure is silently downgraded: `|| log_warn ...` means a failed reset only produces a warning, while `log_pass` was already emitted above and the function returns 0 — the pre-flight reports success even though trading remains halted in production. Also, `grep API_KEY | cut -d=` truncates any key whose value contains '=', and it can match multiple lines if several keys contain 'API_KEY'. Make the reset result part of the pass/fail decision and use `$CONFIG_FILE` instead of the hardcoded path (see also the secret-exposure issue below).

---

### [medium] (bug)

Exit code contract violated: the header documents `2` for warnings, but this branch exits `0`. Any automation (CI, deploy scripts) that distinguishes 'warning' from 'all-clear' via exit code will treat warnings as a clean pass. Change to `exit 2`.

```suggestion
    elif [[ $WARNINGS -gt 0 ]]; then
        echo -e "${YELLOW}⚠ Pre-flight checks passed with warnings${NC}"
        echo "Review warnings before production deployment"
        exit 2
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

When `ntpq -p` has no synchronized peers, `grep -c` prints `0` and exits 1, so the `|| echo "0"` appends a second `0` — `peers` becomes `0
0`, making the `-gt` numeric comparison unreliable (bash prints an arithmetic syntax error and the branch is effectively random). This pattern appears in both ntpq branches. Use `peers=$(ntpq -p 2>/dev/null | grep -c "^\*") || true` (grep -c already prints `0` on no match) or test with `grep -q`.

```suggestion
        peers=$(ntpq -p 2>/dev/null | grep -c "^\*") || true
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The average latency is computed only over successful calls (`${#latencies[@]}` is the success count), so the failure ratio is ignored: 9 failed/timeout requests plus 1 fast success still yields an average well under the 50ms threshold and the check passes. Enforce a minimum success ratio (e.g., require ≥ 8/10 successes) or include timed-out requests (at `--max-time 5`, i.e. 5000ms) in the total and denominator.

---

### [medium] (security)

Security concern: the webhook secret is extracted with `grep`/`cut -d=` (truncates any value containing '=') and then passed as a command-line argument to `openssl dgst -hmac`, making it visible in the process list (`ps`/`pgrep`) to any local user. Same pattern applies to the API key embedded in the curl `Authorization` header above. Prefer sourcing the env file and referencing the variables directly (e.g., `openssl ... -hmac "$CHIMERA_SECURITY__WEBHOOK_SECRET"` via env), or at minimum avoid placing secrets on the CLI.

```suggestion
        local webhook_secret
        webhook_secret="${CHIMERA_SECURITY__WEBHOOK_SECRET:-}"
```

## ops/process-evaluation-metrics.py (4 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

The column indexing does not match how the collector writes the docker stats file. `collect-evaluation-data.sh` writes `docker stats --format "table {{.Container}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}\t{{.MemPerc}}\t{{.NetIO}}\t{{.BlockIO}}"`. Because `{{.MemUsage}}` renders as e.g. `10.2MiB / 100MiB` (contains a space), `split()` shifts the columns: `parts[3]` becomes `"/"`, so `float(parts[3].rstrip('%'))` raises `ValueError`. The broad `except` then aborts the whole loop and `containers` is returned empty, silently discarding all system stats. Additionally, `parts[0]` is the container ID (`{{.Container}}`), not the container name. Parse robustly (e.g., regex for `name cpu% mem%`) or use a delimiter-free format without the spaced `MemUsage` column.

```suggestion
                for line in lines[1:]:
                    match = re.match(r'^(\S+)\s+([0-9.]+)%\s+([0-9.]+)%', line)
                    if match:
                        container_name = match.group(1)
                        cpu_percent = float(match.group(2))
                        memory_percent = float(match.group(3))
```

---

### [high] (bug)

When the operator metrics file is absent or empty (handled just above, where `operator_metrics` stays `{}`), the code still calls `store_evaluation_snapshot` and commits a zero-filled row (0% CPU, 0 trades, 0 PnL). Downstream analytics, averages and anomaly detection will treat these as genuine observations of an idle system, polluting the evaluation data. Skip the snapshot (and the dependent system-resource/anomaly writes) when no operator metrics were parsed, or record an explicit "no data" marker.

```suggestion
            if not operator_metrics:
                print("Warning: No operator metrics available; skipping snapshot for this cycle")
                return False

            # Store evaluation snapshot
            snapshot_id = self.store_evaluation_snapshot(
                day_number=day_number,
                hour_number=hour_number,
                timestamp=timestamp,
                operator_metrics=operator_metrics,
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The label section `{...}` is captured but immediately discarded, and `metrics` is keyed by bare metric name only. Any labeled series sharing a name (e.g., per-outcome counters, histogram `_bucket`/`_created` lines) silently overwrites the previous one and only the last value survives, corrupting the data consumed by `store_evaluation_snapshot`. Also, `\w+` cannot match Prometheus metric names containing `:` (e.g., `chimera:trades_total`), so those lines are skipped entirely. Preserve the labels when keying metrics (or select the intended series explicitly) and widen the name regex to `[A-Za-z_:][A-Za-z0-9_:]*`.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Anomaly rows are stamped with `datetime.now().isoformat()` — naive local time — while `evaluation_snapshots.snapshot_time` is stored from the UTC `--timestamp` (parsed as timezone-aware). This breaks time alignment/joins between the two tables. For backfilled runs (`--day`/`--hour` with a historical timestamp) it is also the wrong wall-clock time entirely. Pass `timestamp` into `detect_and_store_anomalies` and reuse the same aware UTC datetime derived from it (as `store_evaluation_snapshot` does) instead of `datetime.now()`.

```suggestion
                    datetime.fromisoformat(timestamp.replace('Z', '+00:00')),
                    day_number, hour_number,
```

## ops/recover-postgres.sh (7 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

psql without `-d` connects to a database named after POSTGRES_USER (default `chimera`), which is the very database being dropped when POSTGRES_DB also defaults to `chimera`. `DROP DATABASE` then fails with "cannot drop the currently open database"; the error is swallowed by `2>&1`, and the subsequent `CREATE DATABASE` also fails because the database still exists, so recovery always aborts with the default configuration. Connect to a maintenance database instead.

```suggestion
if docker-compose exec postgres psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d postgres -c "DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS $POSTGRES_DB;" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The script never enables `set -o pipefail`, so pipeline exit status comes from the last command only. Here a failing `pg_dump` (e.g. connection error or lock) is masked by `gzip` returning 0, so the safety backup is reported as successful even when it is empty/partial. The same problem applies to the restore pipeline `gunzip -c ... | psql` (a corrupt dump can be silently truncated). Add `set -o pipefail` immediately after `set -e` at the top of the script.

---

### [high] (bug)

If the primary restore fails midway, the safety dump is piped into psql on the same partially-restored database without dropping/recreating it first, and the restore result is never checked — so the "recovery" can leave an inconsistent database. Worse, the script then `exit 1` without restarting `operator`/`scout`, leaving the application services stopped. Drop/recreate the database before restoring the safety backup, verify the restore exit status, and restart services (ideally via a `trap`) before exiting.

---

### [medium] (security)

POSTGRES_DB is interpolated directly into the DROP/CREATE DATABASE SQL. A database name containing quotes or SQL metacharacters will corrupt the statement or allow SQL injection. Validate the name against a safe pattern (e.g. `^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$`) before running DROP/CREATE, rather than relying on it being a trusted env var.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The glob `chimera_*.sql.gz` also matches safety snapshots created as `chimera_before_recovery_*.sql.gz` in earlier runs, so the "latest backup" auto-discovered here may be a safety snapshot rather than the intended archived backup. Restrict the pattern (e.g. `chimera_[0-9]*.sql.gz`) or filter out `before_recovery`. Also, parsing `ls` output is fragile for names with whitespace; prefer null-delimited `find` if such names are possible.

```suggestion
    BACKUP_FILE=$(ls -t "$BACKUP_DIR"/chimera_[0-9]*.sql.gz 2>/dev/null | head -1)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Most `docker-compose exec` invocations here omit `-T`, which allocates a TTY by default. In non-interactive/CI contexts this can emit "the input device is not a TTY" and fail (the restore step already uses `-T`). Add `-T` to the exec calls used for DROP, CREATE, and verification so the script behaves consistently in automation.

```suggestion
TABLE_COUNT=$(docker-compose exec -T postgres psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -t -c "SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'public';" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ')
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

If CREATE DATABASE fails (or any step after `docker-compose stop operator scout` fails), the script exits without restarting `operator`/`scout`, leaving the application down. Consider registering a `trap` (e.g. `trap 'docker-compose start operator scout' EXIT`) so services are always restored even on failure paths.

---

## ops/report-generator-entrypoint.sh (6 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

The trigger is an exact string-equality check against the HH:MM value, performed once per ~60s loop. Any drift — a delayed wake from `sleep`, NTP/clock jump, CPU throttling, or signal handling — that moves the check past the scheduled minute means the report is silently skipped for the entire day with no catch-up; it will only run again the next day at the same minute. Track the last run date and also trigger when the current time is at/after REPORT_TIME and today's report hasn't run yet.

```suggestion
    # Check if it's time to generate report; also catch up if the minute was missed
    TODAY=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
    if [ "${CURRENT_TIME}" = "${REPORT_TIME}" ] || { [ "${CURRENT_TIME}" \> "${REPORT_TIME}" ] && [ "${LAST_RUN_DATE}" != "${TODAY}" ]; }; then
        LAST_RUN_DATE=${TODAY}
```

---

### [high] (bug)

On Python failure the script prints '❌ Report generation failed' but then falls through to 'Report generation complete.' and sleeps ~24h before trying again. A broken report thus silently becomes a missing daily report with no retry, backoff, or alerting, and the final log line is misleading. Exit non-zero on failure (letting the orchestrator restart/alert) or implement a retry with backoff and an explicit error marker.

```suggestion
        else
            echo "❌ Report generation failed"
            # Retry after a short backoff instead of waiting 24h
            sleep 300
            continue
        fi
```

---

### [high] (bug)

With `set -e` active, if neither `stat -f%z` (BSD syntax) nor `stat -c%s` (GNU syntax) is available — common in busybox/minimal container images — both commands fail and this assignment returns non-zero, terminating the whole service right after a successful report generation. Add a portable fallback such as `wc -c` and/or a trailing `|| true`.

```suggestion
                FILE_SIZE=$(stat -f%z "${LATEST_REPORT}" 2>/dev/null || stat -c%s "${LATEST_REPORT}" 2>/dev/null || wc -c < "${LATEST_REPORT}" 2>/dev/null || true)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

REPORT_TIME is compared with an exact string match against CURRENT_TIME (always zero-padded 'HH:MM') and later split with `cut -d:`. Values such as '2:00', '02:00:00', or ones with surrounding whitespace will never match, so the report silently never runs. Validate and normalize the value to HH:MM before entering the loop, and fail fast on invalid input.

```suggestion
REPORT_TIME=${REPORT_GENERATION_TIME:-02:00}
# Normalize/validate to HH:MM before use
REPORT_TIME=$(date -d "${REPORT_TIME}" +%H:%M 2>/dev/null || true)
if [[ ! "${REPORT_TIME}" =~ ^([01][0-9]|2[0-3]):[0-5][0-9]$ ]]; then
    echo "❌ Invalid REPORT_GENERATION_TIME: ${REPORT_TIME} (expected HH:MM)" >&2
    exit 1
fi
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

`date -d` is GNU-only and `date -v` is BSD-only; on busybox-based images both fail and this line prints an empty 'Next report time'. This only affects a log line, but since the service is meant to run in containers, compute the next-run time portably (e.g., from the already-computed epoch seconds) or pin the base image so one variant is guaranteed.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Any pre-existing file at DB_PATH (empty, truncated, or from an older schema) is treated as a valid database and skips initialization, so report generation can later fail against an uninitialized/outdated DB. Consider validating the schema (e.g., `sqlite3 "${DB_PATH}" ".tables"` and checking for the expected tables) and re-initializing/repairing otherwise. Also, only EVAL_DIR is created here — if EVAL_DB_PATH points into a directory that does not exist, `sqlite3` fails and `set -e` aborts startup.

## ops/rollback.sh (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Dead-code defect that would corrupt production if this block is ever re-enabled: a raw `.db` backup is piped into `sqlite3` as if it were SQL (`sqlite3 "$DB_PATH" < "$BACKUP_FILE"`), and even the `.gz` branch streams the decompressed binary database through the SQL engine instead of writing it back as a file. A binary SQLite file interpreted as statements will fail and can partially overwrite `DB_PATH`. A database restore must copy bytes, not execute them.

```suggestion
    if [[ "$BACKUP_FILE" == *.gz ]]; then
        gunzip -c "$BACKUP_FILE" > "$DB_PATH" || error_exit "Failed to restore database"
    else
        cp "$BACKUP_FILE" "$DB_PATH" || error_exit "Failed to restore database"
    fi
```

---

### [high] (security)

Dead-code SQL injection: `$BACKUP_FILE` and `$(basename "$BACKUP_FILE")` are interpolated unescaped into the SQL INSERT. A backup path/filename containing a single quote (e.g. `/tmp/chimera_x'||<payload>...db.gz`) would break out of the string literal and execute arbitrary SQL against the restored database. Escape single quotes (double them) before interpolation, or write the audit event through a parameterized mechanism instead of string-built SQL, before this block is ever re-enabled.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The retirement guard fails closed for direct execution, but if this script is ever sourced (e.g. `source ops/rollback.sh` from CI or another automation that still references the retired path), the bare `exit 1` terminates the caller's shell outright instead of returning an error to the caller. Make the guard mode-aware so it fails gracefully whether executed or sourced.

```suggestion
echo "ERROR: ops/rollback.sh is RETIRED. It targets the decommissioned SQLite/systemd stack." >&2
echo "Use the git-revert + Compose rebuild rollback described in AGENTS.md." >&2
if [[ "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" == "$0" ]]; then
    exit 1
else
    return 1
fi
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Nearly 300 lines of unreachable, decommissioned SQLite/systemd logic remain below the guard (the double `exit 1` at line 29 is the only thing keeping it inert). Preserving this inside an executable script creates a re-enablement hazard: removing one guard would re-activate a flow that targets a stack that no longer exists (restores a nonexistent `data/chimera.db`, calls `systemctl` on an unmanaged service), and it buries the actual live behavior. Move the historical implementation to an archived document (e.g. docs/archive/) and keep only the fail-fast guard in this file.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The plain pre-restore copy `CURRENT_BACKUP` is deleted immediately after the restored DB passes its integrity check, but the rollback is not yet complete: if the service fails to start or health checks fail (steps 7-8), the script exits with an error while production is left on the restored DB and the only automatic known-good copy has just been removed (recovery would require manual use of the step-3 gzipped safety backup). Keep `CURRENT_BACKUP` until the final health check passes (or add a trap that reverts on failure) and clean up only on success.

---

## ops/run-paper-trading-scenario.sh (7 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

The final summary is hardcoded and does not reflect the actual run: even if every signal was rejected, metrics are missing, or the anomaly count is zero/unreadable, the report still claims 'Operational/Active/Running/Monitoring'. This defeats the purpose of an evaluation script. Derive the summary from the collected data (success rate, health payload, anomaly count, metric availability) instead of printing unconditional success.

---

### [medium] (bug)

If the signal file is empty (or contains no valid signals / SIGNALS_TO_PROCESS=0), `processed` stays 0 and `successful * 100.0 / processed` raises ZeroDivisionError. Since the script runs under `set -e`, the Python process exits non-zero and the entire evaluation aborts before steps 4/5 execute. Guard the division when no signals were processed.

```suggestion
if processed > 0:
    print(f"  Success Rate: {successful * 100.0 / processed:.1f}%")
else:
    print("  Success Rate: N/A (no signals processed)")
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The JSONL file is parsed wholesale with a list comprehension outside the per-signal try/except. A single malformed line raises json.JSONDecodeError (and a missing file raises FileNotFoundError), which under `set -e` kills the whole run instead of being reported as a failed signal. Parse line-by-line, skip blank lines, and catch per-line parse errors so bad input degrades gracefully.

```suggestion
signals = []
with open(signal_file, 'r') as f:
    for line in f:
        line = line.strip()
        if not line:
            continue
        try:
            signals.append(json.loads(line))
        except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
            print(f"Skipping malformed signal line: {e}")
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Without `set -o pipefail`, the exit status of `curl | grep | head -5` is that of `head`, which is 0 even when curl fails or grep matches nothing — so the `|| echo "Some metrics unavailable"` fallback never fires and missing metrics look like empty output. The same masking pattern repeats in the RPC-latency query (`grep ... | head -3`) and the `sqlite3 | while` anomaly query below. Add `set -o pipefail` after `set -e` (or restructure the pipelines) so the intended fallbacks actually trigger.

```suggestion
set -e
set -o pipefail
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The health check only verifies the HTTP status via `curl -f`; a 200 response carrying an unhealthy/degraded JSON body still passes, and the final summary prints 'System Health: Operational' unconditionally. Validate the health payload (e.g., check a `healthy`/`status` boolean) at this point and propagate the result to the final report, otherwise a degraded operator produces a false-positive 'Operational' evaluation.

---

### [medium] (bug)

This checks an absolute path `/evaluation/day-1`, while the rest of the script uses repo-relative paths (`evaluation/signals/...`, `evaluation/evaluation.db`), so a real local `evaluation/day-1` directory is reported as 'not found'. Use a repo-relative path and drive it from the already-defined but unused `DAY_NUM` variable for consistency.

```suggestion
EVALUATION_DIR="evaluation/day-${DAY_NUM}"
if [ -d "$EVALUATION_DIR" ]; then
    echo "✅ Day ${DAY_NUM} data directory exists"
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

In this pipeline the last command is the `while` loop, which always exits 0 even when sqlite3 fails (missing DB, missing table, or query error with stderr suppressed), so the `|| echo "No recent anomalies"` fallback never fires and the section silently prints nothing. The earlier `ANOMALY_COUNT=$(sqlite3 ... || echo "0")` works because it has no trailing pipeline element. Add `set -o pipefail` or check the sqlite3 exit status explicitly.
