## operator/src/circuit_breaker.rs (6 findings, 1 critical, 2 high)

### [critical] (bug)

`evaluation_in_progress` is set to `true` at the top of `evaluate()`, but this Tripped→Cooldown branch returns without resetting it (the `?` on `enter_cooldown()`/`check_breach_conditions()`/`trip()`/`exit_cooldown()` can also skip the clear on the other paths). After any real trip, the next `evaluate()` call runs this branch and leaks the flag, so every subsequent call short-circuits at the "already in progress" guard. The breaker then sits in Cooldown forever — automatic cooldown exit, recovery and further loss detection all stop. This also fires at startup via `restore_from_db()`. Recommend an RAII drop-guard that always clears the flag, or explicitly clear it on every exit path.

---

### [high] (bug)

`Handle::block_on` panics when called from within an async execution context. `record_jupiter_failure` is invoked from async code (e.g. the retry/swap paths in `jupiter_error_handling.rs` and `transaction_builder.rs`), so on a tokio worker thread `try_current()` succeeds and `block_on` panics instead of tripping cleanly; it also blocks the worker while `trip()` awaits DB/notification work. Make `record_jupiter_failure` async and `await self.trip(reason)` directly (or `tokio::spawn` it) so it is cancellation-safe and never blocks a runtime thread.

---

### [high] (bug)

A failed read of the persisted breaker state is silently converted to `Ok(None)`, and `restore_from_db()` treats that as "Active or absent — no restore needed". If the DB read fails at startup, the operator can silently resume trading even though the breaker was Tripped/Cooldown before the restart — fail-open on a safety-critical path. Propagate the error (or at least log at error level and refuse to start) rather than swallowing it.

---

### [medium] (bug)

If the persisted `tripped_at` is NULL or fails RFC3339 parsing, `tripped_at` becomes `None`. The state is then restored to Tripped and `evaluate()` moves it to Cooldown with `tripped_at = None`; the cooldown-expiry check in `evaluate()` returns `false` when `tripped_at` is None, so the breaker is stuck in Cooldown indefinitely until a manual reset. Fall back to `Utc::now()` (or fail the restore) when the persisted timestamp is missing/unparseable so the breaker can still recover.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Any system trip restored from the DB is re-labeled as `TripReason::Manual`, so status/logs/notifications show "Manual: 24h loss $... exceeded threshold $...", misattributing a system trip to an admin action. Consider parsing the persisted reason back into its original variant, or adding a dedicated `Restored` variant.

---

### [low] (bug)

There is no guard that the breaker is already Tripped/Cooldown before tripping again, so concurrent Jupiter failures (or failures during an existing trip) each call `trip()`, producing duplicate config-change logs, duplicate notifications and `trips_total` increments, and resetting `tripped_at`/the cooldown clock each time. Consider short-circuiting when the current state is not Active, and resetting `jupiter_failure_count` on `reset()`/`exit_cooldown()`.

---

## operator/src/config.rs (7 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

`AppConfig` top-level fields `circuit_breakers`, `strategy`, and `jito` have no `#[serde(default)]` and are never covered by `set_default(...)` in this builder, so `load_config()` fails to deserialize whenever the config file omits those sections — contradicting the documented "Default values" priority. `load()` is worse: it calls no `set_default` at all, so `server`/`rpc`/`database`/`security`/`queue` are also mandatory there. Since these structs already define per-field serde default fns (and `CircuitBreakerConfig` implements `Default`), add `#[serde(default)]` to the required sections or `set_default(...)` entries so an env/YAML-only deployment actually falls back to the advertised defaults.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

`AppConfig::default()` diverges from the serde field defaults in many places, so runtime behavior depends on which construction path is used. Examples: `security.webhook_rate_limit` is 10000 here vs `default_webhook_rate_limit()` = 100 (and burst 15000 vs 150); `jito.helius_fallback` is false vs `default_helius_fallback()` = true, plus tip_floor/ceiling/tip_percent_max differ from their default fns; `queue.parallel_enabled` false vs true, num_workers/max_concurrent_rpc None vs Some(4)/Some(8); `strategy` quality thresholds 0.65/0.50 vs 0.55/0.55; `MonitoringConfig` also diverges (`enabled` false vs serde `default_true`, `webhook_processing_rate_limit` 100 vs `default_monitoring_webhook_rate_limit()` = 45); and `ProfitabilityGateConfig::default()` (derived) yields refresh_interval_seconds=0 / inconclusive_size_factor=0.0 instead of 300/0.5. Make the hand-written `Default` impls delegate to the same serde default fns so `AppConfig::default()` and a deserialized config are equivalent.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`JupiterConfig` derives `Default`, but `#[derive(Default)]` does not invoke the `#[serde(default = ...)]` fns: `api_url`/`price_api_url` become empty strings and `multi_dex_comparison`/`enable_rtse` become false. Because `AppConfig::default()` uses `JupiterConfig::default()`, anything built through that path gets an unusable Jupiter config (empty base URL), unlike a deserialized config. Implement `Default` manually using the same default fns (`default_jupiter_api_url`, etc.).

---

### [medium] (bug)

The doc comment claims `false` (fail-open dry-run) is the default for `helius_auth_enforce` and `rpc_verify_enforce`, but the serde default is `default_true` and `MonitoringConfig::default()` also sets `true`. Deployments that rely on the documented fail-open behavior will instead reject events with HTTP 401 / drop mismatched events. Align the docs with the actual fail-closed default (or flip the default fns if fail-open is really intended).

---

### [medium] (bug)

`TradeMode::default()` is `Paper`, and this branch returns any non-Live `config_mode` immediately, so the `rpc_url.contains("devnet")` auto-detection branch below is unreachable unless the config explicitly sets `trade_mode: live`. A fresh deploy that points RPC at a devnet endpoint silently runs `Paper` (rule 2 wins) instead of auto-detecting `Devnet`, and the intended "Auto-detected devnet RPC URL" log never fires as designed. Reorder so devnet detection runs before the Paper short-circuit (e.g. only early-return for a value that was explicitly set), or drop the dead branch and document that devnet must be configured explicitly.

---

### [medium] (security)

`SecurityConfig` derives `Debug` but contains `webhook_secret` unredacted, so any `{:?}`/tracing print of `AppConfig` leaks the HMAC secret — inconsistent with the explicit redaction implemented for `ApiKeyConfig` and `JupiterConfig`. The same leak applies to `MonitoringConfig` (`helius_api_key`, `helius_webhook_auth_header`) and `TelegramNotificationConfig` (`bot_token`). Add redacting `Debug` impls (like the existing `ApiKeyConfig`/`JupiterConfig` pattern) to these structs.

---

### [low] (bug)

The field doc says `0 = auto-detect`, but `validate()` rejects `server.worker_threads == 0`, so the documented auto-detect value can never be used — any config setting 0 fails validation. Either allow 0 in `validate()` (and handle it when building the runtime) or update the doc to state 0 is invalid.

## operator/src/db/experiment_schema.sql (6 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

experiment_trades has no run_id and no foreign key to experiment_manifest, so individual trades cannot be attributed to a specific experiment run. This makes it impossible to reconcile the denormalized manifest counters (total_trades, tracer_trades, toxic_wallets) against actual trade rows, and cross-run queries (e.g., per-wallet or per-verdict analysis) require guessing ownership. Add a NOT NULL run_id column referencing experiment_manifest(run_id) and an index on it.

```suggestion
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS experiment_trades (
    -- Primary identification
    trade_uuid TEXT PRIMARY KEY,

    -- Experiment reference
    run_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES experiment_manifest(run_id),
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Financial/monetary columns (paper_fill_price, paper_pnl, real_fill_price, real_pnl, execution_gap, jito_tip_sol, dex_fee_sol, control_random_pnl, sol_bench_pnl, and the budget columns below) are stored as REAL. Floating-point arithmetic is approximate and can silently corrupt PnL/fee/budget totals, especially when summing many small values or comparing against credit budgets. Consider storing integer base units (lamports / smallest token unit) or a fixed-decimal TEXT representation, and convert at the application layer.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Enumerated/flag columns accept arbitrary strings: signal_side (BUY/SELL), strategy (Shield/Spear), status (running/completed/aborted), verdict (GO/KILL/INCONCLUSIVE), toxic_reason ('roi_drop'/'local_top_squeeze'), and operation_type. A typo or future code path can persist invalid experiment states that downstream logic does not expect. Add CHECK constraints to these columns (and to is_tracer/toxic_flag, e.g., IN (0,1)).

```suggestion
    signal_side TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (signal_side IN ('BUY','SELL')),  -- BUY/SELL
    strategy TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (strategy IN ('Shield','Spear')),    -- Shield/Spear
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

SQLite only enforces foreign keys when every connection runs PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON; without it, this FK (and the one in experiment_credits) is a no-op and orphaned rows can be created. In addition, there is no ON DELETE behavior, so deleting an experiment_manifest row leaves toxic_wallets/experiment_credits orphaned. Recommend enabling foreign_keys on all connections and adding explicit ON DELETE CASCADE/SET NULL policy (and similarly backfill a FK from experiment_trades).

```suggestion
    -- Metadata
    created_at TEXT DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TEXT DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,

    FOREIGN KEY (run_id) REFERENCES experiment_manifest(run_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Timestamp columns (entry_time, exit_time, t0, start_time, end_time, verdict_time, detected_at, timestamp) are unconstrained TEXT. Range/ordering queries (e.g., idx_experiment_trades_entry_time) rely on lexicographic comparison, so mixing formats (ISO-8601 with 'T'/'Z' vs the 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' produced by CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) or timezones will silently break time windows. Standardize on ISO-8601 UTC consistently across the app, and consider a CHECK constraint (e.g., GLOB pattern) or INTEGER unixepoch storage.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

toxic_wallets.wallet_address has no UNIQUE constraint (the index on it is non-unique), so the same wallet can be inserted multiple times for the same run or with different toxic flags, producing ambiguous 'toxic wallet' counts in the manifest. If a wallet should be tracked once per run, add UNIQUE(run_id, wallet_address); if it must be re-promoted, add an explicit versioning/attempt column instead of duplicate rows.

```suggestion
    -- Wallet identification
    wallet_address TEXT NOT NULL,
```

## operator/src/db_abstraction/export.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (security)

CSV formula injection: `token_symbol` is chain/user-controlled data (a token mint symbol), and `csv_escape` only quotes fields containing `,`, `"`, or `\n`. A symbol starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` (e.g. `=HYPERLINK(...)` or `=cmd|'/C calc'!A0`) is written as a live cell, and spreadsheet apps (Excel/Sheets/LibreOffice) will evaluate it as a formula when the CSV is opened, enabling formula injection. Quote-wrapping alone is not a reliable defense here since `token_symbol` doesn't need quoting. Prefix such cells with `'` (or a tab) before further escaping.

```suggestion
fn csv_escape(s: &str) -> String {
    // Neutralize spreadsheet formula injection for cells starting with =, +, -, or @
    let s = if s.starts_with('=') || s.starts_with('+') || s.starts_with('-') || s.starts_with('@') {
        format!("'\u{feff}{s}")
    } else {
        s.to_string()
    };
    if s.contains(',') || s.contains('"') || s.contains('\n') || s.contains('\r') {
```

---

Incomplete line-break handling: the escape check covers `\n` but not `\r`. A value containing a lone carriage return (or `\r\n` is caught via `\n`, but a CR-only break is not) will be emitted as a raw newline inside a field, producing a malformed/row-splitting CSV that cannot be parsed correctly. Include `\r` in the quoting condition.

```suggestion

```

### [medium] (bug)

Only `token_symbol` is passed through `csv_escape`; the other string fields (`strategy`, `side`, `status`, `tx_signature`, and `created_at`) are written raw into the CSV. Since these are user/DB-derived strings, any embedded comma, quote, CR/LF, or leading `=`/`+`/`-`/`@` will either corrupt the row structure or enable formula injection when the file is opened in a spreadsheet. Apply `csv_escape` to every string/option-string field (and the `trade_uuid`, `wallet_address`, `token_address` values as well) rather than only the symbol.

```suggestion
            csv_escape(trade.token_symbol.as_deref().unwrap_or("")),
            csv_escape(&trade.strategy),
            csv_escape(&trade.side),
```

`trades_to_pdf` is a stub that unconditionally returns `Internal` and its doc comment claims it "Generate[s] PDF content from trades", which is misleading for callers. Either remove the dead code or clearly document that PDF export is unimplemented so callers can branch on availability instead of discovering the hard error at runtime.

## operator/src/db_abstraction/postgres.rs (9 findings, 0 critical, 4 high)

### [high] (bug)

This INSERT (and the `UPDATE positions SET ... updated_at` in `update_trade_status_and_position`) references columns that do not exist in the canonical `positions` schema used by every other query in this file. The correct columns are `entry_amount_sol`, `entry_price`, and `last_updated` (there is no `amount_sol`/`entry_price_sol`/`created_at`/`updated_at` on positions), so these methods will fail at runtime with "column does not exist". Worse, both methods are duplicated verbatim in the inherent `impl PostgresBackend` block at the bottom of the file, so the broken SQL exists twice and the inherent copies shadow the trait methods for direct method-call syntax. Align the column names with the schema and remove the duplicate copies.

---

### [high] (bug)

The advisory lock is keyed on `wallet_address:token_address`, but the duplicate-position check immediately below is token-wide (`WHERE token_address = $1 ...`). Two concurrent opens of the same token from *different* wallets hold different lock keys, both see count = 0 under READ COMMITTED, and both insert — creating duplicate ACTIVE positions, which is exactly what the lock is supposed to prevent. The lock key must match the uniqueness scope: either take the lock on `token_address` alone (if one position per token globally) or scope the duplicate check to `wallet_address + token_address`. Note also that the portfolio-wide heat sum is only serialized per wallet+token, so concurrent opens of different tokens can jointly exceed `max_heat_sol`.

```suggestion
        sqlx::query("SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext($1))")
            .bind(token_address)
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The active positions are read without `FOR UPDATE`, and the partial-close branch (`exit_fraction < 1`) reads the current `entry_amount_sol` / `realized_pnl_sol` and then writes back absolute computed values (`remaining_amount`, `new_realized_sol`, `new_realized_usd`). Two concurrent partial closes of the same position can both read the same snapshot and then overwrite each other — a classic lost update. The `state IN ('ACTIVE','EXITING')` guard does not help because the state stays ACTIVE in the partial branch. Add `FOR UPDATE` to the positions SELECT so concurrent closes serialize on the row lock.

```suggestion
                SELECT id, entry_price, entry_amount_sol, trade_uuid, entry_sol_price_usd
                FROM positions
                WHERE wallet_address = $1 AND token_address = $2 AND state IN ('ACTIVE', 'EXITING')
                FOR UPDATE
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`reverted_amount` is computed as `buy_signal_amount_sol - confirmed_exit_amount` with no non-negative guard. When confirmed sells equal or exceed the original buy (i.e. the position was fully closed), the code still sets `state = 'ACTIVE'`, clears `exit_price`/`closed_at` and writes a zero or negative `entry_amount_sol` — re-activating a position that no longer has exposure. Clamp `reverted_amount` to zero and only re-activate the position when `reverted_amount > 0`; otherwise leave it CLOSED.

```suggestion
                    let reverted_amount = (buy_signal_amount_sol - confirmed_exit_amount).max(Decimal::ZERO);
                    if reverted_amount <= Decimal::ZERO {
                        tracing::warn!(trade_uuid = %position_trade_uuid, "Revert would leave zero/negative exposure; keeping position CLOSED");
                        tx.commit().await?;
                        return Ok(());
                    }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The `let _ = ... .await;` discards the execution result, so a failing audit insert (connection loss, constraint violation, schema error) is completely invisible — lifecycle events silently disappear from the audit trail and the caller believes the event was recorded. Log the error at minimum (`if let Err(e) = ... { tracing::error!(...) }`) and consider returning `AppResult<()>` so failures propagate instead of being swallowed.

---

### [medium] (bug)

In PostgreSQL, `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` reports exactly 1 row affected whether the row was inserted or updated, so `rows_affected() != 1` is always `false` and this return value carries no information about insert-vs-update. If callers rely on it to distinguish a fresh insertion from an update, use `RETURNING (xmax = 0)` (the xmax trick) to detect insertion, or drop the misleading boolean.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The final bucket's FILTER is `lat >= $n AND lat < $(n+1)` — closed above — but its label is `{upper}ms+`, and any row with `lat >=` the top bound is counted nowhere. The histogram therefore undercounts and mislabels the highest-latency trades. Either make the top bucket open-ended (`lat >= $n` for `i == len-1`) or relabel it with the actual range it covers.

```suggestion
            let range = if i == bucket_bounds.len() - 1 {
                format!("{}+ms", lower_bound)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The read-modify-write of `jito_tip_sol`/`dex_fee_sol`/`slippage_cost_sol` is split across a SELECT and an UPDATE with no transaction and no row lock, so concurrent callers can lose each other's increments. Use a single atomic UPDATE where each column accumulates with COALESCE so the increment is applied against the latest committed value.

```suggestion
        let result = sqlx::query(
            r#"
            UPDATE trades
            SET jito_tip_sol = COALESCE(jito_tip_sol, 0) + $1,
                dex_fee_sol = COALESCE(dex_fee_sol, 0) + $2,
                slippage_cost_sol = COALESCE(slippage_cost_sol, 0) + $3,
                total_cost_sol = COALESCE(total_cost_sol, 0) + ($1 + $2 + $3)
            WHERE trade_uuid = $4
            "#,
        )
        .bind(jito_tip_sol)
        .bind(dex_fee_sol)
        .bind(slippage_cost_sol)
        .bind(trade_uuid)
        .execute(&self.pool)
        .await?;
```

---

### [low] (bug)

Within a single UPDATE statement, column references in SET expressions evaluate against the pre-update row, so `WHEN registration_attempts >= 2` is checked against the old count. As a result the status only flips to 'failed' on the call *after* the count reaches 2 (i.e. on the 3rd failure). If the intent is to mark failed once attempts reach 2, compare against `registration_attempts + 1`.

```suggestion
                webhook_status = CASE
                    WHEN registration_attempts + 1 >= 2 THEN 'failed'
                    ELSE webhook_status
                END
```

### [high] (bug)

`pnl_data_valid` is hardcoded to `true` here, which contradicts the field's own documentation above: "false for rows produced by the pre-fix accounting model (quarantined). Decision metrics must exclude these rows." The internal `Trade` struct (db_abstraction/mod.rs) doesn't carry `pnl_data_valid` at all, so this conversion silently marks every trade — including quarantined rows — as valid. `DatabaseConfig` derives `Debug` while holding `url: Option<String>`; `DATABASE_URL` conventionally embeds credentials (`postgres://user:password@host:port/db`). Any accidental `{:?}` log of a `DatabaseConfig` (e.g., in startup/error diagnostics) will dump the password in plain text. Implement a manual `Debug` that redacts the URL (or at least masks the password portion), and similarly avoid deriving `Clone`-based logging paths that print the URL.

Since there is currently only one backend, this is harmless functionally, but it defeats config validation. Prefer returning `Result`/emitting a warning on unknown values so configuration mistakes are surfaced.

### [low] (maintainability)

`rpc_polling_active` and `monitoring_enabled` are encoded as `i32` rather than `bool`, so invalid states (e.g., `2`, `-1`) are representable and every caller must guess the convention (`== 0`, `> 0`, `== 1` — see handlers/monitoring.rs, monitoring/polling_task.rs, monitoring/webhook_lifecycle.rs). The sqlx layer already reads `monitoring_enabled` as `bool` elsewhere (postgres.rs:4450) and the upsert API takes `bool`, so these fields should be `bool` too (cast/interpret at the DB boundary if the column is an integer type).

## operator/src/engine/channel.rs (5 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

TOCTOU race: the `total_len` capacity check and the subsequent `fetch_add` are not atomic across sub-queues. Two threads pushing into different sub-queues (e.g. `medium` and `low`) each hold only their own lock, so both can observe `total_len < capacity` and both push, exceeding `capacity`. The comment at lines 114-116 claims the lock-held increment prevents a TOCTOU race, but it only serializes pushes to the single `spear_high_wqs` queue. Consider guarding check-and-increment with a shared capacity lock (or a CAS loop on `total_len` that also re-checks before the final increment) so the capacity contract holds under concurrency.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The high-WQS SPEAR branch bypasses the global capacity and load-shedding checks entirely. Because `spear_high_wqs_capacity` has a hard minimum of 10 (`(capacity / 10).clamp(10, 50)`), a queue configured with capacity 2 or 10 can grow well past `capacity` — e.g. capacity 10 allows 10 shields + 10 high-WQS SPEARs = 20 queued items (200% of capacity), and `should_shed_load()` is only consulted after the dedicated queue is already full, so high-WQS signals keep being accepted while the overall queue is over capacity and shedding is active. Unlike `Strategy::Exit`, there is no documented "always allow" intent for this path. Consider also checking `total_len < capacity` (and/or load shedding) in the high-WQS branch, and sizing the dedicated queue relative to the configured capacity for small queues (e.g. `(capacity / 10).min(50)` with a ceiling at `capacity`).

---

### [medium] (bug)

Unvalidated load-shed threshold: if `load_shed_threshold_percent` is configured as 0, `threshold` becomes 0 and `current >= 0` is always true, so every low-WQS SPEAR push is rejected even when the queue is completely empty. `PriorityQueue::new` never validates the percentage (values > 100 silently disable shedding). Clamp or reject the input in `new`, e.g. `let load_shed_threshold = load_shed_threshold_percent.clamp(1, 100);`, so the documented "percentage of capacity" semantics hold.

---

### [low] (bug)

Check-then-wait ordering around `Notify` is fragile. Because `notify_one()` only stores a single permit, a burst of pushes while no consumer is registered collapses into one wakeup, and a consumer woken by a stale permit can re-enter `notified().await` and sleep even though a push is racing with its state check. The tokio-recommended pattern is to create the `notified()` future *before* checking the queue so the waiter is registered up front. Also note this function never returns `None` (it loops forever) and has no shutdown/termination mechanism, so waiting workers can never be cancelled.

```suggestion
    pub async fn pop_wait(&self) -> Option<Signal> {
        loop {
            let notified = self.push_notify.notified();
            if let Some(signal) = self.pop().await {
                return Some(signal);
            }
            notified.await;
        }
    }
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`push` (and `pop`) are declared `async` but contain no `.await` points and use only synchronous `parking_lot` mutexes. This forces callers to `.await` a future that can never yield, and masks the fact that a contended mutex briefly blocks the executor thread inside an async context. Making them plain synchronous methods would be clearer; if they must remain async, prefer `tokio::sync::Mutex` or keep the critical sections guaranteed-tiny and document that.

## operator/src/engine/decision_recorder.rs (4 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

Completeness ratio can be read outside [0,1] or spuriously low. `attempted` is incremented synchronously in `record`, while `persisted` is incremented later inside the spawned task — both with `Ordering::Relaxed` and both read with `Relaxed` here. Because the two counters are independent relaxed atomics, a concurrent `completeness()` call can observe `persisted` ahead of `attempted` (ratio > 1.0) or a fresh `attempted` with a stale `persisted` (transient 0.0), undermining the C4 ≥99% go/no-go gate. Use Release stores (in `record`) with Acquire loads here so that seeing a persisted increment also makes the matching attempted increment visible, and clamp the result to [0,1] as defense in depth.

```suggestion
    pub fn completeness(&self) -> f64 {
        let a = self.attempted.load(Ordering::Acquire);
        if a == 0 {
            return 1.0;
        }
        let p = self.persisted.load(Ordering::Acquire);
        // Clamp so transient read skew can never yield a ratio outside [0,1].
        (p as f64 / a as f64).clamp(0.0, 1.0)
    }
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

Unbounded detached task spawning on the hot trading path. Every `record`, `update_quote`, `update_fill_model`, and `link_trade` call spawns a new tokio task with no in-flight limit, no semaphore, and no graceful shutdown drain (the `JoinHandle` is dropped immediately). Under high decision rates this can pile up tasks (memory) and saturate the DB pool since each task must acquire a connection to execute its statement; on runtime shutdown all pending writes are silently dropped, permanently diverging from `attempted`. Consider a bounded channel feeding a small number of dedicated worker tasks (or a `Semaphore` to cap concurrent writes) and a drain/shutdown step so in-flight rows are flushed before exit.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Best-effort updates with no retry, backoff, or accounting: a failure here only emits a warn and the row stays permanently missing `quote_json` (same pattern in `update_fill_model` and `link_trade` for `trade_uuid`). Because these updates never touch `persisted`, `completeness()` can report 1.0 while rows are actually incomplete, and the C4 completeness gate gives no visibility into the loss. Add bounded retries with backoff (or a reconciliation/reaper query) and/or track these update failures in the completeness metric.

---

### [low] (bug)

Silent integer truncation in the persistence path: `consensus_wallet_count` is `Option<usize>` (64-bit on typical platforms) and casting with `as i32` wraps to a negative value for counts above `i32::MAX`. The same applies two lines below to `source_slot: Option<u64>` cast with `as i64`. Use checked conversion (e.g. `i32::try_from(c).ok()` / `i64::try_from(s).ok()`) so out-of-range values become NULL rather than corrupting the row.

```suggestion
            consensus_wallet_count: decision.consensus_wallet_count.and_then(|c| i32::try_from(c).ok()),
            source_slot: req.source_slot.and_then(|s| i64::try_from(s).ok()),
```

## operator/src/engine/degradation.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Fail-deadly `df` parsing: `cols[3].parse().unwrap_or(0.0)` silently converts malformed output into "0% free", and `df`'s exit status is never checked (a failed/error df run can produce unexpected stdout). Since `prune_logs_if_needed` interprets free space below thresholds as a signal to delete aggressively, a transient parse/df failure can trigger deletion of logs instead of failing safely. Parse with `?` (propagating `AppError`) and verify `output.status.success()` before trusting the columns.

---

### [high] (bug)

`is_log_file` matches any name ending in `.log` or `.gz`, including the currently open `operator.log` and unrelated archives. Consequently Phase 1 can delete the live log if its mtime is older than `max_age_days` (e.g. during idle periods), and Phase 2 deletes the oldest remaining candidates regardless of age or liveness — writes after removal go to an unlinked inode and are permanently lost. Restrict matches to the operator log naming (`operator.log`, `operator.log.*` and their `.gz` forms) and explicitly exclude the active log file from both pruning phases.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Non-atomic read-modify-write on `RPC_BACKOFF_MULTIPLIER`: `load` then `store` is a check-then-act race. Two concurrent rate-limit hits can both read the same multiplier and both store the same doubled value, losing an increment (backoff stays flat instead of growing exponentially); a concurrent `reset_rpc_backoff()` store can also be overwritten by a stale `store`. Use `fetch_update` (or a `compare_exchange` loop) so the read and increment are one atomic operation.

```suggestion
    let multiplier = RPC_BACKOFF_MULTIPLIER
        .fetch_update(Ordering::Relaxed, Ordering::Relaxed, |m| Some((m * 2).min(64)))
        .unwrap_or(1);
    let delay_ms = INITIAL_BACKOFF_MS * multiplier;
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Same fail-deadly defaults as the async `check_disk_space`: a parse error here becomes 0% free and can drive `prune_logs_if_needed` into critical/aggressive deletion. This also duplicates the entire df-parsing logic from `check_disk_space`; extract one synchronous helper (that returns `AppResult`) and wrap it in `spawn_blocking` for the async path so the two implementations can't drift.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Two issues in Phase 2: (1) `check_disk_space_sync(...).unwrap_or(0.0)` turns any failed re-check into "still critically full", so the loop keeps deleting every remaining candidate (including the active log) instead of aborting on error — fail-deadly again; (2) it spawns a `df` subprocess after every single deletion, i.e. O(n) process spawns for n log files. Propagate the error and stop pruning on a failed check, and re-check free space less frequently (e.g. every N deletions).

---

### [low] (documentation)

Doc/return mismatch: the doc says "return current usage percentage" but the function returns `usage_percent / 100.0`, i.e. a 0–1 fraction. Comparing against `MEMORY_PRESSURE_THRESHOLD` (0.90) happens to work, but any caller treating the result as a percentage will misread the memory load. Align the doc with the actual return unit (or return a percentage consistently).

## operator/src/engine/dex_comparator.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

The v2 path never applies the DEX restriction, yet still labels the quote with the requested DEX: `dexes=` is only appended when `!use_v2`, but `selected_dex` is set unconditionally from `dexes` (`dexes.unwrap_or("Jupiter")`). Since the default constructor uses `https://api.jup.ag/swap/v2`, every 'restricted' query is just another unrestricted aggregate quote mislabelled as a specific DEX — the per-DEX comparison is non-functional and `multi_dex` fan-out sends N identical aggregate requests (wasted API quota), while `selected_dex`/logging report false attribution. Note the repo's own v2 usage (`transaction_builder.rs::get_jupiter_v2_order`) also requires a `taker` param and has no DEX filter, confirming v2 `/order` cannot express per-DEX restriction this way. Fix: on the v2 path, either implement a real restriction (e.g. `excludeDexes`-based if available), or skip the fan-out entirely and always label the result as aggregate (`"Jupiter"`), and add the required `taker` param.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The cache key omits `multi_dex` and `dex_labels`, which are both part of the route-selection policy. `set_multi_dex(false)` followed by `set_multi_dex(true)` (or reconfiguring the candidate labels) returns the previously cached aggregate-only selection for the same key within the 5s TTL, so the returned route does not reflect the current routing options. Include `multi_dex`/`dex_labels` in the key or invalidate/version the cache when they change.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The response body is parsed as JSON before the HTTP status is checked. On a 4xx/5xx response with a non-JSON body (plain-text/HTML error page or empty body), `response.json()` fails first and the caller gets a misleading "Failed to parse Jupiter response" error — the real status and Jupiter error message are discarded. Worse, the intended silent-skip of unsupported DEX labels (the 400/404 check below) is unreachable for non-JSON error bodies. Check `status.is_success()` before parsing, then read the body as JSON-or-text for the error path.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`feeAmount` entries are parsed strictly as `u64` strings (`parse::<u64>().ok()`), so entries that are decimal strings (e.g. "123.45") or JSON numbers are silently dropped, and an absent/unparseable `routePlan` yields `unwrap_or(0)`. `fee_sol` is therefore systematically understated with no diagnostic. Note `transaction_builder.rs` parses the same field via `Decimal::from_str`. Parse as `Decimal` (matching the repo's other v2 handling) and log a warning when the field is present but unparseable.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Price-impact parse failures silently become `Decimal::ZERO`: a `priceImpactPct` string that fails `Decimal::from_str` or a `priceImpact` value that isn't a float yields `.unwrap_or(Decimal::ZERO)`, understating `slippage_sol` without any warning. If the field is present but unparseable, log a warning (or return an error) instead of silently reporting zero cost.

---

### [low] (test)

This unit test performs live network calls (two `select_route` invocations against the real Jupiter API) but is not marked `#[ignore]`, unlike the repo's actual Jupiter integration tests which are all `#[ignore]`d. In CI/unit runs it will make real HTTP requests (and can hang up to the 2s timeout per request) and is environment-dependent. Mark it `#[ignore]` or mock the HTTP layer.

## operator/src/engine/execution_lock.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Check-then-insert race: `get_mut` returns None (shard lock released), then between that check and `self.locks.insert(...)` another worker can insert the same trade_uuid. This `insert` then silently overwrites the other worker's entry, both workers receive guards, and mutual exclusion is broken. Use DashMap's atomic `entry()` API so the occupancy check and insertion happen under a single shard lock.

```suggestion
            worker_id: worker_id.to_string(),
            acquired_at: now,
            expires_at,

        let trade_uuid_owned = trade_uuid.to_string();

        match self.locks.entry(trade_uuid_owned.clone()) {
            dashmap::mapref::entry::Entry::Occupied(_) => {
                // Another worker acquired in the meantime; treat as held.
                return None;
            }
            dashmap::mapref::entry::Entry::Vacant(v) => {
                v.insert(entry);
            }
        }
```

### [medium] (bug)

Fixed TTL with no renewal/heartbeat: a worker that legitimately runs longer than `lock_timeout_seconds` (default 120s) has its lock expired and reclaimed while it is still processing, allowing a second worker to acquire the same trade_uuid and duplicate execution. Add a heartbeat/renewal mechanism that extends `expires_at` while the guard is actively processing, or explicitly document/enforce a maximum processing duration.

### [low] (maintainability)

These `unsafe impl`s are redundant and lack a full safety rationale. `LockGuard` only contains `Arc<dyn LockImpl>`, and since `trait LockImpl: Send + Sync`, the trait object is already `Send + Sync`, making the `Arc` Send + Sync automatically. Remove the unsafe impls (or document the precise invariant being upheld if kept).

### [low] (bug)

Metrics noise/incorrectness: on the expired-reclaim path the actual previous holder's held duration (`now - existing.acquired_at`) is available, but `Duration::from_secs(0)` is recorded instead. Combined with the identical call on the fresh-insert path, `record_lock_held_duration(0)` on every acquire pollutes the held-duration metric. Record `existing.acquired_at.elapsed()` when reclaiming and only record held duration on release.

### [high] (bug)

`rand::random::<f64>()` was removed in rand 0.9 (the project depends on `rand = { version = "0.9", features = ["small_rng"] }`), so this line fails to compile. The rest of the file uses the 0.9 API (`rand::rng().random_range(...)` in `calculate_retry_backoff`). Use `rand::rng().random_range(0.75..1.25)` to match the 0.9 API used elsewhere.

### [high] (bug)

`ExecutionOutcome::live` hardcodes `executed_output_sol: None`, yet the struct's own doc contract (A1) states SELL attribution must use the Jupiter quote's real `outAmount` gross SOL proceeds, never the copied wallet's signal amount. As a result, every live SELL's `cost_basis_sol` in `execute()` falls back to `signal.payload.amount_sol`, so exit-side cost attribution (dex fee/slippage) is computed against the wrong notional. `execute_jito`/`execute_standard`/`execute_via_helius_staked` have the quote's out amount available in `built_tx` but never plumb it into the outcome. Plumb the executed notional through `ExecutionOutcome::live` so live SELL attribution matches the documented A1 contract.

### [medium] (bug)

This rate-limit retry branch only matches `Err(ExecutorError::Rpc(..))`, but both `submit_transaction` (legacy) and `submit_versioned_transaction` wrap all `sendTransaction` failures — including HTTP 429 / rate-limit responses — in `ExecutorError::TransactionFailed`. Therefore the dedicated degradation backoff (up to 10 attempts via `handle_rpc_rate_limit`) never fires for the primary TPU submission path; a rate-limited send returns `TransactionFailed` and goes straight to the failure handler. Either classify rate-limit hints from `TransactionFailed` messages here too, or preserve the `Rpc` variant when the underlying RPC request is rate-limited.

The retry loop logs "retrying with increased tip" but never actually increases the tip: `calculate_adaptive_jito_tip` (which applies the 20%/attempt multiplier) is defined but never called, and the retry simply re-invokes `execute_jito`, which recomputes the same tip via `calculate_jito_tip`. So insufficient-tip / bundle-timeout failures are retried with the identical tip and can burn all retries. Either apply `calculate_adaptive_jito_tip(signal, attempts).await` in the retry path (and pass it into `execute_jito`), or correct the log message.

In fallback mode the primary RPC is typically the unhealthy endpoint that triggered the failover, so `get_signature_status` will error/stall on every poll and a landed transaction will be reported `false` (unconfirmed), leaving the position stuck in EXECUTING until the recovery manager reconciles. ## operator/src/engine/jito_searcher.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

This parser returns the last transaction signature even when the bundle entry reports an error (`err` is non-null, e.g. `{"Err": ...}`) or a non-finalized status. `getBundleStatuses` returns the `transactions` array for failed bundles too, so a swap that never executed (or failed) will be reported as a landed swap signature and `resolve_bundle_status` will stop polling on it. Callers then treat the trade as confirmed and skip recovery reconciliation. Filter out entries whose `err` is non-null/`Ok` is absent, and ideally verify `confirmation_status` before returning a signature.

```suggestion
    value
        .get("result")
        .and_then(|r| r.get("value"))
        .and_then(|v| v.as_array())
        .and_then(|a| a.first())
        .filter(|entry| {
            entry
                .get("err")
                .map_or(true, |e| e.is_null() || e.get("Ok").is_some())
        })
        .and_then(|entry| entry.get("transactions"))
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The comment claims "~2.5s total over 6 attempts", but that only counts the sleep backoff. Each `send()` can block up to the 10s reqwest client timeout, so six attempts can stall for ~60s on a slow/hung endpoint — far too long for the time-sensitive confirmation path this is used in, and there is no overall deadline. Wrap the whole loop in `tokio::time::timeout` (e.g. a few seconds) so worst-case wall time is bounded, and drop out early once the bundle reaches a terminal errored state.

### [medium] (bug)

Contract mismatch: `send_bundle` returns the tagged ref `bundle:<uuid>`, but `resolve_bundle_signature` passes its argument straight to `getBundleStatuses` without stripping the `bundle:` prefix. Anyone passing the value returned by `submit_bundle`/`submit_single_bundle` directly into this method gets a permanent resolution failure. The current caller in executor.rs strips the prefix manually, which works only by convention — the public API should normalize the input itself so the two methods are composable.

```suggestion

        let bundle_id = bundle_id.strip_prefix("bundle:").unwrap_or(bundle_id);
        let url = format!("{}/api/v1/bundles", self.endpoint);
        resolve_bundle_status(&self.http_client, &url, bundle_id).await
    }
```

### [low] (maintainability)

The tip set is frozen at compile time and the only guard is a parse-time `expect` in `next_tip_account`. Jito does rotate these accounts; if one is retired or replaced, the two-tx bundle is rejected (tip not in allowlist) or the tip silently goes to an address Jito no longer controls, with no runtime signal. Consider a defense-in-depth approach that doesn't blindly trust the endpoint but still detects drift: e.g. periodically fetch `getTipAccounts`, require every returned account to be in this verified allowlist, and emit a hard error/alert if any allowlisted account is missing from the live list (instead of rejecting out of hand).

## operator/src/engine/kelly_sizer.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Unit mismatch in the Kelly formula. `avg_win`/`avg_loss` are per-trade return percentages (`pnl / amount_sol`), not full-stake odds, so the classic edge/odds form k = (p·b − q)/b with b = avg_win/avg_loss is only the growth-optimal *allocation fraction* when a losing trade costs the entire stake (avg_loss = 1). With, say, avg_loss = 5%, the correct growth-optimal allocation is f* = (p·avg_win − q·avg_loss)/(avg_win·avg_loss), i.e. a factor 1/avg_loss (~20×) larger than what this code computes. As written, `full_kelly` (and therefore `conservative_kelly`, `recommended_size_percent`, and `calculate_position_size`) is actually the fraction of capital *at risk per trade*, not the fraction allocated — so the sizer is systematically ~avg_loss× too small and is not Kelly-optimal. The [T-H1] comments claiming "avg_loss is already embedded in the Kelly formula" are only partially right: avg_loss appears in the numerator (q·avg_loss) but is missing from the denominator (should be avg_win·avg_loss). Fix the denominator (and the misleading comments), or — if 'full Kelly' is deliberately intended as the risk fraction — divide by avg_loss when converting to a position size.

```suggestion
            let p = win_rate;
            let q = loss_rate;
            // Growth-optimal allocation: f* = (p*avg_win - q*avg_loss) / (avg_win*avg_loss)
            let k = (p * avg_win - q * avg_loss) / (avg_win * avg_loss);
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Break-even trades inflate `valid_trades_count` without contributing to `wins` or `losses`, so win_rate + loss_rate < 1 in the Kelly computation. The formula k = p − q/b then silently discards that probability mass (making k too small), while `expected_return_pct` recomputes loss_rate as `1 - win_rate`, reclassifying every break-even trade as a full average loss — biasing the expected return downward and contradicting the empirical `loss_rate = loss_count / total_trades` used in `calculate_kelly`. Handle break-even trades consistently: either exclude them from `valid_trades_count` (preserving p + q = 1) or count them explicitly in both functions.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`trades.first()` / `trades.last()` are assumed to be the newest and oldest trades, but `Database::get_trades_filtered` does not document any row-ordering guarantee in its trait contract — only the current Postgres implementation happens to append `ORDER BY created_at DESC`. If a mock or alternate backend returns trades unsorted, `(newest_time - oldest_time)` becomes negative/meaningless and, after `.max(1.0)`, yields a bogus timespan and trades-per-day velocity multiplier. Sort the trades by `created_at` explicitly (or take the min/max over the vector) before computing the span. Note the span is also computed over *all* returned trades including `pnl_data_valid = false` rows, while `valid_trades_count` only counts valid ones — mixing sample definitions.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`trade_count` reports `trades.len()`, which includes rows that were explicitly skipped from the Kelly computation (pnl_data_valid = false, missing `net_pnl_sol`, zero `amount_sol`), contradicting the struct doc "Number of closed trades used to compute this result". Downstream consumers can therefore overestimate the effective sample size and confidence in the sizing. Report `valid_trades_count` instead.


This test body contains only a doc comment and no assertions, so the Kelly formula has zero unit coverage — despite the subtle unit semantics of avg_win/avg_loss discussed above. Add an assertion-based test (e.g. p = 0.6, avg_win = 0.1, avg_loss = 0.05) that verifies `full_kelly` / `conservative_kelly` to lock in the intended behavior.

## operator/src/engine/market_regime.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

update_price_history unconditionally pushes the cached SOL entry without checking it is newer than the current back of the deque or distinct from the last push. PriceCache::get_price returns the same PriceEntry until the cache refreshes (TTL/15s refresh cadence), so calling this more often than the refresh rate appends many duplicate (fetched_at, price_usd) entries with identical timestamps. Because the pruning cutoff is derived from that same fetched_at (price_entry.fetched_at - 24h), the duplicates are never evicted (front.0 < cutoff is never true for them), so the deque grows unboundedly and detect_regime's first/last price comparison can be dominated by arbitrarily stale entries, misclassifying the regime. Suggest skipping the push when the new entry's fetched_at is not newer than the back, and pruning relative to the newest timestamp actually present.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

detect_token_regime never bounds the window itself; the 24-hour calculation claim depends entirely on PriceCache::set_price pruning price_history to 24h at insert time. If cache retention changes, history is backfilled with older timestamps, or a token's updates are sparse/out of order, the first/last comparison here can silently span more than 24h (or be skewed by stale points) while the comment promises a 24h calculation. Enforce the window locally (drop entries older than back().0 - 24h) before computing the trend.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

This getter exposes the detector's internal Arc<RwLock<VecDeque<...>>>; any caller can take a write lock and mutate price_history, contradicting the documented read-only access and risking corrupted regime signals that drive position sizing. Return an immutable snapshot (e.g., a cloned VecDeque) or a read guard instead of handing out the raw writable lock.

---

### [medium] (bug)

update_volume_history has no deduplication or cadence guard: calling it more than once per day pushes multiple snapshots for the same day. get_volume_trend_multiplier averages per entry rather than per day, so duplicate snapshots distort the week-over-week multiplier (and snapshots near the 7-day boundary can land in different buckets, changing whether they count as last week or previous week). Skip the push when the latest entry is already within the same day, or key the history by date.

---

### [low] (performance)

Unnecessary allocation: the full history is copied into a Vec only to read the first/last elements, when history.front()/history.back() are already available (they are used just above for the timestamps). The 24h SOL history can hold tens of thousands of points, and this runs on every token/position evaluation, so use the deque's front/back directly. Same pattern exists in detect_token_regime.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Silently defaulting to Decimal::ZERO if the literal fails to parse would flip the classification logic (any positive change would look greater than 5% and be labeled Bull) while hiding the error. These are compile-time constants, so use dec!(5.0)/dec!(-5.0) (or expect with a clear invariant) instead. The same pattern is duplicated in detect_token_regime.

## operator/src/engine/mev_protection.rs (3 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

This helper applies a fixed 50-200ms delay with no awareness of signal urgency, but the module's whole purpose is to prioritize EXIT / consensus signals (they get the highest Jito tips specifically to land quickly and avoid MEV). If this delay is applied before submitting any trade, high-priority EXIT exits are delayed just as much as low-priority single BUYs, which can push bundle submission past the current slot and undermine the priority that `calculate_tip` establishes. Consider making the delay urgency-aware (e.g. skip or shrink it for `Strategy::Exit` / consensus signals) or accept an urgency parameter so callers can choose the trade-off between latency and predictability.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The tip values are returned directly from user-controlled configuration (deserialized from YAML and updateable at runtime via `UpdateMevProtectionConfig`) without any validation or clamping. A zero or negative `exit_tip_sol`/`consensus_tip_sol`/`standard_tip_sol` would silently disable effective MEV protection (or produce an invalid bundle tip), and since `calculate_tip` returns `Decimal` with no error path, misconfiguration is undetectable at the call site. Validate (and clamp to a sane minimum) at construction/config-load time, or reject non-positive tips when the config is updated.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`Decimal::from_str("1.5")` cannot fail for this hard-coded literal, so the `unwrap_or` fallback is dead code and is misleading (it looks like runtime validation of a parsed value). Worse, `unwrap_or` evaluates its argument eagerly, so `Decimal::from(3) / Decimal::from(2)` is recomputed on every consensus call even though the `Ok` path is always taken. Prefer a plain constant: `Decimal::new(15, 1)` (or `const CONSENSUS_TIP_MULTIPLIER: Decimal = Decimal::new(15, 1);`) which is `const`, cheaper, and self-documenting.

```suggestion
            // Use higher tip for consensus (1.5x the standard consensus tip)
            const CONSENSUS_TIP_MULTIPLIER: Decimal = Decimal::new(15, 1);
            return self.config.consensus_tip_sol * CONSENSUS_TIP_MULTIPLIER;
```

## operator/src/engine/momentum_exit.rs (7 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

RSI readiness gate mismatch: `calculate_rsi` only rejects fewer than 12 samples here, but `compute_rsi_from_prices` requires `prices.len() >= 16` (a 14-period Wilder RSI needs 15 price changes = 16 prices). Between 12 and 15 samples the check below passes yet the subsequent call always returns None, so RSI is effectively unavailable until ~7.5–8 minutes at 30s sampling — not the ~6 minutes stated in this comment and the module header. Because the price-drop base threshold widens from 5% to 8% at `elapsed_minutes >= 6`, the 6–8 minute window loses both the tighter base threshold and the intended RSI backup. Align the gate/comment with the actual requirement (16 samples) or move the base-threshold widening to match real RSI availability.

```suggestion
        if prices.len() < 16 {
            // A 14-period Wilder RSI needs 15 changes (=16 prices) to produce both a
            // previous and current RSI value; at 30s sampling this is ~8 minutes.
            return None;
        }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`current_price` from the cache is never sanity-checked, even though `entry_price` has an explicit zero guard right above. If the cache returns 0 (or a negative/corrupt value), `price_drop_percent` computes to 100%+ and forces an exit on corrupt data — the opposite of the intent behind the entry_price guard. Mirror the entry_price guard: log a warning and skip (or handle explicitly) when `current_price <= Decimal::ZERO` instead of converting it into an exit signal.

```suggestion
        // Guard: corrupt price data — skip momentum check rather than force exit
        if current_price <= Decimal::ZERO {
            tracing::warn!(
                trade_uuid = %trade_uuid,
                token_address = token_address,
                current_price = ?current_price,
                "CORRUPT_PRICE: current_price is zero/negative — skipping momentum check"
            );
            return MomentumExitAction::None;
        }
        let price_drop_percent = if !entry_price.is_zero() {
            let diff = entry_price - current_price;
            let ratio = diff / entry_price;
            ratio * Decimal::from(100)
        } else {
            Decimal::ZERO
        };
```

### [medium] (bug)

`entry_time.elapsed()` returns `Err` when `entry_time` is in the future (clock skew), and `unwrap_or_default()` silently maps that to `Duration::ZERO`. A zero elapsed time makes `in_wick_window == true` and `volume_check_ready == false`, so the price-drop, volume, and RSI checks are all silently suppressed until the clock catches up — momentum protection is disabled without any diagnostic. Surface the error explicitly (log it and clamp to zero, or otherwise handle it) so clock skew can't silently disable exits.

```suggestion
        let elapsed = match entry_time.elapsed() {
            Ok(d) => d,
            Err(e) => {
                tracing::error!(
                    trade_uuid = %trade_uuid,
                    token_address = token_address,
                    error = ?e,
                    "CLOCK_SKEW: entry_time is in the future — momentum checks suppressed"
                );
                Duration::ZERO
            }
        };
```

The documented threshold and time boundary don't match the code and can mislead operators about when a momentum exit triggers. Update the header to reflect the actual 5%-then-8% logic and the 6-minute boundary.

## operator/src/engine/portfolio_heat.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Registry fast path and DB fallback compute different exposure sets: registry.calculate_portfolio_heat_fast() counts only ACTIVE positions plus PENDING/QUEUED/EXECUTING BUY trades, while the fallback below additionally counts EXITING positions within the 1800s cutoff and RETRY BUY trades. Because of this, calculate_heat(), can_open_position(), and is_critically_overexposed() (which drives force-liquidation) can return materially different results depending on whether the registry is populated — e.g., EXITING positions and RETRY trades silently drop out of the fast path. Align both paths on the same exposure rules (EXITING cutoff, RETRY inclusion, staleness policy) or pick one canonical source and document the divergence.

---

### [high] (bug)

check-then-act race: can_open_position()/can_open_strategy_position() read current exposure and decide without any reservation or lock, so concurrent callers can both observe headroom and pass, collectively exceeding the heat cap before any position is persisted. Introduce an atomic reservation — e.g., a mutex held across the check and position insertion, or a pending-reservation counter that is decremented when the position fails to open — so capacity allocation is serialized.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Inconsistent stale-trade handling between the two gates: get_strategy_heat() excludes BUY trades older than 5 minutes, while calculate_heat() (fallback) counts every PENDING/QUEUED/EXECUTING/RETRY BUY trade regardless of age. The general heat gate therefore keeps blocking on stale queue entries that the strategy-allocation gate ignores, so the two checks disagree and stale entries can lock up new trades indefinitely. Apply the same staleness cutoff to the total heat calculation (or remove it from get_strategy_heat) so both gates use identical rules.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

This warn! fires on every calculate_heat() call whenever the registry is absent — e.g., between construction and with_registry(), or in configurations that never set a registry. Since calculate_heat() is invoked per position attempt and by the background liquidation task, this can spam warn-level logs. Consider logging the fallback once at startup, or demoting this to trace/debug with a one-time warning.

---

### [low] (bug)

position_size_sol is never validated: a zero or negative value passes the general gate and new_heat_percent <= max_heat_percent check, and a negative value would actually reduce reported exposure. Unless all callers are guaranteed to pass positive sizes, reject position_size_sol <= 0 explicitly (return Err or Ok(false)) to keep the capacity accounting sound.

---

### [low] (test)

Empty test stub: the nontrivial heat logic (EXITING 1800s cutoff, stale-trade rules, RETRY inclusion, boundary at exactly max heat, strategy allocation) has no coverage. Add unit tests with a mock Database and a stub StateRegistry so the two code paths' parity can be verified.

## operator/src/engine/reconciliation.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

The exit check unconditionally overwrites any entry-level outcome: for an EXITING position, every branch of this match reassigns `outcome`, discarding an earlier `MISSING_TX`/`TX_CHECK_ERROR` produced by the entry check. Consequences: (1) an exit `NotFound` downgrades a genuine entry discrepancy to `Pending`, so it is never logged or counted; (2) an exit `Found` auto-resolves/closes the position even though its entry transaction was never confirmed on-chain — the position gets closed based on an unverified entry. Only set the exit outcome when the entry check left `outcome == Outcome::Ok` (or merge/prioritize severities) so entry findings are preserved.

---

### [high] (bug)

ACTIVE positions are appended before EXITING and the combined list is then truncated to MAX_POSITIONS_PER_RUN with no offset/progress tracking. `get_positions` orders by `last_updated DESC` per state, and this pass never touches `last_updated` for checked-but-still-ACTIVE positions, so whenever there are ≥500 ACTIVE positions every run re-inspects the same leading ACTIVE set and EXITING positions (the only ones eligible for exit auto-resolution) are never reached. Recommend interleaving/prioritizing EXITING positions or using per-state caps/offsets so the sweep makes progress.

---

### [high] (bug)

When `close_position_full` returns `false` (no ACTIVE/EXITING position matched), `auto_resolve_exit` returns `Ok(())` without inserting a `reconciliation_log` row, yet the caller treats it as success: `result.auto_resolved += 1` and `outcome = Outcome::AutoResolved`, which suppresses the row for this position. This breaks the documented one-row-per-position accounting, overstates `auto_resolved`, and silently hides that the exit could not be matched to a position. Return a distinct result (or `Err`) when `position_closed == false` so the caller logs the position instead of counting it as resolved.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`Outcome::Ok` always writes `actual_on_chain = "FOUND"`, but this path also fires when the entry signature is empty (no on-chain check was performed at all) or when an entry `NotFound` fell inside the finalization grace window (the on-chain result was actually `NotFound`, just not yet definitive). The log therefore records a misleading `FOUND` status and downstream counts over-report confirmed transactions. Use `None` or a distinct status (`PENDING`/`NOT_CHECKED`) in these cases instead of `Some("FOUND")`.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Classifying RPC failures by string-matching the lowercased error message for "not found" is fragile: it depends on the exact wording/version of the RPC provider, and a different message containing "not found" (e.g. an account-not-found error) would be misclassified as a legitimate absent transaction, suppressing a real discrepancy. If the client exposes a structured error (e.g. `RpcError::RpcResponseError { code: .. }`), match on that instead.

---

## operator/src/engine/recovery.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Balance check ignores the position's owning wallet. `PositionRecord` carries `wallet_address` (see db_abstraction/types.rs), but `check_is_balance_zero` always loads the single default wallet from vault secrets. In any multi-wallet setup, the query `get_token_accounts_by_owner` returns an empty list for the wrong wallet, `max_balance` defaults to 0, and `revert_or_close_position` marks the position CLOSED — even though the exit sell was never executed and the token balance is still held in the actual owner wallet. This can silently drop a live position (capital/PNL loss). Pass the position's `wallet_address` into this function and derive the Pubkey from it instead of loading the default keypair.

```suggestion
        let wallet_pubkey = wallet_address
            .parse::<Pubkey>()
            .map_err(|e| AppError::Internal(format!("Invalid wallet address: {}", e)))?;
```

---

### [high] (bug)

After 300s of RPC errors the position is reverted EXITING → ACTIVE while the exit transaction's on-chain status is genuinely unknown. If the original exit tx was actually submitted and later confirms, the sell executes, while the now-ACTIVE position can be picked up again by the normal exit/stop-loss path and sold a second time — a duplicate exit / inverted position. The dead-letter entry only ensures eventual human review; nothing prevents the automatic re-exit before that review happens. Consider keeping such positions in EXITING (or a dedicated REVIEW state) and gating re-exit on the DLQ entry, or verifying via the failover client before reverting.

---

### [medium] (bug)

A transaction that was found on-chain but failed (`meta.err.is_some()`) is mapped to `TransactionNotFound`. This conflates two very different situations: a tx that never landed (blockhash expired / never submitted) vs. a tx that landed and reverted. The failure reason is discarded (only logged), and the recovery path treats it as MISSING_TX, driving the wrong reconciliation log and stats. Return a distinct state (e.g. `TransactionFailed`) so the failure reason is preserved and the correct recovery/logging path is chosen.

```suggestion
                        Ok(OnChainState::TransactionFailed)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`update_position_state` and `update_trade_status` are two separate DB calls and the second one's `Result` is swallowed with `let _`. If the trade-status update fails (or the process dies between the two calls), the position row is CLOSED while the trade status remains EXITING — a permanently inconsistent state that is never retried. Propagate the error (or better, wrap both updates in a single transaction) so a partial failure is detectable and retryable.

```suggestion
                self.db
                    .update_position_state(&position.trade_uuid, "CLOSED")
                    .await?;
                self.db
                    .update_trade_status(&crate::db_abstraction::UpdateTradeStatus {
                        trade_uuid: position.trade_uuid.clone(),
                        status: "CLOSED".to_string(),
                        tx_signature: position.exit_tx_signature.clone(),
                        error_message: None,
                        network_fee_sol: None,
                    })
                    .await?;
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Every `Ok` result — including `RecoveryAction::StillPending` (RPC error under the 300s threshold) — increments `recovered` and logs "Position recovered". A position can thus be reported as "recovered" every 30s cycle while no recovery action was actually taken, inflating metrics and hiding no-op cycles from operators. Only count `MarkedClosed`/`RevertedToActive` as recovered and log `StillPending` separately (e.g. at debug/warn level without incrementing).

```suggestion
                Ok(RecoveryAction::StillPending) => {
                    tracing::debug!(
                        trade_uuid = %position.trade_uuid,
                        "Position still pending; no recovery action taken"
                    );
                }
                Ok(action) => {
                    tracing::info!(
                        trade_uuid = %position.trade_uuid,
                        action = %action,
                        "Position recovered"
                    );
                    recovered += 1;
                }
```

---

### [low] (performance)

`check_is_balance_zero` reloads vault secrets and reconstructs/validates the wallet keypair synchronously on every invocation — i.e. once per stuck position, per 30s cycle — and does so inside the async recovery task. `load_secrets_with_fallback` may perform blocking file/network I/O, which stalls the tokio worker. Hoist the secret load and keypair derivation out of the per-position loop (or derive the owner pubkey from `position.wallet_address`, per the wallet-ownership finding) and only perform the async RPC balance query per position.

## operator/src/engine/rent_scavenger.rs (6 findings, 1 critical, 2 high)

### [critical] (bug)

RPC `jsonParsed` token-account data nests `tokenAmount`, `delegate`, and `delegatedAmount` under `parsed.info` (with `parsed.type == "account"`), not directly under `parsed`. So `parsed.parsed.get("tokenAmount")` always returns `None` and the empty-account filter never matches — the scavenger silently closes nothing. Additionally, `delegatedAmount` only exists in the payload when a `delegate` is set, so even after fixing the nesting, accounts without a delegate (exactly the accounts meant to be closed) would be skipped by the `Some(delegated_amount)` requirement. Read `parsed.parsed.get("info")` and only require `info.tokenAmount.amount == "0"` plus absence of a non-system `delegate`. The identical bug exists in `verify_empty_accounts` below.

```suggestion
                if let Some(info) = parsed.parsed.get("info") {
                    if let Some(amount_str) = info
                        .get("tokenAmount")
                        .and_then(|t| t.get("amount"))
                        .and_then(|a| a.as_str())
                    {
                        if amount_str == "0" {
                            let has_delegate = info
                                .get("delegate")
                                .and_then(|d| d.as_str())
                                .map(|s| !s.is_empty() && s != "11111111111111111111111111111111")
                                .unwrap_or(false);
                            if !has_delegate {
                                // ... existing closeAuthority/state checks and push logic
                            }
                        }
                    }
                }
```

### [high] (performance)

`RpcClient` is a synchronous, blocking client. `get_token_accounts_by_owner`, `get_latest_blockhash`, and `send_and_confirm_transaction` (the last one also inside the `retry_rpc` closure) are all executed directly on a Tokio worker thread from the spawned scavenger task. During retries/backoff this stalls the runtime and can delay every other task sharing the executor. Wrap the blocking RPC work in `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` (or use an async RPC client).

---

### [high] (bug)

Selection only checks zero balance and absence of a delegate. A token account whose `closeAuthority` is set to a key other than the funding keypair cannot be closed with the funding keypair's signature, and accounts in `state: "frozen"` also cannot be closed; including either kind will make the entire batch transaction fail. Filter on `info.closeAuthority` (absent/equal to the funding pubkey) and `info.state != "frozen"` in both the initial scan and `verify_empty_accounts`.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Hardcoding 165 bytes underestimates rent for Token-2022 accounts with extensions (data length can be several times larger), so `batch_rent`/`max_rent_lamports` safety cap and the `total_rent_reclaimed` accounting are both inaccurate and the safety cap can be exceeded. The RPC is also called once per candidate account (repeated blocking calls) and errors are silently swallowed by `unwrap_or(2_040_000)`. Use the actual `parsed.space` reported by the RPC and propagate errors with `?` instead of defaulting.

```suggestion
                                        let space = parsed.space.unwrap_or(165) as usize;
                                        let rent = rpc_client
                                            .get_minimum_balance_for_rent_exemption(space)
                                            .map_err(|e| AppError::Rpc(format!("Failed to get rent exemption: {}", e)))?;
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

All CloseAccount instructions are packed into a single transaction. If any account in the batch is already closed, frozen, has a mismatched closeAuthority, or changes between re-verification and send, the whole transaction fails and none of the batch is closed; the error is only logged, so the same bad batch will be retried on every run. Consider per-account transactions (or smaller batches) and treat per-account failures as non-fatal so one bad account does not block the others.

---

### [low] (performance)

`verify_empty_accounts` re-fetches ALL owner token accounts via `get_token_accounts_by_owner` for every batch (chunks of `max_batch_size`, default 10), so a run with many accounts performs O(batches × total_accounts) blocking RPC round-trips and data transfers. Fetch the current empty set once per run/program and filter from it, or re-check each candidate with a single `get_account_info`.
