## operator/src/engine/rpc_cache.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

`get()` ignores the TTL captured at `set()` time and instead applies the caller-supplied `ttl`. A caller passing a larger TTL can read back data that should already be expired, while a smaller TTL needlessly invalidates still-valid entries; the `CachedResponse.ttl` field is only consulted by `clear_expired()`. The expiry check should use the stored `cached.ttl` (the TTL passed to `set()`), and the `ttl` parameter should be removed from `get()` so the semantics are unambiguous.

```suggestion
        if let Some(cached) = cache.get(key) {
            // Check if expired using the TTL stored at set() time
            if cached.cached_at.elapsed().unwrap_or_default() < cached.ttl {
                return Some(cached.data.clone());
            }
        }
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Eviction is neither LRU nor FIFO: `HashMap::keys().next()` returns an arbitrary key (std `HashMap` iteration order is not insertion-ordered), so the "oldest" entry removed here is effectively random — despite the module doc claiming an LRU cache. Additionally, when `max_size == 0`, `cache.len() >= 0` is always true, but only one entry can be removed before the insert, so the cache permanently ends up holding 1 entry, exceeding the configured limit. Track insertion order explicitly (e.g., a `VecDeque` of keys or insertion timestamps) for real FIFO/LRU eviction and return early when `max_size == 0` so no entry is ever stored.

```suggestion
        if self.max_size == 0 {
            return;
        }
        if cache.len() >= self.max_size {
            // Remove oldest entry (tracked in insertion order)
            if let Some(first_key) = cache.keys().next().cloned() {
                cache.remove(&first_key);
            }
        }
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

Expired entries are only purged by an explicit `clear_expired()` call; `get()` returns `None` for expired entries but leaves them in the map. Over time stale data accumulates, wasting memory and triggering eviction of live entries before `clear_expired()` is ever invoked. Purge expired entries opportunistically (e.g., `retain(...)` inside `set()` before inserting, or remove the entry in `get()` once expiry is detected) so the cache self-cleans even if callers never call `clear_expired()`.

---

### [low] (performance)

`get()` clones the entire `Vec<u8>` payload on every cache hit while holding the read lock, which allocates and copies on each lookup and stalls writers for large RPC responses. Consider storing the payload as `Arc<Vec<u8>>` / `Arc<[u8]>` and returning an `Arc` clone so cache hits are cheap and the read guard is not held during a large copy.

```suggestion
struct CachedResponse {
    data: Arc<Vec<u8>>,
```

---

### [low] (test)

The `test_rpc_cache_expiration` test never exercises expiration — the only assertion runs immediately after insertion, and the comment explicitly defers the real expiry check. Add a short sleep (or introduce a clock abstraction) and assert that `get()` returns `None` after the TTL elapses, including the case where the caller passes a TTL different from the one used at `set()`.

```suggestion
        // Should be available immediately
        assert!(cache.get("test_key", Duration::from_secs(1)).is_some());

        std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1100));
        assert!(cache.get("test_key", Duration::from_secs(1)).is_none());
```

---

## operator/src/engine/run_context.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

`started_at.timestamp()` has 1-second resolution. Any restart within the same second (e.g. a crash/restart loop, or two operator replicas starting concurrently) produces an identical `run_id` even though they are distinct runs — directly contradicting the module's documented guarantee that "a restarted process always gets a fresh run_id". Since `run_id` is the key used to cohort decision evidence in C4, colliding IDs silently merge records from different runs. Use millisecond/nanosecond resolution (and update the `run_id` format docs) or append a monotonic counter/nonce.

```suggestion
        let start_unix = started_at.timestamp_millis();
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Only the first 8 hex chars (32 bits) of the config hash are embedded in `run_id`. Distinct `SelectionConfig`s sharing that prefix yield the same `run_id`, so any grouping keyed on `run_id` alone will conflate runs that had different admission thresholds (the birthday-bound collision risk grows with the number of configs). Even though the full `config_hash` is stored separately, the run identifier itself no longer uniquely identifies a run. Consider embedding more of the hash (e.g. 16 chars) so the identifier is collision-resistant in practice.

```suggestion
        let config_hash_short: String = config_hash.chars().take(16).collect();
```

---

### [low] (bug)

Any build without `GIT_HASH` is stamped `"unknown"`. If a stripped/untracked build is deployed (the fallback's own doc comment contemplates this), its records become indistinguishable from every other `"unknown"` build, silently conflating distinct code revisions during C4 evidence cohorting. Consider failing the release build at compile time (`env!("GIT_HASH")`) or at least emitting a prominent build-time warning, so an untracked revision cannot quietly poison the evidence grouping.

```suggestion
            code_revision: env!("GIT_HASH").to_string(),
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

SHA-256 is truncated to 8 bytes (64 bits), giving a ~50% collision chance around 2^32 distinct rosters. That is a reasonable compact fingerprint for realistic roster counts, but if any downstream cohorting ever groups solely by `roster_hash`, a collision will silently merge two different wallet rosters into one evidence cohort. Worth documenting this bound (or using the full digest) where roster counts could grow large.

---

## operator/src/engine/selection.rs (5 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

`req.exit_fraction` is documented on SelectionRequest (“For SELL: the fraction of the position to exit (None = full)”) but is never applied here: `size_sol` is always the full `source_amount_sol` (capped at `max_position_sol`). The webhook handler then overwrites `signal.payload.amount_sol` with `decision.size_sol`, so a partial exit (e.g. exit_fraction = 0.5) is recorded/queued as the full source amount while the executor later scales the on-chain balance by `exit_fraction` — the decision record and trade row misrepresent the exit size. Either apply the fraction when computing `size_sol`, or remove the unused field and make the “full position handled downstream” contract explicit.

```suggestion
        let exit_fraction = req.exit_fraction.unwrap_or(Decimal::ONE);
        let size_sol = Some((req.source_amount_sol * exit_fraction).min(self.config.max_position_sol));
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The comment above this fallback says the source amount is “clamped to the configured capital ceiling”, but the code returns `req.source_amount_sol` unclamped (the warn message even admits “unclamped sizer”). If `PositionSizer` is unavailable, a copied-wallet amount larger than `max_position_sol` yields an admitted position that violates the configured cap. Clamp the fallback to the ceiling so the cap holds regardless of sizer availability.

```suggestion
            tracing::warn!("PositionSizer unavailable; using source amount clamped to max_position_sol");
            req.source_amount_sol.min(self.config.max_position_sol)
```

---

### [medium] (security)

When `fast_check` errors, the decision is returned as admitted with `fast_check_errored = true`, and safety is delegated to the caller setting `force_slow_path` — but only the webhook handler honors this flag; the Helius monitoring handler never checks `decision.fast_check_errored`. The documented contract (“The caller sets force_slow_path on the signal so the engine enforces slow-path verification before entry”) is therefore not uniformly enforced: for the Helius ingress a token whose safety check failed (RPC/network error) is admitted and queued with no slow-path requirement, and if `token_parser` is ever unavailable at execution time the trade proceeds with zero token-safety verification. Consider rejecting with a distinct code (fail-closed) or running the slow-path verification inside `decide_buy` before admitting.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`add_signal` is invoked at step 7 — before the quality threshold (step 8), the sizer (step 10) and the heat-admission gates (step 11). Signals that are later rejected on quality/sizing/heat are still inserted into the aggregator’s 5-minute window and wallet clusters, so they can inflate `consensus_wallet_count` and fabricate consensus for subsequent signals (the same applies to the `persist_signal_aggregation` INSERT, which runs regardless of admission). Record the signal only after the decision is admitted, or make the aggregator admission-aware, otherwise rejected noise drives false consensus and larger position sizes.

---

### [low] (security)

The portfolio/strategy heat gates fail open: on `Err` from `can_open_position` / `can_open_strategy_position` the trade is allowed. Every other gate in this pipeline is fail-closed (unknown wallet, wallet lookup error, position lookup error, liquidity fetch defaulting to $0), so failing open on the risk-control gate means a transient DB error lets positions exceed the configured portfolio/strategy heat limits. Consider failing closed (or at least surfacing these as errors rather than silently allowing the trade).

---

## operator/src/engine/shadow_fill.rs (6 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

The p50 delay is measured from the *completion* of the decision-time quote round-trip, not from `decided_at` as documented. `get_jupiter_quote` is a network call that can itself retry up to 3 times (200/400/800 ms backoff), so the requote actually fires at roughly `decided_at + decision_quote_latency + p50`, systematically pushing the requote later than specified and biasing `modeled_slippage_pct`. Capture a `tokio::time::Instant` deadline before the decision quote and sleep until that deadline after the quote returns, so the requote lands at `decided_at + p50` regardless of fetch duration.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`(size_sol * 1e9).round() as u64` is a saturating, lossy f64→u64 cast. Negative or NaN `size_sol` silently becomes 0 (then dropped by the `== 0` guard), and values above 2^53 lamports (≈9M SOL) lose precision or saturate to `u64::MAX`, producing a bogus Jupiter amount. Validate/range-check `size_sol` and convert via `u64::try_from(...)` (or explicit `clamp`) so invalid sizes fail loudly instead of silently corrupting the modeled fill.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Parsing `inAmount`/`outAmount` as f64 loses precision once amounts exceed 2^53 (9.007e15) — reachable with high-decimal tokens or larger orders — and strings like `"NaN"`/`"inf"` parse successfully, yielding a poisoned price/slippage (which serde then silently collapses to `null` in the JSON payload). Parse the amounts as integers (u64/u128) and compute the ratio as f64 from the integers, with an explicit NaN/Inf guard.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

An unparseable or out-of-range `CHIMERA_NONLANDING_PROB` silently falls back to the 0.03 default, so an operator typo changes simulation behavior with no signal. When the env var is present but invalid/out of range, emit a `tracing::warn!` (or fail fast) so the misconfiguration is visible.

---

### [low] (performance)

`s.remove(0)` shifts the whole sample buffer on every record, making `record` O(cap) per decision despite the doc comment calling it cheap; `LatencyTracker::default()` (cap = 0) additionally panics here because `0 >= 0` is true and `remove(0)` on an empty Vec is out of bounds. Use a `VecDeque`/ring buffer (or pop-front only when full) and guard the `cap == 0` case.

---

### [low] (performance)

`percentile` clones the entire sample buffer (up to ~16 KB at cap 2048) and sorts it while still holding the mutex, blocking `record` for the whole O(n log n) sort. Take the clone (or a length snapshot) under the lock and sort *after* releasing it; a smaller window or kept-sorted structure would also remove the per-call sort.

---

## operator/src/engine/signal_quality.rs (4 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

Liquidity thresholds use strict `>` so a value exactly equal to a boundary (50000/20000/10000/5000) falls into the lower bucket. This is also inconsistent with `passes_liquidity_floor`, which uses `>=` — a token with exactly `min_liquidity` USD passes the hard floor but is scored one tier lower here. Use `>=` for the upper thresholds (or otherwise align the two APIs) so boundary behavior is consistent.

```suggestion
        let liquidity_score: f64 = if liquidity_usd >= Decimal::from(50000) {
            1.0
        } else if liquidity_usd >= Decimal::from(20000) {
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`wallet_wqs` is documented as 0-100 but is only clamped on the upper side. A negative value produces a negative `wallet_score` that silently drags down the composite score, and a NaN input yields `wallet_score = 1.0` (f64::min ignores NaN), inflating the score — both without any validation error. Additionally, `factors.wallet_wqs` stores the raw unclamped value while every other stored factor is normalized to 0.0-1.0, making the struct internally inconsistent. Clamp to 0.0-100.0 (or validate and return a typed error) and store a normalized value consistent with the other factors.

```suggestion
        // 1. Wallet quality (40% weight)
        let wallet_wqs = wallet_wqs.clamp(0.0, 100.0);
        let wallet_score = wallet_wqs / 100.0;
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

As the doc comment itself acknowledges, a high WQS/consensus signal can pass the 0.7 quality gate with near-zero liquidity, and the protection relies entirely on callers remembering to invoke this detached associated function. Since `passes_liquidity_floor` takes no `self`, nothing structurally prevents the floor check from being skipped, and its `>=` boundary semantics differ from the `>` thresholds in `calculate`. Consider folding the liquidity floor into `calculate`/`should_enter` (or providing a combined API) so the invariant cannot be forgotten.

---

### [low] (documentation)

The doc claims `min_quality` has a default of 0.7, but it is a mandatory positional argument with no default and no zero-arg overload exists. Callers reading the docs may assume they can omit it, and a caller passing 0.0 would silently accept every signal. Either provide a default/no-arg variant or fix the doc to state the value is required.

```suggestion
    /// * `min_quality` - Minimum quality score required
```

## operator/src/engine/slippage.rs (4 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

Jupiter's `priceImpactPct` is trusted unconditionally. A negative value (Jupiter can return negative impact on some routes) produces a negative `expected_fraction`: `expected_cost_sol` becomes negative (misleading cost bookkeeping) and the bps conversion below fails (`to_u16()` returns `None` for negatives), falling back to `bounds.ceil_bps` — silently widening the on-chain tolerance to the strategy maximum instead of rejecting the quote. Absurdly large values also push tolerance to the ceiling and can overflow later arithmetic. Clamp `pct` to `[0, 100]` (or at least reject negatives) before converting.

```suggestion
    if let Some(pct) = jupiter_impact_pct {
        // pct is a percent (1.5 = 1.5%); convert to fraction.
        // Clamp malformed (negative/absurd) feed values instead of trusting them.
        return pct.max(Decimal::ZERO) / Decimal::from(100);
    }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`amount_sol`, `sol_price_usd`, and `liquidity_usd` are externally supplied on the live quoting path, and rust_decimal's `Mul`/`Div` panic on overflow (and `Div` panics on a zero divisor). A malformed or extreme feed value here can crash the quoting task. Use `checked_mul`/`checked_div` and degrade to the size-tier fallback on arithmetic failure instead of panicking.

```suggestion
            match amount_sol.checked_mul(sol_price) {
                Some(trade_usd) => {
                    // ... compute sqrt/linear estimate with checked_div ...
                }
                None => return fallback.fraction_for(amount_sol),
            }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Two issues here: (1) `tolerance_fraction * 10000` is unchecked multiplication — with an unvalidated Jupiter pct (or extreme amount/liquidity inputs) `expected_fraction` can be large enough that this overflows and panics in rust_decimal mid-quote; (2) `unwrap_or(bounds.ceil_bps)` maps every conversion failure (negative or overflowing) to the *maximum* strategy tolerance — the opposite of a safe fallback. A negative/overflowing fraction must not widen the on-chain tolerance; fall back to the floor (or reject the quote) instead, after validating/clamping the input so legitimate large impacts still clamp to the ceiling via `clamp`.

```suggestion
    let raw_bps = match (tolerance_fraction.checked_mul(Decimal::from(10_000u64)))
        .and_then(|bps| bps.to_u16())
    {
        Some(bps) => bps,
        // Negative/overflowing fraction must not widen tolerance.
        None => bounds.floor_bps,
    };
    let tolerance_bps = raw_bps.clamp(bounds.floor_bps, bounds.ceil_bps);
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The model is documented (module header and this comment) as a "square-root market impact" approximation, but `trade_usd / (2 × liquidity_usd)` is linear in trade size. For larger trades on thin books the linear model understates real impact, so the derived tolerance under-buffers exactly where reverts/MEV risk is highest (and the 15% ceiling caps it). Either implement an actual sqrt model (`Decimal::sqrt`) or correct the docs/comments to describe the linear approximation and its known limitation for large trades.

---

## operator/src/engine/stop_loss.rs (9 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

True Range is miscalculated: `high` and `low` are both bound to the same close price, so `high - low == 0` and TR degenerates to `|close - prev_close|`. The resulting ATR measures only day-over-day price change, not intra-period range, so any ATR-based stop distance derived from it is incorrect. Additionally, `period` is only used as a minimum-length guard — the loop runs over the entire `price_history` instead of the last `period` samples, so a true lookback ATR is never computed. (Note this method is currently unused in the operator crate; if it is ever wired in, both defects will propagate.)

---

### [medium] (concurrency)

The `signal_aggregator` read guard is held across both `.await` points (the in-memory `is_consensus_token` call and the fallback SQL query). This runs on every position tick (every 5s), and a slow DB query under the fallback blocks `set_signal_aggregator` writers for the whole duration. Better: clone the `Arc` out under a short-lived guard and drop the guard before awaiting.

---

### [medium] (error-handling)

DB errors in the consensus fallback query are swallowed with `unwrap_or(0)`, so a transient database failure is silently treated as "no consensus". That silently tightens stops on consensus tokens during exactly the kind of outage when consensus widening is most relevant. Log the error instead of discarding it.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Volatility is applied twice when `atr_stop_loss_enabled` is set: the same `price_cache.calculate_volatility` value first drives the ATR-based override (`calculate_atr_stop_loss`) and then the adaptive volatility multiplier below. E.g. a low-volatility token gets an ATR-tightened threshold that the adaptive 0.9x multiplier then partially undoes (and vice-versa for volatile tokens). The two adjustments compound the same signal and likely don't reflect configuration intent — apply only one volatility-based adjustment, or compute them from independent signals.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

The wick-protection bypass re-hardcodes `dec!(-25)` even though `is_hard_stop` (computed from the same condition at the top) is already available. The module doc header also claims a -15% hard stop while the code enforces -25%. If the hard-stop level is ever changed in one spot but not the other, catastrophic-drop protection silently drifts. Reuse `is_hard_stop` here and update the header doc to match the actual -25% level.

```suggestion
                if is_hard_stop {
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

If `entry_time` is ahead of the local clock (clock skew, or a position timestamped from a future-dated source), `elapsed_secs` is negative and therefore always `< wick_protection_secs`. The wick-protection grace period then suppresses legitimate stop-loss exits indefinitely until the clock catches up, and the hard-stop bypass becomes the only way out. Clamp elapsed time to `>= 0`.

```suggestion
        let elapsed_secs = chrono::Utc::now()
            .signed_duration_since(entry_time)
            .num_seconds()
            .max(0);
```

---

### [low] (error-handling)

A `get_wallet` DB error (the `_ =>` arm) silently defaults WQS to 50.0, and a missing `wqs_score` is also mapped to 50.0. Both failures flip the wallet into the "medium WQS" tier (-15%) without any log signal, so an operator watching stop behavior cannot tell that the dynamic stop is running on defaults. Distinguish the DB-failure case and log it.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`from_str` collides with the name of the std `FromStr` trait method but does not actually implement the trait, which prevents `str::parse::<MarketRegime>()` from working and makes the API less discoverable. Worse, the `_ => Neutral` fallback silently maps any config typo (e.g. "BULLL") to Neutral with no warning. Prefer implementing `std::str::FromStr` (optionally returning a `Result`) or at least log an unknown value.

---

### [low] (bug)

This force-exit branch is dead code: `price_cache.is_price_stale` returns `false` when no cache entry exists (it only reports staleness for an existing entry older than the threshold), and if an entry existed, `get_price_usd` above would have returned `Some`. So a token with no cached price can never take this exit path — the intended "no price on tracked token" safety net never fires. Use `is_tracked_price_stale` (or a tracked-token membership check) if this is the intent.

---

## operator/src/engine/tips.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Scale mismatch makes this failure-rate estimate wrong and it degrades over time. `recent_tips` is bounded at 100 rows (WHERE success = TRUE), but `total` is the all-time count of successful tips. As history grows past 100, `success_count / total` shrinks toward 0 and `failure_rate` approaches 1.0 forever — so `calculate_dynamic_tip_with_load` will permanently apply the ~1.5x tip multiplier even when bundles are landing fine. Note both numbers count only *successful* tips, so this is really 'fraction of all history in the last window', not a failure rate at all. Compute the rate over a consistent window (e.g. successes vs attempts within the same 100-tip window), ideally by exposing success/failure counts from the Database trait, and clamp the result.

```suggestion
        let recent_tips = self.db.get_recent_jito_tips(100).await?;
        let recent_count = recent_tips.len() as f64;
        // total is all-time; use the same 100-row window on both sides,
        // otherwise the estimate converges to 1.0 as history grows.
        let window_total = total.min(100) as f64;
        let failure_rate = 1.0 - (recent_count / window_total.max(1.0));
        Ok(failure_rate.clamp(0.0, 1.0))
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Seeding condition contradicts the documented contract. The doc above claims "The seed only runs when the history is empty" and "Live mode never seeds ... so the percentile data is never polluted", but this guard only checks `count < MIN_SAMPLES_FOR_PERCENTILE`. If 1-9 real tips already exist (e.g. from an earlier live run sharing the same DB), paper mode inserts 12 fake seeds that are permanently persisted into `jito_tip_history` with no distinguishing filter — later live runs will count them toward the 10-sample threshold and blend them into percentile calculations, polluting live data exactly as the docs say it won't. Also, the check-then-act across multiple awaits means two concurrent calls can both pass the guard and double-insert. Guard on an actually-empty history (count == 0) or tag seeds so `get_recent_jito_tips`/percentile computation can exclude them.

```suggestion
        let count = self.db.get_jito_tip_count().await?;
        // Only seed a completely empty history — mixing paper seeds with real
        // tips pollutes persisted live percentile data.
        if count > 0 {
            return Ok(());
        }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

This measures distribution overlap of recent *successful* tips, not actual landing success. `get_jito_tip_count`/`get_recent_jito_tips` only return successful rows (WHERE success = TRUE), so `in_range / len` is just 'what fraction of successful tips are near our proposed tip' — it cannot detect whether that tip would have landed. Worse, with zero history (`total == 0`) it returns 1.0, so `is_tip_success_rate_acceptable` reports success with no evidence at all. This overstates success probability and can wrongly suppress fallback/retry behavior. Return a neutral/no-data signal (or false) when there is no data, and compute success from actual attempt outcomes (success vs failed rows) for the tip range instead.

```suggestion
        let recent_tips = self.db.get_recent_jito_tips(500).await?;
        let in_range = recent_tips
            .iter()
            .filter(|t| **t >= min_tip && **t <= max_tip)
            .count();
        if recent_tips.is_empty() {
            return Ok(0.0); // No evidence of landing success — don't assume 1.0
        }
        Ok(in_range as f64 / recent_tips.len() as f64)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

When history is empty, `stats()` returns `TipStats::default()` which hard-codes `is_cold_start: false`, without consulting the actual `cold_start` flag. Since cold start is exactly when history tends to be empty, monitoring/telemetry will report the manager as NOT in cold-start mode while it still uses cold-start tips — misleading operators. Return the real flag instead of the default.

```suggestion
        if history.is_empty() {
            return TipStats {
                is_cold_start: *self.cold_start.read(),
                ..TipStats::default()
            };
        }
```

---

### [low] (bug)

`percentile_tip_from_history` panics on an empty input: `tips.len() - 1` underflows (panic in debug, wraps to usize::MAX in release) and `tips[index]` indexes out of bounds. It is currently only reachable via the guarded `percentile_tip`, but as a standalone pure helper it's a footgun for future callers/tests. Add an early return for the empty case.

```suggestion
    if tips.is_empty() {
        return config.tip_floor_sol;
    }

    let index = (tips.len() * percentile / 100).min(tips.len() - 1);
    let percentile_tip = tips[index];
```

## operator/src/engine/transaction_builder.rs (7 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

fill_price_lamports_per_base is computed unconditionally as inAmount/outAmount, which is only correct for BUY (SOL→token, i.e. lamports per token base unit). For a SELL (token→SOL), in_amount is in token base units and out_amount is in lamports, so this yields token-units-per-lamport — the inverse of the documented 'lamports per base unit' semantics that the executor feeds into lamports_per_base_to_sol_per_token() for cost/fill tracking. Note get_quote_prices() below is direction-aware (out/in when output is SOL). This path doesn't know the trade direction, so thread it in (or compare output_mint to SOL) and mirror the get_quote_prices formula.

```suggestion
        let fill_price_lamports_per_base = match (in_amount, out_amount) {
            // BUY (SOL→token): lamports per base unit. SELL (token→SOL):
            // invert so the value is always lamports per token base unit.
            (Some(inn), Some(out)) if out > 0 && inn > 0 => {
                if output_mint == Pubkey::from_str(crate::constants::mints::SOL).unwrap() {
                    Some(Decimal::from(out) / Decimal::from(inn))
                } else {
                    Some(Decimal::from(inn) / Decimal::from(out))
                }
            },
            _ => None,
        };
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Same inversion bug as the v2 path: fill_price_lamports_per_base is computed as inAmount/outAmount unconditionally. For a SELL (token→SOL) this is token-units-per-lamport, contradicting the documented 'lamports per base unit' semantics and get_quote_prices()'s direction-aware formula. Since the swap paths only receive mints (not the Action), derive direction from output_mint == SOL or pass the signal's action through.

```suggestion
        let fill_price_lamports_per_base = match (in_amount, out_amount) {
            (Some(inn), Some(out)) if out > 0 && inn > 0 => {
                if output_mint == Pubkey::from_str(crate::constants::mints::SOL).unwrap() {
                    Some(Decimal::from(out) / Decimal::from(inn))
                } else {

### [medium] (bug)

A consumer that assumes transaction_bytes and blockhash() agree will submit a stale-blockhash tx while reporting a fresh one. Consider returning the message's actual blockhash in that case, or failing closed so the caller can re-request Jupiter (executor has a BlockhashExpired retry path).

Sum all parseable balances with saturating add — or, if Jupiter's swap only drains the primary source account, filter to that account and document the choice so the sell amount matches what will actually be spent.

If the v2 API ever reports priceImpact as a percent or as a string, as_f64() returns None and the field is silently dropped; a Decimal::from_f64 failure also silently becomes Some(0.0) instead of None, which cost tracking will treat as a genuine 0% impact. Additionally .abs() strips the sign while the v1 path preserves it. Centralize the parsing (as dex_comparator does) and return None on missing/unparseable values so cost tracking is not skewed by 100x or fabricated 0%.

## operator/src/engine/v0_reconstruction.rs (3 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

Returning `Result<_, String>` for a public API loses structured error context and forces callers into either `to_string()`-based matching or silent fallback. Both call sites (executor.rs / transaction_builder.rs) only log the error and fall back to the original message, which is a misuse-friendly design: the failure here is really a programming/API-contract violation (passing a Legacy message), not a runtime condition the caller can recover from. Prefer a small typed error enum (e.g. `RefreshBlockhashError::LegacyMessageNotSupported`) with `thiserror`/`Display`, so callers can branch on the variant and the contract is documented in the type system instead of in a log string.

```

The clone copies the entire `v0::Message`, including `account_keys`, `instructions`, and `address_table_lookups`. For large V0 transactions (e.g. Jupiter swaps with many instructions and ALT lookups) this allocates and copies a non-trivial amount per refresh. Both call sites already own the transaction and must re-sign and rebuild it anyway, so an API taking `VersionedMessage` (or the transaction) by value and returning the refreshed message — or an in-place variant that mutates `recent_blockhash` — would eliminate the copy while keeping the same semantics. At minimum, note this is O(message size) per refresh.

The comment claims the message is preserved "byte-for-byte apart from the blockhash", but the test only asserts `header` and `account_keys` are unchanged — `instructions` and `address_table_lookups` (which would differ if a field-swap ever touched them) are never verified. Since the whole point of this module is that only `recent_blockhash` changes, lock the contract down by asserting `instructions` and `address_table_lookups` equality as well, or the test would not catch an accidental mutation of those fields.

## operator/src/engine/volume_cache.rs (4 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

`get_24h_average_volume` and `get_current_volume` report data regardless of freshness: unlike `has_volume_drop`, they do not reject samples when the most-recent entry is older than ~10 minutes. After indexer lag/downtime the deque still holds (potentially >24h-old) entries and callers in `momentum_exit.rs` will act on stale volume signals, e.g. exit based on a meaningless "24h average". Apply the same staleness guard used in `has_volume_drop` (return `None` / skip when the newest sample is too old).

```suggestion
    pub fn get_24h_average_volume(&self, token_address: &str) -> Option<Decimal> {
        let history = self.volume_history.read();
        let token_history = history.get(token_address)?;

        // Reject stale data (same guard as has_volume_drop).
        if let Some((newest_time, _)) = token_history.back() {
            if Utc::now().signed_duration_since(*newest_time).num_minutes() > 10 {
                return None;
            }
        }

        if token_history.is_empty() {
            return None;
        }

        let total_volume: Decimal = token_history.iter().map(|(_, volume)| *volume).sum();
        let count = Decimal::from(token_history.len());

        Some(total_volume / count)
```

### [medium] (performance)

Token entries are never evicted from `volume_history`: `entry().or_default()` inserts a key on the first sample and nothing removes keys once a token stops being updated (idle/transient tokens). In a long-running operator processing many ephemeral tokens this grows memory without bound, with per-token deques that may also retain stale >24h entries when updates stop. Consider evicting deques whose newest entry is older than 24h on each `record_volume`, or run a periodic sweep / cap on the number of tracked tokens.

```suggestion
        let mut history = self.volume_history.write();
        // Evict idle tokens (no updates for 24h) to bound memory usage.
        history.retain(|_, h| {
            h.back().is_none_or(|(t, _)| now.signed_duration_since(*t) <= Duration::hours(24))
        });
        let token_history = history.entry(token_address.to_string()).or_default();
        token_history.push_back((now, volume_usd));
```

### [medium] (bug)

In the sparse-data fallback, `avg` is computed over the entire history *including* the most-recent (possibly depressed) sample, so a single low `current` drags the average down and understates `drop_pct`, masking genuine volume drops (the exact false-negative the momentum-exit detector is meant to catch). Exclude the current sample from the baseline average and guard the divisor.

```suggestion
        if let Some(current) = token_history.back().map(|(_, v)| *v) {
            // Compare against the remaining history so the depressed current
            // sample does not dilute the baseline average.
            let n = token_history.len().saturating_sub(1);
            if n > 0 {
                let total: Decimal = token_history.iter().take(n).map(|(_, v)| *v).sum();
                let avg = total / Decimal::from(n);
                if avg > Decimal::ZERO {
                    let drop_pct = (avg - current) / avg * Decimal::from(100);
                    return drop_pct >= threshold_percent;
                }
            }
        }
```

## operator/src/engine/worker_pool.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

`active_workers` is manually incremented here and decremented only after `process_signal` completes. If `process_signal` (or anything in between) panics, the counter is never decremented, permanently inflating `stats().active_workers`. Worse, the worker task dies with no respawn — the pool silently shrinks to N-1 workers — and the reserved `panic_count` field (line 52) is never incremented, so the intended circuit-breaker signal is lost. Prefer an RAII guard that decrements on drop (e.g., a small scoped struct holding the Arc + count), and track panics by inspecting `JoinSet` join results at runtime (or `catch_unwind` around the processing step), incrementing `panic_count` and optionally respawning the worker.

---

### [high] (bug)

Cancellation is only checked at the top of this `biased` select, before a signal is popped. Once a worker has popped a signal it then awaits `rpc_semaphore.acquire()` and `process_signal(...)` with no cancellation awareness and no timeout. If all permits are held (semaphore saturated by slow RPCs) or `process_signal` blocks indefinitely on an external call, `shutdown()` (which awaits `join_next()` with no timeout) hangs forever. Make the permit acquisition cancellation-aware (e.g., wrap `acquire` in a `tokio::select!` with `cancel_token.cancelled()` and return), wrap `process_signal` with a timeout, and add an overall timeout to `shutdown` for forced completion.

---

### [medium] (performance)

`signal` is already owned (moved out of `pop_wait`) and is dead after this point — `trade_uuid` was already cloned earlier for logging and the `debug!` borrow of `signal.payload.strategy` has ended. Cloning the entire `Signal` on every item is an unnecessary allocation/copy in the hot path; pass the owned signal directly instead.

```suggestion
                    signal_processor.process_signal(&mut signal).await;
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`rpc_rate_limit` is stored in `WorkerPoolConfig` (and documented as "RPC rate limiter (requests per second)") but is never read anywhere in this file — only `max_concurrent_rpc` is enforced via the semaphore. Per-second rate limiting is actually handled elsewhere (`RateLimiter` in `main.rs`/`monitoring`, and RPC-error backoff in `executor.rs`), so this field is misleading dead config at the worker-pool boundary. Either implement the limiter here or remove the field/document that it is enforced downstream.

## operator/src/error.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (security)

Internal error details are serialized verbatim into the API response. `Config` errors can expose the database URL/connection string, and `Database` errors can leak SQL or connection details to clients. Log the full error server-side and return a generic message (e.g. `details: None` or a fixed string) for these internal-failure variants to avoid information disclosure.

```suggestion
            AppError::Config(e) => {
                tracing::error!(error = %e, "Configuration error");
                (
                    StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
                    ErrorResponse {
                        status: "error",
                        reason: "configuration_error".to_string(),
                        details: None,
                    },
                )
            }
```

---

### [high] (security)

The same verbatim-details leak applies to the `Database` variant: `e.to_string()` is echoed to the client, potentially exposing SQL statements, table names, or connection details. Log the full error and return a generic response.

```suggestion
            AppError::Database(e) => {
                tracing::error!(error = %e, "Database error");
                (
                    StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
                    ErrorResponse {
                        status: "error",
                        reason: "database_error".to_string(),
                        details: None,
                    },
                )
            }
```

### [medium] (bug)

`Parse` errors are mapped to 502 Bad Gateway, which tells clients/monitoring that an upstream server is at fault. A parse/deserialization failure is normally caused by malformed client input (→ 400) or an internal invariant bug (→ 500), not an upstream gateway problem. Unless this variant is exclusively for parsing responses from downstream services, it should map to BAD_REQUEST.

```suggestion
            AppError::Parse(msg) => (
                StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST,
                ErrorResponse {
                    status: "rejected",
                    reason: "parse_error".to_string(),
                    details: Some(msg.clone()),
                },
            ),
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Every error — including 4xx client mistakes such as Validation, Auth, Forbidden, NotFound, BadRequest and InvalidInput — is logged at `tracing::error!`. This floods the error log with expected client behavior and obscures genuine server failures. Log 4xx-class errors at `debug`/`warn` (or omit them) and reserve `error!` for 5xx responses.

```suggestion
        if status_code.is_server_error() {
            tracing::error!(
                error_type = %self,
                status_code = %status_code,
                "Request error"
            );
        } else {
            tracing::warn!(
                error_type = %self,
                status_code = %status_code,
                "Request rejected"

```

### [low] (maintainability)

`Validation`, `BadRequest`, `InvalidInput`, `Signal` and `Parse` are all stringly-typed variants that overlap semantically yet map to inconsistent statuses (Signal→400, Parse→502, BadRequest→400, Validation→400). This makes it easy to pick the wrong variant and return misleading status codes. Consider consolidating into a single typed error (e.g. `BadRequest { code, message }`) or deriving status codes from one place so equivalent failures get equivalent responses.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The `Queue` variant maps to `reason: "queue_full"`, but the variant represents any queue error (e.g. queue unreachable or down), so the fixed reason string can misstate the cause. Consider naming the variant `QueueFull` or making the reason reflect the actual failure.

## operator/src/experiment/controls.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

The "random" token selection is not random: the index is derived from wall-clock microseconds, so two fires within the same microsecond always pick the same token, the sequence is fully predictable from the clock, and `timestamp % len` has modulo bias when `len` doesn't divide the counter. The `use rand::prelude::*;` import at the top is unused. Use a real RNG instead, e.g. `rand::thread_rng().gen_range(0..self.liquid_tokens.len())`.

        let idx = rand::thread_rng().gen_range(0..self.liquid_tokens.len());

### [high] (bug)

When multiple open trades share the same `token_mint` (common here because selection is non-random and `liquid_tokens` can be small — the test itself fires 3 trades on a single token), `close_random_control` closes the *first* open match, and `close_sol_benchmark` closes the first open SOL trade regardless of entry price. Repeat or concurrent fires can therefore associate an exit price/PnL with the wrong entry, corrupting the control-arm statistics that this module exists to produce. Close by trade identity (e.g. `entry_time` or a trade id) or at least close the most recent open trade (`.iter_mut().rev().find(...)`), and make `ControlTrade::close` idempotent.

### [medium] (bug)

Returning `ControlStats::default()` for an unknown control type or when there are no closed trades yields `total_trades = 0` with `win_rate = 0.0` — indistinguishable from a losing record in downstream reporting. Return `Option<ControlStats>` (or add an explicit "no data" flag) so empty results aren't reported as a 0% win rate.

### [low] (bug)

`ControlTrade::close` unconditionally overwrites `exit_time`/`exit_price`/`pnl`. Calling it twice on the same trade (possible if a caller bypasses the manager, or if close is raced in a retry) silently discards the original exit and recomputes PnL. Guard against closing an already-closed trade.

A zero (or negative) `entry_price` silently maps to `Decimal::ZERO` PnL instead of signaling invalid data. Statistics mix inconsistent populations, producing misleading experiment metrics: (1) `total_trades` counts only closed trades while `tracer_count` counts all tracer trades (open and closed), so `tracer_count` can exceed `total_trades`; (2) the early `if total_trades == 0` return discards tracer stats entirely even when open tracer trades exist; (3) `wins`/`losses`/`win_rate` are derived only from paper PnL, and zero-PnL trades are counted as losses (`losses = len - wins`), so flat trades skew the verdict metrics. ### [medium] (bug)

Decision (`should_fire_tracer`) and recording (`record_tracer`) each acquire the mutex in a separate scope, creating a check-then-act race: two concurrent callers can both observe `tracer_count < tracer_cap`, both return true, and both increment `tracer_count`, exceeding the configured cap. Since these are real money trades, consider an atomic method that checks the cap, samples, and increments under a single lock (e.g., `try_record_tracer`) or document that the cap is only approximate.

### [medium] (bug)

After `tracer_cap` is reached the sample rate is tapered (cap/(count+1) * initial) but never reaches zero, so `should_fire_tracer` can keep returning true indefinitely and tracer trades remain unbounded — each being a real 0.02 SOL order. If `tracer_cap` is meant to bound live-trade exposure/cost, this doesn't do it; make the cap a hard stop (or taper to 0 at the cap) or clearly document that it is only a soft rate-reduction point.

Note the existing test cannot catch this because its assertions are tautological (`lower >= ZERO || lower < ZERO`).

---

### [high] (bug)

Same without-replacement bug as in `calculate_bootstrap_ci`: `choose_multiple` with `strategy.len()`/`control.len()` yields permutations of the original vectors, so every bootstrap diff equals the observed `mean_diff`, the CI collapses, and `p_value` degenerates to exactly 0 or 1. The "hypothesis test" reduces to a deterministic point comparison and reflects no sampling variability, so `beats_control` (Rule 3) is decided by the raw point estimate. Resample with replacement; also, if the field is meant to be a two-sample test, the one-sided proportion `d <= 0` should be doubled (with the usual +1/(B+1) correction) rather than compared to 0.05 directly.

```suggestion
            let strategy_sample: Vec<f64> = (0..strategy.len())
                .map(|_| *strategy_float.choose(&mut rng).unwrap_or(&0.0))
                .collect();

            let control_sample: Vec<f64> = (0..control.len())
                .map(|_| *control_float.choose(&mut rng).unwrap_or(&0.0))
                .collect();
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The Wilson interval variance term is wrong: `(z * z / (4.0 * n as f64).powi(2))` expands to z²/(4n)² = z²/(16n²), but the Wilson formula requires z²/(4n²), so the interval is narrower than it should be. More fundamentally, the Wilson score interval bounds the *win rate* (proportion of winning trades); multiplying it by the profit factor does not produce a valid confidence bound for the PF ratio (gross_profit/gross_loss). This quantity is used in the hard Kill rule (Rule 2), so strategies can be misclassified. Either compute a proper bootstrap/parametric CI for the PF ratio or document this as an ad-hoc heuristic rather than a confidence bound.

```suggestion
        let margin = z * ((p_hat * (1.0 - p_hat) / n as f64) + (z * z / (4.0 * (n as f64).powi(2)))).sqrt() / denominator;
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

When `gross_loss == 0` the comment says "Infinite PF when no losses" but the code returns `gross_profit` instead of infinity. `profit_factor_lb` then becomes `gross_profit * Wilson_lower_bound`, and with many zero-PnL trades the win-rate lower bound can be very small (e.g. 2 wins out of 50 → LB ≈ 0.02), pushing `profit_factor_lb` below 1.2 and wrongly triggering Kill for a strategy that has *no losing trades at all*. Handle the no-loss case as unbounded (skip the PF rule or use `Decimal::MAX`) rather than substituting the finite gross profit.

```suggestion
        let profit_factor = if gross_loss > Decimal::ZERO {
            gross_profit / gross_loss
        } else {
            Decimal::MAX // Infinite PF when no losses
        };
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`peak` is initialized to 0, so any losses incurred before the equity curve turns positive hit the `peak <= 0` branch and are reported as drawdown 0. A strategy that opens with a losing streak is therefore measured with `max_drawdown == 0` and passes Rule 4 even though it began in a deep drawdown relative to its starting equity. Track drawdown from the running equity peak (including the initial 0 baseline) or report the drop below starting equity explicitly instead of returning 0. Note the suggested code treats the pre-peak loss as a percentage relative to the initial equity, so the drawdown rule will correctly flag strategies that start underwater.

```suggestion
            let drawdown = if peak > Decimal::ZERO {
                (cumulative - peak) / peak * Decimal::from(100)
            } else {
                cumulative * Decimal::from(100)
            };
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`d.to_f64().unwrap_or(0.0)` silently converts any PnL value that overflows or cannot be represented as f64 into 0.0. These converted values drive the bootstrap mean, CI, and control-arm comparisons, so a single out-of-range trade can silently distort the expectancy and flip the final verdict. Convert explicitly and fail with context (or clamp after validation) instead of defaulting to zero.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`Decimal::from_f64_retain(...).unwrap_or(Decimal::ZERO)` silently maps non-finite or out-of-range f64 results to `Decimal::ZERO` for the mean, CI bounds, and control-comparison metrics. This masks data corruption and can change the verdict (e.g. a large mean turning into 0 triggers Kill in Rule 1). Propagate an error or validate the values before substituting zero.

---

### [low] (bug)

`(experiment_end - experiment_start).num_days() as u32` silently wraps a negative `i64` into a huge `u32` when `experiment_end < experiment_start` (e.g. swapped inputs). This bypasses the `duration_days < self.min_days` Inconclusive guard and can produce a Go/Kill decision on invalid data. Validate the time ordering (and the cast) before proceeding.

```suggestion
        let duration_days = if experiment_end >= experiment_start {
            (experiment_end - experiment_start).num_days() as u32
        } else {
            return VerdictResult {
                verdict: Verdict::Inconclusive,
                ..Default::default()
            };
        };
```

## operator/src/handlers/api.rs (12 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

`get_dead_letter_entries(1, 0)` fetches only the FIRST dead-letter row, so `find()` can only ever match that one item — any other `trade_uuid` in the queue will always 404. The endpoint should look the item up by `trade_uuid` (pass the uuid to the DB query) instead of scanning a single row. Additionally, unlike sibling operator endpoints (`update_wallet`, `retry` docs say “Requires: operator+ role”), this handler has no `AuthExtension` role check; if route-level middleware doesn't enforce roles, unauthenticated/lower-privilege callers could trigger retries.

---

### [high] (bug)

`config_snapshot` is only restored when the final `config.validate()` fails. All earlier `return Err(AppError::Validation(...))` paths (e.g. `webhook_processing_rate_limit > 50`, profit-target ordering, position-sizing range checks, daily_summary hour/minute, load-shed > 100) exit the function directly AFTER earlier fields in the same request have already been mutated in shared memory — those mutations persist without audit entries while the API reports an error. Restore the snapshot on every error path (e.g. a scope guard that reverts unless committed) so a rejected request cannot partially apply.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The `config` read guard is acquired and then held across `notifier.notify(...).await` (and remains alive through the webhook auto-registration block below). A slow Telegram send therefore blocks all `update_config` writers — and every config reader — for the duration of the network I/O. Copy only the needed values (notification rule flag, webhook config, auth header) into locals and drop the guard before any `.await`.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The `let _ =` swallows the kill-switch persistence error: if writing "INACTIVE" to `kill_switch_state` fails, the handler still reports success, and after a restart main.rs may re-trip the circuit breaker from the stale ACTIVE row — exactly the crash-safety scenario this table is designed to prevent. Propagate the error (return 500) so the admin knows the reset is not durable.

```suggestion
    state
        .db
        .set_kill_switch_state("INACTIVE", None)
        .await
        .map_err(|e| AppError::Internal(format!("Failed to persist kill-switch reset: {}", e)))?;
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The in-memory config is already mutated (and the write lock released) before these audit writes run. If any `log_config_change` fails, the handler returns an error while the config has already changed — the API state and the audit trail diverge, and a client retrying the same request sees the new values (partial/duplicated application). Consider writing the audit entries atomically with the update, or at least warn-and-continue / return a distinct partial-failure status so the divergence is visible.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`ttl_hours` is accepted as `i64` and converted with `as i32` without a range check: any value above `i32::MAX` truncates/wraps and produces an unintended demotion TTL. Also, negative values are never rejected. Validate the range (e.g. `0..=some_max`) and use `i32::try_from(h)` returning `AppError::Validation` on overflow.

---

### [medium] (security)

`date_from`/`date_to` come directly from user query params (`from`/`to`) and are interpolated into the `Content-Disposition` header. URL-decoded CR/LF (e.g. `%0D%0A`) produces an invalid `HeaderValue`, and axum's `(HeaderName, &str)` header path panics on invalid values — a crafted `from`/`to` can crash the request handler (and, if the value were accepted, inject response headers). Sanitize the filename inputs (strip control characters/quotes) or build the header with `HeaderValue::from_str(...)` and return a `400` on failure.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`update_config` stores `hard_stop_loss` as a NEGATIVE percentage in `max_stop_loss_distance` (per the comment: -25.0 means 25% loss), but this GET path returns the raw stored value, so clients see `hard_stop_loss: -25.0`. That breaks round-tripping — PUT rejects negatives with a validation error — and misleads any dashboard. Negate on read (or store positive) so GET and PUT use the same sign convention.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`successful_count` is computed only from `run_responses` — which were fetched with `limit` (default 10) — while the denominator `total` comes from `count_reconciliation_runs()` over ALL runs. Once history exceeds the limit, the reported success rate is wrong (e.g. 10 successes in the last 10 fetched runs / 1000 total runs = 1%). Compute the success rate over the same population (e.g. query completed-run count from the DB) or explicitly document that it is windowed.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`RECONCILIATION_RUNNING` is reset only on the normal completion path of the spawned task. If `run_reconciliation` panics (or the task is aborted during shutdown), the flag stays `true` forever, so every subsequent manual trigger fails with `Duplicate` until process restart. Make the reset panic-safe — e.g. a small RAII guard whose `Drop` clears the flag — instead of a bare `store(false)` after the `await`.

---

### [low] (other)

This admin endpoint performs no actual cache clearing (all counters hard-coded to 0, `liquidity_cleared` unused beyond the log) yet always returns success and logs “Monitoring caches cleared successfully”. Returning a misleading success for a no-op is worse than an explicit 501/410. Either implement the clearing or remove/disable the route. Additionally, the doc comment above this function describes `debug_backtest_smoke` (endpoint path and purpose), so the documentation is attached to the wrong handler.

---

### [low] (security)

`limit` is only clamped with `.min(1000)`, so a negative value (e.g. `limit=-1`) is passed straight through — and since `get_trades_filtered` treats `-1` as “no limit” (see `export_trades`), a readonly caller can bypass pagination and dump the entire trades table. Clamp to at least 1 (e.g. `params.limit.unwrap_or(100).max(1).min(1000)`) and reject negative `offset` as well.

```suggestion
    let limit = params.limit.unwrap_or(100).max(1).min(1000);
    let offset = params.offset.unwrap_or(0).max(0);
```

---

## operator/src/handlers/health.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (performance)

Every health request executes two DB queries with no timeout: `get_trade_statistics()` (a full-table `COUNT`/`SUM` aggregation over `trades`, which grows with table size) and `get_recent_trades(1, 0)`. Load balancers typically poll health endpoints every few seconds, so this adds measurable load to an already struggling DB, and if a query *hangs* rather than erroring, the health endpoint hangs indefinitely — the grace window only triggers on errors, not on stalls. Consider caching probe results with a background refresh, wrapping calls in `tokio::time::timeout`, or using a cheap `SELECT 1` for liveness.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Circuit-breaker snapshot is not atomic: `status()` and `is_trading_allowed()` each acquire the internal `RwLock` in separate reads. If the breaker trips or recovers between the two calls, the response can expose contradictory state (e.g., `state` reports Tripped/Cooldown while `trading_allowed` is true, or vice versa), and `overall_status` is computed from the earlier `cb_status` snapshot. Derive `trading_allowed` from the same `cb_status` snapshot so the response is internally consistent.

```suggestion
    let cb_status = state.circuit_breaker.status();
    let circuit_breaker_health = CircuitBreakerHealth {
        state: cb_status.state.to_string(),
        trading_allowed: cb_status.state == CircuitBreakerState::Active,
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

A complete RPC outage can never make the overall status `Unhealthy`: `rpc_health.status == Unhealthy` only maps to `Degraded`, and `Unhealthy`/HTTP 503 is reserved for DB failures. Since trading is impossible without a working RPC endpoint, this can mask a critical outage to load balancers and operators (they keep seeing 200). Consider mapping persistent RPC failure to `Unhealthy` (optionally with the same grace-window treatment as the DB check), or document why a full RPC outage is intentionally only `Degraded`.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`health_simple` unconditionally returns 200. If load balancers are pointed at `/health` as stated in its doc comment, it will never signal unavailability — a node with a dead DB, tripped circuit breaker, or broken RPC still reports OK, defeating the purpose of a readiness probe. Either route load balancers to `/api/v1/health` (which does return 503 when unhealthy) or make `health_simple` accept `AppState` and reuse the same overall-status computation.

---

### [low] (test)

This boundary test is a tautology: it calls `determine_db_grace_status(now, now)` twice and asserts the two identical results are equal, so it can never fail and doesn't validate the grace-window boundary. Replace it with a real boundary assertion, e.g. `Degraded` at `now - (DB_GRACE_WINDOW_SECS - 1)` and `Unhealthy` at `now - DB_GRACE_WINDOW_SECS`.

---

## operator/src/handlers/mod.rs (2 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

All 12 submodules are re-exported via `pub use *` globs, making the crate's public surface implicit and collision-prone. If any two submodules ever export a name with the same spelling (very likely given the overlapping domains here, e.g. `webhook` vs `webhook_lifecycle`, `monitoring` vs `api` config types), the resulting ambiguity (E0659) only surfaces at each call site as a confusing compile error, and every new `pub` item silently expands the public API. Note the `ws` module was deliberately given an explicit re-export list instead of a glob — the same discipline should be applied to the other modules (or at least a CI check enforcing unique exported names) so the re-export surface stays intentional and auditable.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`profitability` is the only submodule declared `pub mod`; the rest are private `mod` whose items are surfaced exclusively through the `pub use` globs. As a result, `handlers::profitability::evaluate_gates` becomes a second, unintended public entry point alongside `handlers::evaluate_gates`, while equivalent types in the other modules are only reachable through the re-export. Change this to `mod profitability;` for a uniform, single-path public surface (the glob re-export on line 21 already exposes everything needed).

```suggestion
mod profitability;
```

---

## operator/src/handlers/profitability.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Admitted BUY decisions with a non-NULL trade_uuid whose trade is not CLOSED (e.g. still OPEN/CANCELLED), whose side is not SELL, or whose `pnl_data_valid` is NULL are silently dropped here: `fetch_outcomes` requires `t.status='CLOSED' AND t.pnl_data_valid=TRUE AND t.side='SELL'`, while `count_invalid_pnl` only counts `pnl_data_valid=FALSE`. `count_missing_outcomes` only counts `trade_uuid IS NULL`. So a material share of incomplete trades is neither part of the outcome sample nor counted against integrity — the integrity gate can report PASS on incomplete data and the verdict is computed on a biased subset. Consider a LEFT JOIN over admitted BUY decisions that counts every row without a qualifying closed/valid SELL outcome (and treat NULL `pnl_data_valid` as invalid).

---

### [high] (bug)

When no run_id is provided and `state.run_context` is None, `unwrap_or_default()` yields an empty string, and the SQL predicate `($1 = '' OR dr.run_id = $1)` treats an empty run_id as "match every run". The verdict then aggregates decision_records/trades across all unrelated runs while the completeness counter reflects only the current run — mixing scopes in a single verdict, contrary to the "defaults to the current run" documentation. Return an explicit error (or STOP/INCONCLUSIVE) when a run cannot be resolved, or change the SQL so an empty run_id matches nothing.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`confidence_interval` only ever returns PASS or INCONCLUSIVE, and the verdict precedence treats INCONCLUSIVE as "insufficient evidence". A run whose returns are clearly and significantly negative (upper CI below the threshold) therefore never produces a FAIL/STOP — a persistently losing strategy can never be halted by this gate, and the response's `net_return.status` can never indicate failure. Add a FAIL branch when the upper bound is below `NET_RETURN_THRESHOLD` and make the overall verdict treat that net FAIL as a halt (STOP) rather than INCONCLUSIVE.

```suggestion
    let status = if lower > NET_RETURN_THRESHOLD {
        "PASS"
    } else if upper < NET_RETURN_THRESHOLD {
        "FAIL"
    } else {
        "INCONCLUSIVE"
    };
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Max drawdown orders cumulative PnL by `dr.decided_at` (decision time) rather than the trade close time at which the PnL is actually realized. Execution lag between decision and close can reorder PnL events and materially distort the drawdown gate. `fetch_outcomes` doesn't even select a close timestamp — add `t.close_time` (or the equivalent close column) to the outcome query and sort by it here.

---

### [medium] (security)

When `state.decision_recorder` is None the completeness gate is hardcoded to PASS (`(1.0, true)`). "No recorder → no evidence of loss" fails open for a go/no-go safety gate: a deployment where the recorder was never wired up silently disables the completeness check while the verdict still reports a PASS. Consider failing closed (FAIL/INCONCLUSIVE) or requiring the recorder to be present before serving the verdict.

---

### [low] (security)

Fail-open in the bias gate: if no outcome carries a `price_impact_pct` value, `declared_bias` defaults to 0.0 and the gate passes. Missing bias data is thereby treated as zero bias, so an unpopulated/broken `price_impact_pct` column silently makes this gate always PASS. Consider reporting INCONCLUSIVE (or FAIL) when `bias_vals` is empty instead of 0.0/PASS.

---

## operator/src/handlers/risk.rs (9 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

The `loss_prevented_sol` aggregate can be (partially) negative: the WHERE clause admits exits up to `stop_loss_price * 1.01`, so when `exit_price` is slightly above the stop price, `(stop_loss_price - exit_price)` is negative and *reduces* the reported total. The same formula is reused in the by-strategy query. Clamp each term with `GREATEST(et.stop_loss_price - p.exit_price, 0)` (or restrict the filter to `exit_price <= stop_loss_price`) so an overshoot does not cancel out loss prevented by other positions.

---

### [high] (bug)

`loss_prevented_sol` for recent activations uses a hardcoded `0.01` multiplier instead of the position quantity used by the aggregate query (`(stop - exit) * entry_amount_sol / entry_price`). The two sets of numbers are therefore not comparable and the per-activation value is essentially arbitrary. Select `entry_amount_sol` in the recent-rows query and compute `(stop - exit) * entry_amount_sol / entry_price` (clamped to >= 0) for consistency.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`hit_rate` is hardcoded to 100.0 for every strategy, making the per-strategy hit-rate metric meaningless. The query only returns rows that already hit at least one target, so it cannot derive a hit rate. Compute it separately per strategy (e.g., hits / total closed positions grouped by strategy) or drop the field until it can be measured.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`total_targets` is populated from `total_closed_count` (the number of closed positions), which does not match the documented meaning of "total targets". The field should represent the number of profit targets in the period (e.g., SUM(jsonb_array_length(targets_hit))), or the response field should be renamed/re-documented. Note `StrategyProfitTargetData.total_hits` is likewise a count of positions, not targets.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`target_level` is set to `jsonb_array_length(targets_hit)`, i.e., the *count* of targets hit, not the level reached. If the array holds non-contiguous levels (e.g. `[1, 3]`), the reported level (2) is wrong, and if a target can be hit more than once the count is not a level at all. Extract the actual (e.g., max) target level from the `targets_hit` array instead.

---

### [medium] (bug)

For an even number of positions, `OFFSET COUNT(*)/2 LIMIT 1` returns only the upper of the two middle elements; the median of an even-sized dataset should be the average of the two middle values. Also the median is a separate full sort from the stats query. Use `percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY entry_amount_sol)` (single pass, handles even counts correctly) instead of the OFFSET trick.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Wallet balance silently degrades on failure: a DB error from `get_total_realized_pnl()` becomes `Decimal::ZERO`, a failed `f64 -> Decimal` conversion of exposure becomes `ZERO`, and a failed `to_f64()` becomes `0.0`. The endpoint returns a 200 with an arbitrarily wrong balance instead of an error. Since this handler already returns `AppResult`, propagate the DB error with `?` and handle the decimal conversions explicitly (e.g., a typed error on `try_from` failure) rather than substituting zero.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`max_drawdown_percent` in both `ExposureData` and `DrawdownData` is always equal to `current_drawdown_percent`: `get_max_drawdown_percent()` returns the drawdown at the *current* point (peak PnL vs. current PnL), and the handler assigns that same value to both fields (since `exposure.max_drawdown_percent` is initialized to 0.0). Consequently the response never reports the historical worst drawdown, `drawdown_duration_days` is always 0.0, and `recovery_percent` is always 0 while in a drawdown. Track the peak (worst) drawdown separately from the current one, or document that these are both current values.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`kelly_criterion_usage` is a hardcoded placeholder (`0.0`) that is exposed as a real metric in the public API response. Consumers may mistake the constant zero for an actual computed value. Either implement the metric, omit it from the response, or use an `Option<f64>`/explicit null so clients can distinguish "not computed" from a real zero.

---

## operator/src/handlers/scout.rs (14 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

`very_high` (ACTIVE, updated within 1 hour) is a strict subset of `high` (ACTIVE, updated within 24 hours), so both are summed into `total_entries` and the derived hit/miss rates and `cache_efficiency` are inflated/double-counted. Make the categories mutually exclusive, e.g. `high` = updated > 1 hour AND <= 24 hours.

---

### [high] (bug)

This predicate overlaps the `low` bucket (CANDIDATE, updated <= 7 days, which is also <= 30 days) and `medium` (CANDIDATE updated > 7 days but <= 30 days), so `inactive` double-counts rows already tallied elsewhere; `REJECTED` rows may also satisfy other buckets' status/date conditions. The activity categories are not mutually exclusive, corrupting `total_entries` and all derived efficiency metrics.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The bucket query uses half-open [min, max) semantics (`wqs_score >= $1 AND wqs_score < $2`), so the last "80-100" bucket excludes any wallet with `wqs_score == 100`, and out-of-range scores (< 0 or > 100) are silently dropped. The reported bucket percentages can therefore sum to less than 100%. Use an inclusive upper bound for the final bucket (e.g., `wqs_score <= 100.0`) or add an explicit `>= 100` bucket, and ideally compute all buckets in a single GROUP BY query.

---

### [medium] (bug)

This endpoint returns hard-coded simulated budget figures as if they were live production data. API consumers (dashboards, alerting) may act on fabricated numbers, and `usage_percentage` can exceed 100% when `credits_used > monthly_credits` since it is not clamped. Either wire this to the real budget manager or return an explicit "not implemented"/503 response instead of plausible-but-fake data.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Hard-coded simulated allocation (`total_budget: 5000`, fixed 70/20 split, fabricated `roi_score` values and credit multipliers) is returned as live HighConvictionAllocator data. Prefer reading from the real allocator, or return a not-implemented error rather than fabricated numbers that callers will trust.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`total_credits_allocated` is set to only the high-conviction portion (70% of `total_budget`), ignoring the `emerging` and `reserve` buckets listed in `budget_remaining`; `average_credits_per_wallet` then divides that same high-conviction-only budget by `total_wallets_analyzed` (which spans all buckets). Sum the three allocations (or use `total_budget`) so the summary is internally consistent with the breakdown.

---

### [medium] (bug)

This handler returns a successful `run_id`/`scheduled_at` without actually scheduling or invoking any Scout run — callers will believe a run was triggered when nothing happened. Either implement real scheduling (enqueue in a run-request table and signal the Scout process) or return an explicit not-implemented error so clients can distinguish a real trigger from a placeholder.

---

### [medium] (bug)

When no wallet has ever been analyzed, `last_run_at` defaults to the current wall-clock time, making the API claim Scout just ran. Change the field to `Option<String>` and return `None` (or an explicit "never" sentinel) when there is no analysis history.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`notes` and `wqs_score` are likely nullable columns, but they are decoded as non-null `String`/`f64`; a single row with NULL in either column makes `fetch_all` fail with a DB decode error and the entire endpoint returns 500. Use `COALESCE(notes, '')` / `COALESCE(wqs_score, 0)` in the SQL or decode into `Option<String>`/`Option<f64>` and handle absence. The same applies to the rejection queue query.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Deriving "completed" merely from the existence of any wallet rows misrepresents the actual Scout process state, which could be running, failed, or never executed. Track real run state (or return an explicit unknown/not-tracked value) instead of fabricating the status.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`backtest_success_rate` and `validation_pass_rate` divide by `total_analyzed`, which includes REJECTED and CANDIDATE wallets that were never backtested or promoted, producing misleadingly low percentages. Divide by the relevant populations instead (e.g., wallets with backtest results for the success rate, and ACTIVE+CANDIDATE for the validation pass rate).

---

### [medium] (bug)

Same denominator problem as `backtest_success_rate`: `validation_passed` (ACTIVE wallets) is divided by `total_analyzed` (ACTIVE + CANDIDATE + REJECTED), so the pass rate is systematically understated. Use the ACTIVE + CANDIDATE population (or whichever set actually underwent validation) as the denominator.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Comment says "2.5x multiplier" but the code applies `saturating_mul(2)`. Either correct the comment or the multiplier so the reported `credits_used` matches the intended policy.

---

### [low] (performance)

This loop issues one COUNT query per bucket plus a separate total-count query — six round trips per request. Compute all buckets and the total in a single GROUP BY / conditional-aggregation query to avoid the N+1 pattern on a request path.

## operator/src/handlers/signals.rs (7 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

`cutoff_str` (an RFC3339 string like `2026-08-02T00:59:00+00:00`) is interpolated into SQL without quotes or a bind parameter. PostgreSQL rejects this as a syntax error (`created_at >= 2026-08-02...`), so all three queries in this handler fail and the `.unwrap_or(...)` fallbacks silently return defaults (0, (0,0), 50.0) — the entire /quality endpoint returns meaningless data. Use a parameterized query and bind the timestamp, e.g. `sqlx::query_scalar("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM trades WHERE created_at >= $1").bind(cutoff)`, and propagate the error instead of defaulting.

```suggestion
    let total_signals: i64 =
        sqlx::query_scalar("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM trades WHERE created_at >= $1")
            .bind(cutoff)
            .fetch_one(&pool)
            .await
            .unwrap_or(0);
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The result of `get_active_clusters(...)` is stored in `_active_clusters` and then discarded; the response hard-codes `active_clusters: Vec::new()`, so GET /signals/consensus always returns an empty cluster list even when clusters exist. `get_wallet_clustering` has the same pattern (`_clusters` is dropped and `clusters: Vec::new()` is returned). Additionally, `get_active_clusters` actually returns `Vec<QualityTrendPoint>` (hourly WQS averages), not `Vec<Cluster>`, so the helper can't be wired in as-is — and it issues 24 sequential DB queries per request. Fix the helper to return real `Cluster` data and populate the response fields.

---

### [high] (bug)

`&token_address[..8]` is a byte slice, not a character slice: it panics if `token_address` is shorter than 8 bytes, and can also panic mid-way through a multi-byte UTF-8 character (slicing at a non-char boundary). Since `token_address` comes from database data, a short or non-ASCII address crashes the handler. Use safe truncation, e.g. `token_address.chars().take(8).collect::<String>()` or `token_address.get(..8).unwrap_or(&token_address)` (same issue on the `sellers_` line below).

```suggestion
                cluster_id: format!("holders_{}", token_address.chars().take(8).collect::<String>()),
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`COUNT(*)` is cast to `INTEGER` (PostgreSQL INT4 / i32) but the row is decoded as `i64` (BIGINT). sqlx's strict type checking rejects decoding an INT4 column into `i64`, so `try_get("signal_count")` errors and `unwrap_or(0)` silently sets every wallet's signal count to 0. Use `COUNT(*)` directly (already BIGINT) or decode as `i32`.

```suggestion
            COUNT(*) as signal_count,
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`MAX(t.created_at)` returns a TIMESTAMPTZ, but the row is decoded into a Rust `String`; sqlx cannot decode a timestamp column as `String` (unlike the other queries in this file, which cast `created_at::text` precisely for this reason — see lines 222/390), so `try_get("last_signal_at")` fails and `unwrap_or_default()` silently yields an empty string for every source. Cast in SQL (`MAX(t.created_at)::text`) or decode into a timestamp type.

```suggestion
            MAX(t.created_at)::text as last_signal_at,
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

`.unwrap_or_default()` on `fetch_all` converts real database/query failures into empty responses, so API consumers cannot distinguish a DB outage from a legitimate "no signals" result. The same pattern is used for `query_scalar`/`query_as` throughout this file (`.unwrap_or(0.0)`, `.unwrap_or((0, 0))`, etc.), which also hides the unquoted-timestamp bug above. Prefer propagating `AppError` with context so failures surface; reserve defaults for genuinely optional values.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The documented contract says `divergence_type` is one of `"directional" | "timing" | "amount"`, but the code emits `"directional_bullish"` / `"directional_bearish"`, and the field is serialized under the misleading name `divergence_score`. Also `severity` and `wallets_clustered` are `skip_serializing`, so the API never returns the alert severity or the clustered-wallet breakdown. Align the serialized shape and value set with the documented API.
