## operator/src/handlers/webhook.rs (7 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

If `update_trade_status(DEAD_LETTER)` fails here, the `?` propagates the DB error before the DLQ insert runs. The trade is then stuck in PENDING (it was inserted as PENDING earlier), has no DLQ audit entry, and the client receives a 500 that masks the original queue error. A subsequent retry would be rejected as "duplicate" (row exists in `trades`), silently losing the trade. Since the comment above calls the status update authoritative, treat its failure as a non-fatal but serious condition: log it, still attempt the DLQ insert, and return the original queue error to the client.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`get_token_decimals` returns `None` on RPC failure or for unknown tokens, and that `None` is stored as-is, leaving `signal.token_decimals` unset. Downstream, the executor's `lamports_per_base_to_sol_per_token` then silently falls back to 9 decimals — producing wrong SOL amounts for USDC/USDT (6 decimals), exactly the mispricing the `[B-M1]` comment above warns about. A fetch failure should not be silently equivalent to "token uses default decimals": when decimals are required but could not be resolved, reject the signal or force the slow-path/retry instead of proceeding with the default.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Check-then-act race: `trade_uuid_exists` followed by `insert_trade` is not atomic. Two concurrent identical webhooks can both pass the duplicate check and both run the full selection pipeline. The DB schema does enforce `UNIQUE` on `trades.trade_uuid`, so the loser's `insert_trade` fails with a unique-violation that surfaces as `AppError::Database` (HTTP 500) via the `?` — instead of the PDD-shaped `duplicate_signal` response, and no DLQ entry is written. Make dedupe atomic (e.g. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (trade_uuid) DO NOTHING` and treat 0 affected rows as the duplicate path) so the losing request gets a clean duplicate response.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The dedupe key from `generate_trade_uuid` is only `SHA256(wallet|token|action|amount)` — strategy, `token_address`, and `exit_fraction` are not included. Two distinct signals (e.g. a SHIELD and a SPEAR for the same wallet/token/action/amount, or the same symbol resolving to different `token_address`es) therefore hash to the same UUID, so the second legitimate signal is wrongly rejected as `duplicate_signal` and never executed. Either extend the UUID derivation to include the full request semantics or, before rejecting here, verify the existing trade actually matches the incoming payload.

---

### [low] (security)

Silently substituting `Utc::now()` when `X-Timestamp` is missing or unparseable defeats the middleware's drift/replay protection if the middleware guarantee ever changes (the handler is only safe today because hmac.rs rejects missing/invalid/expired timestamps with 401/400). For defense in depth, return an error here instead of accepting the request with server time — otherwise a stale/retried webhook without a valid header is accepted and stamped with a fresh server timestamp.

---

### [low] (bug)

The DLQ insert error is discarded with `let _` and never logged. If this best-effort write fails, a rejected signal leaves no server-side audit trail at all (the client only sees the 400). At minimum log the failure at warn level so rejections remain traceable.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Circuit-breaker and validation-failure responses return an empty `trade_uuid`, while every other rejection path returns the real UUID. Return a correlation/trade identifier here as well so clients can consistently correlate rejections (and so dedupe/audit can trace them).

---

## operator/src/handlers/webhook_lifecycle.rs (7 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (security)

`get_webhook_stats` is the only handler in this file that omits the `auth.0.role.has_permission(Role::Operator)` check. The router applies only `bearer_auth` middleware, which authenticates but does not authorize (role enforcement here is per-handler, as every other webhook lifecycle handler does it inline). As a result any authenticated user — including Readonly and even anonymous users when `allow_anonymous_readonly` is enabled — can read internal webhook statistics, leaking monitoring data. Add the same operator-role check used by the sibling endpoints.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`get_webhook_url` returns an empty string when the `monitoring` config is absent or `helius_webhook_url` is unset. That empty string is then used to build `WebhookLifecycleConfig` (bulk/retry/toggle) and passed directly to `reconcile_internal`/`health_check_internal`, which perform external Helius calls — producing requests against an invalid URL instead of a clear error. Validate that the URL is non-empty at the handler boundary and return `AppError::Validation` when the config is missing.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`BulkRegisterRequest.force_recreate` is deserialized (with `#[serde(default)]`) but never forwarded to `WebhookLifecycleManager::bulk_register_webhooks` — only `request.wallets` is passed. Callers that set `force_recreate: true` get silently different behavior than requested. Either thread the flag through to the manager (and the underlying Helius call) or remove the field so the API doesn't advertise an option it ignores.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

This `WebhookLifecycleConfig` is hand-built with hard-coded values (`health_check_interval_secs: 3600`, `stale_threshold_days: 7`, `max_registration_retries: 3`) in four handlers (bulk-register, bulk-cleanup, retry, toggle). This ignores `state.config.monitoring.webhook_lifecycle`, so admin operations can disagree with the configured policy — note that `manual_health_check` above reads `stale_threshold_days` from config, so the same endpoint family uses inconsistent thresholds. Build the config from the actual monitoring config (ideally via one shared helper) instead of duplicating hard-coded values.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Both branches (failed result and hard error) return `Ok(StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)`, bypassing the `AppError` machinery that every other handler in this file uses. Clients receive a bare 500 with no error body, and a transient registration failure is indistinguishable from a real server failure. Return `Err(AppError::...)` (or map to an appropriate status) so the error context reaches the caller.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`toggle_wallet_webhook` maps every error to `Ok(StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)`, so not-found / validation-type failures are indistinguishable from server failures and the error detail is lost from the response. Return `Err(AppError::...)` instead of swallowing the error into an `Ok()` status code, consistent with the other handlers.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`WebhookStatsResponse` is defined but never used anywhere — the stats handler returns `ApiResponse<WebhookStats>` instead. Remove this dead struct (or use it) to avoid confusion about the actual response type.

## operator/src/handlers/ws.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (security)

Security: the authenticated user identifier embeds the full API key secret (`api_key:<token>`). This identifier is later logged at info level in `ws_handler` (`identifier = %identifier`) and repeatedly in `handle_socket` and both spawned tasks (`user = %user_id`), so the raw credential is written to logs. Use a non-sensitive identifier (e.g., a hash of the token or a stored key name) for the authenticated user.

---

### [high] (security)

Authorization bypass: when anonymous readonly access is enabled, the connection is created with only `Some("anonymous")` and no role is attached. The broadcast loop in `handle_socket` sends every `WsEvent` (positions, trades, alerts) to every client regardless of identity or role — the readonly restriction is defeated, and even authenticated readonly users would receive the full stream because the role obtained in `authenticate()` is only logged, never used for filtering. Thread the user's role into `handle_socket` and filter events (or reject subscription) based on it.

---

### [high] (bug)

Panic risk: `&token[..token.len().min(8)]` performs a byte-indexed slice. If the first 8 bytes of the token are not a UTF-8 character boundary (e.g., a token containing multi-byte UTF-8), this panics, and a remote client can trigger it by sending a crafted token in the query string. Use `token.get(..token.len().min(8))` or `token.chars().take(8)` instead (also note the same slice is repeated at the 'invalid token' log line).

```suggestion
    tracing::info!(token_prefix = %token.chars().take(8).collect::<String>(), "WebSocket connection attempt");
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Task leak / incomplete cleanup: `tokio::select!` moves the `JoinHandle`s into the branches, and when one branch completes the losing future is dropped, which only *detaches* the other spawned task rather than cancelling it. If the send task fails first (client gone), the recv task keeps polling the split receiver and may keep the socket half open; if the recv task exits, the send task keeps waiting on `rx`. Connection cleanup is never joined or cancelled. Abort the losing task after the `select!` (e.g., using `&mut` handles and `JoinHandle::abort()`) so both halves are dropped deterministically.

```suggestion
    tokio::select! {
        _ = &mut send_task => {
            recv_task.abort();
        }
        _ = &mut recv_task => {
            send_task.abort();
        }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Data correctness: `decimal.to_f64().unwrap_or(0.0)` silently converts a Decimal that cannot be represented as f64 (NaN, overflow -> None) into a misleading `0.0` in outgoing real-time data, and serializing Decimal as f64 generally loses precision for large values — problematic for financial position/trade data. Prefer serializing as a string (preserves exactness) or handle the `None` case explicitly instead of defaulting to zero.

```suggestion
        Some(decimal) => serializer.serialize_str(&decimal.to_string()),
```

---

### [low] (bug)

Slow clients are silently disconnected: `rx.recv()` returns `Err(Lagged(_))` once the receiver falls more than the channel capacity (100) behind, and since the loop only continues on `Ok`, the send task simply ends and the client is dropped without a close frame or any notice. If dropping slow consumers is intended, consider logging it; otherwise handle `Lagged` by catching up to the latest event or sending a close message so the disconnect is explicit.

---

## operator/src/jupiter_error_handling.rs (8 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

The retry loops retry every `AppError` unconditionally; the `JupiterError` classification and its `retryable` flag are never consulted. Non-retryable failures (bad request 400, auth 401/403, parse errors) will be retried with backoff, adding latency, masking client bugs, and generating avoidable load. The operation should be classified first (e.g., match on `JupiterError`/`JupiterErrorType` or expose retryability on `AppError`) and only transient errors retried.

---

### [high] (bug)

Same issue in the circuit-breaker variant: every `AppError` (including non-transient ones) is retried with backoff. The retryable classification is never used to decide whether to retry, so a permanent bad request or parse failure still burns all retries and adds latency.

---

### [medium] (bug)

After retries are exhausted, the original `AppError` variant and context are discarded — only `e.to_string()` survives and is re-wrapped in `AppError::Internal`. Callers can no longer distinguish a rate-limit (429), timeout, or server error, so they cannot react appropriately. Keep the last `AppError` object and return it directly (e.g., `last_error.unwrap_or_else(...)`) instead of flattening it to a string and reclassifying it. This applies to both `retry_with_backoff` and `retry_with_circuit_breaker`.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The circuit breaker records every failure using `e.to_string()`, which flattens away the error classification (`JupiterErrorType`). Consequently non-transient errors (bad request, auth, parse) also increment the consecutive-failure counter and can trip the breaker, and diagnostics only see an opaque string. Record only transient failures and pass a classified error type (e.g., derive it from `JupiterErrorType`) so the breaker and logs can distinguish recoverable from permanent failures.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`cb.record_jupiter_failure(error_type)?` propagates a circuit-breaker-side error (e.g., poisoned lock) directly via `?`, silently discarding the original operation error; the caller is left with an unrelated error and no context about the Jupiter failure. Similarly, the tripped path returns a generic `AppError::Internal` message that drops `last_error`. Preserve the original error by attaching context instead of `?` (e.g., map_err to wrap `e`), and include the original error when reporting a trip.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Unclassified statuses (including 4xx client errors such as 404, 422, 409) default to `retryable: true`, so client-side bugs will be retried with backoff, masking the root cause and adding load. Classify known 4xx codes as non-retryable and only default unknown 5xx / network-level statuses to retryable.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Mapping an authentication failure to `AppError::Config(ConfigError::Message(..))` is semantically wrong — an upstream 401/403 is a runtime/API credential problem, not a configuration problem. This misclassification can trigger config-oriented handling paths (e.g., config reload/validation logic) downstream. Use a dedicated error variant (e.g., an auth/permission variant) instead.

---

### [low] (bug)

`attempt as i32 - 1` underflows for `attempt == 0` (public function with no documented precondition). While the retry loops start at 1, a zero/out-of-range attempt silently yields a sub-initial or fractional delay. Use saturating arithmetic (`attempt.saturating_sub(1)`) or clamp `attempt` to >= 1.

---

## operator/src/jupiter_http_client.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

The running average is computed from `metrics.total_requests`, but that counter is only incremented by `update_request_status`, not by `record_request_duration` itself. The sample count is therefore wrong, and when `total_requests == 0` the term `total_requests - 1.0` becomes `-1.0`, producing a negative multiplier. Example: recording durations 100 then 200 yields avg = 100 instead of 150. Track a dedicated sample counter (e.g., add `duration_samples` to `ClientMetrics`) and use `avg = (avg * n + x) / (n + 1)`.

```suggestion
        // Update rolling average using a dedicated sample counter
        let n = metrics.duration_samples as f64;
        metrics.avg_request_duration_ms =
            (metrics.avg_request_duration_ms * n + duration_ms as f64) / (n + 1.0);
        metrics.duration_samples += 1;
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Check-then-act race: `health_check` snapshots `consecutive_failures` under a read lock, releases it, then writes `is_healthy` from that stale value under a separate write lock. If a concurrent `update_request_status(false)` bumps the failure count between the two lock acquisitions, `health_check` overwrites it and can mark the client healthy despite 3+ consecutive failures. Read and write under a single lock acquisition instead.

```suggestion
        // Compute and persist health state under a single lock to avoid stale overwrites
        let mut status = self.health_status.write();
        let is_healthy = status.consecutive_failures < 3;
        status.is_healthy = is_healthy;
        status.last_check = chrono::Utc::now();
        Ok(is_healthy)
```

Wire them into the builder (e.g., `http2_max_concurrent_streams`, `tcp_keepalive`, conditional `pool_max_idle_per_host`) or remove the unused fields.

        let mut builder = Client::builder()
            .timeout(config.request_timeout)
            .connect_timeout(config.connect_timeout)

            builder = builder.pool_max_idle_per_host(config.max_idle_connections_per_host);
        }
        if config.tcp_keepalive {
            builder = builder.tcp_keepalive(config.keep_alive_duration);
        }

        let client = builder.build().map_err(|e| {
```

### [low] (other)

Despite its name, `health_check` performs no network probe — it only re-reads the locally recorded `consecutive_failures` set by `update_request_status`. It cannot detect a dead TCP/TLS connection or an upstream outage that hasn't yet produced 3 recorded failures, so it adds no signal beyond the existing counters (and it always returns `Ok`, making the `AppResult` wrapper unnecessary). Either issue a lightweight real request (e.g., HEAD/OPTIONS to a health endpoint) or rename/document this as a local state evaluation.

The doc comments on these two fields appear swapped: `max_idle_connections` is documented as "per host" while the actual per-host field is `max_idle_connections_per_host` (which is documented as "overall"). Update the comments to match the field names to avoid API confusion.

## operator/src/jupiter_monitoring.rs (7 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

The per-endpoint histogram `jupiter_request_duration_by_endpoint_seconds` is never observed: `record_request` ignores the `_endpoint` argument and only observes `jupiter_request_duration_seconds`. Moreover, the histogram is a plain `Histogram` with a *const* label `endpoint="unknown"`, so even if observed, all endpoints would be lumped into one series and the "by endpoint" breakdown would never work. Use a `HistogramVec` keyed by `endpoint` and observe with the actual endpoint here.

```suggestion
    pub fn record_request(&self, endpoint: &str, duration_secs: f64, success: bool) {
        self.jupiter_requests_total.inc();

        if success {
            self.jupiter_requests_success_total.inc();
        } else {
            self.jupiter_requests_failed_total.inc();
        }

        self.jupiter_request_duration_seconds.observe(duration_secs);
        self.jupiter_request_duration_by_endpoint_seconds
            .with_label_values(&[endpoint])
            .observe(duration_secs);
    }
```

`export_metrics` converts every failure into a normal-looking `String` ("Error exporting metrics: ..." / "Error encoding metrics"). A caller serving this string (e.g. as an HTTP 200 response) would silently break Prometheus scraping instead of signaling an explicit failure. Return `Result<String, prometheus::Error>` and propagate the error so the caller can respond with a non-200 status.

```suggestion
    pub fn export_metrics(&self) -> Result<String, prometheus::Error> {
        use prometheus::Encoder;

        let mut buffer = Vec::new();
        let encoder = prometheus::TextEncoder::new();
        encoder.encode(&self.registry.gather(), &mut buffer)?;
        String::from_utf8(buffer).map_err(|_| {
            prometheus::Error::Msg("gathered metrics are not valid UTF-8".to_string())
        })
    }
```

## operator/src/keypair_utils.rs (4 findings)

### [medium] (security)

A base58 string consisting of 64 '1' characters is valid base58 (each '1' is the digit 0, and bs58 encodes each leading zero byte as '1'), so it decodes to exactly 64 zero bytes. This passes the `bytes.len() != 64` check and is returned as a 'valid' keypair whose Ed25519 secret half is all zeros — a degenerate/weak key that downstream code may import without noticing. Since this helper is the shared import path for both `import_keypair` and `load_wallet_keypair`, consider rejecting all-zero secrets here (or validating the buffer via `Keypair::try_from`) so weak/malformed keys never leave the normalizer.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Only the decoded byte count is validated — the 32-byte public half is never checked against the secret half. A corrupted or mismatched buffer (e.g. a secret from one key paired with a public key from another) is returned as a valid keypair. solana-sdk's `Keypair::try_from` does verify the halves match, but callers of this shared helper must remember to do so. The `base58_86_chars_accepted` test explicitly asserts that mismatched pairs are accepted, so if that is deliberate, at least document at the API boundary that the returned 64 bytes are not guaranteed to form a valid keypair; otherwise derive the pubkey from the secret half and compare before returning.

---

### [low] (documentation)

The wipe guarantee in the module docs is narrower than it reads: the input `&str` is borrowed and never wiped, and the decoder internals (`serde_json`/`hex`/`bs58`) and any temporary copies they make can hold secret bytes until their own drop. `Zeroizing` only covers the decoded `Vec<u8>` and the returned array. If a strong 'secret bytes wiped from memory' guarantee is intended, document precisely what is and isn't wiped so callers don't assume the source text is erased.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The rejection message advertises base58 as '86-88 chars' while the code accepts any length ≤ 88 and defers wrong-length rejection to the later byte-count check. A truncated hex string of ≤88 chars that happens to contain none of the excluded chars (`0`, `O`, `I`, `l`) is silently decoded as base58 and then fails with a confusing 'Decoded keypair is N bytes' error rather than a hex-format error. Consider rewording to 'base58 (up to 88 chars, must decode to 64 bytes)' or validating the decoded length within the branch to produce a clearer message.

## operator/src/main.rs (8 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

DLQ retry ordering bug: Phase 3 marks items `processed_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` (see `update_dlq_items_batch` SQL: `WHERE ... processed_at IS NULL`) *before* Phase 4 re-injects the signal into the engine. If `queue_signal` fails, only the `trades` row is reverted to DEAD_LETTER — the `dead_letter_queue` row stays `processed`, so the item is never picked up by future retry cycles and the signal is silently dropped. Mark items as processed only after a successful `queue_signal`, or clear `processed_at` in the failure/revert path.

---

### [high] (security)

These routes are registered on the unauthenticated `public_api_routes` router (described as "public read-only API routes, no auth required"), yet they perform state changes: `retry_dead_letter_item` rewrites the DLQ row and re-queues a failed trade, and `trigger_scout_run` triggers a scout run. Anyone on the internet can flip a dead-lettered trade back into the queue (potentially leading to real trades) without any authentication. Move these endpoints under `protected_api_routes` (with `bearer_auth`) or at least a POST-specific auth/role check.

---

### [medium] (bug)

When Helius is unavailable, this branch can never share the original metadata cache: `token_fetcher` is an `Arc<TokenMetadataFetcher>` that is also held by `token_parser` (and MonitoringState), so `Arc::try_unwrap(token_fetcher.clone())` always fails (clone raises the refcount ≥ 2) and a brand-new `TokenMetadataFetcher` with a fresh internal cache is built. The background cache updater therefore populates a different metadata cache than the one consumed by `token_parser`, so cached liquidity/metadata stays stale in the hot path. Reuse the existing fetcher's cache (e.g. build the updater fetcher from the same instance / share the metadata cache) instead of constructing an independent one.

---

### [medium] (security)

The webhook rate limiter is constructed from `config.security.webhook_rate_limit`/`webhook_burst_size` but never applied: `_governor_layer` is unused (the `_` prefix suppresses the warning) and the `.layer(governor_layer.clone())` call is commented out. The public `/webhook` endpoint therefore has no rate limiting at all, despite the comment on the limiter claiming it is enabled. Re-enable the layer (or remove the dead limiter) — leaving an unauthenticated, publicly reachable endpoint unbounded is a DoS/abuse risk.

```suggestion
    let governor_layer = tower_governor::GovernorLayer {
        config: governor_conf,
    };
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`build_exit_signal` sizes a full exit from `pos.entry_amount_sol`, which is the *original* entry size. After a partial profit-target exit (`ProfitTargetAction::ExitAmount` -> `build_exit_signal_amount`), the remaining balance is smaller, but the full-exit path (stop-loss, profit-target full exit, force-liquidation) still requests `entry_amount_sol` with `fraction = 1`. This can oversell the remaining position — the exact class of bug the adjacent `build_exit_signal_amount` docstring says was fixed for partial exits. Size full exits from the remaining balance (e.g. reuse `build_exit_signal_amount` with the current remaining amount) or ensure `entry_amount_sol` is decremented after each partial exit.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Many background tasks are spawned with `tokio::spawn` and never added to `task_handles` nor selected on `cancel_token` — notably the PnL refresh task (which performs DB writes every 30s), the price cache updater, and the unified cache updater. On shutdown, `main` only awaits `server_handle` and `task_handles`; the rest are abandoned and aborted mid-write when the runtime is dropped after `main` returns. Track these handles and/or give them a cancellation token and drain them (with the same timeout) during shutdown so in-flight DB writes finish cleanly.

---

### [low] (bug)

`&key_config.key[..key_config.key.len().min(8)]` slices a `String` by raw byte index. For any non-ASCII (multi-byte UTF-8) API key with length ≥ 8 bytes, byte 8 can land in the middle of a character and this panics at startup on untrusted config input. Use a char-boundary-safe prefix (e.g. `key_config.key.chars().take(8).collect::<String>()`) or slice via `get(..n)` with a fallback.

### [low] (bug)

`rent_scavenger_config.interval_secs` (parsed from `RENT_SCAVENGER_INTERVAL_SECS`) is passed to `RentScavenger::new` but the spawned task hardcodes a 6-hour ticker, silently ignoring the configured interval. Use `rent_scavenger_config.interval_secs` in the `tokio::time::interval` duration.

## operator/src/metrics.rs (8 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

The slow-query count is wrong: it takes the cumulative count of the first bucket whose upper bound is >= 100ms. A cumulative count includes every sample up to that bound (including all fast queries), so it over-counts "slow" queries. Worse, `chimera_db_query_latency_ms` is created with the library default buckets whose largest finite bound is 10, so the first bucket >= 100ms is the +Inf bucket — meaning `slow_queries_count` will equal `total_queries_count` for essentially all runs (every query reported as slow). To count queries above the threshold use `total - cumulative count of the last bucket below the threshold`, and give the histogram explicit millisecond-scale buckets so it is actually informative at these latencies.

```suggestion
                        // Count slow queries (> 100ms): total minus cumulative count of the last bucket below the threshold
                        let below_slow = histogram.bucket.iter()
                            .take_while(|b| b.upper_bound() < SLOW_QUERY_THRESHOLD_MS)
                            .last()
                            .map(|b| b.cumulative_count() as u32)
                            .unwrap_or(0);
                        slow_queries_count = sample_count.saturating_sub(below_slow);
```

None of the collectors created by `ExecutionLockMetrics::new()` / `RentScavengerMetrics::new()` are ever registered with a Prometheus `Registry` — confirmed call sites (engine/mod.rs:415, main.rs:1942) only construct them and wrap them in `Arc`. As a result, every counter/histogram recorded by the execution lock and rent scavenger is invisible in /metrics; operators get no data for these subsystems. Fix: have `new()` accept a `&Registry` (or the shared `MetricsState`) and register each collector, or register them centrally at startup so the recorded values are actually scraped.

This file already implements the standard Prometheus `histogram_quantile()` algorithm (`histogram_quantile`/`quantile_from_buckets`) — use it to compute real p95/p99 from the histogram buckets (capture the `histogram` reference while iterating) instead of scaling the mean.

### [medium] (maintainability)

`unwrap_or_else` silently replaces a failed metric with a collector named "dummy", swallowing the initialization error with no log. If the hardcoded name/help were ever rejected (or these metrics were registered, as the unregistered-collector finding suggests), the operator would simply see no data, and multiple "dummy" fallbacks would collide with each other on registration. Prefer returning `Result` (as `MetricsState::new()` does) or at minimum `tracing::error!`/`warn!` on the failure path so instrumentation problems are surfaced instead of hidden.

### [medium] (bug)

`MetricsState::new()` deliberately returns `Result` so the caller can degrade gracefully on a metrics registration failure, but `Default::default()` panics via `expect()`. `Default` is frequently invoked implicitly (`..Default::default()`, struct update syntax, generic bounds), so a registration failure in such a path would crash the whole process rather than degrade. Since `new()` already exists, consider dropping this `Default` impl (tests can call `MetricsState::new().unwrap()` directly) or making it non-panicking to keep the graceful-degradation contract.

### [medium] (bug)

`chimera_db_query_latency_ms` uses the library default histogram buckets, whose largest finite bound is 10. Since observations are recorded in milliseconds, typical DB query latencies (>10ms) all land in the +Inf bucket, making the histogram (and the slow-query/percentile logic in `get_db_query_stats`) effectively useless. Specify explicit millisecond-scale buckets (e.g. 1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000) via `HistogramOpts::buckets(...)`.

## operator/src/middleware/hmac.rs (9 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (security)

Replay protection is process-local: `seen_nonces` lives only in this process's `HmacState`. In a multi-instance / scale-out deployment (or after any restart), a captured signed request can be replayed once per instance within the drift window, defeating replay protection — an attacker who intercepts one valid request can re-deliver it to every replica. If horizontal scaling is supported, the nonce store must be shared (e.g., Redis) or the limitation explicitly documented so operators don't rely on this as a hard replay guard.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`(now - timestamp).abs()` performs unchecked i64 subtraction with an attacker-controlled `timestamp` (any value < ~now - i64::MAX, e.g. `i64::MIN` = "-9223372036854775808", parses and reaches this line before any signature check). Debug builds panic — a cheap remote DoS — and release builds wrap so the computed `drift` is garbage; a crafted timestamp can even land inside the accepted window. Use saturating/checked arithmetic, e.g. `now.saturating_sub(timestamp).abs()`.

```suggestion
    let now = Utc::now().timestamp();
    let drift = now.saturating_sub(timestamp).abs();
```

---

### [medium] (security)

`HmacState::new` accepts an empty secret, unlike `with_rotation` which filters and rejects empty strings. An empty HMAC key is trivially forgeable — anyone who knows the scheme (HMAC-SHA256 over timestamp||body) can produce a valid signature, silently disabling webhook authentication after a misconfiguration. Validate the secret in `new` as well (reject empty, ideally return `Result` like `with_rotation`).

```suggestion
    pub fn new(secret: String, max_drift_secs: i64) -> Self {
        assert!(!secret.is_empty(), "HMAC secret must not be empty");
        Self {
            secrets: Arc::new(vec![secret.into_bytes()]),

```

---

### [medium] (security)

`#[derive(Debug)]` on `HmacState` will print the raw webhook secrets in `secrets` whenever the state is logged or included in an error/debug dump, leaking credential material into logs. Implement `Debug` manually and redact secret bytes (log only the count or a redacted form).

```suggestion
impl std::fmt::Debug for HmacState {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
        f.debug_struct("HmacState")
            .field("secret_count", &self.secrets.len())
            .field("max_drift_secs", &self.max_drift_secs)
            .finish_non_exhaustive()
    }
}
```

---

### [low] (bug)

The comment claims strict `<` matches the rejection gate `drift > max_drift_secs`, but the boundaries actually disagree: the drift gate accepts `drift == max_drift_secs` while `retain` evicts a nonce at exactly `now - ts == max_drift_secs`. A replay arriving exactly at the drift boundary (first request seen at the header timestamp, replay `max_drift_secs` later) passes the drift check but finds its nonce already evicted — a small replay window. Make the two boundaries consistent, e.g. keep entries with `now - *ts <= self.max_drift_secs`.

```suggestion
        store.retain(|_, ts| now - *ts <= self.max_drift_secs);
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

When the nonce store reaches `MAX_NONCE_STORE`, every new (otherwise valid) request is rejected with a generic "Replay detected" 401. This conflates a capacity/DoS condition with an authentication failure: legitimate senders get misleading errors and operators cannot distinguish real replays from store pressure (or a burst of valid traffic). Return a distinct status/reason (e.g. 503 "Too many requests") and emit a metric so the condition is diagnosable.

---

### [low] (security)

The constant-time comparison iterates `max(a_len, b_len)` bytes, so the timing still scales with the submitted signature length: an attacker varying the header length can observe where execution time stops growing and infer the expected digest length (64 hex chars). The comment's claim that length is not leaked is inaccurate. Because the expected value is a fixed-format 64-char hex digest (a public fact), validate the canonical length/format up front and then do a fixed-length comparison — this also bounds per-request comparison work.

```suggestion
fn constant_time_compare(a: &str, b: &str) -> bool {
    // Expected digest is a fixed 64-char lowercase hex string (public format);
    // reject other lengths up front so the compare always runs a fixed length.
    if a.len() != b.len() {
        return false;
    }
    a.as_bytes().ct_eq(b.as_bytes()).into()
}
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`VerifiedTimestamp` is documented as an "extension trait to add the verified timestamp to request extensions", but it is a plain struct that is never inserted into `request.extensions_mut()` nor read anywhere — dead code that misleads readers. Either actually populate `request.extensions_mut().insert(VerifiedTimestamp(timestamp))` and consume it in handlers, or remove the type.

---

### [low] (performance)

Every verified request acquires the global `seen_nonces` mutex and performs an O(n) `retain` scan of the whole store (up to 100k entries), serializing the hot path and making per-request cost grow linearly with store size. Consider periodic/amortized eviction (e.g. a timestamp-keyed `BTreeMap` or ring buffer with sparse cleanup) or sharding the store so per-request work stays bounded.

## operator/src/middleware/rate_limit.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

Direct public connections are rejected outright with `GovernorError::UnableToExtractKey`. In tower_governor this is an extraction failure that short-circuits the request with an error response (typically 500) — it does NOT rate-limit by peer IP. This contradicts the module-level doc which states "Direct connections from public IPs always use the peer address". The comment claims peer addresses are "easily spoofed", which is inaccurate for TCP (the peer socket address cannot be spoofed like a header can). The referenced authentication-based limiting is not implemented anywhere in this file, so the practical effect is that all direct public traffic fails or is unthrottled. Either fall back to the peer IP as the rate-limit key, or explicitly handle this rejection path (e.g., a configured error handler) so the behavior is intentional and documented.

---

### [high] (security)

The `ip.contains('.') || ip.contains(':')` check accepts any string as a rate-limit key without validating it is a real IP address. Values like `1.2.3.4.5`, `garbage:value`, or `example.com` pass this test. A malformed/spoofed proxy header then becomes an arbitrary rate-limit key — and since each distinct string maps to its own governor bucket, an attacker behind a trusted proxy can mint an unbounded number of unique keys to bypass throttling. This applies to all three header branches (X-Real-IP, Forwarded, X-Forwarded-For). Parse the value with `IpAddr::from_str` (or `SocketAddr` where ports can appear) and reject invalid input.

```suggestion
                if let Ok(ip) = header_value.to_str() {
                    let ip = ip.trim();
                    if ip.parse::<IpAddr>().is_ok() {
                        return Ok(ip.to_string());
                    }
                }
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The RFC 7239 `Forwarded` parsing is incorrect for multi-hop chains. `Forwarded: for=1.2.3.4, for=5.6.7.8` splits on ';' into a single element, so `strip_prefix("for=")` leaves `"1.2.3.4, for=5.6.7.8"` — the whole remainder becomes the key. That both yields an unstable/garbage key and selects the leftmost (client-supplied) value instead of the trusted proxy's rightmost value, inconsistent with the XFF rightmost rule. It also fails to strip brackets/ports for IPv6 (`for="[2001:db8::1]:8080"`). Split on ',' first, take the last hop element, then parse the `for=` parameter as `IpAddr`/`SocketAddr`.

```suggestion
            if let Some(header_value) = req.headers().get("Forwarded") {
                if let Ok(header_str) = header_value.to_str() {
                    // Last element is closest to the trusted proxy.
                    if let Some(last_hop) = header_str.split(',').next_back() {
                        for part in last_hop.split(';') {
                            let part = part.trim();
                            if let Some(ip_raw) = part.strip_prefix("for=") {
                                let ip = ip_raw
                                    .trim_matches('"')
                                    .trim()
                                    .trim_start_matches('[')
                                    .trim_end_matches(']');
                                if let Ok(addr) = ip.parse::<SocketAddr>() {
                                    return Ok(addr.ip().to_string());
                                }
                                if ip.parse::<IpAddr>().is_ok() {
                                    return Ok(ip.to_string());
                                }
                            }
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

IPv6 trusted-proxy detection only trusts `::1` loopback. Internal IPv6 proxies using unique-local (`fc00::/7`) or link-local (`fe80::/10`) addresses are treated as untrusted, so their forwarded headers are ignored and their requests are rejected. Dual-stack deployments that present peers as IPv4-mapped IPv6 (`::ffff:10.0.0.1`) are also missed. Consider also trusting unique-local/link-local ranges and IPv4-mapped addresses.

```suggestion
        IpAddr::V6(v6) => {
            v6.is_loopback()
                || v6.is_unique_local()
                || (v6.segments()[0] & 0xffc0) == 0xfe80 // link-local
                || v6
                    .to_ipv4_mapped()
                    .map(|v4| v4.is_loopback() || v4.is_private())
                    .unwrap_or(false)
        }
```

---

### [low] (security)

This `tracing::warn!` fires on every direct public request (extraction fails before any rate-limit bucket check, so the warn is unconditional for that traffic class). A single attacker sending requests from a public IP can therefore flood the log sink. Use a rate-limited/aggregated logger, or demote this to debug and log once at startup.

## operator/src/models/trade.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Serde representation of `DeadLetter` diverges from the rest of the system. `rename_all = "UPPERCASE"` converts `DeadLetter` to `"DEADLETTER"` (serde just uppercases the variant name, it does not insert underscores), but `Display`/`FromStr` and the rest of the codebase (e.g., `state/registry.rs`, `engine/signal_pipeline.rs` writing `"DEAD_LETTER"` to the DB) all use `"DEAD_LETTER"`. As a result, a `Trade`/`TradeStatus` serialized via serde cannot be matched against values produced by `Display`/`FromStr`, and persisting a `"DEAD_LETTER"` string and later deserializing it through serde will fail. Add an explicit rename on the variant, e.g. `#[serde(rename = "DEAD_LETTER")] DeadLetter,`, so serde and Display/FromStr agree.

```suggestion
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "UPPERCASE")]
pub enum TradeStatus {
    /// Signal received, awaiting validation
    Pending,
    /// Validated, in priority buffer awaiting execution
    Queued,
    /// Transaction submitted to RPC, awaiting confirmation
    Executing,
    /// On-chain position confirmed, actively tracked
    Active,
    /// Exit signal received, selling transaction in flight
    Exiting,
    /// Position fully exited, PnL calculated
    Closed,
    /// Transaction rejected (insufficient funds, slippage, etc.)
    Failed,
    /// Failed transaction queued for retry
    Retry,
    /// Max retries exhausted, requires manual intervention
    #[serde(rename = "DEAD_LETTER")]
    DeadLetter,
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`mark_failed` force-sets `status` to `Failed` from any state without consulting `can_transition_to`. According to the state machine, only `Executing -> Failed` (and `Retry -> Executing -> Failed` in the retry cycle) is legal; calling `mark_failed` on a terminal trade (e.g. `Closed`/`DeadLetter`) revives it into `Failed` and allows `queue_retry` to push it back into the retry cycle, corrupting the lifecycle invariants and the PnL/closure semantics. Validate the transition first (e.g., return a `Result` and reject when `!self.status.can_transition_to(TradeStatus::Failed)`), or at minimum document that it is only allowed from `Executing`/`Retry`.

```suggestion
    pub fn mark_failed(&mut self, error: String) -> Result<(), String> {
        if !self.status.can_transition_to(TradeStatus::Failed) {
            return Err(format!(
                "Invalid state transition: {} -> FAILED",
                self.status
            ));
        }
        self.error_message = Some(error);
        self.status = TradeStatus::Failed;
        self.updated_at = Utc::now();
        Ok(())
    }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`queue_retry` unconditionally increments `retry_count` and moves to `Retry`; it never consults `MAX_RETRY_ATTEMPTS`, so a trade can be retried indefinitely unless every caller independently remembers to check `max_retries_exceeded`. Additionally, `Failed -> DeadLetter` is not a valid transition in `can_transition_to`, so once the retry budget is exhausted there is no direct route from `Failed` to the terminal `DeadLetter` state (the only path is the awkward `Failed -> Retry -> DeadLetter` via a manual `transition_to`). Enforce the limit inside `queue_retry`: when `max_retries_exceeded(MAX_RETRY_ATTEMPTS)`, move directly to `DeadLetter` (add `(Failed, DeadLetter)` to `can_transition_to`) and record the error, instead of silently allowing unbounded retries.

```suggestion
    pub fn queue_retry(&mut self) -> Result<(), String> {
        if self.status != TradeStatus::Failed {
            return Err("Can only retry from Failed state".to_string());
        }
        if self.max_retries_exceeded(MAX_RETRY_ATTEMPTS) {
            self.error_message = Some("Max retry attempts exceeded".to_string());
            self.status = TradeStatus::DeadLetter;
            self.updated_at = Utc::now();
            return Ok(());
        }
        self.retry_count += 1;
        self.status = TradeStatus::Retry;
        self.updated_at = Utc::now();
        Ok(())
    }
```

---

### [low] (test)

These tests do not exercise `Trade::max_retries_exceeded` at all — they only re-implement the `>=` comparison against the constant inline. A regression in the actual method (e.g., wrong comparison operator or off-by-one) would go undetected. Construct a `Trade` (or `TradeStatus`) and assert on the real `max_retries_exceeded`/`queue_retry` behavior.

The cache read (fast path, read lock) and cache insert (write lock) are separate lock scopes separated by `.await` (rate limiter + HTTP call). Worse, `at` is reset to `Instant::now()` at insert time, so the stale snapshot gets a fresh full TTL. ### [medium] (bug)

When the response contains pairs but none of them are Solana (or the liquidity/volume fields are missing), `max_liq`/`max_vol` remain `0.0` and a zero-valued snapshot is cached for the full TTL and returned as `Some(...)`. Callers may treat zero volume/liquidity as genuine market data rather than "unknown", silently skewing downstream decisions. Consider returning `None` when no Solana pair contributed any metric (or storing a not-found sentinel) so the fail-open contract is not confused with a real zero reading.

The cache `HashMap` is never evicted: entries for distinct token addresses accumulate for the lifetime of the process, and expired entries are only replaced when the *same* address is re-fetched. A long-running bot polling many addresses will grow this map without bound. Consider pruning expired entries on insert (or via a periodic sweep), or bounding the map size with an LRU-style eviction policy.

### [medium] (security)

`token_address` is interpolated directly into the request URL without validation or percent-encoding. If the address is ever derived from untrusted input, characters such as `/`, `?`, or `&` would alter the API path/query. Validate the address (e.g., allow only alphanumeric/base58 characters, as Solana addresses should be) or percent-encode it before formatting the URL.

### [low] (bug)

`max_liq` and `max_vol` are computed independently across *all* Solana pairs, so the resulting snapshot can pair the liquidity of one pool with the volume of a different pool and correspond to no actual pool on DexScreener. Prefer selecting a single dominant pool (e.g., the one with the highest liquidity) and reading both metrics from it, or explicitly document this approximation.

## operator/src/monitoring/helius_wss_health.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

A connection that has received messages but never recorded a pong falls into the `_ => false` arm and is always reported unhealthy. In the caller (`helius_wss.rs`), `record_pong` is only invoked on server-initiated `Message::Pong` frames or a JSON-RPC `"pong"` method — the client never sends its own pings, so a pong is not guaranteed for a healthy connection that is streaming text messages. Even at connection start (before the first message), both timestamps are `None`, so the first health-check tick reports the freshly connected stream as unhealthy regardless of real health. Pong should be treated as an optional signal (only enforce the pong timeout once a pong has been observed), not as a hard requirement.

```suggestion
                (Some(msg_time), pong_time) => {
                    let now = SystemTime::now();

                    let msg_duration = now.duration_since(msg_time).unwrap_or(Duration::ZERO);
                    if msg_duration.as_secs() > self.unhealthy_threshold_secs {
                        tracing::warn!(
                            elapsed_secs = msg_duration.as_secs(),
                            threshold_secs = self.unhealthy_threshold_secs,
                            "Unhealthy: No messages received recently"
                        );
                        return false;
                    }

                    // Only enforce pong timeout when a pong has actually been observed
                    if let Some(pong_time) = pong_time {
                        let pong_duration = now.duration_since(pong_time).unwrap_or(Duration::ZERO);
                        if pong_duration.as_secs() > self.pong_timeout_secs {
                            tracing::warn!(
                                elapsed_secs = pong_duration.as_secs(),
                                threshold_secs = self.pong_timeout_secs,
                                "Unhealthy: No pong response recently"
                            );
                            return false;
                        }
                    }

                    true
                }
                _ => false,
```

### [medium] (bug)

The failure counter is unbounded — failures accumulate forever and are only cleared by an explicit `reset_failures()` call, with no time window. Sporadic historical failures can keep `should_trigger_circuit_breaker()` returning true long after the connection has become healthy again. Additionally, this function is currently dead code: it is referenced only from the tests in this file and never wired into the reconnection/circuit-breaker path in production code. Consider counting failures within a sliding time window (or clearing the count on `set_state(Connected)`), and actually calling this check from the reconnection loop.

```suggestion
    pub fn should_trigger_circuit_breaker(&self) -> bool {
        const FAILURE_THRESHOLD: u64 = 5;
        const WINDOW_SECS: u64 = 300;

        let now = SystemTime::now()
            .duration_since(SystemTime::UNIX_EPOCH)
            .map(|d| d.as_secs())
            .unwrap_or(0);
        let mut failures = self.failure_times.write();
        failures.retain(|t| now.saturating_sub(*t) < WINDOW_SECS);
        failures.len() as u64 >= FAILURE_THRESHOLD
    }
```

### [low] (performance)

`record_message` is called for every WebSocket text frame, and taking an async `RwLock` write lock per message on `last_message_time` adds lock acquisition cost and contention with the health-check task on the hot path. Since only a wall-clock timestamp is stored, an `AtomicU64` (e.g. unix seconds via `AtomicU64::load/store(Ordering::Relaxed)`) would be cheaper and avoid blocking; the same applies to `last_pong_time`.

```suggestion
    pub fn record_message(&self) {
        self.messages_received.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
        self.last_message_time.store(SystemTime::now(), Ordering::Relaxed);
    }
```

## operator/src/monitoring/polling_task.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

Fail-open monitoring fallback: the error path returns an empty `vec![]`, and then `monitoring_enabled_set.is_empty()` triggers a fallback that polls ALL wallets. This conflates two very different cases: (1) the DB query failed, and (2) no wallet genuinely has monitoring enabled. On a transient DB error — or when the user has explicitly disabled monitoring for every wallet — the task silently polls every wallet and can generate trading signals from wallets the user intended to exclude. This defeats the `monitoring_enabled` intent and can cause unwanted trades. Fix: fail closed on query error (log + `return`) and only poll wallets present in the enabled set; an empty set should mean "poll nothing", not "poll everything".

```suggestion
        // Only poll wallets explicitly marked as monitored; an empty set means nothing to poll
        let monitored_wallets: Vec<String> = wallet_addresses
            .into_iter()
            .filter(|addr| monitoring_enabled_set.contains(addr))
            .collect();
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Delayed exit signals are never dispatched to the engine. When `should_generate_exit` returns true, this task only logs "Generating delayed exit signal", calls `mark_exit_processed`, and removes the entry from the pending list — there is no `Signal`/`SignalPayload` construction and no `engine.queue_signal(...)` call anywhere in this loop, and the `engine` handle is not even captured by this spawned task. The whole delayed-exit mechanism is therefore a silent no-op: exits are marked processed and dropped. Note the `ExitSignal` struct (wallet/token/exit_type/delay_secs) also lacks the amount and timestamp needed to build a `Signal`, so the data model must be extended and the processor must queue an `Action::Sell` signal to the engine. Additionally, these pending exits are in-memory only and are lost on restart, so exits will never fire after a restart either.

---

### [high] (bug)

`trade_uuid_exists(...).await.unwrap_or(false)` swallows DB errors: on failure the transaction is treated as "not a duplicate" and queued again. Since the duplicate check is the idempotency guard against re-processing on restart/pagination gaps, a flaky DB can cause the same on-chain transaction to be queued multiple times (potentially duplicate trades). The check should fail closed: on error, log a warning and skip the transaction rather than assume it is safe to queue.

```suggestion
    let trade_uuid = payload.generate_trade_uuid(tx.timestamp);
    match db.trade_uuid_exists(&trade_uuid).await {
        Ok(true) => {
            tracing::debug!(
                trade_uuid = %trade_uuid,
                wallet = %tx.wallet_address,
                token = %token_address,
                "Duplicate polling signal skipped"
            );
            return Ok(());
        }
        Ok(false) => {}
        Err(e) => {
            // Fail closed: if idempotency cannot be verified, do not queue.
            tracing::warn!(
                error = %e,
                trade_uuid = %trade_uuid,
                "Duplicate check failed, skipping polling signal"
            );
            return Ok(());
        }
    }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The `pending_exits.write()` guard is held across `.await` calls (`should_generate_exit` and `mark_exit_processed`), and `mark_exit_processed` additionally acquires the ExitDetector's internal write lock while this task still holds the Vec write lock. Any concurrent writer — e.g. `process_transaction` pushing a newly detected exit — is blocked for the whole iteration. Since `should_generate_exit` only inspects the detector's timestamp map, collect the due signals under a short read lock (or clone), release the lock, dispatch/process them, then re-acquire the write lock to remove the entries.

```suggestion
                _ = exit_interval.tick() => {
                    // Determine due signals without holding the write lock across awaits
                    let due: Vec<(usize, super::ExitSignal)> = {
                        let pending = pending_exits_clone.read().await;
                        let mut v = Vec::new();
                        for (idx, s) in pending.iter().enumerate() {
                            if exit_detector_clone.should_generate_exit(s).await {
                                v.push((idx, s.clone()));
                            }
                        }
                        v
                    };

                    for (idx, exit_signal) in due {
                        // ... dispatch exit signal to engine ...
                        exit_detector_clone.mark_exit_processed(&exit_signal).await;
                        let mut pending = pending_exits_clone.write().await;
                        pending.remove(idx);
                    }
```

### [high] (bug)

Unit mismatch between the async and local slippage estimators. `estimate_slippage` (async path) returns a percentage (`impact * 100`), but `estimate_slippage_local` returns a raw fraction here — the same trade yields values ~100x apart (e.g. a $3k trade against $20k liquidity: 0.3 locally vs 30 in the async path). Since the 3% threshold in `validate` and any caller-side comparison are in percent units, a trade rejected by the async path can pass via `validate_local`, and the `max_slippage = 5` cap is effectively 500% for the fraction. Multiply by 100 to match `estimate_slippage` (and the documented `price_impact ≈ ... * 100` formula), and document the return unit.

            // Square-root market impact estimation (returns %)

            return impact.min(max_slippage);

If the fail-open policy is intentional, make it explicit/configurable; otherwise fail-closed on unknown age. Also, the function is declared `Result<bool>` but never returns `Err` — every path returns `Ok`, so the `Result` wrapper is misleading; return a plain `bool` or propagate real errors.

## operator/src/monitoring/rpc_polling.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Check-then-act race: `has_seen` and `mark_seen` acquire the `RwLock` in two separate steps, so two concurrent `poll_wallets_batch` invocations (multiple polling tasks/tiers run simultaneously) can both read the signature as unseen and both emit the same transaction, producing duplicate signals downstream. Fix by making dedup atomic under a single write lock, e.g. a `mark_seen_if_absent(&self, sig) -> bool` method that checks `contains` and `put` while holding the write guard, and use only that here.

```suggestion
                for tx in txs {
                    if polling_state.mark_seen_if_absent(tx.signature.clone()).await {
                        chunk_transactions.push(tx);
                    }
                }
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The DB anchor is advanced to the *newest* signature whose `getTransaction` succeeded and is persisted as the next poll anchor. Because pagination collects everything newer than the anchor, any collected signature older than that point is permanently skipped on future polls: (1) signatures beyond the `.take(15)` cap, and (2) signatures whose fetch/parse failed (they log a warning but never retry). This creates permanent gaps where swap signals can be missed. Fix by capping the *collection* (stop paginating once 15 signatures are collected) and only persisting the anchor after the whole collected batch has been processed, so every collected signature is handled before the cursor advances.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Polling errors are silently discarded (`if let Ok(txs)`) with no logging and no backoff. Since `update_last_poll` only runs on success, a wallet whose RPC polling persistently fails (network error, rate limit, transient 5xx) remains eligible via `should_poll` and is retried on every cycle, burning rate-limit credits and hammering the RPC endpoint. Log the error and record a failure timestamp (or advance `last_poll` with a longer backoff interval) so failing wallets are retried less aggressively.

---

### [medium] (performance)

`last_poll` is a `HashMap` that is only ever inserted into and never evicted, unlike the bounded LRU used for `seen_signatures`. Over a long-running operator with a rotating set of monitored wallets this grows without bound (memory leak). Use an LRU cache (like `seen_signatures`) or periodically prune entries older than the maximum poll interval.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`serde_json::to_value(...)?` propagates a single serialization failure out of the entire poll, aborting the remaining collected signatures and skipping the anchor DB update for the transactions already processed in this poll. Since `poll_wallets_batch` swallows the error, the wallet just re-fetches the whole window next cycle (wasted credits), and this transaction's swap info is dropped. Log and `continue` to the next signature instead of failing the whole poll.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Matching the RPC error by string (`error.to_string().contains("-32020")`) is fragile: the substring could appear in unrelated error text, and the rendering may change across Solana client versions. Prefer the structured form `ClientError::RpcError(RpcError::RpcResponseError { code, .. })` and compare `code` directly to -32020, which is stable and version-agnostic.

## operator/src/monitoring/signal_aggregator.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

The `recent_signals` write guard (`signals`) is still alive when `update_wallet_clusters(...).await` acquires the separate `wallet_clusters` write lock. This keeps every reader of `recent_signals` (`is_consensus_token`, `check_divergence`, `get_all_recent_signals`) blocked for the whole cluster-update section, which itself is O(n²) in the number of distinct wallets. It is also a lock-order hazard: if any future code path acquires `wallet_clusters` before `recent_signals`, this becomes a deadlock. Build the `ConsensusSignal` first, `drop(signals)`, and only then call `update_wallet_clusters`.

```suggestion

                token_address: token_address.to_string(),
                wallet_count: unique_wallets.len(),
                total_amount_sol: total_amount,
                wallets: unique_wallets,
                confidence,
            };
            drop(signals);
            self.update_wallet_clusters(&consensus.wallets).await;
            return Some(consensus);
```

### [medium] (bug)

`total_amount_sol` sums every stored BUY signal, but the dedup comment above states that a single wallet retrying must not be able to fake consensus. Only `wallet_count` is deduplicated: if one wallet buys several times within 5 minutes, all its amounts count toward the total, inflating the reported SOL volume and any downstream amount-based logic. Sum only the first (or the max) signal per unique wallet instead of every signal.

```suggestion

            // Dedup amounts per wallet so repeated buys don't inflate the total
            let total_amount: Decimal = unique_wallets
                .iter()
                .map(|w| {
                    token_signals
                        .iter()
                        .find(|s| &s.wallet_address == w)
                        .map_or(Decimal::ZERO, |s| s.amount_sol)
                })
                .sum();
```

Each entry also duplicates the pair as a `Vec<String>` value that is never read (`get_wallet_cluster` only uses the key), doubling the memory footprint. ### [high] (bug)

The `wallet_address` parameter is ignored (`_wallet_address`), so this function aggregates balance changes from *every* account in the transaction instead of only the tracked wallet. ```

### [high] (bug)

Token amounts are parsed from `uiTokenAmount.uiAmount` as `f64` and then converted with `Decimal::from_f64_retain`, which silently loses precision for large or high-decimal token amounts (exactly the case for meme coins tracked by this operator). The same issue exists in the post-balances loop below. Prefer the raw `uiTokenAmount.amount` string together with `decimals` to keep exact integer precision.

```suggestion
            let raw_amount = balance
                .get("uiTokenAmount")
                .and_then(|v| v.get("amount"))
                .and_then(|v| v.as_str());
            let decimals = balance
                .get("uiTokenAmount")
                .and_then(|v| v.get("decimals"))
                .and_then(|v| v.as_u64())
                .unwrap_or(0);
            let amount = raw_amount
                .and_then(|s| Decimal::from_str(s).ok())
                .map(|a| a / Decimal::from(10u64.pow(decimals as u32)))
                .unwrap_or(Decimal::ZERO);
```

---

### [high] (bug)

When no non-SOL token change is found, the function still returns `Ok` with an empty `token_out`, `amount_in = 0` and `amount_out = 0`. Since all sub-parsers (Jupiter/Raydium/Orca/Pump.fun) funnel through this function and `parse_transaction` treats any `Ok` as a detected swap, a non-swap transaction that merely contains one of the DEX program IDs (e.g. a plain transfer routed through the program) is reported as a valid swap with bogus data. Return an error here so the caller can distinguish "not a swap" from a real swap.

```suggestion
        } else {
            return Err(anyhow::anyhow!("No token balance change found; not a swap"));
        }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

When `sol_change == 0` (e.g. a token-to-token swap via an aggregator, or a SOL-only transfer), the direction unconditionally defaults to `Sell`, and the amount extraction below then produces `token_in = token`, `token_out = SOL` with `amount_out = 0`. A token-to-token swap with no SOL leg is misreported as a sell with a zero SOL amount. Handle the zero-SOL-change case explicitly (token-to-token) instead of defaulting to Sell.

---

### [medium] (bug)

All `native_transfers` are summed unconditionally without filtering by wallet or direction. A single swap typically produces two legs (wallet → pool and pool → wallet change/refund), so both get summed and `sol_amount`/`amount_in` is inflated; unrelated transfers in the same transaction (tips, other users' legs when `tracked_wallet` is None) are also included. Filter transfers to those involving the tracked wallet and select only the leg matching the swap direction (outgoing for Buy, incoming for Sell).

---

### [medium] (bug)

Each matching LaserStream token transfer overwrites `token_in`/`amount_in` or `token_out`/`amount_out` (last write wins). For multi-hop swaps (e.g. SOL → USDC → TOKEN) the wallet sends and receives multiple mints, so `token_in`/`token_out` end up holding an intermediate hop (e.g. USDC → TOKEN instead of SOL → TOKEN) and the amounts reflect only the last transfer. Aggregate transfers by mint / direction, or reject multi-hop payloads explicitly instead of silently returning an incomplete swap.

---

### [medium] (bug)

When multiple non-SOL mints have significant balance changes (e.g. a transfer and a swap bundled in the same transaction, or fee tokens), `token_change` is overwritten each iteration and the final value depends on the iteration order of the `HashSet` from `all_accounts`, which is non-deterministic. Combined with the ignored wallet filter, this can report an arbitrary token/amount as the swap. Choose deterministically (e.g. largest absolute delta) or return an error when more than one non-SOL token changes.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`parse_transaction` uses `if let Ok(...)` for each DEX parser, so any error — not just "not this DEX" — is silently swallowed and the parser falls through to the next heuristic. Because `parse_balance_changes` also returns bogus `Ok` swaps (see the fallback path), genuine parse failures and false positives are indistinguishable. Consider having the sub-parsers return a typed "not this DEX" result distinct from real errors, or at least log the error before falling through.

---

### [low] (bug)

A LaserStream message without `tokenTransfers` (e.g. any non-swap notification) produces an `Err`, which forces the caller in `helius_wss.rs` onto the fallback RPC parser and logs a warning for every unrelated message. Since this function already returns `Result<Option<ParsedSwap>>`, missing `tokenTransfers` should map to `Ok(None)` (not a swap) rather than an error.

```suggestion
    let Some(token_transfers) = payload.get("tokenTransfers").and_then(|t| t.as_array()) else {
        return Ok(None); // Not a swap / unsupported payload
    };
```

## operator/src/notifications/discord.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Check-then-act race: `can_send` and `mark_sent` are two separate lock acquisitions with an `.await` (the network POST) in between. When two `notify` calls for the same event type run concurrently (e.g., two strategies fire `PositionExited` simultaneously), both can read `can_send() == true`, both send, and both mark — duplicating the alert and defeating the rate limiter. Fix by making the check+mark atomic under a single write lock (e.g., a `try_acquire(key) -> bool` that inserts `Instant::now()` only if the last send is stale), and drop the separate `mark_sent` call after the await.

```suggestion
        if event.level() != AlertLevel::Critical && !self.rate_limiter.try_acquire(&rate_key) {
            tracing::debug!(
                key = %rate_key,
                "Rate limited, skipping Discord notification"
            );
            return Ok(());
        }
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

Unbounded `last_sent` map growth: keys are derived from dynamic values (`position:{token}:{strategy}`, `wallet_promoted:{address}`, `system_crash:{component}`), and entries are inserted forever and never pruned even after the rate-limit interval expires. In a long-running operator with many tokens/addresses, this leaks memory as unique events accumulate. Consider evicting expired entries when they are encountered during `can_send`/`try_acquire`, and/or capping the map size (e.g., LRU or periodic purge of entries older than `self.interval`).

---

### [medium] (bug)

`notify` only checks `self.enabled`, but `is_enabled` additionally requires a non-empty `webhook_url`. `DiscordConfig` is a public struct (and `Default` yields an empty URL), so a config with `enabled: true` and an empty webhook URL will reach `client.post("")` and fail at request time instead of being a clean no-op. Guard the empty URL inside `notify` as well (or validate the config at construction).

---

### [low] (bug)

`std::env::var("DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL").ok()?` collapses both `VarError::NotPresent` and `VarError::NotUnicode` into `None`, so a non-UTF-8 or otherwise malformed `DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL` silently disables Discord notifications with no diagnostic. Distinguish the error cases and at least emit a `tracing::warn!`/`error!` before returning `None` for `NotUnicode` (and log the reason for other errors), rather than silently degrading.

---

## operator/src/notifications/mod.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Panic risk in a production notification path: `&address[..4]` and `&address[address.len() - 4..]` both panic if the address is shorter than 4/8 characters (e.g. an empty or malformed wallet address from config/mocks). `address.len() - 4` underflows for `len < 4` (panic in debug, index-out-of-bounds in release), and byte-slicing can also panic on a non-UTF-8 boundary if the address ever contains multi-byte characters. Guard the length before slicing (Solana base58 addresses are >8 chars, but this is a public API and the value isn't validated).

```suggestion
                let (head, tail) = if address.len() > 8 {
                    (&address[..4], &address[address.len() - 4..])
                } else {
                    (address.as_str(), "")
                };
                format!(
                    "{prefix}📊 Wallet promoted: {}...{} (WQS: {:.2})",
                    head, tail, wqs_score
                )
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

Sequential fan-out with no timeout: services are awaited one after another, so a slow or hung Telegram/Discord client (network call with no timeout) delays every subsequent notifier, including critical circuit-breaker/wallet-drained alerts. Consider dispatching notifications concurrently (e.g. `futures::join_all` over the enabled services, or `tokio::spawn` per service) and wrapping each call in a timeout so one bad service can't stall the rest.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`latency_ms.unwrap_or(0)` renders a missing latency as "0ms", which falsely reads as an excellent (impossible-to-beat) latency instead of "unknown". This can mislead operators diagnosing Jito health. Display "N/A"/"unknown" when no latency was reported.

```suggestion
                let latency = match latency_ms {
                    Some(ms) => format!("{}ms", ms),
                    None => "N/A".to_string(),
                };
```

---

### [low] (bug)

Silent fallthrough: any `trade_mode` other than exactly `"paper"`/`"devnet"` (e.g. `"Paper"`, `"paper "`, or a typo) produces a live-style message with no prefix. Since `format_message` is public and can be called with arbitrary strings, a mislabeled paper/devnet alert could be mistaken for a real live event. Normalize the input and handle unknown modes explicitly (at minimum log a warning).

```suggestion
        let prefix = match trade_mode.trim().to_lowercase().as_str() {
            "paper" => "[PAPER] ",
            "devnet" => "[DEVNET] ",
            "live" | "" => "",
            other => {
                tracing::warn!(mode = other, "Unknown trade mode, treating as live");
                ""
            }
        };
```

## operator/src/notifications/telegram.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (security)

The bot token is interpolated directly into the request URL. `reqwest::Error` carries the request URL in its Display/Debug output, so any propagated error from `send_message` (timeout, DNS, connection reset) embeds the token and it can be written to logs/metrics by callers — leaking a full bot credential. Since the Telegram Bot API requires the token in the URL path, sanitize errors before propagation instead: map the reqwest error to a message without the URL/token (e.g., log status only, keep the original error in an internal-only context).

---

### [medium] (bug)

Check-then-act race in the rate limiter: `can_send()` and `mark_sent()` each acquire the lock separately, with an `await` on `send_message()` in between. Two concurrent `notify()` calls for the same key can both pass `can_send()` before either calls `mark_sent()`, so duplicate messages get sent and the throttle is defeated — precisely the behavior this limiter exists to prevent. Make check-and-mark atomic (e.g., a single method that checks and inserts under one write lock and returns whether it reserved the slot), or mark the key as sent immediately after the check passes and only roll it back on send failure.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Rate-limit keys are derived from high-cardinality values (`token:strategy`, wallet addresses, component names), and `mark_sent()` inserts a new entry per key with no eviction. In a long-running process, this HashMap grows without bound (a memory leak), especially since `SystemCrash`, `PositionExited`, and `WalletPromoted` each produce unique keys. Bound the map size (e.g., cap entries and evict the oldest), or lazily prune entries whose last-sent time is older than the rate-limit interval when the map exceeds a threshold.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`mark_sent()` only runs after `send_message()` succeeds. During a Telegram API outage, every event therefore performs a full HTTP attempt (10s timeout each) because the rate limiter is never updated on failure — throttling is exactly absent when the API is failing, potentially piling up requests and 10s stalls per event. Record the attempt (or a failure timestamp) before/independent of the HTTP result so failures are also rate-limited and back off.

---

### [low] (security)

The message is sent with `parse_mode: "HTML"` but `text` is inserted without any HTML escaping. Event-derived strings (reasons, component names, token symbols, wallet addresses, error text) can contain `<`, `>`, `&`, or quotes, which Telegram will interpret as markup — corrupting the alert or injecting unintended links/formatting into the chat. Escape the text (e.g., escape `<`, `>`, `&` before sending) or use plain-text parse mode.

---

## operator/src/price_cache.rs (7 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (performance)

`get_price` is a read-only hot-path lookup (called by the position monitor / circuit breaker for every token read) but acquires the exclusive `write()` lock, serializing all concurrent readers and blocking the background updater's `set_price` writes for the duration of the lookup. The write lock exists only because `cache_hits`/`cache_misses` are plain `u64` counters — convert those to `AtomicU64` and use a read lock for the lookup so reads never contend with the writer.

---

### [high] (bug)

Zero-price results are treated as success: `fetch_prices_jupiter` returns `Ok` with empty vectors when the API returns no prices (it only logs), and this branch then returns `Ok` straight away — for attempts 1/2, or when the lite-api fallback also returns empty on attempt 0. The cache silently goes stale with no error and no further retry, while risk/monitor logic keeps consuming outdated prices. Return a `PriceCacheError` (or keep retrying) whenever `tokens` is non-empty but the fetched price list is empty.

---

### [medium] (performance)

Same issue as `get_price`: `get_decimals` is a lookup path (called per position when computing values) but takes the exclusive `write()` lock. Only the expired-entry removal and miss counter need write access; the actual lookup can use `read()`. Reserve the write lock for the mutation and the counter can be an atomic.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`#[serde(flatten)]` merges every remaining top-level field into the `data` map and tries to deserialize each value as `JupiterPriceData` (which requires `usdPrice`). Any metadata field added by the API — e.g. `timeTaken`, a request id, or a `data` wrapper — fails the deserialization of the entire batch, dropping all token prices at once instead of just skipping the unknown field. Prefer an explicit `data: HashMap<String, JupiterPriceData>` field (or deserialize to `serde_json::Value` and extract the token entries) so unknown top-level fields are ignored.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`get_sol_price_usd_fallback` returns whatever is cached for SOL even if it is zero, contradicting the documented 'last known non-zero' contract — a zero price would be treated as a valid SOL price by risk logic. It also bypasses the staleness threshold (the doc intends 'expired is OK', but there is no age bound at all, so a price from hours ago can be fed into market-condition checks). Guard the fallback with a `!price_usd.is_zero()` check and at least bound the age.

```suggestion
        let inner = self.inner.read();
        let entry = inner.prices.get(&self.sol_mint)?;
        if entry.price_usd.is_zero() {
            return None;
        }
        Some(entry.price_usd)
```

---

### [low] (bug)

The module invariant (stated in the header and above `STALENESS_THRESHOLD_SECS`) requires `DEFAULT_CACHE_TTL_SECS >= STALENESS_THRESHOLD_SECS` because `get_price_usd` checks both the staleness flag and the TTL. But `with_ttl` accepts any value without validation; a TTL below 90s makes `get_price` expire prices that are still inside the staleness window, so the stale-price extension never kicks in. Validate `ttl_secs >= STALENESS_THRESHOLD_SECS` (returning an error) or clamp it.

```suggestion
    pub fn with_ttl(ttl_secs: i64) -> Result<Self, PriceCacheError> {
        if ttl_secs < STALENESS_THRESHOLD_SECS {
            return Err(PriceCacheError::HttpError(format!(
                "ttl_secs {} must be >= STALENESS_THRESHOLD_SECS ({})",
                ttl_secs, STALENESS_THRESHOLD_SECS
            )));
        }
        Ok(Self {
```

---

### [low] (bug)

`updater_running` is set to `true` in `start_updater` but never reset when the supervisor exits. If the inner loop ever returns normally or the task is cancelled, a subsequent `start_updater` call logs 'already running' and refuses to start even though no updater is active. Clear the flag when the supervisor loop breaks (and ideally in the panic-restart path the flag is fine to stay, since the supervisor re-runs the loop).
