## operator/src/retry.rs (5 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

The documented 30s cap is unreachable: `attempt.min(4)` bounds the base at 16s, so with +25% jitter the maximum wait is 20s and the `min(30.0)` branch is dead code. The `test_calculate_backoff` cap assertion (`<= 30`) is therefore vacuous. Also, the comment above `with_jitter` claims a "1 second minimum" while `.max(100.0)` actually enforces only 100ms, so the first retry can fire after 100ms instead of the documented ~1s. Suggest capping the base itself rather than the exponent, and aligning the floor with the intended value.

```suggestion
    let base = 2_u64.pow(attempt).min(30);
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`status == 0` makes *every* non-reqwest error (and any reqwest error without a status) retryable — including permanent application/programming errors. This masks real failures, contradicts the docstring ("Non-retryable errors (400, 401, ...) fail immediately"), and delays error reporting by the full backoff sequence (~31s for the default 5 attempts). Note the success test actually relies on this behavior: its `anyhow!("HTTP error: 500")` is not a `reqwest::Error`, so it is retried only because of the `status == 0` branch. Restrict retry-on-unknown to errors that are explicitly transient.

---

### [medium] (bug)

reqwest's `is_request()` indicates the error occurred while *building* the request (e.g., invalid URL or header) — a permanent, non-transient failure, not a network problem. Classifying it as a network error causes wasted retries through the full backoff sequence and obscures the root cause. Only `is_timeout()` and `is_connect()` are transient network conditions.

```suggestion
        e.is_timeout() || e.is_connect()
```

---

### [low] (bug)

With `max_retries = 0` the `0..0` loop body never runs and the function falls through to this misleading "Internal error" result. Validate the argument up front (or document that 0 means "no attempts") and return a meaningful error instead.

---

### [low] (test)

These tests perform real wall-clock sleeps through `retry_with_backoff` (1s + 2s in each of the two tests, ~6s total), slowing the test suite and making it flaky under CI load. Consider using `tokio::time::pause()`/`advance()` (test-util feature) or injecting a mock clock.

### [high] (bug)

`merge_roster` unconditionally returns an error, so any caller expecting roster updates will always fail. The doc comment above advertises a real implementation (attaches roster_new.db, runs integrity check, merges wallets in a transaction, detaches) — none of that exists, and the error message merely points at a "direct SQL import" path that isn't provided by this module. The integration test pins the rejection on PostgreSQL, but the API surface (name, `AppResult<MergeResult>` return, doc comment) still implies a working merge. Either implement the actual ingestion path or remove/decommission this dead API and update the docs so callers aren't misled.

### [high] (bug)

`validate_roster` can never return `Ok`, so callers cannot distinguish a valid roster file from an invalid one — the `AppResult<bool>` return type is misleading. The doc comment claims it "checks if a roster file is valid (exists and passes integrity check)", but the function body never performs that check and always errors. If the PostgreSQL backend truly doesn't support this operation, return a clear typed rejection as documented and drop the misleading bool contract, or implement the validation for real.

### [medium] (maintainability)

Stale/contradictory documentation: the module doc describes an SQLite `ATTACH DATABASE` merge (Scout writes `roster_new.db`, Operator merges it), but the API takes a `sqlx::Pool<sqlx::Postgres>` and both functions unconditionally reject the operation as "not supported with PostgreSQL". The design intent (SQLite era, decommissioned per `postgres.rs` comments) no longer matches the code. Update the module docs to state that SQLite ATTACH-based roster ingestion is intentionally unsupported on PostgreSQL so future readers aren't misled about this module's behavior.

### [low] (maintainability)

Both functions are `async` yet contain no `.await` points (triggers `unused_async`), and `MergeResult` is only ever constructed in the unit test — its fields (`wallets_merged`, `wallets_removed`, `integrity_ok`, `merged_at`, `warnings`) are dead in production since the production functions always return an error. ## operator/src/state/coordinator.rs (9 findings, 0 critical, 5 high)

### [high] (bug)

This sync is strictly one-directional: DB entries are only added or updated in the registry; entries that no longer exist in the DB are never removed. Worse, `db.get_active_positions()` only returns ACTIVE positions, so once a position leaves ACTIVE in the DB it stops appearing in the query and the registry keeps it as ACTIVE forever. The same applies to trades that moved to CLOSED/FAILED and deleted wallets. These stale entries keep contributing to `calculate_portfolio_heat` and decision-making indefinitely. The registry has no removal API either — add `remove_trade`/`remove_position`/wallet removal and reconcile by diffing the DB result set against the registry.

---

### [high] (bug)

Only `status` is reconciled for trades. If the DB row's `amount_sol`, `strategy`, `side`, `token_address`, etc. change while status stays the same, the registry never picks up the change — so portfolio heat (computed from `amount_sol`/`strategy`) and trade decisions use stale data. Compare against the full DB row and update all fields (or add a full-field `update_trade` to the registry) instead of only patching status.

---

### [high] (bug)

Only `state` is reconciled for positions. `current_price`, `unrealized_pnl_sol` (which change frequently in the DB) and `entry_amount_sol`/`strategy` are never propagated when `state` is unchanged, so the registry's price/PnL/exposure used for decisions stays stale. Replace the full position from the DB row on each sync rather than only patching `state`.

---

### [high] (bug)

Only `status` is reconciled for wallets. Changes to `wqs_score` or `win_rate` in the DB are never propagated when status is unchanged, so wallet-scoring data used for selection stays stale. Upsert the full wallet state unconditionally on each sync.

---

### [high] (bug)

The spawned task's `JoinHandle` is dropped and never observed. If the loop panics — e.g., this `Mutex::lock().unwrap()` once the mutex is poisoned by an earlier panic — periodic synchronization stops forever with no error surfaced and no shutdown/cancellation path. Store the handle, tolerate poisoning (e.g., `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` or `catch_unwind` per cycle), log on failure, and add a cancellation mechanism (e.g., `CancellationToken`/`watch` channel) so the task can be stopped cleanly.

---

### [medium] (bug)

There is no guard between `load_initial_state` and `start_sync_task`. If the sync loop starts while the initial load is still inserting trades/positions/wallets and computing portfolio heat, the two mutate the registry concurrently, producing inconsistent intermediate state and heat values (and resetting `version` counters on re-inserted entries). Run the initial load inside the spawned task before entering the loop, or gate the loop on a startup flag.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Any unrecognized DB status string is silently coerced to `TradeStatus::Failed`. If the DB contains a new legitimate status (e.g., "CANCELED") or a data-integrity problem, a live trade is misclassified as failed and, on the next sync, `update_trade_status` overwrites the registry status to Failed — which can cause downstream logic to drop the trade. Return an error (or at least log a warning) for unknown statuses instead of silently mapping them to Failed.

---

### [low] (bug)

`tokio::time::interval` panics if the period is zero. `new()` accepts an arbitrary `Duration` and never validates it, so a zero `sync_interval` would crash the spawned task at startup. Validate the interval in `new()` (e.g., clamp to a minimum) before constructing the timer.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The `write_queue` field is never used anywhere in this file: all sync logic is strictly DB→registry, and registry mutations are never persisted back through this queue. Either wire registry changes into the queue (to make the coordinator's bidirectional-sync contract real) or remove the unused field, otherwise the field misleads readers into thinking writes are being flushed.

## operator/src/state/write_queue.rs (7 findings, 2 critical, 0 high)

### [critical] (bug)

Critical liveness bug: after any 1-second idle recv timeout, the worker parks on `shutdown.notified().await` and stops receiving new operations until shutdown is signalled. In normal low-traffic operation the queue idles for >1s, so the worker blocks here forever and every subsequently enqueued operation is silently never processed even though `enqueue` returned `Ok`. There is also a missed-notification race: `Notify::notify_waiters()` only wakes waiters already registered, so if `shutdown()` is called while this worker is busy processing a batch, the worker reaches this `notified().await` afterwards and hangs forever — making `shutdown()` consume its full 30s timeout per worker. Finally, the pending `batch_buffer` is only flushed *after* the notification, so acknowledged-but-unpersisted operations can sit in memory indefinitely. Use `tokio::select!` on recv vs. shutdown in the loop (plus an `AtomicBool`/persistent flag checked after each iteration to avoid the missed-notification race) and flush the partial batch on window expiry regardless of shutdown.

```suggestion
                Err(_) => {
                    tokio::select! {
                        _ = shutdown.notified() => {
                            if !batch_buffer.is_empty() {
                                Self::process_batch(&batch_buffer, &db, &retry_config, &metrics).await;
                            }
                            info!("Worker {} shutting down", worker_id);
                            break;
                        }
                        _ = tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(batch_config.batch_window_ms)) => {
                            if !batch_buffer.is_empty() {
                                Self::process_batch(&batch_buffer, &db, &retry_config, &metrics).await;
                                batch_buffer.clear();
                                last_batch_time = Instant::now();
                            }
                        }
                    }
                }
```

---

### [critical] (bug)

Data-loss bug: this arm returns `Ok(())` without invoking any database method, so `UpsertWallet` operations are silently dropped while the queue reports them as successful (`success_count`/`operations_completed` are incremented and the caller sees no error). There is no `upsert_wallet` method on the `Database` trait, so either implement a real write (extend the trait/DB impl) or return an error so the operation is not acknowledged as persisted.

```suggestion
                WriteOperation::UpsertWallet { address, status, wqs_score, win_rate } => {
                    // Implement a real DB write; returning Ok(()) silently loses the operation.
                    db.upsert_wallet(&UpsertWallet {
                        address: address.clone(),
                        status: status.clone(),
                        wqs_score: *wqs_score,
                        win_rate: *win_rate,
                    })
                    .await
                    .map(|_| ())
                }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Two metric bugs in `enqueue`: (1) `operations_queued` is incremented before `try_send`, so operations rejected with `QueueFull`/`QueueClosed` are still counted as queued, making the counter misleading; move the increment into the `Ok` arm. (2) `current_queue_depth` is incremented only *after* the message is placed in the channel, so a worker can `recv()` and `fetch_sub(1)` before the producer's `fetch_add(1)` executes — the unsigned counter underflows (wraps to ~2^64-1) and triggers spurious "queue depth high" warnings. Increment the depth *before* `try_send` and compensate with `fetch_sub` in the error arms so the worker can never decrement before the producer increments.

```suggestion
        let depth = self.metrics.current_queue_depth.fetch_add(1, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Relaxed) + 1;

        match self.operation_tx.try_send(operation) {
            Ok(_) => {
                self.metrics.operations_queued.fetch_add(1, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Relaxed);
                if depth > (self.batch_config.max_queue_depth / 2) as u64 {
                    warn!("Write queue depth high: {}", depth);
                }
                Ok(())
            }
            Err(mpsc::error::TrySendError::Full(_op)) => {
                self.metrics.current_queue_depth.fetch_sub(1, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Relaxed);
                error!("Write queue full, rejecting operation");
                Err(QueueError::QueueFull)
            }
            Err(mpsc::error::TrySendError::Closed(_op)) => {
                self.metrics.current_queue_depth.fetch_sub(1, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Relaxed);
                Err(QueueError::QueueClosed)
            }
        }
```

### [medium] (bug)

`operations_failed` and `operations_retried` are exposed in `QueueMetricsSnapshot` (and presumably consumed by monitoring), but they are never incremented anywhere in this file: failures only bump the local `failure_count`, and `WriteResult.retry_count` is discarded after the loop. Add `metrics.operations_failed.fetch_add(1, ...)` in the failure branch and `metrics.operations_retried.fetch_add(result.retry_count, ...)` so the published counters are truthful.

```suggestion
            if result.success {
                success_count += 1;
            } else {
                failure_count += 1;
                metrics.operations_failed.fetch_add(1, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Relaxed);
            }

            metrics.operations_retried.fetch_add(result.retry_count, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Relaxed);
            metrics.operations_completed.fetch_add(1, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Relaxed);
```

### [medium] (maintainability)

Dead code that masks the intended shutdown design: `_shutdown_rx` is a `Notified` future that is created and never awaited, and `shutdown_interval` is ticked once at startup but never polled in the loop. These look like leftovers of a planned `select!`-based shutdown check that was replaced by the blocking `shutdown.notified().await` in the timeout branch (which is the root cause of the worker-hang bug). Either wire them into the loop (e.g., `tokio::select!` on recv vs. `shutdown_interval.tick()`) or remove them.

---

### [medium] (bug)

When the per-worker shutdown timeout fires, the `JoinHandle` is dropped and the worker task is aborted mid-execution — potentially in the middle of a database write or a retry backoff sleep, leaving an inconsistent record. Because of the missed-notification race in the worker timeout branch, this 30s abort path is actually the likely shutdown path today (up to 30s per worker, sequentially). Make shutdown deterministic by fixing the `notified()` race, and if a timeout must remain, drain/flush in-flight work before aborting rather than cancelling mid-write.

---

### [low] (bug)

Retries run serially inside the batch loop and the backoff `sleep` is not cancellable by shutdown: with the default config (5 retries, 50→800ms backoff ≈ 1.55s per failing op) a full batch of failing operations can stall a worker for minutes, and `shutdown()` cannot interrupt the sleep (it either waits it out or hits the 30s abort). Consider a per-operation total deadline/attempt cap tied to the shutdown signal, and bound how long a single batch can consume.

### [high] (bug)

This holder-concentration computation is not trustworthy and effectively fails open (or misfires):
1. `account.owner` of a token account is the SPL Token / Token-2022 program ID, not the DEX program that created the pool, so `dex_programs.contains(&owner)` will essentially never match — LP/AMM-held supply is never excluded and the "non-DEX" set is meaningless.

Consider deserializing the token-account data to get the real wallet owner, and use raw `amount` (unscaled) consistently with `supply`.

## operator/src/tools/import_keypair.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Unconditionally overwriting `webhook_secret` drops the old current secret. `config.rs::get_all_secrets` (and `main.rs` HMAC verification) checks both `webhook_secret` and `webhook_secret_previous`, and the project's own `ops/rotate-secrets.sh` preserves the old secret as `..._PREVIOUS` precisely so webhooks still signed with the old secret verify during the grace period. If this import is used to rotate the secret (the comment above says rotations are a supported scenario), any in-flight webhook signed with the old secret will fail HMAC verification. Move the old current secret into `webhook_secret_previous` when it differs from the new one, and also honor `CHIMERA_SECURITY__WEBHOOK_SECRET_PREVIOUS` if set.

```suggestion
    if secrets.webhook_secret != webhook_secret {
        // Rotation: keep the old current secret as `previous` so webhooks still
        // signed with it verify during the grace period.
        secrets.webhook_secret_previous = Some(secrets.webhook_secret.clone());
        secrets.webhook_secret = webhook_secret;
    }
```

---

### [medium] (security)

The comment claims this "confirms pubkey matches secret", but `normalize_to_64_bytes` only decodes the bytes (it never re-derives the public half from the secret), and `Keypair::try_from(&[u8; 64])` merely splits the buffer into a 32-byte secret + 32-byte public half. Whether the SDK cross-checks the two halves is version-dependent and not something this code verifies. If a mismatched pair slips through, every transaction signed with this keypair will fail on-chain signature verification. Make the guarantee explicit by signing/verifying a probe message (or deriving the pubkey from the secret half and comparing it to the stored public half) before accepting the keypair.

```suggestion
    // 6. Confirm the bytes are a real Ed25519 keypair (pubkey matches secret).
    let keypair = Keypair::try_from(keypair_bytes_64.as_slice())
        .map_err(|e| anyhow!("Decoded bytes are not a valid Ed25519 keypair: {:?}", e))?;
    // Keypair::try_from only splits the 64 bytes; depending on the SDK version it
    // may not re-derive the pubkey from the secret. Sign/verify a probe message to
    // deterministically reject a keypair whose secret and public halves disagree.
    let probe = b"import_keypair: secret/public consistency probe";
    let sig = keypair.sign_message(probe);
    if keypair.verify(probe, &sig).is_err() {
        bail!("Keypair secret and public halves are inconsistent — refusing to import");
    }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

This pubkey check is tautological and can never fail. `kp` comes from `load_wallet_keypair(&reloaded)`, which internally does `Keypair::try_from(normalize_to_64_bytes(reloaded.wallet_private_key))` — the exact same pipeline used to build `expected` from the same `reloaded.wallet_private_key`. Both pubkeys are therefore identical by construction, so the check cannot detect a wrong-but-self-consistent key being written (e.g. an encode/decode bug or in-memory corruption between the pre-write `derived_pubkey_b58` and what is saved). Compare against the pubkey captured *before* writing (`derived_pubkey_b58`) and pass it into this function, which also lets the redundant re-derivation be removed.

```suggestion
    let reloaded_b58 = bs58::encode(kp.pubkey().as_ref()).into_string();
    if reloaded_b58 != expected_pubkey_b58 {
        bail!(
            "pubkey mismatch after round-trip: expected {}, got {}",
            expected_pubkey_b58,
            reloaded_b58
        );
    }
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`#![allow(warnings)]` disables every compiler/lint diagnostic for this entire security-sensitive tool. Warnings such as unused imports/fields, shadowing, or `unused_mut` here would be silently suppressed, hiding genuine mistakes in a program that handles private keys. Prefer scoped `#[allow(...)]` attributes on the specific items that need them.

---

### [low] (security)

The module safety docs emphasize zeroizing secrets, but the derived `Keypair` (which holds the 64-byte secret material) is kept alive until the end of `main` even though it is only needed to derive the pubkey in step 6. `solana_sdk::signature::Keypair` does not implement `Zeroize`, so the secret stays in memory for the rest of the process. `drop(keypair)` right after computing `derived_pubkey` at least releases it immediately (the `keypair_bytes_64` buffer is already `Zeroizing` and will be wiped on drop).

```suggestion
    let derived_pubkey = keypair.pubkey();
    let derived_pubkey_b58 = bs58::encode(derived_pubkey.as_ref()).into_string();
    // The Keypair is only needed for pubkey derivation; release it now so the
    // raw secret does not stay resident for the remainder of the process.
    drop(keypair);
```

`VACUUM` cannot run inside a transaction block and cannot be executed via a prepared statement; sqlx's default extended query protocol runs it inside an implicit transaction, so this statement typically errors — and the result is silently ignored (`let _ = timeout(...)`). The test therefore asserts that reads work while the VACUUM likely never ran. Use a raw/simple-protocol connection outside a transaction and assert the VACUUM actually succeeded.

## operator/tests/common/mod.rs (3 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

The admin URL is derived by splitting at the last '/' and appending '/postgres', which silently drops any query parameters in TEST_DATABASE_URL (e.g. `?sslmode=require`, `?connect_timeout=...`). This can break TLS/SSL or other connection options, and it also assumes the maintenance database is literally named `postgres` (not true on some managed Postgres instances). Worse, the same `base_url` is reused to build the test DB URL, so those query params are lost there too. Consider parsing with the `url` crate (preserving/merging query params) or at least document the constraint clearly.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Each call creates a new `test_<uuid>` database that is never dropped, so repeated/CI test runs leak databases on the Postgres server indefinitely. If `create_database` or `run_migrations` fails after the CREATE DATABASE, the just-created DB is also leaked. Additionally, the returned `TempDir` is created but never actually used, so it provides no cleanup for anything. Consider tracking created database names and dropping them during teardown (via a separate admin connection, e.g. `DROP DATABASE ... WITH (FORCE)`), and either remove the unused TempDir or put it to real use.

---

### [low] (security)

The SQL identifier is built with unchecked string interpolation. It is only safe today because `db_name` is generated from a UUID, but it is a latent quoting/injection hazard if the naming scheme ever changes. Since SQL identifiers cannot be bound as query parameters, validate `db_name` against a strict identifier pattern (e.g. `[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*`) before interpolating, or quote it defensively.

---

## operator/tests/integration/accounting_characterization_tests.rs (3 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

The helper aliases `entry_amount_sol` as "remaining" and the test asserts it shrinks to 0.5 after a 50% partial close. This pins the behavior that the partial-close path MUTATES `entry_amount_sol` to the remaining exposure. That conflicts with the column's name and its use elsewhere as the original entry/deployed amount (e.g. portfolio heat, docs). If the schema contract is that `entry_amount_sol` stays the immutable original entry size, this assertion (and the tier-2 expectations below) would silently pin the wrong accounting contract. Either document/assert this mutation explicitly or track remaining exposure in a dedicated column so the test is robust to the schema's intended semantics.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The final tranche passes `exit_fraction = Decimal::ONE` while the SELL trade's `amount_sol` is only 0.5. This only closes 0.5 SOL because the tier-1 partial close rewrote `entry_amount_sol` to the remaining 0.5 (verified in `close_position_full`: partial close sets `entry_amount_sol = remaining_amount`). If `entry_amount_sol` ever keeps the original 1.0, this close would compute `exited_amount = 1.0` and gross = 2.0, making the expected total 1.5 wrong. Make this dependency explicit (e.g. assert `remaining == 0.5` immediately before the final close) so the coupling is self-documenting and a regression in the remaining-exposure handling fails here loudly.

### [low] (test)

`#[tokio::test]` defaults to a `current_thread` runtime, so the five spawned tasks only interleave at `.await` points instead of running in parallel. For a race/atomicity characterization, use `#[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 4)]` so the concurrent same-token open path is genuinely stressed; with the current single-threaded runtime, a scheduling-dependent regression in the exclusivity guarantee could go undetected.

## operator/tests/integration/auth_tests.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

`extract_bearer_token` returns `Some("")` for a `Bearer ` header, and `test_extract_bearer_token_empty` (below) codifies this behavior. An empty token is not an authenticated request: any downstream check that only tests `is_some()`/presence of the header would treat it as valid, which is a classic auth bypass. Reject empty tokens at extraction time and update the test to expect `None`. Also consider normalizing case (RFC 7235 auth schemes are case-insensitive) and multiple/leading spaces.

```suggestion
fn extract_bearer_token(header: &str) -> Option<&str> {
    header
        .strip_prefix("Bearer ")
        .filter(|token| !token.is_empty())
}
```

---

### [high] (security)

This mock handler treats any non-empty `signature` as valid and issues a token with role `admin` for any wallet that includes the magic phrase. The signature is never cryptographically verified against the wallet's public key, so this test passes even with a completely bogus signature — masking a potential auth bypass if this pattern is mirrored in production code. The `message.contains(wallet)` substring check is also weak (the address can appear anywhere in the message, and no exact format/timestamp is enforced). Verify the signature (e.g., ed25519/ed25519-dalek verification against the wallet pubkey) and add a negative test asserting that a tampered/invalid signature is rejected with 401.

---

### [high] (test)

All four routes registered in this test ignore the `Authorization` header entirely and always return 200. The test therefore passes for unauthenticated or non-admin requests and does not demonstrate that admin tokens can access all endpoints. Add auth/role enforcement to the handlers (or use the real auth middleware) and include negative assertions (no header → 401, non-admin token → 403) so the test actually validates the access-control claim.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`is_expired` uses `<`, so a token whose `exp` equals the current timestamp is still treated as valid. Per RFC 7519, a JWT MUST NOT be accepted on or after its `exp` time, so the boundary check should be `<=`. The existing tests only cover `exp` in the past/future; add a case for the exact boundary (`exp == now`) which currently would be (incorrectly) considered not expired.

```suggestion
    fn is_expired(&self) -> bool {
        self.exp <= chrono::Utc::now().timestamp()
    }
```

---

### [medium] (test)

This 'format' validation only checks the string length (44 chars), so any 44-character string — including ones with non-base58 characters — would pass. A Solana pubkey is 32 bytes encoded in base58 (typically 43–44 chars), so the test should decode the address with a base58 decoder and assert the decoded length is 32 bytes, and add cases with invalid base58 characters (e.g., `0`, `O`, `I`, `l`) to ensure they are rejected.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The same wallet-auth mock handler is duplicated across four tests (`valid_signature`, `invalid_message`, `address_mismatch`, `missing_fields`) with slightly different logic in each copy. This invites divergence between the tests and the real auth behavior, and makes the intended endpoint contract harder to audit. Extract a single shared handler (or better, exercise the actual auth middleware) so the tests validate one source of truth.

---

## operator/tests/integration/consensus_detection_tests.rs (3 findings)

### [medium] (test)

The return values of the first two `add_signal` calls are discarded. In particular, after Wallet2's BUY there are already 2 distinct wallets, so the second call already returns `Some(ConsensusSignal{wallet_count: 2, total_amount_sol: 2.5})` — this intermediate expectation is never asserted. As written, a regression that triggers consensus on the first signal, or produces wrong `wallet_count`/`total_amount_sol` on the second, would go undetected because only `result3` is checked. Assert the intermediate results too (e.g. result1 `is_none()`, result2 `is_some()` with `wallet_count == 2` and total 2.5) so the test actually pins down the aggregation logic it claims to cover.

---

### [medium] (test)

All five tests hard-depend on an external `TEST_DATABASE_URL`, connect to the same shared Postgres instance, and call `run_migrations()` on it without any cleanup/truncation — yet the code under test never touches the database: `SignalAggregator::add_signal` only manipulates its in-memory `recent_signals` map, and the `db` field in the aggregator is `#[allow(dead_code)]`. Because `#[tokio::test]` runs tests in parallel, the five tests execute `sqlx::migrate!` concurrently against the same shared schema (with no per-test database), which is a source of flaky migration races, and the whole Postgres dependency adds heavy, pointless setup. `temp_dir` is likewise created but never used (it is only meaningful for file-based backends). Consider removing the DB setup entirely and testing the in-memory aggregator directly, or isolating each test in its own database/schema.

---

### [low] (test)

This test is tightly coupled to an implementation detail: `tokio::time::pause()`/`advance()` only manipulate tokio's virtual clock, and the test passes only because `SignalAggregator` happens to record timestamps as `tokio::time::Instant` and performs the 5-minute cleanup inline inside `add_signal`. If the aggregator ever switches to `std::time::Instant`, `SystemTime`, or database-side timestamps, this test will either fail or (worse) pass without actually exercising expiry. Also, the comment claims a background "cleanup loop" removes Wallet1's signal, but no such loop exists — cleanup is synchronous within the next `add_signal` call. Consider documenting the tokio-virtual-time dependency explicitly (and noting the test is a white-box test), or restructuring so the expiry behavior is tested without relying on the aggregator's internal clock source.

## operator/tests/integration/helius_retry_tests.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Wrong retry count: `count < 3` makes the operation fail on counts 0, 1 and 2, i.e. 3 failures + 1 success (4 attempts) with three backoff waits of ~1s + ~2s + ~4s ≈ 7s. The comment and the `2..=6s` assertion assume only 2 failures (1s + 2s ≈ 3s), so `elapsed.as_secs()` (~5.3–8.8s) will exceed the 6s upper bound and the test will fail. Change the condition to `count < 2` (2 failures ≈ 3s total) or update the bounds to reflect three waits (e.g. 5–11s). Note this timing test is also inherently flaky under CI load; prefer asserting the number of attempts/backoff waits rather than wall-clock time.

```suggestion
            if count < 2 {
                Err(anyhow::anyhow!("Simulated transient error"))
            } else {
                Ok::<(), anyhow::Error>(())
            }
```

---

### [high] (bug)

This test does not actually exercise the non-retryable path. `retry_with_backoff` classifies retryability via `extract_status`/`is_network_error`, both of which only recognize `reqwest::Error`. A plain `anyhow!("HTTP 404")` yields `status == 0`, and the implementation treats `status == 0` as retryable. As a result the operation is called 5 times (counter becomes 5, not 1) and `assert_eq!(counter.load(...), 1)` fails after ~15s of sleeps. To test immediate failure on a 404, construct a real `reqwest::Error` with status 404 (e.g. from a mock HTTP server via httpmock/wiremock) rather than an error-message string; otherwise the test only verifies the `status == 0` fallback.

---

### [medium] (test)

The 30s cap is not actually validated here. `calculate_backoff` already clamps the exponent with `2_u64.pow(attempt.min(4))`, so the base is at most 16s and the max jittered value is 20s — the 30s cap (`with_jitter.min(30.0)`) is never reached, and the comment "Without cap, this would be 2^10 = 1024s" is inaccurate for the code under test. Additionally, `as_secs()` truncates, so a real over-cap duration between 30.0s and 30.999s would still pass. If the intent is to verify the documented cap, sample multiple values and compare `as_secs_f64()` against 30.0 (and ideally assert the exponent clamp too).

---

### [low] (test)

This jitter test is probabilistic and unseeded: it relies on 20 random samples producing a spread of at least 1s. With a 2s support ([3s,5s]) the flake probability is small (~(1/2)^19) but nonzero, and the `range >= 1.0` check does not verify the documented ±25% envelope — e.g. a much narrower jitter could still occasionally pass. Seed the RNG (or expose a jitter function accepting a seed) and/or assert the empirical min/max fall within [3s, 5s] to make the test deterministic and meaningful.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Both `Duration` and `sleep` are imported at module level but never used anywhere in this file (all sleeps happen inside `retry_with_backoff`), which triggers unused-import warnings. Remove them.

---

### [low] (test)

The assertion message/count is inconsistent with the actual flow even after the condition is fixed: the comment states "1st attempt (fail) + backoff1 + 2nd attempt (fail) + backoff2 + 3rd attempt (success)". Keep the comment, the condition, and the bounds in sync when changing this test.

## operator/tests/integration/position_lifecycle_tests.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (test)

This raw SQL overwrite makes the "Net PnL after fees" assertion tautological and bypasses the production logic entirely. `close_position_full` already computes and persists `net_pnl_sol`/`pnl_sol` itself (postgres.rs:1811–1839), so the test writes 0.0983, reads it back, and asserts it equals 0.0983 — a regression in the production fee/PnL computation would still pass. Worse, the hand-computed expectation (0.1 − jito − dex − slippage = 0.0983) contradicts the production A1 cost model, which treats DEX fee and slippage as attribution-only and computes net = gross − entry costs − exit jito tip − exit network fee (here 0.1 − 0.001 = 0.099). To genuinely test "PnL accuracy with fees", call `update_trade_costs` *before* `close_position_full` and assert the `net_pnl_sol`/`realized_net_pnl_sol` values that production persists, using the documented cost model.

The `trades` table is never checked, so a regression where `close_position_full` accidentally inserts/updates a trade row on the no-op path would go undetected. The test comment states the goal is "exactly one trade row (UNIQUE constraint on trades.trade_uuid) and one position", but only the `positions` table is asserted. The idempotency invariant is partially implied by the second `insert_trade` failing, yet nothing verifies that the `trades` table still holds exactly one row for this uuid. Also note the semantics: the duplicate is rejected with an error (UNIQUE violation) rather than being treated as an idempotent no-op — so the test documents that callers must swallow the error on retry. Fetch the value as `Decimal` (sqlx supports NUMERIC → rust_decimal) and assert exact equality instead of casting to f64; the same applies to the `net_stored` assertion below.

## operator/tests/integration/profitability_verdict_tests.rs (2 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

`seed_outcome` silently rewrites any unrecognized strategy to "SHIELD" in the trades row, while the linked decision_records row keeps the caller's original string. A typo such as "SHILED" would therefore pass silently, producing a decision↔trade strategy mismatch that could misgroup cohort-positivity buckets or mask test-data errors. Fail loudly instead (e.g. assert the strategy is one of SHIELD/SPEAR/EXIT) and pass it through unchanged, so bad fixtures break the test rather than being silently normalized.

```suggestion
    assert!(
        matches!(strategy, "SHIELD" | "SPEAR" | "EXIT"),
        "unexpected strategy in seed_outcome: {strategy}"
    );
    let trade_strategy = strategy;
```

### [low] (maintainability)

Each `seed_n_outcomes` call restarts the wallet/token counter at 0, so the second and third batches reuse `w0..wN`/`tok0..tokN` from the first batch within the same run. The same `wallet_address`/`token_address` then appears on unrelated trades; any query that groups or dedups by wallet would silently merge these rows, and the fixture is harder to reason about. Consider parameterizing a per-batch wallet/token prefix or offset so names stay unique (same issue exists in `drawdown_exceeds_20pct_fails`).

## operator/tests/integration/safety_validation_tests.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Silent blockhash failure masks safety validation: `latest_blockhash().await.unwrap_or_default()` turns an RPC failure into a zero blockhash, and `inline_jito_tip` happily produces a valid legacy message with that zero blockhash. All downstream assertions (instruction count, verbatim preservation, tip last) still pass, so this harness can green-light the D3 tip-inlining path with no real blockhash. The parallel v0 test correctly SKIPs on the same failure. Use the same SKIP-on-error pattern.

```suggestion
    let fresh = match latest_blockhash().await {
        Ok(h) => h,
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("SKIP (no blockhash): {e}");
            return;
        }
    };
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Brittle blockhash inequality assertion: `refresh_v0_blockhash` swaps the field to the value returned by `latest_blockhash()`. The swap tx fetched from Jupiter was built with Jupiter's own latest blockhash moments earlier; if it happens to equal the public RPC's latest blockhash (slot hasn't advanced / same cluster view), `m.recent_blockhash == v0.recent_blockhash` and this `assert_ne!` fails spuriously even though the refresh is perfectly correct. The `assert_eq!(m.recent_blockhash, fresh)` above already proves the swap occurred, so drop the redundant inequality check (or gate it on the values differing).

```suggestion
            // No assert_ne! here: the fetched swap tx may already carry the same
            // latest blockhash, which would spuriously fail a correct refresh.
```

---

### [low] (test)

`THROWAWAY_USER` is the System Program id (`111...`), not a neutral throwaway account. Jupiter may reject the request (silently SKIPping the test) or build an atypical swap tx — e.g. the fee payer / SOL-wrap source becomes the system program. The legacy test then uses `legacy.account_keys[0]` (the system program) as the tip source, so neither test validates a representative real-world swap. Use a random valid pubkey (e.g. a hardcoded `Pubkey::new_unique()` value) that is not any well-known program, and add a comment that it is an arbitrary unused account.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Both tests mutate the process-global Jupiter API key via `jupiter::set_api_key`, which is a `OnceLock` with first-wins semantics (`let _ = API_KEY.set(key)`). Under the default parallel test harness, whichever test runs first installs the key and the other call is a silent no-op. This is benign only because both tests read the identical env var; the tests are nevertheless coupled through global state, and if any code in the same process ever installs `None` or a different key first (e.g. the library's own startup path or a future test), the swap requests silently go out without the key and the harness mis-SKIPs. Consider installing the key exactly once (e.g. before both tests via a shared setup) and documenting that the global is process-wide.

```suggestion
    // Install the process-global key exactly once (OnceLock first-wins);
    // subsequent calls from other tests are silently ignored.
    jupiter::set_api_key(Some(key));
```

## operator/tests/integration/token_safety_tests.rs (3 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (test)

This test depends on live mainnet RPC and real token data, making it non-deterministic and flaky. BONK is not in the parser's whitelist (only USDC/USDT/WSOL are), so `fast_check` performs a real RPC metadata fetch. If the RPC is unreachable, `fast_check` returns `unsafe_with_reason(...)` WITHOUT inserting into the cache (see parser.rs error path), so the final `assert!(cache.get(...).is_some())` fails. Additionally, both results are discarded (`_result1`/`_result2`), so the test cannot distinguish a true cache hit from a second RPC fetch (the metadata cache could mask it). Recommend injecting a mock/fake `TokenMetadataFetcher` so the test is deterministic, and asserting on the returned values (e.g., second call returns the same `TokenSafetyResult` as the first, proving the cache hit).

---

### [medium] (test)

The assertion only checks `result.is_ok()`, so a wrong verdict (e.g., the whitelist path returning unsafe) would go undetected. The note claiming verification 'requires RPC access' is inaccurate: `fast_check` calls `is_whitelisted()` before any RPC fetch (parser.rs), so a whitelisted USDC returns a safe result without network access. The test should assert the actual safety value, e.g. `result.expect(...).safe`, which would also make the whitelist fast-path behavior verifiable deterministically.

---

### [low] (test)

The test relies on wall-clock timing: sleeping 2s for a 1s TTL leaves only ~1s margin and forces a 2s wait in CI. This is timing-sensitive (scheduler stalls, NTP clock jumps) and unnecessarily slow. For a deterministic check, use a 0-second TTL (immediate expiry, as the cache.rs unit test does) or inject a controllable clock into `TokenCache`, so no wall-clock sleep is needed.

---

## operator/tests/integration/volatility_tests.rs (4 findings)

### [medium] (test)

`Decimal::from_f64(price).unwrap_or_default()` silently turns any conversion failure (NaN, infinity, or out-of-range values) into 0, which corrupts the price history and the resulting volatility without the test ever surfacing the real cause. Since these are fixed test constants, use `Decimal::from_f64(price).expect("test price must convert")` (or `Decimal::try_from`) so a conversion failure fails loudly. The same pattern is duplicated in `test_get_sol_volatility` (line ~93) and `test_volatility_high_volatility_detection` (line ~113).

---

### [medium] (test)

This test claims to verify the 24h window, but every price is inserted at 'now', so the window pruning logic (`cutoff = now - Duration::hours(24)` in `set_price`) is never exercised — the test would pass even if entries older than 24h were never evicted. To actually test the window, entries with timestamps more than 24h old must be inserted. Note that the `#[cfg(test)]` `set_price_with_time` helper is not visible to integration tests, so this requires a non-`cfg(test)` timestamp-injectable API (or a clock parameter) on `PriceCache`.

---

### [low] (test)

These tests are wall-clock/timing dependent: each sample is preceded by a 10ms real sleep purely to get distinct `Utc::now()` timestamps, which adds ~100–200ms of wall time per test and relies on clock granularity being finer than the sleep interval. On a coarse-granularity clock or under heavy scheduling, samples can share timestamps (and would silently change results if `calculate_volatility` ever becomes time-weighted, a natural evolution of the metric). Since the current calculation only depends on entry order, the sleeps are unnecessary — consider removing them, or injecting a controllable clock to make the tests deterministic and fast.

---

### [low] (test)

The 30% threshold is hardcoded from this particular sample set rather than derived from the documented volatility formula (std-dev of consecutive % changes), so any legitimate change to the metric (e.g., time-weighting or annualization) will break this test without indicating a real regression. Consider computing the expected value independently from the formula in the test (or documenting the derivation), so the assertion is tied to the metric's definition rather than to an arbitrary constant.

## operator/tests/integration/webhook_flow_tests.rs (6 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (test)

The "full webhook flow" route is an inline stub that only checks header presence — it never verifies the HMAC signature, timestamp drift, replay nonce, or idempotency, so the end-to-end security pipeline (middleware/hmac.rs -> handlers/webhook.rs) is completely bypassed. A broken signature/timestamp check in production would still pass this test. The stub also returns 200 OK while the real `webhook_handler` returns 202 Accepted. Wire the actual `webhook_handler` behind the real `hmac_verify` middleware (same composition as main.rs's webhook route) and assert on the real behavior. The same stub-handler problem applies to `test_webhook_missing_signature` below.

### [medium] (test)

These HMAC tests reimplement signature verification in the test itself using the same hmac crate rather than invoking the production `hmac_verify` middleware / `verify_with_secrets` (operator/src/middleware/hmac.rs). Any regression in the production path — signature update order, hex handling, constant-time comparison, secret rotation — would go completely undetected. Recommend building a test router with the real `hmac_verify` middleware + `webhook_handler` (as main.rs does) and sending signed requests through it.

---

### [medium] (test)

These "rejection" tests never send a request — they only assert that a locally-built 5000-char string is longer than 4096. The middleware's `MAX_HEADER_SIZE` rejection path (400 `Signature/Timestamp header too large` in hmac.rs) is therefore never exercised, so the DoS-protection behavior is untested. Note also `secret`, `timestamp`, and `body` are declared but never used here (dead-code warnings). Replace with a real request carrying an oversized X-Signature/X-Timestamp header through the `hmac_verify` middleware and assert the 400 response.

---

### [medium] (test)

The timestamp-drift tests only validate plain integer arithmetic (`(now - req_time).abs()`) — they never invoke the middleware's drift gate or its nonce/replay store. Replay protection, the strict boundary (`drift > max_drift_secs` rejected), and nonce dedup across repeat requests are thus completely untested against the real middleware. These assertions can also be flaky at the boundary because `now` is captured before the assertion runs. Send requests with out-of-window / repeated timestamps through `hmac_verify` and assert the 401 responses instead.

---

### [medium] (test)

Despite the test name, this only checks that `trade_uuid_exists` returns true after an insert — it never sends a duplicate webhook through the handler, so the idempotent-rejection path (webhook_handler returning 200 with `status: rejected`, `reason: duplicate_signal`) is never verified. It also never exercises `SignalPayload::generate_trade_uuid`. Recommend inserting via one signed request and submitting the same signed payload a second time, asserting the second response is rejected with `duplicate_signal`.

### [low] (test)

This test only hashes a locally-concatenated `timestamp+token+action+amount` string; it never calls the production `SignalPayload::generate_trade_uuid` (models/signal.rs), which hashes `wallet_address||token||action||amount_sol` (no timestamp — intentionally, so retries with the same payload dedupe) and truncates to 16 bytes. So the real idempotency-key determinism is not validated, and the doc comment "Same inputs should generate same UUID" is misleading. ## operator/tests/integration_tests.rs (7 findings, 4 critical, 1 high)

### [critical] (bug)

SQLite-style `?` bind placeholder used against a `Pool<Postgres>` (from `pg_pool`/`common::create_test_db`, which is PostgreSQL-only). sqlx/Postgres only supports `$1`-style positional binds; this query will fail at runtime with a syntax error, so this test never runs as written. Use `$1` (as in `db_abstraction/postgres.rs` and other test files).

```suggestion
    let row: (i64,) = sqlx::query_as("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM trades WHERE trade_uuid = $1")
        .bind(uuid)
```

---

### [critical] (bug)

Same `?` placeholder issue as in `test_trade_idempotency`: this SELECT runs against a PostgreSQL pool, where `?` is not valid bind syntax (only `$1`… is). The UPDATE above it correctly uses `$1/$2`, making the inconsistency obvious.

```suggestion
    let row: (Decimal,) = sqlx::query_as("SELECT net_pnl_sol FROM trades WHERE trade_uuid = $1")
        .bind(uuid)
```

---

### [critical] (bug)

Same `?` placeholder problem: this SELECT is executed on a PostgreSQL pool (from `common::pg_pool`) and must use `$1` instead of `?`, otherwise the test fails with a syntax error and `update_trade_status` is never actually verified.

```suggestion
    let row: (String,) = sqlx::query_as("SELECT status FROM trades WHERE trade_uuid = $1")
        .bind(uuid)
```

---

### [critical] (bug)

Same `?` placeholder issue as the other tests: the INSERT and the two SELECTs in this test run against a PostgreSQL pool and will fail with a syntax error. Replace `?` with `$1` (and the second SELECT likewise). Note the numeric literals (55.0, 0.65, etc.) are fine, but the bind marker is not valid Postgres syntax.

```suggestion
    sqlx::query(
        "INSERT INTO wallets (address, status, wqs_score, roi_7d, roi_30d, trade_count_30d, win_rate, max_drawdown_30d, avg_trade_size_sol)
         VALUES ($1, 'CANDIDATE', 55.0, 12.0, 30.0, 25, 0.65, 10.0, 0.5)",
    )
    .bind(address)
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`net_pnl_sol` is `NUMERIC(30,18)` on Postgres: sqlx cannot decode NUMERIC into `String` (no such `Decode` impl), so `query_as::<_, (String,)>` fails even after the placeholder is fixed. And even if decoding succeeded (e.g. SQLite TEXT column), round-tripping a 30-digit financial value through `f64` is lossy, while `unwrap_or(0.0)` silently turns any parse failure into 0.0 and masks data corruption. Decode directly to `rust_decimal::Decimal` (the `sqlx` `rust_decimal` feature is enabled) and compare exactly.

```suggestion
    let (net_pnl,): (Decimal,) = sqlx::query_as("SELECT net_pnl_sol FROM trades WHERE trade_uuid = $1")
        .bind(uuid)
        .fetch_one(&pool)
        .await
        .unwrap();
    assert_eq!(net_pnl, Decimal::from_str("-2.5").unwrap(), "net_pnl_sol should be -2.5");
```

---

### [medium] (test)

This test only asserts `upsert_wallet` returned `Ok` — it never re-reads the wallet or verifies the persisted fields, so a no-op implementation (or a write to the wrong table/backend) would pass. It should re-query the row and assert the stored status/score fields. Also, the doc comment claims it falls back to SQLite, but `common::create_test_db_from_env()` always creates a PostgreSQL database (and requires `TEST_DATABASE_URL`), so the comment is misleading and the harness is not actually backend-agnostic.

```suggestion
    result.expect("upsert_wallet should work on both backends");

    // Verify the write actually persisted: re-read the row and assert stored fields
    let pool = pg_pool(&db);
    let (status,): (String,) = sqlx::query_as("SELECT status FROM wallets WHERE address = $1")
        .bind("test-wallet-backend-agnostic")
        .fetch_one(&pool)
        .await
        .expect("wallet should have been persisted");
    assert_eq!(status, "CANDIDATE");
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

This UPDATE is executed as raw SQL, bypassing the `Database` trait abstraction used in production. The test therefore verifies only the schema, not the actual persistence code path (`db_abstraction/postgres.rs` `update_trade_pnl` etc.). Prefer driving mutations through the trait where possible, or add a companion assertion that goes through the trait, so a regression in the production query layer is caught.

## operator/tests/reconciliation_tests.rs (4 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

The aging here is ineffective and the comment is misleading. `run_reconciliation` has NO exit-confirmation grace window — `reconcile_position` checks the exit signature for every `EXITING` position regardless of age and auto-resolves immediately on `Found`, so aging the position changes nothing and the test would pass without this call. Worse, this `UPDATE` fires the `positions_updated_at` trigger which resets `last_updated = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, so if an exit-staleness check based on `last_updated` is ever added, this test would not actually create a stale exit (exactly the trap the comment claims to set). Remove the dead `age_opened_at` call, or — if exit staleness is meant to be pinned — plant `last_updated` via the `set_last_updated` helper instead.

---

### [medium] (test)

The test's stated goal is to verify "A log row was inserted recording the confirmed entry," but the assertions only check aggregate counters (`status.checked_count >= 1`, `metrics.reconciliation_checked.get() >= 1`). A regression that stops writing the per-position `reconciliation_log` row would still pass, and `>= 1` is too loose even for the aggregates (the run inspected exactly one position). Query `reconciliation_log` directly for `trade_uuid` and assert the `discrepancy` is `NONE` (as `test_reconciliation_handles_null_values` does), and tighten the counter assertions to `== 1`.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`set_last_updated` is not panic-safe: if the UPDATE between `DISABLE TRIGGER` and `ENABLE TRIGGER` fails or panics (the `.unwrap()` is a live panic point), the `positions_updated_at` trigger is left disabled in the test database. Because every test creates its own isolated DB the blast radius is small, but this is fragile. Since PostgreSQL DDL is transactional, wrap the disable/update/enable in a transaction (rollback restores the trigger), or use a guard type whose `Drop` re-enables the trigger so cleanup always runs.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

These helpers hard-code schema internals — the `positions` table, `opened_at`/`last_updated`/`trade_uuid` columns, and the `positions_updated_at` trigger name — duplicating knowledge already encapsulated by the `Database` abstraction. A trigger rename or column change fails with a confusing `ALTER`/`UPDATE` error at best, and a semantic change (e.g. the trigger behavior) silently diverges. Consider exposing timestamp-planting through `db_abstraction` or centralizing these helpers in `tests/common` with a single source of truth.

## operator/tests/test_volume_cache.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (test)

The `has_volume_drop` results are only printed, never asserted — a regression in drop-detection logic would not fail this test. Worse, with the current implementation both calls actually return `false` here: `has_volume_drop` needs ≥12 baseline samples for the windowed comparison, then falls back to a single-point-vs-24h-average check that is guarded by `now.signed_duration_since(oldest).num_minutes() < 30 -> false`. This test only records ~100ms of history, so both thresholds return `false` and the test passes vacuously while the printed diagnostics claim a drop was detected. Assert on the booleans, and restructure the test (e.g., an injectable clock or bulk history loader in `VolumeCache`) so the windowed comparison is exercised with real 24h-spanning data.

```suggestion
    let has_dropped = cache.has_volume_drop("declining_token", dec!(50));
    assert!(has_dropped, "50% threshold should detect the decline");
    println!("✓ Volume drop detected (50% threshold): {}", has_dropped);

    let has_dropped_lower = cache.has_volume_drop("declining_token", dec!(20));
    assert!(has_dropped_lower, "20% threshold should also detect the decline");
    println!("✓ Volume drop detected (20% threshold): {}", has_dropped_lower);
```

### [high] (test)

The test claims to verify that stale data (>10 minutes old) doesn't trigger false drops, but only 100ms elapse and `record_volume` stamps `Utc::now()` internally, so no entry can ever be older than the 10-minute staleness guard in `has_volume_drop`. The staleness branch is never reached and the assertion passes trivially for the wrong reason (the newest entry is recent and the history spans <30 minutes). To actually test this path, `VolumeCache` needs an injectable clock or a test-only `record_volume_at(token, volume, timestamp)` so genuinely stale entries can be created.

### [medium] (test)

Wall-clock sleeps are used to create "timestamp variation," but drop detection operates on minute/hour windows (60-min recent vs 23-h baseline, 30-min minimum history), so 10–100ms gaps have no effect on the results — they only slow the tests down and make them timing-dependent on loaded CI machines. Prefer an injectable clock (or passing timestamps to `record_volume`) so the tests are deterministic and fast.

### [medium] (test)

Each thread writes to a distinct token, so this test only exercises lock contention on the shared map, not concurrent mutation of a single token's history (the `VecDeque::push_back` plus 24h pruning protected by the write lock). Races on shared per-token state would go undetected. Add a test where multiple threads record to the same token and then assert invariants — e.g., the final entry count equals the total number of writes, the most recent value is the largest written, and no entries are lost.

This file lives in `tests/`, so `cargo test` compiles it as a test crate whose harness generates its own entry point; this `fn main()` is dead code under `cargo test` (it is never executed) and can conflict with the harness-generated `main` depending on the toolchain. Remove it and rely on the `#[test]` functions.

## operator/tests/unit/circuit_breaker_real_tests.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

SQLite dialect executed against PostgreSQL: this helper runs on a `Pool<Postgres>` (pg_pool panics unless the backend is PostgreSQL), but `INSERT OR IGNORE` is SQLite-only syntax — PostgreSQL raises a syntax error at `OR`, so `execute().await.unwrap()` panics in every test that calls `insert_closed_position_with_pnl`. The file also mixes SQLite `?` placeholders (helpers, drawdown test) with Postgres `$1` / `NOW() + ($1)::interval` (consecutive-loss tests), and the module doc still says "real in-memory SQLite database" while the code requires `TEST_DATABASE_URL`/PostgreSQL. Convert the helper to `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` with consistent Postgres syntax, and update the module docs.

---

### [medium] (test)

This test does not exercise the behavior it claims to document. After `enter_cooldown()`, it never calls `evaluate()` on the cooldown CB — it creates a fresh `cb2` and evaluates that, so the "cooldown exit without re-evaluation" path is untested. Moreover the premise is stale: `evaluate()` in circuit_breaker.rs explicitly calls `exit_cooldown()` when the cooldown expires, and `exit_cooldown()` re-checks breach conditions and re-trips ("Circuit breaker cooldown expired but breach condition still present — re-tripped"). To actually test the documented behavior, call `cb.evaluate()` after `enter_cooldown()` (cooldown_minutes=0) and assert the resulting state transition.

### [medium] (test)

Wrong insert helper: `insert_closed_trade_with_pnl` populates only `trades`, but `get_consecutive_losses()` does `SELECT COALESCE(p.realized_pnl_sol, 0.0) FROM trades t LEFT JOIN positions p ...` — a trade without a position row reads as 0.0 (a non-loss), so the consecutive counter breaks on the first row and the `Active` assertion passes vacuously regardless of the LOSE/WIN/LOSE/LOSE pattern. Additionally, all rows share `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` created_at, so `ORDER BY created_at DESC` has ties and the order is nondeterministic. Use `insert_closed_position_with_pnl` (both tables) and backdate created_at/closed_at as the sibling `test_consecutive_losses_resets_at_intervening_win` does.

---

### [medium] (test)

SOL/USD conflation: the helper writes the same numeric value into both `realized_pnl_sol` and `realized_pnl_usd`, and the tests then assert against the USD threshold (`max_loss_24h_usd`). However, the current implementation (`get_evaluation_data`) sums `positions.realized_pnl_usd` (24h, pnl_data_valid) and `evaluate()` compares that USD total against `max_loss_24h_usd` — there is no "SOL treated as USD" path, so these tests only pass because they inject fake USD values. The comments claiming a unit-mismatch bug ("potential unit mismatch bug") are stale, and the tests would silently pass even if the close path incorrectly wrote SOL into the USD column. Insert USD-denominated values (e.g. SOL × price) explicitly and update the comments to reflect the real SQL semantics.

Stale and timing-sensitive rate-limit test: the module doc and this test describe a "30-second rate limit", but `CircuitBreaker::new` now sets `check_interval: Duration::seconds(5)` (comment: "Reduced from 30s to 5s for faster loss detection"). The second `evaluate()` call is only skipped if it happens within 5s; if the 10 DB inserts between the two calls take longer than 5s on a slow CI runner, the second call re-evaluates, trips on the -1000 loss, and this test fails spuriously. Update the docs to the 5s interval and make the assertion robust (e.g., assert on rate-limit accounting/last_check rather than wall-clock timing).

## operator/tests/unit/db_integrity_tests.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (test)

This test asserts that the FK constraint blocks trade deletion, but the actual schema (operator/migrations_postgres/0001_full_schema.sql, positions table) declares `FOREIGN KEY (trade_uuid) REFERENCES trades(trade_uuid) ON DELETE CASCADE`. A plain `DELETE FROM trades` therefore succeeds and cascade-deletes the child position, so `delete_result.is_err()` is false and this test fails. The test's premise (and its 'SQLite PRAGMA foreign_keys / sqlite3 chimera.db' commentary) also describes SQLite behavior, while the pool here is PostgreSQL where FK enforcement is schema-level, not per-connection. The real orphaning risk is the reverse: CASCADE silently deletes positions/PnL data when a trade is removed. Either assert the actual CASCADE semantics (delete succeeds, position removed) or remove CASCADE from the schema if blocking is intended, and rewrite the SQLite-specific comments.

```suggestion
    // Schema uses ON DELETE CASCADE: deleting the trade also deletes its position.
    let delete_result = sqlx::query("DELETE FROM trades WHERE trade_uuid = $1")
        .bind(uuid)
        .execute(&pool)
        .await;

    assert!(
        delete_result.is_ok(),
        "trade deletion should succeed (FK is ON DELETE CASCADE)"
    );
    let pos_count: (i64,) = sqlx::query_as(
        "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM positions WHERE trade_uuid = $1",
    )
    .bind(uuid)
    .fetch_one(&pool)
    .await
    .unwrap();
    assert_eq!(pos_count.0, 0, "cascade should remove the child position");
```

---

### [medium] (test)

This test codifies the silent no-op as the expected contract (`Ok(false)`), even though its own comment documents it as a bug ('the caller has no way to detect a missed close') and the file's stated purpose is to eliminate silent failures that corrupt trade state. `close_position_full` currently returns `Ok(false)` with only a WARN log (postgres.rs:1499-1507), so the test enshrines the buggy behavior instead of driving the fix described in the header. If the intent is for callers to detect a missed close, assert `Err`/a typed no-op result; if `Ok(false)` is the deliberate contract, remove the 'BUG DOCUMENTED' framing so the test does not contradict itself.

---

### [medium] (test)

The cost columns are NUMERIC(30) in PostgreSQL, but the test decodes them as String, parses to f64, and compares with an absolute epsilon. This weakens the assertion in two ways: (1) f64 round-trip can mask accumulation/precision errors that a Decimal comparison (rust_decimal is already imported) would catch, and (2) `.unwrap_or(0.0)` silently converts a NULL or parse failure into 0.0, which could make a missing-cost bug appear to pass. Query the columns as Decimal and assert exact Decimal equality, or propagate the parse error instead of defaulting to zero.

```suggestion
    let jito = Decimal::from_str(&jito_str).unwrap();
    let total = Decimal::from_str(&total_str).unwrap();

    assert_eq!(jito, Decimal::from_str("0.003").unwrap());
    assert_eq!(total, Decimal::from_str("0.0051").unwrap());
```

---

### [low] (documentation)

Stale documentation: the file header and this comment describe `update_trade_status()` as silently returning `Ok(())` for a missing UUID, but the actual implementation (postgres.rs:288-290) returns `Err(AppError::NotFound(...))` when `rows_affected() == 0`, and this very test asserts `result.is_err()`. The comment contradicts both the code and the assertion, which will confuse future readers about whether the bug is fixed. Update the header and comment to state the fix is in place (rows_affected == 0 now returns an error).

```suggestion
    // FIXED: update_trade_status returns Err (NotFound) when 0 rows were updated.
    // This lets the caller distinguish "updated successfully" from "UUID not found"
    // and prevents phantom state transitions that leave the actual trade stuck in PENDING.
```

### [low] (maintainability)

`create_test_db` creates a `TempDir` that serves no purpose for the PostgreSQL backend used here (the test helper panics unless the pool is PostgreSQL; TempDir only matters for a file-backed SQLite DB). Drop the TempDir, or scope it to an SQLite variant of the helper.

```suggestion
    let db = create_database(&config).await.unwrap();

```

## operator/tests/unit/jupiter_error_handling_tests.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (test)

Flaky test: the variation denominator `delays[0]` is a random sample, not the minimum or a deterministic baseline. With jitter_factor=0.2 at attempt 2, each delay is uniform in [160, 240]ms. When `delays[0]` lands near the low end (e.g., ~165ms) and the 10-sample range (max-min) approaches ~70-80ms, the ratio exceeds 0.4 and the assertion fails. Given the distribution of the range for 10 uniform samples, the failure probability is roughly 10-15% per run, causing intermittent CI failures. Fix: normalize by the theoretical base delay (initial_delay_ms * backoff_multiplier^(attempt-1), capped), which makes the bound deterministic: max-min ≤ 2*jitter_factor*base = 0.4*base exactly.

```suggestion
    // Variation should be reasonable (not too extreme)
    let base_delay = (config.initial_delay_ms as f64
        * config.backoff_multiplier.powi(1))
        .min(config.max_delay_ms as f64);
    let variation =
        (max_delay.as_millis() - min_delay.as_millis()) as f64 / base_delay;
```

---

### [medium] (test)

Fragile test: the 1.5-2.5x ratio bounds are only valid for the current jitter model (uniform ±jitter_factor, clamped at 0). For the default config the true range is [1.64, 2.44], which just fits inside the window — but any small change to how jitter is applied (asymmetric jitter, additive on the raw base, no clamp, jitter scaled differently once the cap is hit) will push consecutive-delay ratios outside the asserted bounds and make this test nondeterministic. Consider deriving the bounds from the config values (e.g., min/max ratio = multiplier * (1±jitter_factor)/(1∓jitter_factor)) or computing ratios against the deterministic un-jittered capped base instead of hard-coded 1.5/2.5.

### [medium] (test)

This test codifies a policy where every unclassified HTTP status code (e.g., 418, 404, 422) is `retryable` with a retry delay. Verify this matches the production retry policy: since the retry loop will re-attempt these permanent client errors, this can cause avoidable retry storms and additional load on the Jupiter API. Consider asserting a narrower classification (retryable only for 5xx/timeout/429/network) or documenting why unknown statuses are intentionally retried.

### [low] (test)

This assertion silently couples the test to the current `RetryConfig::default()` (initial_delay_ms=100, jitter_factor=0.1). If the defaults are ever changed (e.g., jitter raised to 0.2 or initial delay changed), this test fails with a misleading message that says nothing about the actual cause. Use an explicit config (e.g., `RetryConfig { jitter_factor: 0.1, ..Default::default() }`) or derive the expected bounds from the config values so the assertion self-documents its assumptions.

## operator/tests/unit/kelly_sizer_tests.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (test)

These tests are not re-runnable and are unsafe to run concurrently against a shared `TEST_DATABASE_URL`. All tests insert trades with fixed UUIDs ("win-0"…"loss-7", "neg-win-0"…, etc.) and never clean them up, while `trade_uuid` is `NOT NULL UNIQUE` in the schema and `insert_trade` performs a plain `INSERT` with no `ON CONFLICT` clause. The first run succeeds, but any subsequent run against the same database panics at `db.insert_trade(...).unwrap()` with a duplicate-key error. Stale trades from prior runs also sit inside the 30-day lookback window and silently contaminate results. Fix: delete seeded trades before each test (e.g., `DELETE FROM trades WHERE wallet_address = $1` in `setup_test_db` or per-test) or generate unique UUIDs (e.g., `Uuid::new_v4()`).

---

### [medium] (test)

Seeded data does not match the scenario described in the test comments. KellySizer computes `pnl_pct = net_pnl_sol / amount_sol` (kelly_sizer.rs), so here wins are 0.1/0.1 = 1.0 (100%) and losses are 0.05/0.05 = 1.0 (100%) — not the intended 10%/5% used in the comment "full_kelly = (0.6 * 0.1 - 0.4 * 0.05) / 0.1 = 0.4". With this seeding the actual result is avg_win=avg_loss=1.0, b=1.0, full_kelly = (0.6*1.0 - 0.4)/1.0 = 0.2, i.e. half the documented value. The same mismatch exists in `test_kelly_negative_edge` and `test_expected_profit_negative_edge` (amount_sol set equal to net_pnl_sol). Use `amount_sol = 1.0` for all trades (as `test_expected_profit_calculation` already does) so pnl percentages are the intended 0.1/0.05.

---

### [medium] (test)

Assertions are far weaker than the comments claim: the test documents exact expected values (full_kelly=0.4, conservative=0.1) but only checks positivity and `conservative <= full`. A regression in the Kelly formula (e.g., wrong b ratio or missing cap) could change 0.4 → 0.2 and this test would still pass. Assert concrete values, e.g. `assert_eq!(result.full_kelly, dec!(0.4))` after fixing the amount_sol seeding (see related comment). Note the conservative value in the comment (0.1) is also stale: with the velocity multiplier (all trades share the same created_at → span clamped to 1 day → 20 trades/day → multiplier 1.25), the correct conservative value would be min(0.4*1.25*0.25, 0.4, 1.0) = 0.125. Either update the comment to the true expected value or control created_at to make the velocity multiplier deterministic.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

These tests bypass the `Database` abstraction and execute raw `sqlx::query("UPDATE trades SET net_pnl_sol = ...")` against the Postgres schema directly. This couples the tests to exact column names and the PostgreSQL backend: if the trades table is refactored (e.g., net_pnl_sol renamed or moved into a side table) or a non-Postgres backend is introduced, these tests break silently at the SQL layer rather than through the trait contract. Consider adding a small `set_net_pnl_sol` helper on the Database trait (or seeding via existing trait methods) so the tests exercise the same interface as production code.

## operator/tests/unit/momentum_exit_tests.rs (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (test)

These "unit" tests require a live Postgres instance: setup hard-panics via `expect`/`unwrap` when TEST_DATABASE_URL is unset or the DB is unreachable, so the suite cannot run in an offline/sandboxed CI at all. Worse, this dependency is entirely unnecessary here — the MomentumExit engine keeps `db` as `#[allow(dead_code)]` and `check_momentum` never touches it; the DB is only used for `run_migrations()`. Consider an in-memory/mock Database so these stay true unit tests, or at minimum skip gracefully when the env var is missing. Also note `TempDir::new()` is unused and dropped at the end of the function, adding a needless panic point.

---

### [medium] (test)

Every test calls `run_migrations()` against the same shared TEST_DATABASE_URL. cargo runs each `#[tokio::test]` on its own thread in parallel, so multiple concurrent DDL migration runs can race (lock contention, duplicate-object errors), and there is no cleanup or per-test schema isolation — leftover state can make the suite order-dependent and flaky across runs. Prefer migrating once (e.g., a lazily-initialized shared setup / dedicated schema per worker) and cleaning up test state.

---

### [medium] (test)

Position age is derived from wall-clock time (`SystemTime::now() - Duration::from_secs(120)`), and the engine flips its base drop threshold from 5% to 8% at `elapsed_minutes < 6`. All three sub-checks share the same `entry_time_new`, so if slow CI delays the "6% drop on a 2-minute-old position" assertion by more than ~4 minutes, elapsed crosses 6 minutes, the threshold becomes 8%, and the expected `Exit` assertion fails. Inject a clock into the detector (or compute entry time as close as possible to each assertion) to make the test immune to wall-clock drift.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

These comments state the base threshold switches at 16 minutes (RSI availability), but the engine (`momentum_exit.rs`) switches at 6 minutes: `base_drop_threshold = if elapsed_minutes < 6 { 5 } else { 8 }`. The assertions happen to hold either way, but the stale "16 minutes" description misleads maintainers about the boundary these tests exercise — the 2-min and 20-min cases sit on the 5%→8% edge defined at 6 minutes, not 16.

## operator/tests/unit/position_sizer_tests.rs (5 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

Compile error: `..*cfg` attempts to move the remaining fields out of `*cfg`, which is a place behind a shared `Arc` deref. `PositionSizingConfig` is not `Copy`, so the compiler rejects this with "cannot move out of dereference of `Arc<PositionSizingConfig>`" and this test (and the whole test binary) fails to build. Use `..(*cfg).clone()` instead.

```suggestion
    let kelly_cfg = chimera_operator::config::PositionSizingConfig {
        use_kelly_sizing: true,
        kelly_fraction: Decimal::from_str("0.25").unwrap(),
        ..(*cfg).clone()
    };
```

---

### [high] (bug)

sqlx 0.8 with the `postgres` feature requires `$1`-style positional placeholders; `?` is only supported for MySQL/SQLite. These queries are sent to PostgreSQL verbatim, which will raise `syntax error at or near "?"` for every bind. The same problem exists in the `positions` INSERT below and in `insert_closed_trades`. Replace `?` with `$1` (and `$2`, ... for additional binds).

```suggestion
        sqlx::query(
            "INSERT INTO trades (trade_uuid, wallet_address, token_address, strategy, side, amount_sol, status) \
             VALUES ($1, 'wallet_x', 'token_x', 'SHIELD', 'BUY', 1.0, 'ACTIVE')"
        )
```

---

### [high] (test)

This test permanently drops the `positions` table in the shared `TEST_DATABASE_URL` database that every test in this file connects to (each `create_test_db()` uses the same URL, and re-running migrations won't recreate a table that was already recorded as migrated). Consequences: (1) any other test in the same run that inserts into or reads `positions` (e.g. `test_max_concurrent_positions_enforced`, `test_one_below_max_allows_new_position`) will fail afterwards or race with the drop since cargo runs tests concurrently; (2) those two tests also share the same table and both insert ACTIVE positions, so their counts contaminate each other. The suite needs per-test DB isolation (unique schema/database per test or transactional rollback) instead of mutating shared schema.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Contradictory and incorrect confidence assumptions. `test_new_token_age_penalty_halves_size` states 5 closed trades → confidence ≈ 0.70, while this test claims the same 5 trades yield ≈ 0.33 and that a "Kelly fallback" is active. In the actual implementation: `use_kelly_sizing` defaults to `false` (Kelly is not enabled here), so the size is `base * wqs_factor * confidence` with `confidence = wqs_confidence.unwrap_or(0.50)` for trade_count < 15 → 0.50, not 0.33 or 0.70. If the confidence model ever matches the 0.70 claimed in the other test, this test's ratio ≈ 0.30+ and the `ratio <= 0.3` upper bound below fails. Align both tests' comments with the real model (0.50) or fix the model comments.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Brittle hard-coded magic bounds (0.10 and 0.30) that encode unstated assumptions about the confidence model, penalty defaults and the (non-enabled) "Kelly fallback". The comment even references "old compounding ~0.21x" while asserting against 0.10. The pass/fail outcome depends entirely on the current confidence value; the same test also claims an expected ratio of ~0.144 while the real model produces ~0.217. Prefer asserting a relative relationship (e.g. vs the equivalent non-hybrid test) or derive the bound from the configuration used, rather than hard-coded constants.
