## ops/start-evaluation.sh (9 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Invalid cron job entry. `crontab -` installs a *user* crontab whose line format is `minute hour day month weekday command` — the extra `root` field is parsed as the command to execute, so the hourly data collection either fails or the entry is rejected by cron and never runs. Additionally, `${EVAL_DIR}/ops/collect-evaluation-data.sh` is never created by this script (only `ops/` in the current working directory is made executable), so for the default EVAL_DIR the path does not exist either. Use the symlink created just below instead.

```suggestion
CRON_JOB="0 * * * * ${EVAL_DIR}/collect-data.sh"
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Two problems under `set -e`: (1) if this psql command fails (DB not ready, service missing), the script exits immediately and the `if [ $? -ne 0 ]` fallback never executes; (2) `psql -c '\dt'` returns exit code 0 even when there are no tables (it prints "Did not find any relations"), so on a fresh database the schema is reported as existing and `01-schema.sql` is never applied. Check for a known table explicitly (e.g. via `to_regclass`) and initialize when it is missing.

```suggestion
if docker-compose exec postgres-eval psql -U chimera -d chimera_evaluation -tAc "SELECT to_regclass('public.alerts')" | grep -q .; then
    echo -e "${GREEN}✓ Evaluation database schema exists${NC}"
else
    echo -e "${YELLOW}⚠ Database schema not found, initializing...${NC}"
    docker-compose exec postgres-eval psql -U chimera -d chimera_evaluation -f /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/01-schema.sql
fi
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The detection above also checks docker-compose.yml, but the restart only passes docker-compose.evaluation.yml. If `vector` is declared in the base compose file, this restart fails with "no such service" and Vector never reloads its configuration. Restart with both files, matching how the services were started.

```suggestion
            docker-compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.evaluation.yml restart vector
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`docker ps` only proves the container exists; a crash-looping or exited Scout is still reported as "running", and any container whose name merely contains "chimera-scout" is matched as well — this is not a readiness check. Also, unlike the other health checks, a missing Scout only prints an error and the script continues; decide whether Scout is required and fail fast (or query an actual status/health endpoint).

---

### [medium] (bug)

The anomaly detector (and the signal collector backgrounded in realtime mode above) has no lifecycle management: no `trap` to terminate it when the script exits or fails (with `set -e` any later failure orphans the process), no check of the existing PID file before overwriting it, and no supervision/restart. Re-running this script silently starts duplicate processes that all write to the same log file and bind the same port. Check for a live PID first and add `trap` cleanup for both background jobs.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Under `set -euo pipefail`, a non-zero exit from `docker-compose ps` (e.g. `grafana-eval`/`prometheus-eval` not defined in the compose files) aborts the whole script *before* the completion summary, Telegram notification, and the `evaluation-started-*` marker are written — the `else` warning branch is dead code. The same `$?`-after-command pattern after `up -d` has the same issue (its failure branch is also unreachable). Put the command directly in the `if` condition.

```suggestion
if docker-compose ps grafana-eval prometheus-eval > /dev/null 2>&1; then
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

This `until` loop has no retry limit: if the `postgres-eval` service is missing, misconfigured, or never becomes ready, the evaluation startup hangs forever (errors are suppressed by `2>&1`). Bound the wait with an attempt counter (like `check_service_health`) and fail with a clear message after a timeout.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`COMPOSE_PROFILE` is read from `$1` but never used: the compose command hardcodes `--profile evaluation`, so passing any other profile argument is silently ignored while the banner still prints it. Either use `--profile "${COMPOSE_PROFILE}"` or drop the parameter to avoid misleading configuration.

```suggestion
docker-compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.evaluation.yml --profile "${COMPOSE_PROFILE}" up -d
```

---

### [low] (bug)

`curl -d` sends the value raw without URL-encoding; STARTUP_MESSAGE contains newlines, spaces, and box-drawing characters, and would be misinterpreted if it ever contains `&` or `=` (they would become extra form fields). Use `--data-urlencode "text=${STARTUP_MESSAGE}"`.

```suggestion
        --data-urlencode "text=${STARTUP_MESSAGE}" > /dev/null 2>&1
```

## ops/test-vector-integration.sh (7 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

All verification failures in steps [5/6] and [6/6] only print yellow warnings (and the operator content miss prints a warning while the metrics failure prints red) but never set a failure flag or exit non-zero. The script always prints 'Integration Tests Complete!' and returns 0, so a CI pipeline or automated run would report success even when Vector is not producing evaluation logs at all. Track failures with a variable and exit non-zero at the end when any verification failed.

```suggestion
        echo -e "${YELLOW}⚠ Operator test logs not found yet${NC}"
        FAILED=1
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

EVAL_DIR is declared but never used; all verification paths (lines 68-93, 117) hardcode the relative path 'evaluation/logs/evaluation/...'. The script therefore depends on the caller's current working directory and will look in the wrong location (or report false negatives) when invoked from anywhere other than the repo root — and it ignores the /opt/chimera/evaluation setting entirely. Use EVAL_DIR (or a derived LOG_DIR) consistently for all log checks instead of hardcoded relative paths.

```suggestion
EVAL_DIR="${EVAL_DIR:-/opt/chimera/evaluation}"
LOG_DIR="${EVAL_DIR}/logs/evaluation"
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

A fixed 30-second sleep makes the test timing-dependent and brittle: slower log processing (slow disk, container startup, Vector backpressure) produces false failures, while a shorter wait wastes time when logs arrive quickly. Replace the sleep with a polling loop (with an overall timeout) that checks for the expected content, e.g. loop up to 30s checking `grep -q "test-integration-123"` on the evaluation log and break early on success.

```suggestion
for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
    if grep -q "test-integration-123" "${LOG_DIR}/chimera-${EVAL_TODAY}.log" 2>/dev/null; then
        break
    fi
    sleep 1
done
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The script appends synthetic test entries directly to the real /var/log/chimera/operator.log and scout.log files (the same streams Vector tails) and never removes them. Every run permanently pollutes the real log streams and all downstream outputs (evaluation logs, metrics, external sinks), and repeated runs accumulate duplicate entries that can corrupt later analysis or production evaluation. Write test data to dedicated test-only log files that Vector also tails, or record and remove the injected lines after verification.

---

### [medium] (test)

The scout specialized log is only checked for existence, not content — if Vector's scout transform/route is broken (wrong filter, parse failure), the file may be created empty while the test still reports success. Verify the scout-specific content as well, e.g. grep for the injected marker ("discovery_count: 42") in scout-${EVAL_TODAY}.log, mirroring the operator log content check.

```suggestion
if [ -f "evaluation/logs/evaluation/scout-${EVAL_TODAY}.log" ] && grep -q "discovery_count: 42" "evaluation/logs/evaluation/scout-${EVAL_TODAY}.log"; then
```

---

### [low] (bug)

The script invokes `sudo mkdir` and `sudo tee` with no check that sudo is available, that the user is permitted to write /var/log/chimera, or that the directory is writable. Under `set -euo pipefail` this produces a cryptic raw failure instead of a clear diagnostic. Add an explicit preflight check (e.g. `command -v sudo` and `sudo test -w /var/log/chimera`) with a helpful error message and exit before any log generation.

```suggestion
if ! command -v sudo >/dev/null 2>&1 || ! sudo test -w /var/log/chimera; then
    echo -e "${RED}✗ Cannot write to /var/log/chimera (sudo required)${NC}" >&2
    exit 1
fi
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/chimera
```

---

### [low] (bug)

The injected operator log uses a UTC timestamp (`date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ`) but EVAL_TODAY is derived from the local timezone (`date +%Y-%m-%d`), and the scout log line uses local time while the operator log uses UTC. In non-UTC environments (or around midnight) the script checks for a file named after the local date while Vector names output files by the timestamp of the processed event, so the correct file may be missed. Use `date -u +%Y-%m-%d` consistently for both the injected timestamps and the expected output filename.

```suggestion
EVAL_TODAY="$(date -u +%Y-%m-%d)"
```

## production-deploy-simple.sh (7 findings, 2 critical, 2 high)

### [critical] (security)

Real production secrets are hard-coded in this script: the Helius API key, the Jupyter API key, the webhook signing secret, and the monitoring webhook URL. If this file is ever committed, shared, or its terminal output captured, all these credentials leak (the API keys are live in the generated .env). Additionally, `CHIMERA_MONITORING__HELIUS_WEBHOOK_URL` points to an ephemeral `*.ngrok-free.dev` tunnel, which is not a stable production endpoint — webhook deliveries will break whenever the tunnel is restarted. Move all secrets to environment variables / a secrets manager and reference them here instead of embedding literal values.

---

### [critical] (bug)

The geoip and haproxy images are built locally but never pushed to a registry or loaded onto the remote host. On the server, `docker compose pull` cannot fetch them (these services are `build:`-only in docker-compose-haproxy.yml) and that failure is swallowed by `|| true`; the server also cannot rebuild them because only the compose files and `docker/haproxy` are copied, not the full build context (`tools/`, source). `up -d` will therefore run with stale or missing images while the script reports success. Transfer the images explicitly, e.g. `docker save chimera-geoip-lookup:latest chimera-haproxy:latest | ssh ${PRODUCTION_SERVER} "docker load"` (as done in the other deploy scripts in this repo), or push to a registry and reference `image:` in compose.

---

### [high] (bug)

The heredoc delimiter `'ENV'` is quoted, so NOTHING is expanded. The .env deployed to the server will literally contain `$(openssl rand -hex 16)`, `$(openssl rand -hex 32)` and `${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}`. Docker Compose does not run command substitutions, so HAPROXY_STATS_PASSWORD / GRAFANA_PASSWORD / POSTGRES_PASSWORD become static, publicly-known strings instead of per-deployment random values, and `DATABASE_URL` will not match the actual `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` used by the postgres container (empty or literal substitution), breaking DB auth. The Grafana/HAProxy passwords printed at the end are also not the ones actually in the env file. Fix: generate the random values in the shell before the heredoc, then use an unquoted delimiter with `$` escaped where remote expansion is intended.

---

### [high] (bug)

This generates an invalid HAProxy userlist. Valid syntax requires the `user` keyword and a password type, e.g. `user admin insecure-password <hex>`. The lines `admin <hex>` / `operator <hex>` / `viewer <hex>` (a bare name + value with no `user`/`insecure-password` keywords) will cause HAProxy to fail parsing/loading, so the credentials can never be used. Additionally, `docker/haproxy/haproxy.cfg` never references `monitoring_credentials`, so even a correctly formatted file here would not protect any endpoint — wire the file into haproxy.cfg (or generate it with valid `user ... insecure-password ...` lines).

---

### [medium] (bug)

`down` before `up` tears down the whole stack first, causing full downtime and removing the shared network on every deploy (plain `up -d` already recreates changed containers). Worse, the `pull 2>/dev/null || true` silently discards image-pull failures, so the deploy continues (and prints "complete") even when the images it needs are missing or stale, with no health check after startup — `ps` only shows container state. Remove the `down`, fail loudly on pull/build errors, and add a real readiness check before declaring success.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`|| true` silently swallows a failed certificate issuance. If certbot fails (e.g. port 80 already in use, rate limit), the script falls through to the `else` branch and prints "Using existing certificates" even when no certificate exists at all; HAProxy will then fail to start without `chimera.pem`, yet the script still ends with "✅ Production deployment complete!". Remove `|| true` (or check the certbot exit code) and abort the deploy if no valid certificate is present.

---

### [low] (security)

scp installs `.env` (which now contains real API keys and passwords) and `monitoring-auth.cfg` with the remote host's default umask, typically 0644 — making production secrets world-readable on the server. Set restrictive permissions after copying, e.g. `ssh ${PRODUCTION_SERVER} "chmod 600 ${DEPLOY_PATH}/.env ${DEPLOY_PATH}/docker/haproxy/monitoring-auth.cfg"`.

---

## restart-mainnet-paper.sh (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

If `docker compose up` fails after `docker compose down` succeeds, the operator is left stopped with no rollback or cleanup — a risky outcome for a mainnet trading service. Consider capturing the old container state, retrying the `up` command, and failing loudly (non-zero exit) with a clear message so the outage is not silently ignored.

---

### [medium] (bug)

This health check never fails the script. `curl -s` has no `--fail`/`--max-time`, and the `jq` output is only printed, not validated. Even if the operator reports `status != ok` or the circuit breaker is open, the script will still print "✅ Operator restarted successfully!" and exit 0 — misleading for a mainnet trading service. Suggest validating the JSON fields (e.g., `jq -e '.status == "ok"'`) and exiting non-zero with a clear error when unhealthy. Also add `--max-time` to curl to avoid hanging indefinitely.

```suggestion
curl -sf --max-time 10 http://localhost:8080/api/v1/health | jq -e '.status == "ok" and .circuit_breaker.trading_allowed == true' || { echo "❌ Operator is unhealthy" >&2; exit 1; }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`set -e` alone does not propagate failures inside pipelines. Commands like `docker logs chimera-operator 2>&1 | grep "RPC polling task started" | tail -1` return the exit status of `tail` (0), so a missing log line (grep exit 1) is silently ignored and the script reports success. Add `set -o pipefail` so these pipelines fail loudly when expected output is absent.

```suggestion
set -euo pipefail
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

A fixed 10-second sleep is a fragile readiness check: slow startup (image pull, RPC sync, config load) can leave the health check executing before the operator is ready, producing misleading output or false failures, while a fast startup wastes time. Prefer polling the health endpoint in a retry loop (e.g., up to 60s) until it returns healthy, then proceed.

```suggestion
echo "⏳ Waiting for operator to become healthy..."
for i in $(seq 1 60); do
  if curl -sf --max-time 5 http://localhost:8080/api/v1/health >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "Operator is ready."
    break
  fi
  [ "$i" -eq 60 ] && { echo "❌ Operator did not become healthy in time" >&2; exit 1; }
  sleep 1
done
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The container name `chimera-operator` is hardcoded. If the compose service or container name changes (or is overridden via `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME`/`container_name`), `docker exec`/`docker logs` here will fail or hit the wrong container. Prefer compose-aware commands such as `docker compose exec -T operator printenv ...` and `docker compose logs operator`, which resolve the actual container.

```suggestion
COMPOSE_PROFILE=mainnet-paper docker compose exec -T operator printenv | grep -E "SOLANA_NETWORK|PRIMARY_URL"
```

---

## run-fresh-paper-trade.sh (8 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (security)

Hardcoded privileged credential `dev-admin-key` is embedded in the script as a bearer token. If this script is committed/shared, anyone with the repo can call admin-level API endpoints (roster merge, etc.). The operator also exposes these endpoints on the host via port 8080. Recommend reading the token from an environment variable or a git-ignored local file (e.g., `ADMIN_TOKEN="${ADMIN_TOKEN:-$(cat "$PROJECT_ROOT/.admin-token" 2>/dev/null)}"`) instead of a literal value.

---

### [high] (bug)

Without `set -o pipefail`, the exit status of this pipeline is `tee`'s, not `docker exec`'s. If the scout container is missing/not running or `main.py` exits non-zero, the `if` still evaluates to true and the script logs "Scout completed wallet discovery", then falls through to the roster-merge/verify steps which may silently do nothing. Capture the scout's real exit code (e.g., run `docker exec ... > /tmp/scout-output.log 2>&1` and check `$?`, or add `set -o pipefail`).

---

### [medium] (bug)

With `set -e`, this line defeats error detection: the pipeline's exit status is `grep`'s, and `|| true` swallows everything. A failed `docker build` is silently ignored, so the script proceeds to `start` with stale or missing images and only fails later with a misleading error (or not at all if old containers are still running). Check `PIPESTATUS[0]` after the pipeline, or run the build without the grep filter and handle its exit code explicitly.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Two problems in the readiness loop: (1) `curl -s` returns exit code 0 for any HTTP response, so a 503/error page from the operator counts as "healthy" and the loop breaks early; (2) when the 30-attempt timeout is hit, the script only logs a warning and continues into scout/merge/verify, which then fail in confusing ways against a down operator. Use `curl -sf` (or check the JSON `status`) and fail fast — e.g., `exit 1` with a diagnostic on timeout — or gate all later steps on readiness.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`curl -s` returns exit 0 even when the server responds with 4xx/5xx, so a failed roster merge (e.g., 404/500) is logged as "Roster merged successfully". Use `curl -sf` or inspect the HTTP status/response body (`-w '%{http_code}'`) before declaring success; the current silent failure is exactly the kind of false-positive that masks a broken paper-trading session.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Racy/shaky DB cleanup: `docker-compose stop` failures are suppressed with `|| true` (so containers may still be running), and only a fixed 2s sleep is allowed before `rm -f` (whose own errors are also suppressed). If Docker is still tearing down, SQLite WAL/SHM handles may not yet be released, leaving a half-deleted DB that makes `init-db` fail or produce stale state. Check that `stop` succeeded, then wait until the DB files are actually gone (polling loop) before initializing.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The "fresh session" cleanup may not reset the actual trading state: the compose stack runs the operator with `CHIMERA_DB_MODE=postgres` (default in docker-compose.yml, not overridden in `docker/env.mainnet-paper`), so trades/positions/roster live in PostgreSQL. Deleting `data/chimera.db` and running `init-db` (which creates a fresh SQLite file) does not clear Postgres, so old trades and state can persist — defeating the purpose of a fresh paper-trading session. Verify which DB backend the operator actually uses at runtime, and reset that backend (drop/recreate Postgres schema) as part of Step 1.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Container/service names are hard-coded (`chimera-scout`, `chimera-operator`, port 8080) and bypass `$PROFILE`. They happen to match the mainnet-paper compose stack today, but they silently break if the profile is switched to a stack with different naming (e.g., evaluation/HAProxy variants), and `docker exec chimera-scout python main.py` also assumes the image WORKDIR is `/app`. Derive names from the running compose project (e.g., `docker compose --profile "$PROFILE" ps --format '{{.Name}}' --filter 'status=running'`) or from the profile instead of literals.

---

## scout/config.py (7 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Duplicate definitions: the earlier "Advanced Cache Configuration" section already defines get_redis_enabled()/get_redis_url() reading SCOUT_REDIS_ENABLED/SCOUT_REDIS_URL with default 'false'. This later "Redis Configuration" section silently overrides them (last definition wins in the class body) with REDIS_ENABLED/REDIS_URL and default 'true'. Consequences: any deployment that sets SCOUT_REDIS_* has those settings silently ignored, and Redis L2 cache flips to enabled-by-default, which may cause unexpected Redis connection attempts/failures in environments without Redis. Consolidate into a single pair of accessors with one env-var prefix and one consistent default.

---

### [medium] (bug)

get_alert_webhook_url() is defined twice. The earlier ML Monitoring definition returns Optional[str] (None when unset); this later Validation Reporter definition returns str with '' default and silently wins. Callers that check `url is None`/`url is not None`, or that rely on the Optional type contract, will silently change behavior. Keep a single definition with one explicit absent-value contract (None or '').

---

### [medium] (bug)

is_valid is initialized to True and is never set to False anywhere in this method, even when warnings are appended. The returned tuple therefore always reports (True, [...]), so the validity flag does not reflect any actual configuration problem and misleads callers. Either set is_valid=False for critical issues, or drop the flag and let callers rely on the warnings list.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Default mismatch: get_liquidity_allow_fallback() defaults SCOUT_LIQUIDITY_ALLOW_FALLBACK to "true" (fallback allowed), but validate_config() reads the same env var with default "false". When the env var is unset, the accessor enables fallback while validation believes it is disabled, so the survivorship-bias warning can be suppressed even though fallback is actually active. Align the defaults (and ideally have validate_config call the accessor).

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Several accessors are defined twice in this class; the later definitions silently shadow the earlier ones, making the first copies dead code and obscuring which env var/default is actually in effect: get_validation_enabled, get_alert_high_error_threshold, get_alert_drift_threshold, get_alert_low_accuracy_threshold, get_alert_dir, get_growth_optimized (get_redis_*/get_alert_webhook_url are flagged separately). Remove the duplicate copies and keep a single canonical definition per setting.

---

### [low] (bug)

Default path mismatch: validate_production_config() defaults CHIMERA_DB_PATH to "data/chimera.db", but get_db_path() defaults to "../data/chimera.db". When the env var is unset, the DB directory check/creation here targets a different directory than the one actually used by the application. Use ScoutConfig.get_db_path() so validation checks the real path.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

get_min_wqs_whale()/get_min_wqs_swing() are annotated Optional[float] but never return None (they always fall back to 70.0/72.0). The misleading annotation invites callers to write None-handling branches that can never execute. Change the return type to float.

## scout/core/activity_cache.py (8 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

Memory accounting drift: when `set()` replaces an existing key, the old entry's `size_bytes` is never subtracted from `_total_memory_bytes`. Combined with the expired-entry deletion in `get()` also not decrementing, the counter grows monotonically past the real usage. This eventually triggers premature LRU evictions (the `MAX_MEMORY_MB` check) and corrupts `get_cache_stats()` memory reporting. Subtract the old entry's size on overwrite.

```suggestion
            # Add to cache (account for overwrite)
            old_entry = self._cache.get(key)
            if old_entry is not None:
                self._total_memory_bytes -= old_entry.size_bytes
            self._cache[key] = entry
            self._total_memory_bytes += size
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Expired entries removed here are deleted from `self._cache` without subtracting `entry.size_bytes` from `_total_memory_bytes`. This is the second source of memory-accounting drift (the first being overwrites in `set()`), inflating `_total_memory_bytes` and causing wrong memory-limit eviction decisions and stats.

```suggestion
            # Check if expired
            if entry.is_expired():
                del self._cache[key]
                self._total_memory_bytes -= entry.size_bytes
                self._stats['expirations'] += 1
                self._stats['misses'] += 1
                return None
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Passing `time.time()` as `last_activity` makes `time_since_activity = time.time() - time.time() ≈ 0`, so `RECENT_ACTIVITY_MULTIPLIER` applies unconditionally for every cached wallet — the recent-activity branch inside `get_cache_ttl` is effectively dead logic and the TTL is always inflated by 1.5x. The wallet's actual `last_activity_timestamp` (tracked in `_activity_data`) should be passed instead. Note that for a wallet not yet tracked, this also yields a 36h INACTIVE-level TTL, which is inconsistent with the entry's recorded `ActivityLevel.INACTIVE`.

```suggestion
                last_activity = self._activity_data[wallet].last_activity_timestamp if wallet in self._activity_data else time.time()
                ttl = self.get_cache_ttl(wallet, last_activity)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Strict `>` comparisons against the `*_MIN_TX` thresholds misclassify boundary values: exactly 10 tx/day becomes MEDIUM (should be HIGH per the documented 10-50 range) and exactly 1 tx/day becomes LOW (should be MEDIUM per the 1-10 range). Boundary wallets therefore get 1-hour/6-hour TTLs instead of the intended 15-minute/1-hour, i.e., longer stale data for moderately active wallets. Use `>=` so the lower bounds match the documented inclusive ranges.

```suggestion
        if activity.tx_count_24h >= self._config.VERY_HIGH_MIN_TX:
            return ActivityLevel.VERY_HIGH
        elif activity.tx_count_24h >= self._config.HIGH_MIN_TX:
            return ActivityLevel.HIGH
        elif activity.tx_count_24h >= self._config.MEDIUM_MIN_TX:
            return ActivityLevel.MEDIUM
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Sliding-expiry design hazard: `is_expired()` is based on `last_accessed`, and `get()` refreshes `last_accessed` on every hit, while `created_at` is stored but never consulted. A frequently accessed entry therefore never expires, so TTL-based freshness guarantees (e.g., aggressive 5-minute invalidation for very active wallets) silently stop applying and stale data can live in the cache indefinitely. Consider combining idle expiry with an absolute cap derived from `created_at`, or make the freshness semantics explicit.

```suggestion
    def is_expired(self) -> bool:
        """Check if cache entry is expired (idle expiry with absolute created_at cap)."""
        return ((time.time() - self.last_accessed) > self.ttl_seconds or
                (time.time() - self.created_at) > self.ttl_seconds)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`wallet in k` performs substring matching over every cache key. If keys are composite strings (e.g., `"<wallet>:<asset>"`), a wallet address that is a prefix/substring of another address will also match that wallet's entries, causing spurious invalidation; it is also O(entries) per wallet and will raise `TypeError` if `wallet` is `None` (which `set()` explicitly permits). Prefer structured keys with a wallet prefix mapping (or store a per-wallet index of keys) and guard against `None`.

---

### [low] (performance)

Eager f-string formatting is passed to the logger, so the string is built even when the DEBUG level is disabled. Use lazy `%s`-style formatting for these debug/info calls.

```suggestion
            logger.debug("Updated activity for %s...: %s tx/24h", wallet[:8], tx_count_24h)
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Dead fields: `tx_count_1h` and `tx_count_5m` are always set to 0 on creation and never updated or read; `last_cache_update` is never assigned after construction; `predicted_hit_rate` is never read (prediction is computed statically in `predict_cache_hit_rate`). Similarly, `CacheConfig.PREDICTION_WINDOW_HOURS`, `MIN_PREDICTION_SAMPLES`, and `STATE_FILE` are never used (state persistence is never implemented). Either implement the intended tracking/persistence or remove the dead fields to avoid misleading readers.

## scout/core/adaptive_weights.py (5 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

Per-component threshold of `len(pairs) < 5` defeats the documented `MIN_SAMPLES = 3` behavior. With 3–4 records, every component has < 5 pairs, so all components are skipped, `component_corrs` stays empty, and `calibrate()` returns `None`. The class docstring promises "MIN_SAMPLES reduced to 3 for faster initial adaptation", but calibration cannot produce weights until at least 5 usable records exist. Derive the per-component threshold from `MIN_SAMPLES` (or lower it consistently) so the early-adaptation path is actually reachable.

```suggestion
        for comp_name, pairs in component_pairs.items():
            if len(pairs) < self.MIN_SAMPLES:
                continue
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Confidence is computed from the raw record count, but records with `None` `actual_copy_pnl_30d_sol` or `wqs_components_json` are skipped during pair collection and never contribute to the regression. As a result, `n_records` can be much larger than the number of data points actually backing the adaptive weights, causing the confidence blend (and the `BAYESIAN_THRESHOLD`/`WARM_START_SAMPLES` branches) to overstate how much real evidence supports the regression output. Track the number of records that actually produced pairs and use that for the confidence calculation.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Components with `abs(corr) < min_correlation` are never updated: `new_weights` is initialized as a copy of `current_weights` and only strong-correlation components are modified. Combined with the blend logic (`new_weights.get(key, old_w)` falls back to the old weight), noise components below the threshold permanently keep stale weights — e.g., a component previously boosted to 2.0 that now correlates at 0.02 stays at 2.0 forever. This contradicts the module docstring's "noise components get deweighted". If deweighting is intended, below-threshold components should be pulled toward neutral (1.0) rather than left untouched.

```suggestion
        for comp_name in component_pairs:
            if comp_name not in component_corrs:
                new_weights[comp_name] = 1.0

        for comp_name, corr in component_corrs.items():
            adjusted = 1.0 + corr
            new_weights[comp_name] = max(self.MIN_WEIGHT, min(self.MAX_WEIGHT, adjusted))
```

---

### [low] (bug)

`float(v)` on cached JSON values can raise `TypeError` (e.g., for `null` or array values), which is not covered by the `(json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError)` except clause. A malformed or hand-edited cache would then propagate the exception out of `get_current_weights()` instead of falling back to the seeded defaults. Include `TypeError` in the except clause.

```suggestion
                    if isinstance(cached, dict) and cached:
                        return {k: float(v) for k, v in cached.items()}
            except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError, TypeError):
                pass
```

---

### [low] (performance)

f-string passed eagerly to `logger.info(...)` defeats lazy formatting — the message is formatted even when the INFO level is disabled. This instance (and the "Adaptive weights saved to ..." one in `save_weights`) should use %-style lazy args, as the rest of the file already does.

```suggestion
            logger.info(
                "Adaptive weights: insufficient data (%d < %d records)", len(records), self.MIN_SAMPLES
            )
```

## scout/core/advanced_cache.py (7 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Bug in the convenience setter: `set()`'s third positional parameter is `value`, so the literal string `"metrics"` is stored as the cached value while the actual `metrics` dict is treated as an extra key part (`args`). The resulting key (`wallet:<addr>:<repr-of-dict>`) never matches the getter's `get("wallet", address, "metrics")`, so these helpers write and read different keys and cache the wrong value — effectively breaking caching for them. The same misuse affects `set_token_metadata`, `set_token_creation_time`, `set_high_wqs_wallet_data`, `set_analysis_results`, `set_discovery_results` and `set_backtest_results` (only `set_liquidity_data` is correct because it has no literal suffix). Pass the data as `value` and the literal suffix as an `*args` element.

```suggestion
    cache.set("wallet", address, metrics, "metrics", category=CacheCategory.WALLET_METRICS)
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`TTLDefaults` attributes are defined with UPPERCASE names (`WALLET_METRICS`, `PRICE_DATA`, ...) while `CacheCategory.value` is the lowercase string (`wallet_metrics`, ...). `getattr(cls, category.value, 300)` therefore never finds the attribute and every category silently falls back to the 300s default — e.g. `PRICE_DATA` (intended 60s) is cached for 5 minutes and `TOKEN_METADATA` (intended 24h) expires after 5 minutes. Use `category.name` to look up the intended TTL.

```suggestion
        return getattr(cls, category.name, 300)  # Default 5 minutes
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The L2 branch of `invalidate_category` is a no-op (`pass`), so Redis entries belonging to the category are never removed and keep being served as valid hits until their TTL expires — explicitly invalidated data survives in L2 and is re-promoted into L1 on the next `get()`. Scan the Redis keys (e.g. maintain a per-category key set, or `SCAN` a key pattern) and delete matching entries, or bump a per-category epoch/version that `get()` validates.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`_set_l1` mutates `self._l1_cache` (including `_evict_l1_entries`, which deletes keys) without holding `_l1_lock`, while `get()`, `invalidate()` and `cleanup_expired()` access the same dict under the lock. A concurrent `invalidate()`/`cleanup_expired()` can delete a key between the eviction sort and `del self._l1_cache[key]`, raising `KeyError`; conversely a promotion triggered by `get()` can re-insert an entry right after it was invalidated (stale value resurrected). Acquire `_l1_lock` inside `_set_l1` (and `_evict_l1_entries`) so all L1 mutations are serialized.

---

### [medium] (bug)

When `_deserialize_value` fails (corrupt/partial Redis payload) it returns `None`, and this branch still records an L2 hit and returns `None`, bypassing the caller's `default` and inflating the hit rate. Since `set()` never stores `None`, a `None` here can only mean deserialization failure — treat it as a miss (fall through to L3/default and delete the corrupt key) instead of returning `None` as a hit.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Same issue as the L2 path: when `_deserialize_value` fails on a corrupt SQLite BLOB it returns `None`, which is counted as an L3 hit and returned instead of the caller-supplied `default`. Treat deserialization failure as a miss (and consider deleting the corrupt row) rather than a hit.

---

### [low] (bug)

Each L3 operation opens a fresh `sqlite3` connection, but `conn.close()` is only reached on the happy path: if `cursor.execute`/`fetchone` raises, the exception is swallowed by the outer `except` and the connection (and its file descriptor) leaks. Use `with sqlite3.connect(...) as conn:` or close in a `finally` block in the `get`/`set`/`invalidate`/`invalidate_category`/`_update_l3_hit_count`/`cleanup_expired` paths.

---

## scout/core/advanced_risk_features.py (5 findings, 0 critical, 4 high)

### [high] (bug)

`pnl_array` holds per-trade PnL in absolute SOL, not returns. `returns = np.diff(pnl_array)` is the change in trade PnL between consecutive trades (no financial meaning), and `total_return = pnl_array[-1] - pnl_array[0]` is just the difference between the last and first trade's PnL — it is not a portfolio/trade return. As a result `sharpe_ratio`, `sortino_ratio`, `calmar_ratio` and `sterling_ratio` are all computed from dimensionally meaningless inputs and should not be treated as risk-adjusted return ratios. Build an equity curve (`equity = np.cumsum(pnl_array)`) and compute percentage returns from it, e.g. `returns = np.diff(equity) / equity[:-1]` (guarding zero equity) and `total_return = (equity[-1] - equity[0]) / equity[0]`.

```suggestion
        equity = np.cumsum(pnl_array)
        prev = np.where(equity[:-1] != 0, equity[:-1], 1.0)
        returns = np.diff(equity) / prev
        total_return = (equity[-1] - equity[0]) / equity[0] if equity[0] != 0 else 0.0
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The first loop already advanced `peak` to the global maximum of `cumulative`. In this second pass `peak` is never reset, so `value > peak` can never be true; every index below the global max falls into the `elif` branch and `in_drawdown` stays True for the remainder of the series. Result: `drawdowns` collapses into a single unclosed drawdown spanning from the first non-peak trade to the end, making `avg_drawdown_duration_trades` meaningless. Use a per-episode running peak that is reset on each new high (e.g. a local `episode_peak` initialized to `cumulative[0]`).

```suggestion
        episode_peak = cumulative[0]
        for i, value in enumerate(cumulative):
            if value > episode_peak:
                if in_drawdown:
                    drawdowns.append(i - dd_start)
                    in_drawdown = False
                episode_peak = value
            elif not in_drawdown:
                in_drawdown = True
                dd_start = i
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Dividing by `abs(peak) + 1e-8` makes the percentage drawdown explode when the running peak is zero or near zero — e.g. if the first trade PnL is 0 (peak stays 0) and later trades lose, a -0.01 SOL drawdown is reported as depth 1,000,000 (i.e. 100,000,000%). This produces absurd `max_drawdown_depth` values and contaminates downstream metrics and the risk regime. The same near-zero-peak pattern exists in `_calculate_max_drawdown` and `_calculate_avg_drawdown`. Guard against a zero/near-zero peak rather than adding a tiny epsilon to the denominator.

```suggestion
                denom = abs(peak) if abs(peak) > 1e-8 else 0.0
                depth = (peak - value) / denom if denom else 0.0
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Same near-zero-peak defect as the drawdown depth calculation, but amplified: when `peak` is 0 (e.g. first trade PnL is 0 followed by small losses), `drop = (0 - value) / 1e-8 * 100` yields values on the order of 10^8, so `ulcer_index` explodes to ~10^8 even for a wallet with trivial losses. This in turn pushes `_classify_risk_regime` to "EXTREME" regardless of actual risk. Guard against a zero/near-zero peak when computing the percentage drop.

```suggestion
            denom = abs(peak) if abs(peak) > 1e-8 else 0.0
            drop = (peak - value) / denom * 100 if denom else 0.0
```

---

### [low] (bug)

`float('inf')` (also used for `calmar_ratio`, `sterling_ratio` and `tail_ratio`) is returned whenever the denominator is zero and the numerator is positive. These values end up in the enriched features dict, which is persisted as a JSON cache (`_cache_features` in feature_enrichment.py). Python's json emits `Infinity`, which is non-standard JSON and will break strict JSON consumers or any downstream arithmetic. Consider returning a bounded sentinel (e.g. 0.0) or `None` instead of `float('inf')`.

```suggestion
            features['sortino_ratio'] = float('inf') if total_return > 0 else 0.0  # replace inf with a finite sentinel (e.g. 0.0) to keep JSON output valid
```

---

## scout/core/analyzer.py (9 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

Cross-wallet race on shared instance state: `_cached_avg_entry_delay` is written here and read later inside `_detect_insider_patterns` — after several `await`s (e.g. `_get_wallet_creation_time_cached`). With `analyze_wallets_batch` concurrency (default 5), another wallet's coroutine can overwrite the attribute between the write and the read, so a wallet's insider/fresh-wallet classification can be based on another wallet's avg entry delay (and the stale value lingers for later reads). Pass `avg_entry_delay` into `_detect_insider_patterns` as an explicit parameter (or return it in `insider_metrics`) instead of storing it on `self`.

---

### [high] (bug)

`_load_sample_data` replaces the `OrderedDict` caches initialized in `__init__` with plain `dict` literals (`self._metrics_cache = {...}` and `self._trades_cache = self._generate_sample_trades()`). Later `_metrics_cache_set`/`_trades_cache_set` call `move_to_end`/`popitem`, which plain dicts lack → `AttributeError`. Since `_trades_cache_set` is invoked inside `_fetch_real_wallet_metrics` before metrics are computed, a successfully fetched real wallet is thrown away and `get_wallet_metrics` silently falls back to sample data after logging the exception. Keep these as `OrderedDict` (or re-wrap when assigning sample data).

---

### [high] (performance)

The parse cache is written here with a direct dict assignment, bypassing the `_parse_cache_set` helper (maxlen=5000) that `__init__` says bounds this cache to prevent memory growth. `_parse_cache` therefore grows without bound across the run (one entry per unique tx signature). Additionally, `None` results (failed parses) are stored but never served — the read guard `if cached is not None` treats them as misses, so failed transactions are re-parsed every time while still occupying memory. Route writes through `_parse_cache_set` and store a sentinel that distinguishes “not cached” from “cached failure”.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The `fromUserAccount`/`toUserAccount` net-delta blocks are duplicated — applied once before the `userAccount` block and again right after it. For transfers where the direct from/to accounts match the wallet, the delta is subtracted/added twice, corrupting `token_deltas`. This mislabels `no_primary_token`/`direction_ambiguous` parse-failure reasons and produces misleading debug diagnostics. Remove the duplicated trailing block.

---

### [medium] (performance)

Launches `_fetch_token_creation_time` for every unique buy token with no concurrency cap, and each invocation can make up to 4 external HTTP calls (Birdeye, Jupiter, Helius, token-metadata). Under batch analysis (5 concurrent wallets) this can burst into dozens–hundreds of parallel requests and trip rate limits on Birdeye/Jupiter/Helius, degrading discovery and analysis. Bound the gather with an `asyncio.Semaphore` (e.g. 5–10) and reuse a shared aiohttp session.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The honeypot freeze-authority check builds the `getAccountInfo` URL from `CHIMERA_RPC__PRIMARY_URL`/`SOLANA_RPC_URL` or a hardcoded Helius mainnet URL, ignoring `self.rpc_url` passed to `WalletAnalyzer.__init__`. If the analyzer is configured with a different RPC endpoint, this check hits the wrong node and — under the default `closed` fail mode — tokens can be silently rejected (or wrongly accepted) based on the wrong chain state. Prefer `self.rpc_url` (falling back to the env vars) for this request.

---

### [medium] (security)

Only the `resp.status == 200` branch is handled in the honeypot check; a non-200 response (RPC error/timeout) or a `value: null` result (account not found) falls straight through to `return True` — i.e. the token is assumed safe. This bypasses the `SCOUT_SAFETY_FAIL_MODE=closed` policy, which is only consulted inside the `except` path, so a degraded RPC can cause honeypots/freeze-authority tokens to pass the filter. Treat non-200 responses and missing account data as check failures and apply the fail-mode logic.

---

### [medium] (performance)

`RedisClient.get`/`.set` (scout/core/redis_client.py) are synchronous redis-py calls with 2s socket timeouts, but they are invoked directly inside these `async def` methods (`_get_token_symbol`, `_get_token_symbol_async`, `_fetch_token_creation_time`). On the hot per-token path this can block the event loop for up to the socket timeout per call, stalling all concurrently analyzed wallets. Run the Redis calls via `asyncio.to_thread` (or make the wrapper async), or at least batch/avoid them in the per-token loop.

---

### [low] (bug)

When `self.helius_client` is unavailable (or has no API key), a new `aiohttp.ClientSession` is created per token-creation lookup and never closed — the `async with` only closes the response. Repeated fallback fetches leak connections/file descriptors. Reuse a client-managed session or close the created session explicitly.

## scout/core/api_health_monitor.py (6 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

`_trigger_failover` always enters offline mode. `get_best_endpoint()` mutates `self.current_primary` to the selected endpoint before returning, so when a candidate endpoint exists, `best_endpoint != self.current_primary` is always False. The `if` branch is never taken; the `else` branch logs "No healthy endpoints" and calls `enter_offline_mode()` even when a healthy endpoint was just selected. Capture the previous primary before calling `get_best_endpoint()` (or stop mutating `current_primary` inside `get_best_endpoint`), then switch only when the returned endpoint differs from the previously known primary.

```suggestion
        previous_primary = self.current_primary
        best_endpoint = self.get_best_endpoint()

        if best_endpoint is not None:
            logger.warning(f"Failover triggered: {previous_primary} -> {best_endpoint}")
            self.current_primary = best_endpoint
        else:
            logger.error("No healthy endpoints available, entering offline mode")
            self.enter_offline_mode()
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`get_best_endpoint()` only filters by `enabled`, never by health status. If every enabled endpoint is DOWN, it still returns one of them instead of `None`, contradicting its docstring ("None if no healthy endpoints") and causing callers to keep issuing requests against known-down endpoints. Exclude DOWN endpoints from the candidate list (DEGRADED can remain as a fallback).

```suggestion
        # Filter to enabled, healthy endpoints
        enabled_endpoints = [
            (name, ep) for name, ep in self.endpoints.items()
            if ep.enabled and self.get_status(name) != APIStatus.DOWN
        ]
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The retry guard is broken and can call `request_func(None)`. Because `get_best_endpoint()` sets `self.current_primary` to the value it returns, `endpoint_name != self.current_primary` is always False whenever an endpoint is returned, making the guard dead logic. Worse, after a failure `_trigger_failover` enters offline mode, so the next `get_best_endpoint()` returns `None`, and since `None != self.current_primary` is True the loop `continue`s and the next attempt calls `request_func(None)`. Guard against `None` explicitly (break/return instead of retrying).

```suggestion
                if attempt < max_attempts - 1:
                    # Try next endpoint
                    endpoint_name = self.get_best_endpoint()
                    if endpoint_name is None:
                        break
                    logger.info(f"Retrying with endpoint {endpoint_name}")
                    continue
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Rate-limiter race under concurrent async callers: `last_request_time` is only updated after `await asyncio.sleep(...)`, so two coroutines that both observe the same stale timestamp both sleep the full interval and then fire together, defeating the per-endpoint RPS limit. Reserve the slot by recording the timestamp before awaiting the sleep.

```suggestion
        self.last_request_time[endpoint_name] = now
        if time_since_last < min_interval:
            await asyncio.sleep((min_interval - time_since_last) / 1000)
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Dead/unused state: `self.request_queue` and `self.min_request_interval_ms` are initialized but never read, and `self._health_check_task` is declared but never started or awaited (despite the docstring mentioning background health checks). Remove them or implement the intended background task to avoid misleading future maintainers.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The result cache is append-only: entries are written on every success but never evicted when they expire, so distinct `cache_key`s accumulate without bound over the process lifetime. Prune expired entries (e.g., on write or periodically) or cap the cache size.

---

## scout/core/archive/gradient_boost_predictor.py (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

For the `is_sniper`/`is_swing`/`is_scalper`/`is_whale` features this reads `record.get(feature_name[3:].upper())` (e.g. key `'SNIPER'`), while every other feature is read with its lower-case snake_case name, and inference-side `_prepare_features` also looks up `wallet_features.get('is_sniper')`. If upstream records use the same `is_sniper` keys (or store the strategy in a `trader_type` field), these flags silently become 0 during training, producing train/serve skew and models that never see the strategy features. Read the key matching `feature_name` directly (or map from the actual strategy field) so training and inference are consistent.

```suggestion
                elif feature_name.startswith('is_'):
                    value = 1.0 if record.get(feature_name) else 0.0
```

### [medium] (bug)

The LightGBM SHAP branch checks `hasattr(model, 'booster_')`, but the models stored here are the native `lgb.Booster` returned by `lgb.train()` (and loaded via `lgb.Booster(model_file=...)`); native Boosters do not expose a `booster_` attribute (that is specific to the sklearn `LGBM*` wrappers). Use `isinstance(model, lgb.Booster)` (and optionally also accept `hasattr(model, 'booster_')` for sklearn-style models).

```suggestion
                explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model)
```

### [medium] (bug)

`_prune_model_for_latency` is invoked at the end of both training methods, but at that point no prediction has ever been recorded, so `self.inference_times_ms` is empty and the method always returns early here. Even when latency data does exist, the XGBoost/LightGBM branches only log messages without actually reducing the number of trees. The advertised latency-budget pruning is therefore a no-op and the `latency_budget_ms` constraint is never enforced. Either benchmark a few predictions after training before pruning and actually shrink the model (e.g., rebuild/save with `best_iteration` or fewer rounds), or remove this dead path.

The fallback payload omits fields that a successful `predict_profitability` response always includes (`inference_time_ms`, `latency_budget_ms`, `latency_ok`, `training_samples`, `last_trained`) and adds a `warning` key that success responses never contain. Callers relying on a uniform response shape (e.g., reading `latency_ok` or `last_trained`) will break whenever the model is missing. Consider returning the same metadata keys with neutral values (e.g., `inference_time_ms: None`, `latency_ok: False`) so the response contract stays consistent.

## scout/core/archive/hyperopt.py (7 findings, 0 critical, 4 high)

### [high] (bug)

The default `direction="maximize"` contradicts the built-in objectives: `XGBoostHyperparameterOptimizer`/`LightGBMHyperparameterOptimizer` return RMSE (lower is better), and neither the subclasses nor `optimize_xgboost`/`optimize_lightgbm` override the direction. With default settings Optuna will maximize RMSE and return the worst-performing model as the "best" parameters. Change the default to `"minimize"` (or explicitly pass `direction="minimize"` in the subclasses and convenience functions).

```suggestion
        direction: str = "minimize"
```

This convenience wrapper does not pass `direction`, so it inherits the base-class default of `"maximize"` while the objective minimizes RMSE — a default call to `optimize_xgboost()` will select the highest-RMSE (worst) model as "best". Pass `direction="minimize"` explicitly.

```suggestion

```

### [high] (bug)

Same issue as the XGBoost wrapper: `LightGBMHyperparameterOptimizer` is constructed without `direction`, inheriting `"maximize"` while the objective returns RMSE. A default call selects the worst model. Pass `direction="minimize"`.

```suggestion
    optimizer = LightGBMHyperparameterOptimizer(direction="minimize", latency_budget_ms=latency_budget_ms)
```

## scout/core/archive/model_explainer.py (7 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

For typical sklearn classifiers that expose both `predict` and `predict_proba`, `predict` is always chosen, so the KernelExplainer evaluates hard 0/1 labels and the reported `prediction` (and all counterfactual `prediction_change` values) are hard labels rather than probabilities. This makes SHAP values and counterfactuals misleading for classification. `predict_proba` should be preferred when present (binary: column 1), and note the `[:, 1]` indexing silently assumes binary classification — multi-class models would return the wrong column. Only use `predict` for regression models.

```suggestion
        if hasattr(self.model, 'predict_proba'):
            return self.model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
        elif hasattr(self.model, 'predict'):
            return self.model.predict(X)
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`base_value` flattening can crash the whole explanation. `len(base_value)` raises `TypeError: len() of unsized object` when `expected_value` is a 0-d ndarray (e.g. single-output TreeExplainer paths), and a Python list (multi-class/multi-output models) is not an ndarray so it is never flattened — `float(base_value)` then raises `TypeError` and the entire explanation aborts via the outer `except`. Flatten robustly with `np.asarray(...).reshape(-1)` before taking the first element.

```suggestion
            if hasattr(self.explainer, 'expected_value'):
                base_value = np.asarray(self.explainer.expected_value).reshape(-1)
                base_value = float(base_value[0]) if len(base_value) > 0 else 0.0
            else:
                base_value = 0.0
```

---

### [high] (bug)

In the "reverse" branch the direction is derived from `target_change` instead of the feature's current contribution. For `target_change < 0` with a positive SHAP value the code sets `direction = 1`, i.e. it *increases* a feature that is already pushing the prediction up — moving the prediction in the wrong direction (further away from the target). To reduce a positive contribution the feature must be decreased. Base the direction on the SHAP sign: `direction = -1 if shap_val > 0 else 1`. The symmetric case (`target_change > 0`, `shap_val < 0`) has the same inverted logic.

```suggestion
                else:
                    # Opposite direction - reverse: move the feature against its current push
                    direction = -1 if shap_val > 0 else 1
                    magnitude = abs(target_change) / max(abs(shap_val), 0.01)
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

With `model_type="auto"`, sklearn tree/forest estimators (DecisionTree, RandomForest, GradientBoosting, HistGradientBoosting) have no `coef_`, so they fall through to "kernel" and get the slow KernelExplainer with 100 zero-valued background samples instead of the fast, exact TreeExplainer that natively supports these models. Consider detecting sklearn tree estimators (e.g. via `sklearn.base` estimator tags) before defaulting to kernel.

This try block never actually imports anything, so the `except ImportError` is unreachable and `SKLEARN_AVAILABLE` is unconditionally `True`. The flag is also never referenced anywhere else in the file. Either perform a real `import sklearn` (and actually use the flag for the counterfactual/feature-stat path) or remove this dead block.

This is dead state that misleads maintainers; either implement the cache (e.g. keyed by feature dict in `explain_prediction`) or remove these members.

## scout/core/archive/model_router.py (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

A/B group assignment uses Python's built-in `hash()`, which for strings is salted per-process (`PYTHONHASHSEED`). The comment claims "consistent per wallet", but the same wallet_id will be assigned a different group after a process restart (or across multiple worker processes), invalidating A/B test results. Use a stable hash such as `zlib.crc32(wallet_id.encode())` or `hashlib.md5(...)` for deterministic assignment.

```suggestion
            # Assign group based on a stable hash (consistent across restarts)
            import zlib
            hash_val = zlib.crc32(wallet_id.encode()) % 100
            self.ab_test_group[wallet_id] = 'B' if hash_val < self.ab_test_split * 100 else 'A'
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

`ab_test_group` stores one entry per unique wallet_id and never evicts entries. In a long-running process with a growing wallet population this is an unbounded memory leak. Bound the cache size (e.g., an LRU/ordered dict capped at N entries) or store the group assignment elsewhere/persistently instead of accumulating it forever.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`_track_prediction` is called inside the broad `try` block. If performance bookkeeping raises (or a prediction dict lacks expected keys), the exception is misattributed to the model and the code silently falls back to another model, obscuring the real error. Move the tracking call (and ideally the dict-key mutation) outside the try/except so only the actual model inference is guarded.

```suggestion
        except Exception as e:
            logger.warning(f"Prediction with {model_type} failed: {e}")
            self._track_error(model_type, str(e))

        # Track performance (outside the model try/except)
        self._track_prediction(model_type, prediction)

        return prediction
```

---

### [low] (performance)

F-string arguments passed directly to logging defeat lazy formatting: the string is always built even when the log level is disabled. Prefer `logger.warning("Prediction with %s failed: %s", model_type, e)` (same applies to the other f-string log calls in this method).

## scout/core/archive/online_learning.py (7 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Automatic retraining is advertised but never actually performed: when `drift_count >= retrain_threshold`, the code only sets `retrain_triggered = True` and logs — it never calls `_update_weights()` or `trigger_retrain()`, so the model is never retrained as a result of drift. Additionally, because `drift_count` is not reset here, every subsequent drift detection re-flags `retrain_triggered` even though nothing happens. Call `trigger_retrain()` (or `_update_weights()`) when the threshold is reached.

```suggestion
            if drift_status.get('drift_detected'):
                if self.drift_detector.drift_count >= self.retrain_threshold:
                    result['retrain_triggered'] = True
                    logger.info("Retraining triggered due to concept drift")
                    result['retrain_success'] = self.trigger_retrain()
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`self.drift_detected` and `self.warning_detected` are only ever set to True here and never cleared when the z-score returns below the thresholds. As a result, once a single drift/warning is seen, `get_status()` reports `drift_detected`/`warning_detected` as True forever (stale latched state), even after performance recovers. Reset both flags at the start of each `update()` based on the current z-score (set False before the threshold checks).

```suggestion
            if z_score >= self.drift_threshold:
                self.drift_detected = True
                self.warning_detected = True
            elif z_score >= self.warning_threshold:
                self.warning_detected = True
            else:
                self.drift_detected = False
                self.warning_detected = False
```

### [medium] (bug)

`reset_baseline()` clears `drift_detected` and `drift_count` but leaves `warning_detected` latched. Since `warning_detected` is never reset anywhere else, after the first warning `get_status()` will permanently report `warning_detected: True` even after a clean baseline is re-established. Clear `warning_detected` here as well.

```suggestion
    def reset_baseline(self):
        """Reset baseline with current data."""
        self._establish_baseline()
        self.drift_detected = False
        self.warning_detected = False
        self.drift_count = 0
```

### [medium] (bug)

The global registry is keyed only by `model_name`, so a subsequent call requesting a different `model_type` silently returns the already-created learner configured for the wrong backend (e.g., an XGBoost learner reused for a `linear` caller). This causes predictions/training with the wrong model type without any error. Key the registry by `(model_name, model_type)` or verify the existing instance's type and raise/return a new learner on mismatch.

```suggestion

    if key not in _online_learners:
        _online_learners[key] = OnlineLearner(
```

### [medium] (bug)

Feature names are derived from the first buffered sample only. Later samples with missing keys are silently zero-filled and samples with extra keys are silently dropped, producing training matrices that are silently misaligned with the features the model was built on — a real correctness risk. Worse, because `self.X_buffer` is a bounded deque, the "first sample" changes as old samples are evicted, so the feature set can silently shift between consecutive `_update_weights()` calls. Define a fixed feature schema up front and validate each sample's keys against it (logging or raising on mismatch).

### [medium] (bug)

Prediction feature alignment also relies on `self.X_buffer[0].keys()` (or on the caller's dict keys when the buffer is empty). A `predict()` call with a differently keyed features dict silently zero-fills missing keys, which can yield wrong predictions with no error. When the buffer is empty, the keys come from the provided dict and may not match the dimensions the trained model expects (e.g., when `base_model` was passed to the constructor), causing either a crash or a silently wrong alignment. Track an explicit feature schema rather than deriving it from whichever sample happens to be first.

The truthiness check `if self.baseline_mean` reports `None` when the baseline mean/std is exactly 0.0 (e.g., all errors identical), even though a baseline has been established. Use `is not None` so a legitimate zero-valued baseline is reported correctly.

```suggestion
            'baseline_mean': float(self.baseline_mean) if self.baseline_mean is not None else None,
```

## scout/core/birdeye_client.py (7 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

`get_historical_price` is an `async def`, so calling it without `await` returns a coroutine object, never the price and never `None`. Consequently `if price is None` is always False and `LiquidityData(price_usd=price)` receives a coroutine object, yielding invalid data (or a TypeError when consumers try to use `price_usd`). Add `await`.

```suggestion
        price = await self.get_historical_price(token_address, timestamp)
        if price is None:
            return None
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`last_request_time` is shared mutable state with a check-then-act race. Under concurrent async callers, two coroutines can both read a stale `last_request_time` (the `await asyncio.sleep` yields the event loop before the update), so both can issue requests back-to-back and burst past the intended 1-second delay. Serialize the check/sleep/update with an `asyncio.Lock` (or a fixed-rate limiter) to make the throttle reliable.

---

### [medium] (bug)

This method re-implements the request path instead of reusing `_make_request`: it bypasses `_rate_limit()` and the missing-API-key guard (with an empty key the request is still attempted), and `except Exception: return None` silently swallows every failure with no logging, making problems opaque. It also assigns `params` twice (the second assignment is dead duplication). Prefer extending `_make_request` to accept extra headers (e.g. `x-chain`) and reusing it here, and at minimum log the swallowed exception.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

This LiquidityData is built from *current* liquidity used as a fallback proxy, yet `source="birdeye_historical"` labels it as genuine historical data. Consumers storing this to a historical database will be misled. Rename the source to reflect it is a current-liquidity approximation (e.g. `birdeye_current_proxy`) or document it explicitly.

### [low] (bug)

The response parsing here is fragile for the typical `/defi/history_price` response: the series usually arrives under `data.items` (a dict, not a top-level list), so `price_data.get("value")` would return None and `get_historical_price` would silently always return None. Also `price_data[0].get("value")` assumes list elements are dicts. Verify the actual response shape against the API docs and parse `data['data']['items']` with element-type guards.

### [low] (bug)

`_get_session` has a check-then-act race: if two coroutines call it concurrently while `self._session is None`, both create a new session, overwrite `self._session`, and one session object is leaked/unclosed. Create the session eagerly in `__init__` or guard creation with a lock to guarantee a single pooled session.

### [low] (style)

Prefer lazy logging: `logger.debug("Birdeye API request failed: %s", e)` so the message is only formatted when debug level is enabled, instead of eagerly building the f-string on every failure.

## scout/core/caching.py (3 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

`_wallet_activity` and `_last_activity_update` are initialized in `__init__` but never written anywhere in this module — only the underlying `ActivityBasedCache.update_wallet_activity` is called here. As a result `get_wallet_activity_level()` always returns `INACTIVE`, `get_cache_stats()['wallets_tracked']` is always 0, and the local bookkeeping in `invalidate_wallet`/`cleanup_inactive_wallets`/`clear_cache` operates on permanently empty dicts. Populate both dicts here so the wrapper-level tracking actually reflects cached wallets. Also note the class docstring claims thread safety, but these dicts would then be mutated without the lock that `ActivityBasedCache` uses internally — consider guarding them with a lock.

```suggestion
        # Update wallet activity tracking
        self.cache.update_wallet_activity(wallet_address, tx_count_24h, wqs_score)
        self._wallet_activity[wallet_address] = {
            'tx_count_24h': tx_count_24h,
            'wqs_score': wqs_score,
            'last_updated': time.time(),
        }
        self._last_activity_update[wallet_address] = time.time()
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Because `_wallet_activity` is never populated (see `cache_transactions`), this guard is always true and `get_wallet_activity_level()` returns `INACTIVE` for every wallet, even highly active ones. The whole activity-level API on the wrapper is effectively dead code until the tracking dicts are filled in.

---

### [low] (performance)

Eager f-string formatting defeats logging's lazy argument evaluation: this string is built on every cache read even when the DEBUG level is disabled (production default). Use lazy `%s` formatting for all the f-string log calls in this file (`Cache HIT`, `Cache MISS`, `Cached ... transactions`, `Invalidated ...`, `Cleaned up ...`).

```suggestion
            logger.debug("Cache HIT for %s...: %d transactions", wallet_address[:8], len(cached))
```

## scout/core/circuit_breaker.py (9 findings, 2 critical, 1 high)

### [critical] (bug)

Deadlock: `can_trade_wallet` acquires `self._lock` (a non-reentrant `threading.Lock`) and then calls `check_circuit_breaker()`, which acquires the same lock again. On a non-reentrant lock, the same thread blocks forever, so every call to `can_trade_wallet()` deadlocks. Fix by using `threading.RLock()` for `self._lock`, or refactor so the check runs without re-acquiring the lock (e.g., an unlocked `_check_circuit_breaker_locked()` helper).

---

### [critical] (bug)

Deadlock: `record_trade_result` holds `self._lock` and calls `blacklist_wallet()`, which also acquires the same non-reentrant `threading.Lock`. When a wallet reaches `MAX_WALLET_FAILURES`, this blocks forever. Same fix as `can_trade_wallet`: use `RLock` or extract the locked body so it can be called directly.

---

### [high] (bug)

The EMERGENCY branch calls `_trigger()` unconditionally on every `check_circuit_breaker()` call, unlike the WARNING/CAUTION branches which guard on a level change. While drawdown stays above the emergency threshold, every check logs a warning, appends an event to the unbounded `_events` list, inflates `trigger_count`, and writes state to disk. `COOLDOWN_SECONDS` is defined but never enforced anywhere. Add the same level-change guard (and optionally enforce the cooldown) to stop the per-call churn.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`MAX_WALLET_FAILURES` is documented as "max consecutive failures per wallet", but `_wallet_failures[wallet]` is only reset after a blacklist is issued — a successful trade never resets it. A wallet with e.g. 4 failures, 1 success, then 1 more failure (non-consecutive) will be blacklisted. Reset the per-wallet counter in the `success` branch.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`_trigger()` updates `current_level` but never sets `self._state.current_state = CircuitState.OPEN` (`HALF_OPEN` is likewise never used), so `current_state` remains CLOSED even while trading is halted. `get_status_report()`/`print_status_report()` therefore always report 'closed'. Wire the state transitions in `_trigger()`/`_attempt_reset()`, or drop the `CircuitState` field.

---

### [medium] (bug)

CAUTION is documented as halting only Spear (and `_apply_level_adjustments` keeps Shield at 100%), but this branch returns `should_trade=False`, and `can_trade_wallet()` uses that boolean to gate the entire wallet. As a result, at CAUTION level, Shield trading is blocked too, contradicting the module's own documentation. Return `True` with `CAUTION` and let callers act on the level, or align the docs/allocations with the halt-all behavior.

---

### [medium] (bug)

In this branch, when `current_level != NORMAL` but `RESET_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` has not elapsed, `_attempt_reset()` does nothing, yet the method still returns `(True, NORMAL, "Normal operation")`. The caller is told the system is back to normal while the internal state and allocations remain at the elevated level (e.g. EMERGENCY with 0% allocations), and `get_status_report()` still reports the old level. Only report NORMAL after a successful reset, or return the actual current level.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

`CURRENT_CAPITAL` and `PEAK_CAPITAL` are defaulted to `STARTING_CAPITAL`, which at class-body evaluation time is the `Field` object returned by `field(default_factory=...)`, not a float. This only initializes correctly by accident (dataclasses copies `Field` instances and shares the same default_factory); it is fragile and misleading. Give each field its own explicit `default_factory`/default or initialize them in `__post_init__`.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Dead configuration: `SHIELD_REDUCTION_FACTOR`, `SPEAR_REDUCTION_FACTOR`, `COOLDOWN_SECONDS`, and `DAILY_START_TIME` are declared but never referenced anywhere in the module (`_apply_level_adjustments` hardcodes 0.5/0.2/1.0, and the cooldown is never enforced). Either wire them into the logic or remove them to avoid misleading config.

---

## scout/core/cluster_ensemble.py (3 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

Missing/None metrics are coerced to 0.0 via `m.get(..., 0.0) or 0.0`. A wallet with absent `roi_30d` is counted as non-profitable, and absent `profit_factor` drags mean_pf below 1.0 — so a cluster whose members simply lack data gets profit_rate≈0 and risk_score pushed toward 1.0 (max), triggering the full −15 penalty in `apply_cluster_adjustment` even though there is no evidence the cluster is losing money. In the caller (main.py), `r.roi_30d`/`r.profit_factor` can legitimately be None, so this is a realistic path. Consider excluding members without the metric from the aggregate (or requiring minimum coverage) and skipping the risk adders when data is missing.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Cluster membership/size is derived only from the `wallet_records` list; the `cluster_size`/`members` fields documented in `cluster_data` are never read. If a caller passes a filtered/partial record list, a real multi-wallet cluster is sized n<=1, gets risk_score 0.0, and silently bypasses both the bonus and the penalty. Additionally, clusters present in `cluster_data` but with no matching wallet record still appear in the output with size=1 and all-zero metrics (misleading for consumers). Consider sizing clusters from `cluster_data`'s `members`/`cluster_size` while aggregating metrics only over the records actually available, and skipping clusters with no member records.

---

### [low] (other)

The bonus and penalty branches are not mutually exclusive. A cluster can qualify for the +5 bonus (profit_rate > 0.8, mean_wqs > 60) while still having risk_score > 0.5 because of the negative mean_roi (+0.3) and low profit_factor (+0.2) adders — e.g., profit_rate=0.9, mean_roi<0, mean_pf<1 yields risk≈0.6, so the wallet receives both +5 and −9. If a "profitable" cluster should never be penalized, make the conditions exclusive (e.g., an else/elif or a combined guard); otherwise document that both effects are intended.

## scout/core/clustering.py (6 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

The resolver cache is keyed only by `(address, depth)` but the result depends on the per-chain `visited` set. The shared cache is reused across all top-K wallets (each with a fresh `visited`), yet when a cycle is detected the resulting `None` is written to the cache and then served to any other chain that reaches the same address at the same depth — and a valid root cached by one chain can mask a cycle in another. The outcome therefore depends on which chain was resolved first (order-dependent clustering, e.g. the depth-0 boundary: one chain returns the address as root, another chain that hits the same address as an ancestor returns `None`). Fix: do not cache cycle-detected results (or include the visited state in the cache key).

```suggestion
    # Cycle detection
    if address in visited:
        logger.debug(f"Cycle detected at {address[:8]}, returning None")
        return None  # cycle outcome is chain-dependent; do not cache it
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The pre-flight credit estimate omits Phase 1 entirely. Phase 1 calls `get_wallet_funder` once for every ACTIVE wallet (each call costs `SIGNATURES + GET_TRANSACTION` = 2 credits, confirmed in helius_client.py), plus Phase 2 performs up to `hops` additional funder fetches per top-K wallet. `estimated_cost` only counts the top-K hops (`cost_per_wallet * min(multihop_max, len(active))`), so actual spend can exceed the budget that `can_make_request` approved. Include the Phase-1 per-wallet fetch cost in the estimate.

```suggestion
            cost_per_wallet = (CreditCost.SIGNATURES.value + CreditCost.GET_TRANSACTION.value) * hops
            phase1_cost = (CreditCost.SIGNATURES.value + CreditCost.GET_TRANSACTION.value) * len(active)
            estimated_cost = phase1_cost + cost_per_wallet * min(multihop_max, len(active))
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Phase 2 has no per-wallet error handling, unlike Phase 1 (which uses `asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True)` and downgrades failures to `None`). A single exception from `get_wallet_funder` inside `_resolve_funder_root` propagates out of `cluster_and_dedup` and aborts the entire clustering/demotion run, leaving the roster undeduped. Wrap each root resolution in try/except and degrade that wallet to its direct funder (or None) instead of failing the whole run.

```suggestion
                for record in top_k_active:
                    funder = funder_map.get(record.address)
                    if funder:
                        try:
                            root = await _resolve_funder_root(helius_client, funder, hops, cache)
                        except Exception:
                            logger.warning(f"Root resolution failed for {record.address[:8]}, falling back to direct funder")
                            root = funder
                        root_map[record.address] = root
                    else:
                        root_map[record.address] = None
```

---

### [low] (bug)

`deduped = deduped[:top_n]` truncates after one representative per cluster has been selected. When the number of clusters exceeds `top_n`, wallets removed purely because of the cap — including singleton (non-correlated) wallets — are demoted to CANDIDATE with the note "Demoted: cluster dedup (same funder/root as higher-WQS wallet...)" and the summary "Removed N correlated wallets", which is factually wrong for these wallets. Either cap before/after clustering only correlated removals, or make the demotion note/message distinguish cap-based truncation from genuine cluster correlation.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Operational results use `print()` instead of the module logger that is already defined and used elsewhere in this file. In a library/async context, stdout output is not captured by the project's logging configuration and bypasses log levels/formatters. Prefer `logger.info(...)` for these messages.

---

### [low] (documentation)

The docstring promises "Returns: Deduplicated list of WalletRecord objects (ACTIVE only, reduced)", but the function actually returns the full `records` list with demoted ACTIVE wallets mutated in place to CANDIDATE (plus `cluster_id` set on records). Update the docstring to describe the in-place demotion semantics and that callers must filter `status == "ACTIVE"` to obtain the reduced roster.
