This breaks the documented contract ('Output updated roster to roster_new.db', '--output /path/to/roster_new.db') — operators who pass `--output` believing they control the destination will silently write to the production DB instead. Either pass the path through (and make `write_wallets_to_db` honor it), or drop the misleading flag/docstring.

The effective promotion threshold therefore diverges from both the module documentation and the validator's own default unless env vars are explicitly set. ### [medium] (bug)

`setup_logging()` is called at the top of every `main_async()` cycle and unconditionally appends a new `RotatingFileHandler` and `StreamHandler` to the root logger. In `--continuous` mode (`main()` loops calling `main_async()`), handlers accumulate on every iteration: each cycle duplicates every log line to the file/console N times, and each new file handler opens an additional file descriptor on `scout.log` that is never closed — a slow file-descriptor leak in long-running processes. Guard against re-registration (e.g. check `logger.handlers` before adding, or clear existing handlers first).

            logger.addHandler(console_handler)
```

`execute_and_fetchone` is a synchronous psycopg call executed directly inside the async `process_wallet` task (no `await`, and it is not a coroutine — it returns a row dict). Because this runs on the event loop thread while the wallet analysis is intentionally parallelized with a semaphore of up to 10, every gate-admission query blocks the whole event loop and serializes the otherwise-concurrent analysis at this point, defeating the 10-way concurrency and inflating wall-clock time. Wrap it in `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` (or use the async executor) to keep the loop responsive.

```suggestion

                    SELECT COUNT(*) AS total,

Those adjustments never propagate back into `results`, so: (1) wallets promoted to ACTIVE by archetype diversification are never written as promoted (and don't fall into the shadow band unless near threshold), and (2) wallets demoted by cluster/correlation passes are still recorded as 'promoted' and get a correlation record. Since these episodes drive the WQS-to-PnL feedback/calibration, the feedback data is skewed. ## scout/pyproject.toml (3 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Invalid PEP 517 build backend. `setuptools.backends._legacy:_Backend` is not a real setuptools module — pip will fail with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'setuptools.backends'` whenever this package is built (e.g. `pip install .`, `pip wheel .`, or any frontend invoking the backend). The correct backend identifiers are `setuptools.build_meta` (PEP 517) or `setuptools.build_meta:__legacy__` (legacy setup.py mode). Since no setup.py exists in this project, use `setuptools.build_meta`.

```suggestion
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Redundant per-file ignore: E501 is already listed in the global `ignore` list, so this per-file-ignores entry has no effect and gives the false impression that test files are held to a stricter line-length standard. Remove the global `E501` ignore instead, or drop this redundant entry.

```suggestion
"tests/**/*.py" = []
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`[project]` declares no `dependencies`, yet the scout runtime uses third-party libraries (e.g. psycopg/psycopg-pool in core/db.py, networkx in core/network_features.py). The Docker build happens to install via requirements.txt, so the gap is masked in containers, but `pip install .` on this package will silently install it without any runtime dependencies. Declare the runtime dependencies under `[project].dependencies` (or document that requirements.txt is the authoritative dependency source) to keep the package metadata consistent.

## scout/schema_scout_tables.sql (6 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

COMMENT ON TABLE is issued before CREATE TABLE. In PostgreSQL, COMMENT ON TABLE raises "relation does not exist" when the table is absent (there is no IF NOT EXISTS option for COMMENT), so a fresh database apply aborts on this very first statement — and the same pattern repeats before every table in the file (lines 36, 62, 89, 107, 126, 149, 172, 196, 215, 242, 268). Move each COMMENT after its CREATE TABLE, or guard it, e.g.: DO $$ BEGIN IF to_regclass('public.ml_predictions') IS NOT NULL THEN COMMENT ON TABLE ml_predictions IS 'ML predictions for wallet performance'; END IF; END $$;

---

### [medium] (bug)

This FK (repeated in nearly every table) references wallets(address), and exit_recommendations additionally references trades(trade_uuid) — but neither wallets nor trades is created in this file (no definition exists in scout/). A standalone or re-ordered apply will fail on every CREATE TABLE that depends on these missing tables. The cross-file migration ordering is unenforced; either create the referenced tables in the same script or explicitly document/verify the prerequisite order.

---

### [medium] (bug)

trade_uuid and wallet_address are two independent FKs, so the database can store an exit recommendation whose trade_uuid belongs to a different wallet than wallet_address. Per-wallet reporting and any join on both columns would then return inconsistent/corrupted data. Prefer a composite FK on trades (trade_uuid, wallet_address) — which requires a matching UNIQUE constraint on trades — or validate the wallet/trade pairing in the application layer before insert.

---

### [medium] (bug)

growth_history has no UNIQUE constraint on its natural key (wallet_address, timestamp), so repeated cron runs, retries, or concurrent writers can insert duplicate snapshots that skew balance/PnL aggregates and trend calculations. The same problem applies to wallet_performance_history (wallet_address, timestamp), roi_metrics (wallet_address, timeframe), and multi_timeframe_discovery_stats (wallet_address, discovery_timeframe). Add UNIQUE constraints (or upsert logic) on these keys.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Unlike the other categorical columns in this schema (alert_type, event_type, recommendation_type, severity, status all have CHECK constraints), credit_history.operation_type is unconstrained, allowing arbitrary/invalid values to be stored silently and breaking downstream filtering and reporting. Add a CHECK constraint enumerating the allowed operations (or align it with the application enum).

---

### [low] (maintainability)

alerts.trade_uuid is a free TEXT column with no FK to trades(trade_uuid), inconsistent with exit_recommendations.trade_uuid which does declare that FK. Alerts can therefore reference nonexistent trades. Add the FK (with matching ON DELETE behavior) or a CHECK validating the reference.

### [medium] (bug)

wallets.wqs_score is nullable in the schema (wallets.sql: `wqs_score REAL` with no NOT NULL), but this insert writes it into wqs_pnl_correlation.wqs_score_at_promotion which is declared `REAL NOT NULL`. A CANDIDATE wallet with a NULL score would raise sqlite3.IntegrityError mid-loop, aborting the whole backfill before conn.commit() (the pending transaction is then rolled back on close), so no rows get written. Guard the query with `AND w.wqs_score IS NOT NULL` (or COALESCE with a sensible default) before inserting.

## scout/scripts/bench_baseline.py (6 findings, 1 critical, 2 high)

### [critical] (bug)

`CreditTracker` is not defined anywhere in `core.helius_credit_tracker` — the module only defines `HeliusCreditTracker` (plus `CreditCost`, `get_credit_tracker`, etc.). This import raises `ImportError` at startup, so the entire script can never run. Use `HeliusCreditTracker` instead (and update the instantiation at the `CreditTracker()` call site).

```suggestion
from core.helius_credit_tracker import HeliusCreditTracker
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`HeliusCreditTracker` (the only tracker class in that module) has no `get_remaining_credits()` method — credit state is exposed via `get_snapshot().credits_remaining`. Moreover, the tracker is never connected to the client's request path (the replay patch replaces `_make_request` and nothing calls `record_request`), so `initial_credits == final_credits` always and `credits_consumed` is structurally 0 — the credit metric measures nothing. Use `get_snapshot().credits_remaining` and wire the tracker into request accounting, or drop the metric.

```suggestion
        initial_credits = credit_tracker.get_snapshot().credits_remaining
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`self._network_call_count` is initialized once and never incremented anywhere — no code in the fixture replay path touches it. As a result `network_calls` and `network_calls_per_wallet` are always 0, so the reported "network calls per wallet" metric is meaningless. Additionally, because the counter is never reset per wallet, even if it were incremented via a side effect it would accumulate cumulatively across wallets. Track accesses inside `create_replay_patch`/the replayer and reset the counter at the start of each `measure_wallet` call.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`peak_rss` is measured after the wallet benchmarks by running a fresh `FixtureReplayer().get_all_wallets()` — a completely different, much smaller workload. The reported `peak_rss_mb` therefore does not reflect the peak memory of the wallet operations being benchmarked. The `tracemalloc` fallback additionally measures only Python heap allocations traced inside this method, not process RSS. Measure memory around the actual `measure_all_wallets()` workload (e.g., `memory_usage`/`resource.getrusage` during the run) so the metric matches what is being benchmarked.

### [low] (maintainability)

`os` is imported but never referenced anywhere in this file — dead import. Remove it.

### [low] (maintainability)

`pyinstrument` / `PYINSTRUMENT_AVAILABLE` are imported and a warning is printed when missing, but the flag is never read afterwards — the profiling feature this scaffolding implies is not wired up anywhere. Either actually profile the run with pyinstrument or remove this dead import/warning.

## scout/scripts/capture_fixtures.py (6 findings, 1 critical, 2 high)

### [critical] (bug)

`CreditTracker` is not defined in `scout/core/helius_credit_tracker.py` — that module only exports `HeliusCreditTracker`, `get_credit_tracker()`, `reset_credit_tracker()`, etc. (confirmed by searching the whole `scout/` tree; the only other importer, `bench_baseline.py`, has the same broken import). This line raises `ImportError` at module load, so the entire capture script can never run. Use `from core.helius_credit_tracker import HeliusCreditTracker` (or better, the shared `get_credit_tracker()` singleton that `HeliusClient` actually records against).

```suggestion
from core.helius_credit_tracker import get_credit_tracker
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Two problems here: (1) `get_remaining_credits()` does not exist on the tracker — the API is `get_snapshot().credits_remaining`. (2) More fundamentally, this locally-created tracker instance is never connected to `HeliusClient`; the client records request costs on the module-level singleton returned by `get_credit_tracker()` (see `scout/core/helius_client.py` ~line 2841), so `initial_credits - final_credits` will always be 0 and the `credits_consumed` value written into every fixture/manifest is meaningless. Use the shared singleton and snapshot-based remaining credits.

```suggestion
    # Track credit consumption via the same tracker HeliusClient records against
    credit_tracker = get_credit_tracker()
    initial_credits = credit_tracker.get_snapshot().credits_remaining
```

### [high] (bug)

Same non-existent method in the closing half of the function — `credit_tracker.get_remaining_credits()` will raise `AttributeError` even if the import were fixed; use `credit_tracker.get_snapshot().credits_remaining`. Note that if `initial_credits`/`final_credits` both come from the singleton, the snapshot already reflects prior usage, so the subtraction is still an unreliable measure of this run's consumption; a more accurate approach is to record actual page requests made by the client.

```suggestion
    # Calculate credit consumption
    final_credits = credit_tracker.get_snapshot().credits_remaining
    credits_consumed = initial_credits - final_credits
```

If every wallet capture fails (each failure is caught and only printed in the loop), `all_metadata` is empty yet the script still overwrites `manifest.json` with `total_fixtures: 0`, prints "Capture Complete!" and exits with code 0 — a completely failed run looks successful and can silently destroy a previously captured good manifest. ## scout/scripts/evaluate_models.py (5 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

Unit mismatch risk: predictions are always taken from `predicted_pnl_sol` (the model's raw output, labeled as PnL in SOL) while `y_test` is whatever `target_column` is set to (default `roi_30d`). The model is trained on `target_column` (roi_30d), so the units match only when `--target-column` equals the column used at training time; changing the target column silently produces invalid metrics. Worse, `predict_profitability` returns `_fallback_prediction` (a heuristic `roi_30d * 0.1 * win_rate`, a different scale) whenever model load/feature prep fails, and `pred.get('predicted_pnl_sol', 0.0)` masks any missing key with 0.0 — so fallback/heuristic values can be silently mixed into the metric computation. Verify the prediction unit matches `target_column`, and either exclude fallback predictions or record them separately.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Data-loading failure is silently swallowed by the CLI: `evaluate_models` returns `{'error': 'data_loading_failed', ...}` on empty test data, but `main()` never checks `results.get('error')` and still prints a success-looking "EVALUATION SUMMARY" with N/A values, then exits with code 0. This can mislead CI/automation into treating a failed evaluation as successful. Compare with `train_ml_models.py` which does `if 'error' in results: sys.exit(1)`. Add the same check here (and skip printing the summary when an error occurred).

---

### [medium] (bug)

MAPE calculation is not robust to zero/near-zero ROI targets: adding a fixed 1e-8 to `y_true` in the denominator means that for `y_true` values near 0 (common for 30-day ROI), even a tiny prediction error produces astronomically large percentage values (e.g. y_true=0, y_pred=0.01 → ~1e8%), which dominate the mean and make the metric meaningless (and it is then serialized into the saved JSON report). Use a relative-error formulation that clamps the denominator (e.g. `np.maximum(np.abs(y_true), threshold)`) or exclude near-zero actuals and document the behavior.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Both "model" evaluations may actually score the same model. `GradientBoostPredictor._select_model()` returns the model named by `best_model_type` (loaded from `gradient_boost_metadata.json`) before it ever considers the requested `model_type`. So constructing it with `model_type="xgboost"` / `model_type="lightgbm"` does not pin the evaluated model — if `best_model_type` is, say, `lightgbm`, the "xgboost" branch will evaluate the LightGBM model too, making `results['xgboost']` and `results['lightgbm']` identical and the best-model-by-RMSE selection meaningless. Pin the actual model (e.g. call `_predict_with_model` on `xgb_model.xgboost_model`/`lgb_model.lightgbm_model` directly) or verify the `model_type` field returned in each prediction and skip mismatches.

---

### [low] (performance)

Eager f-string in log call defeats lazy formatting: `logger.info(f"...")` always formats the string even when the INFO level is disabled. Prefer `logger.info("Loaded %d test samples with %d features", len(X_test), len(feature_names))`.

---

## scout/scripts/run_shakedown_test.sh (7 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

The 'short experiment test' never actually starts the operator — it copies the config, patches it, logs 'skipping', and deletes the config. Runtime failures (vault access, DB migration, startup panics, broken trade flow) would therefore pass this 24-hour shake-down as long as static files exist. Either launch the operator against the test config for a bounded period and assert on DB/logs/trade count, or explicitly rename/document this phase as static validation only so the 'ready for 21-day test' conclusion is not misleading.

---

### [high] (bug)

validate_experiment_components never returns non-zero when components are missing — it only logs a warning while setting all_found=false. Consequently the call in main() (`validate_experiment_components || failed=$((failed + 1))`) can never increment `failed`, and the script still prints 'All pre-flight checks passed' / 'completed successfully' even when required tables or modules are absent. Return 1 (or the missing-count) when all_found is false.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`tr -d 'false'` deletes every occurrence of the characters f/a/l/s/e, not the literal word 'false'. It corrupts legitimate numeric values (e.g. `1e3` becomes `13`). Worse, for the actual config `grep "tracer_cap"` also matches `tracer_cap_reached: false`, so `tracer_cap` becomes a multi-line value (`60` + `false`) and the embedded newline makes the `^[0-9]+$` test fail — meaning the low-cap check never fires and no validation is actually performed. Strip a trailing 'false' token explicitly (e.g. `awk '{print $2}' | sed 's/false//'`) or, better, parse the YAML with python3/yq and fail on missing or non-numeric values.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Under `set -e`, the exit status of command substitution inside a `local` assignment is masked (local itself returns 0), so a missing key silently yields an empty value and validation continues. Additionally the bare `grep "tracer_cap"` matches the `tracer_cap_reached: false` line too (multi-line $2 output), and this is not real YAML parsing (formatting/spacing/nested keys are missed). Because missing keys degrade to empty strings that bypass every check, an invalid config still gets logged as '✓ Configuration file is valid' at the end of this function. Validate with a proper YAML parser and treat missing/malformed keys as failures.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The sed substitutions are never verified. If the YAML ever changes keys, values, spacing, or indentation, the replacements silently match nothing, and the 'test' config stays identical to the production 21-day config — yet the script still reports success (and this config is deleted right after without ever being used). Verify each substitution actually matched (e.g. `grep -c` before/after) and fail the phase when a pattern produces no change.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The pipeline's exit status comes from `grep`, not `python3`, and stderr is discarded. A runtime crash in verdict.py produces no stdout, so grep fails and the failure is downgraded to a warning — then the function still returns 0 and logs '✓ Verdict script is valid'. The runtime check can never actually fail the shake-down. Capture output, use `set -o pipefail`, and check python3's real exit code (treating a non-zero exit as a validation failure).

---

## scout/scripts/validate_wqs_predictiveness.py (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

The early return `if k >= n: return 1.0` is wrong for the k == n case. The one-tailed p-value of seeing all n trials succeed is p**n (e.g., 0.5**n), which is very small and would indicate strong significance for a perfectly profitable pool — but this function returns 1.0, making such a dataset look completely insignificant and potentially flipping the VERDICT output. Only k > n should be special-cased (return 0.0); for k == n the normal sum already evaluates to p**n.

```suggestion
def binomial_p_value(k: int, n: int, p: float = 0.5) -> float:
    """One-tailed binomial test: prob of >= k successes in n trials with prob p."""
    if k > n:
        return 0.0
    from math import comb
    return sum(comb(n, i) * (p ** i) * ((1 - p) ** (n - i)) for i in range(k, n + 1))
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The query only guarantees `realized_pnl_30d_sol IS NOT NULL`, so `wqs_score` may be NULL in returned rows. `wqs_vals` is then passed to `pearson()` (arithmetic on None → TypeError) and to `sorted(zip(...))` (None vs float comparison → TypeError), crashing the whole script. Filter NULL scores in SQL (or in Python) before numeric use.

```suggestion
        WHERE realized_pnl_30d_sol IS NOT NULL
          AND wqs_score IS NOT NULL
          AND trade_count_30d >= ?
          AND status IN ('ACTIVE', 'CANDIDATE')
```

Yet the verdict uses `profit_rate > 50 and p_value < 0.05` to declare "WQS POSITIVELY PREDICTS profitability" — a pool that is profitable overall would pass this check even if WQS carried zero predictive signal. Tie the binomial test to WQS ranking (e.g., top vs bottom tercile profitability) or remove it from the WQS verdict so the conclusion is supported by the correlation/tercile evidence only.

## scout/scripts/verdict.py (7 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

The pre-committed rule documented at the top of this file allows GO when "PF > 1.2 on >=50 trades" even if the expectancy CI includes zero, but this Rule 1 unconditionally KILLs as soon as ci_lower <= 0, so that documented alternative can never fire. Rule 2 (below) then turns the PF condition into an *additional* KILL trigger (`profit_factor_lb < 1.2 and ci_lower < 5.0`) rather than a rescue, and it only relaxes the kill when the CI is already strongly positive. As written there is no path that yields GO with a non-positive CI, contradicting the module docstring. Restructure so a non-positive CI is only a KILL unless PF > 1.2 on >= min_trades, and don't use PF<1.2 with a weakly positive CI as a separate hard kill.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The module docstring advertises a BCa bootstrap CI, but this is a plain percentile bootstrap: it sorts bootstrap means and takes the 2.5th/97.5th percentiles with no bias-correction or acceleration terms. For the skewed PnL distributions typical of trading results, percentile intervals misstate coverage and can tip the GO/KILL decision. Either implement the actual BCa adjustment or rename/redocument this as a percentile CI.

---

### [medium] (bug)

experiment_days is derived from the earliest entry and latest exit among trades, so an otherwise valid 21-day window whose trades occur away from the boundaries (or end early with a gap) will undercount the window and be wrongly classified INCONCLUSIVE. It is also truncated by `.days` (a 20.9-day span counts as 20). Additionally `exit_times[-1]` is the last exit in entry-order, not necessarily the maximum exit. Use the scheduled experiment start/end (stored config/table) rather than inferring the window from trade timestamps.

---

### [medium] (bug)

profit_factor_lb is computed by multiplying the point-estimate profit factor by the Wilson lower bound of the win *proportion*. That is not a valid lower confidence bound for profit factor — PF depends on gross win/loss sums, not just the win count — so using it as a KILL threshold can mis-decide. Compute a bootstrap/BCa CI over resampled profit factors, or apply the documented threshold to the PF point estimate.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The minimum-trade gate uses total_trades (all rows), but the expectancy/CI is computed only from rows with non-NULL real_pnl (the loader explicitly skips None values). If real_pnl is NULL for some rows, the effective sample backing the verdict can be well below min_trades while the requirement still passes. Count only trades with a real_pnl for the gate (and for the documented "PF > 1.2 on >=50 trades" alternative).

---

### [low] (maintainability)

avg_gap is passed into _apply_decision_rules but never read by any rule — either remove the parameter or actually use it (e.g., as an execution-gap breaker as suggested by its presence in the signature).

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Both bootstrap loops use np.random.choice without a fixed seed, so repeated runs over identical data can produce different CIs, p-values, and potentially different GO/KILL verdicts. Seed the RNG (or persist the resampled statistics) so decisions are reproducible.

AsyncMock forwards `use_retry=True` into `mock_make_request`, which has no such parameter, raising `TypeError: mock_make_request() got an unexpected keyword argument 'use_retry'`. Mirror the real signature (`params: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None, use_retry: bool = True`) or accept `**kwargs`.

```suggestion
    async def mock_make_request(self, endpoint: str, params: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None, use_retry: bool = True) -> Optional[Any]:
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`patch.object` expects an object target and, unlike `patch()`, does not resolve dotted import-path strings. Passing `'core.helius_client.HeliusClient'` here makes the patch fail when it is applied (the string is treated as the object to patch, raising TypeError/AttributeError). The import path itself is valid (`bench_baseline.py` does `from core.helius_client import HeliusClient`), so use the string form of `patch()` instead: `patch('core.helius_client.HeliusClient._make_request', new=AsyncMock(side_effect=mock_make_request))`, or import the module and pass the class object.

```suggestion
    return patch(
        'core.helius_client.HeliusClient._make_request',
        new=AsyncMock(side_effect=mock_make_request)
    )
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Returning `[]` for any unrecognized endpoint silently masks routing mistakes and missing fixtures: a typo'd endpoint or a fixture-less wallet looks like a legitimate empty result. It also violates the real `_make_request` contract of `Optional[Dict]` (None on failure); callers expecting a dict response for other endpoints (e.g. code doing `data.get(...)`) will hit a list instead. Prefer returning `None` (or logging a warning) for unmatched endpoints and return dict/list responses consistent with the endpoint being replayed.

```suggestion
        # Unknown/unmatched endpoints should not silently succeed
        return None
```

## scout/tests/test_db_writer.py (4 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (test)

This suite never imports or calls the production writer `scout/core/db_writer.py`; every test re-implements atomic write/rename and the SQLite schema using stdlib calls. Consequently, all these tests would pass even if the real writer were completely broken, its schema diverged, or its failure cleanup regressed. Import the actual module (e.g. `from core.db_writer import ...`) and drive it directly, using `tmp_path`/monkeypatching for output paths, so the suite guards real behavior.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`conn.close()` only runs on the success path: if `connect`, `execute`, or `commit` raises (e.g. SQLITE_BUSY even with the 10s timeout), the connection is left to be finalized by GC. In this concurrent test that leaks up to N connections with open file handles/WAL locks and makes cleanup non-deterministic. Close the connection in a `finally` block instead.

```suggestion
    conn = None
    try:
        conn = sqlite3.connect(str(db_path), timeout=10)
        conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
        conn.execute(
            "INSERT OR REPLACE INTO wallets (address, status, wqs_score, created_at, updated_at) "
            "VALUES (?, 'ACTIVE', ?, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)",
            (wallet_address, float(idx) * 10.0),
        )
        conn.commit()
        results[idx] = "ok"
    except Exception as e:
        results[idx] = f"error:{e}"
    finally:
        if conn is not None:
            conn.close()
```

This test does not exercise a real DB write failure: it writes plain text to a `.tmp` file and performs the cleanup itself, so the assertions hold trivially — the original DB is never touched, and a same-size corruption would not be detected by the size check. Add tests that inject a known scam address (e.g., monkeypatch `core.denylist._KNOWN_SCAM_ADDRESSES`/`_KNOWN_SCAM_FUNDERS`) and assert `is_known_scam_address` returns True and `check_wallet_correlation` returns False for a correlated wallet, funder, and counterparty.

Consider asserting the concrete expected value and injecting a known scam address.

## scout/tests/test_discovery_integration.py (5 findings)

### [medium] (test)

This mock does not actually simulate an RPC failure. _filter_by_sol_balance uses 'async with session.post(...)', but because mock_session is an AsyncMock, session.post(...) returns a coroutine (AsyncMock calls return coroutines), and a coroutine has no __aenter__. The 'async with' then raises AttributeError (not the intended Exception('RPC error')), which is swallowed by the same except Exception branch. Both test_balance_fail_open_includes_batch and test_balance_fail_closed_excludes_batch therefore pass for the wrong reason, and the side_effect is never exercised. Configure post as a proper async context manager instead, e.g. set mock_session.post = MagicMock() and give mock_session.post.return_value a __aenter__ AsyncMock with side_effect=Exception('RPC error') and a __aexit__ AsyncMock(return_value=False).

Patch and assert-not-called on all strategy methods (_discover_from_recent_blocks, _discover_from_dex_programs, _discover_from_seed_wallets, discover_from_top_performing_tokens) to make the test both robust and network-free.

## scout/tests/test_growth_tracking.py (6 findings)

### [medium] (security)

`tempfile.mktemp` is deprecated (DeprecationWarning since Python 3.12) and uses a predictable path, which is a TOCTOU race/symlink-hijack hazard. Additionally, the tracker enables SQLite WAL mode (`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`), so `-wal`/`-shm` sidecar files are created next to `db_path`, but the cleanup only unlinks the main `.db` file — those sidecars leak after every test. Prefer `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()` (or `NamedTemporaryFile`) and clean up the whole directory.

```suggestion
    import tempfile
    tmp_dir = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
    db_path = os.path.join(tmp_dir.name, "growth.db")
    tracker = GrowthTracker(
        starting_capital=200.0,
        target_capital=1000.0,
        db_path=db_path,
    )
    yield tracker

    # Cleanup
    tmp_dir.cleanup()
```

---

### [medium] (test)

This test is vacuous: after recording the 25% gain it only contains a comment and makes no assertion, so it passes even if no alert is generated at all. Query the `growth_alerts` table for `alert_type = 'significant_gain'` (which `_check_capital_alerts` stores with severity 'info' for changes > 10%) and assert the row exists.

```suggestion
        import sqlite3
        conn = sqlite3.connect(growth_tracker._db_path)
        cursor = conn.cursor()
        cursor.execute("""
            SELECT alert_type FROM growth_alerts
            WHERE alert_type = 'significant_gain'
        """)
        row = cursor.fetchone()
        conn.close()

        assert row is not None
```

### [medium] (test)

The assertions are guarded by `if metrics.growth_rate_daily > 0:`, but with only a single `record_capital(300)` the just-stored snapshot becomes the "day-ago" baseline in `_calculate_growth_metrics`, so `roi_daily`/`growth_rate_daily` compute to 0 and the guard is False — the intended invariant (`days_to_target` is not None for positive growth) is never exercised and the test passes vacuously. Make the assertions unconditional and seed a proper baseline (e.g., record a lower capital or insert a day-old snapshot) so the positive-growth path actually runs.

### [medium] (test)

Same conditional-assertion problem as the positive-growth test: after a single `record_capital(150)` the day-ago baseline equals the current capital, so `growth_rate_daily` is exactly 0 and the guard passes for the degenerate case rather than a genuinely negative rate. The invariant `days_to_target is None` for non-positive growth should be asserted unconditionally (with a controlled baseline), otherwise the test can pass without validating the behavior it claims to test.

### [medium] (test)

Order-dependent test: `get_growth_tracker` caches a module-level singleton (`_growth_tracker`) and ignores its parameters on every call after the first. This test only passes if no earlier test/runner has already created the tracker with different parameters; under another order (or when the file is imported after other tests call it with 300/1500), `tracker1.starting_capital` would no longer be 200.0 and the assertions fail. Add an autouse fixture that resets the module-level `_growth_tracker` to None before this test.

The test name claims to verify the alert; assert against the `growth_alerts` table (as `TestGrowthAlerts.test_target_reached_alert` does) or the returned alert state.

## scout/tests/test_helius_429_handling.py (5 findings)

### [medium] (test)

This test is tautological: it re-implements the same backoff formula (2**attempt, random.uniform(±0.25), min(30.0)) locally instead of exercising HeliusClient._retry_with_backoff or _make_request. It will pass even if all 429/retry handling is removed from the client, so it gives no regression protection for the behavior it claims to verify. Also, the ordering assertion (1*1.25 < 2*0.75, 2*1.25 < 4*0.75) holds with or without jitter, so the ±25% jitter claim is never actually asserted. Test the real code path instead, e.g. mock the transport to return a 429 and call client._make_request / _retry_with_backoff with a failing coroutine, then assert retry count and observed backoff intervals.

---

### [medium] (test)

Same tautological pattern as test_exponential_backoff_with_jitter: this only samples random.uniform() and asserts its average — it never calls the client's retry logic, so an implementation with zero jitter or no backoff at all would still pass. The average-over-100-samples check verifies properties of Python's random module, not of the code under test. Exercise HeliusClient._retry_with_backoff directly with a mocked failing coroutine (as done in test_helius_discovery.py) and assert the retry timing/count.

---

### [medium] (test)

Verifying behavior via inspect.getsource() literal-substring matching is brittle: harmless refactors (renaming _retry_with_backoff, extracting the 429/Retry-After block into a helper, rewording a log string) will break this test even though behavior is unchanged, and getsource raises TypeError for dynamically generated or inherited methods. Assert behavior instead: mock the aiohttp session/response to return 429 with a Retry-After header and verify the client honors it, backs off, and eventually returns a result.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Session cleanup only runs after all assertions pass: if any assertion fails (or _get_session itself raises), the aiohttp ClientSession and its connection pool are leaked, producing 'Unclosed client session' warnings and consuming sockets. This affects test_connection_pooling_configuration, test_session_reuse, and (indirectly) the other tests. Wrap assertions in try/finally, or better, use an async pytest fixture that yields the client and always calls _close_session() in teardown.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

This test couples to aiohttp private internals (_limit, _limit_per_host) which are not part of the public API and can change between aiohttp versions, making the test fragile. It also hardcodes 100/50, duplicating the constants in HeliusClient._get_session — any deliberate tuning of the pool silently breaks the test. Prefer asserting through a stable interface (e.g. the client's configured limits/behavior) rather than reaching into private connector attributes.

## scout/tests/test_helius_discovery.py (7 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

This second scenario is defeated by the global validation cache. The first scenario in this test validates `"test_wallet"` with `min_trades=3, days_back=7` and stores `True` in the process-wide `get_cache()` singleton under key `wallet_validation:test_wallet:test_wallet:3:7` (5-minute TTL, L1 memory). `_validate_wallet_activity` reads this cache at entry, so the second scenario hits the cached `True` and `assert not ...` fails — the test is order-dependent and currently broken. Use a distinct wallet address per scenario (or reset/mock `get_cache` between them) so the negative case cannot be short-circuited by the positive case's cached result.

```suggestion
            mock_get_txns.return_value = [{"signature": "tx1"}]
            assert not await helius_client._validate_wallet_activity("test_wallet_insufficient", min_trades=3, days_back=7)
```

---

### [medium] (test)

This wall-clock timing assertion is flaky under CI load, and it compares against the wrong knob: `_rate_limit()` sleeps based on `self.rate_limit_delay`, while the test derives `min_delay` from `_current_delay` (only equal while no adaptive throttling adjustment has occurred; they diverge if `SCOUT_HELIUS_RATE_LIMIT_MS` is set or adaptive mode has run). Real `time.sleep` plus elapsed-time measurement makes the pass/fail depend on machine load. Prefer patching `time.time`/`time.sleep` and asserting the actual sleep intervals (e.g., 2 * rate_limit_delay) rather than measuring real elapsed time.

### [medium] (test)

Setting `_discovery_cache_time` manually here masks whether the production path actually refreshed the cache. `_set_discovery_cache()` is what updates `_discovery_cache_time`; if a regression stopped refreshing it (stale cache bug), this test would still pass because the timestamp was force-set by the test. Remove the manual override and instead assert `helius_client._discovery_cache` / `_discovery_cache_time` were updated by the first call itself (or mock `time.time`) so a cache-freshness regression is actually caught.

This test re-implements the filtering logic inline (`count >= 3`) instead of invoking any `HeliusClient` method, so it cannot catch a regression in the production filtering inside `discover_wallets_from_recent_swaps`. Same applies to `test_sort_by_activity`, which re-implements the sort. ### [low] (test)

On any machine where those are set (typical dev environment), this test will not return `[]` — it will run real discovery and perform network requests, making the assertion fail. Pin the environment with `patch("core.helius_client.os.getenv", return_value=None)` (or `patch.dict(os.environ, {...}, clear=True)`) before constructing the client so the no-API-key path is deterministically exercised.

## scout/tests/test_prediction_validation.py (6 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

This test isolation strategy is broken. `scout/core/db.py` decommissioned SQLite (2026-07): `get_connection()` ignores the `db_path` argument completely and returns a pooled PostgreSQL connection, raising `ValueError` when `DATABASE_URL` is not set. So the `tempfile.mkstemp('.db')` file is never actually used — every test (all four classes use this same setUp/tearDown pattern) writes to and reads from the same shared Postgres database. Consequences: (1) assertions such as `len(pending) == 1` / `len(matched) == 1` become non-deterministic because predictions left behind by earlier tests are still present in the shared table; (2) the suite permanently pollutes the shared DB with test rows (no cleanup); (3) if `DATABASE_URL` is unset, every test fails in setUp. The `os.close`/`os.unlink` in tearDown is likewise a no-op for the actual backend. The fixtures need to target a dedicated test database and purge `ml_predictions` between tests (or restore a true SQLite test backend).

---

### [medium] (test)

This test never creates any predictions, so `mark_expired` runs against an empty table and `expired_count` is trivially 0 — the `assertGreaterEqual(..., 0)` can never fail. The age-based expiry filtering (`prediction_timestamp < threshold`) is never exercised. Log a pending prediction, backdate its `prediction_timestamp` beyond `max_age_days` (e.g. via an UPDATE), then assert it is marked EXPIRED (count == 1) while a recent prediction is left PENDING.

```suggestion
    def test_mark_expired(self):
        """Test marking old predictions as expired."""
        from datetime import datetime, timedelta

        prediction_id = self.logger.log_prediction(
            wallet_address="test_wallet_expired",
            predicted_pnl_sol=0.15,
            model_type="xgboost",
            features={"roi_7d": 0.05},
            confidence=0.85,
            strategy="SHIELD",
            wqs_score=75.0,
            wqs_components={}
        )

        conn = self.logger._get_connection()
        cursor = conn.cursor()
        cursor.execute(
            "UPDATE ml_predictions SET prediction_timestamp = %s WHERE id = %s",
            ((datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(days=180)).isoformat(), prediction_id)
        )
        conn.commit()
        conn.close()

        expired_count = self.logger.mark_expired(max_age_days=90)
        self.assertEqual(expired_count, 1)
```

## scout/tests/test_token_2022_extensions.py (5 findings)

### [medium] (test)

Mock TLV buffer is too small for the declared extension lengths. The helper allocates only 200 bytes but places the extension header at offset 165 and callers declare lengths of 32/64/16, so the full TLV entry (4 + length bytes) extends past the buffer (e.g. 165+4+32 = 201 > 200 for TransferFeeConfig; 165+4+64 = 233 > 200 for ConfidentialTransferAccount). The analyzer advances via `offset += 4 + ext_len`, so these mocks represent truncated TLV data and the tests only pass because the risky type happens to be read before the overshoot. Size the buffer to accommodate the full entry, e.g. `bytearray(165 + 4 + extension_length)`.

```suggestion
        extension_data = bytearray(165 + 4 + extension_length)
        extension_data[165:167] = extension_type.to_bytes(2, 'little')
        extension_data[167:169] = extension_length.to_bytes(2, 'little')
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Wrong extension type ID: Token-2022 extension type 19 is `ConfidentialTransferFeeConfig` (a confidential-transfer-fee extension), not TokenMetadata — TokenMetadata is type 17. This test labels type 19 as a 'safe extension', so it does not actually verify that only safe extensions are accepted; it is exercising a risky (confidential-transfer-fee) extension that the analyzer's `RISKY_EXTENSIONS` set happens to omit. If the analyzer is ever corrected to flag type 19/20, this test will start failing. Use type 17 for TokenMetadata.

```suggestion
        # Extension 1: TokenMetadata (type 17)
        extension_data[165:167] = (17).to_bytes(2, 'little')
        extension_data[167:169] = (64).to_bytes(2, 'little')
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Wrong extension type ID here too: type 19 is `ConfidentialTransferFeeConfig`, not TokenMetadata (type 17). The 'safe extension before sentinel' is actually a confidential-transfer-fee extension, so this test's premise is incorrect and it would break if the analyzer's `RISKY_EXTENSIONS` set is extended to cover confidential-transfer-fee types. Use type 17 for the safe extension before the sentinel.

```suggestion
        extension_data[165:167] = (17).to_bytes(2, 'little')  # TokenMetadata
        extension_data[167:169] = (64).to_bytes(2, 'little')
```

---

### [low] (bug)

Comment mislabels extension type 19 as 'TokenMetadata - safe extension'. In the Token-2022 spec, type 19 is `ConfidentialTransferFeeConfig` (a risky confidential-transfer-fee extension); TokenMetadata is type 17. This assertion still passes only because the first extension (TransferFeeConfig, type 1) triggers rejection, but the comment/claim about the second extension is wrong and could mislead future maintainers.

## scout/tests/test_wqs_base_score.py (5 findings)

### [medium] (test)

This test does not actually verify a zero base score — it passes because the raw score is a clamped negative. With all-None metrics, the implementation still applies: +5.5 sortino bonus (dd=0 < 5.0, x1.1 weight), -10 pump_spike (avg_trade_size_sol None → `(None or Decimal(0)) < 0.05` is True), -5 smart_accumulation, and -3 enhanced_momentum. Net ≈ 5.5 - 18 = -12.5 → clamped to 0.0 by `raw_score = max(0.0, positive - negative)`. Consequently a hidden base of up to ~12 points would go undetected, so this is not a valid PDD-compliance check. Prefer asserting on the raw components (e.g., `calculate_wqs_with_confidence(...).components`) and constructing a metric set that is truly neutral (avg_trade_size_sol >= 0.05, dd >= 5, trade_sizes present, non-flat momentum) so a genuine zero base can be distinguished from clamping.

---

### [medium] (test)

Same clamping problem as the first test: avg_trade_size_sol=0.0 trips the `(size or Decimal(0)) < Decimal('0.05')` check and adds a -10 pump_spike penalty on top of the -5 smart_accumulation / -3 enhanced_momentum penalties, so the 0.0 result is again a clamped negative (≈5.5 - 18), not evidence of a PDD zero base. 'All zeros' is not a neutral input here.

The claimed arithmetic in the comment doesn't match the implementation and the assertions don't verify it. With default weights the actual score is ≈ 41 (roi 16.5 incl. +1 for roi_7d and +5 wmi bonus, win_rate 6, activity 7, consistency 5, pf 2.6, recency 10, minus drawdown 1.2 + smart_accumulation 5), not 14. Also `profit_factor=1.5` yields +2 (the `> 1.5` branch is False, falls to `>= 1.2`), not +5, and the '-20 unproven penalty' only fires when `is_unproven=True` (defaults to False here), so that comment is doubly misleading. Since the assertions only check `0 < score <= 100`, a regression that dropped the ROI contribution entirely would still pass. Assert the exact expected value (after fixing the comment) or verify individual component contributions.

### [medium] (test)

The hardcoded 27.0 gap (±10 tolerance) is brittle: it assumes a clean composition of '25pt pump penalty + ~2pt 7d bonus', but the two cases also differ in the suppressed 7d ROI bonus, the recency-weighted ROI path, and the wmi bonus. Under the current default weights the actual gap is ≈ 20-21, and the effective weights can be overridden by the adaptive-weight cache file (scout/core/adaptive_weights.py), making this value environment-dependent. A legitimate WQS formula change (e.g., adjusting the pump penalty or 7d suppression) will break this test even when behavior is still correct. Prefer asserting only the directional relation (`score_pump < score_normal`) plus a loose bound, or derive the expected gap from the raw components.

## scout/tests/test_wqs_properties.py (6 findings)

### [medium] (test)

This assertion cannot detect the regression it claims to guard. For this wallet (roi_30d=0.001, roi_7d=50, win_rate=0.7, trade_count=100) the score is ~11 with the -25 pump-spike penalty, but even if the pump-spike penalty were entirely removed the score would only rise to ~34 (roi_7d bonus +5, win_rate +10, activity +20, minus the dust-trader penalty), i.e. still far below 60. So the check passes whether or not the penalty is applied. Note also that avg_trade_size_sol is left unset here, so the wallet unintentionally incurs the -10 'dust trader' penalty, confounding what the test claims to measure. Suggest asserting a relative comparison against an equivalent non-spike baseline wallet, or a threshold derived from the actual penalty components, instead of an absolute bound.

---

### [medium] (test)

The `< 15.0` tolerance is 3x larger than the +5 momentum bonus this test is designed to catch. Under the current formula the two scores differ by only ~2 points (0.4 from the roi_7d bonus plus a ~2-point enhanced-momentum difference), so if a +5 recency bonus were incorrectly applied to near-zero roi_30d the gap would be ~7 points — still well under 15 — and the regression would pass silently. Tighten the bound (e.g., `< 1.0`) or assert an exact expected delta derived from the score formula so the test can actually detect the +5 bonus.

### [low] (test)

A 10-point tolerance defeats the monotonicity property being claimed. The score formula is not strictly monotonic: it has discrete step discontinuities (e.g., +10 bonus as soon as roi_30d > 20, ROI bonus capped at 25), so a genuine non-monotonic step of up to ~10 points would satisfy this assertion and the test would stay green. Use `wqs_high >= wqs_low` (strict) or a tolerance small enough to catch real violations.

---

### [low] (test)

Same weakness as the ROI monotonicity test: win-rate bonuses are discrete +5 steps at 0.5/0.65/0.80/0.90, so a regression that removes one tier (e.g., the 0.65 bonus) drops the score by exactly 5 and would pass the `- 5.0` tolerance. Assert `wqs_high >= wqs_low` (strict) to make the property meaningful.

The guard `if trade_count_low < 20 and trade_count_high >= 20:` is always True — the @given strategies already constrain trade_count_low to [0,19] and trade_count_high to [20,1000], so this branch is dead/redundant. Remove it (or the inner condition) to avoid implying the test handles cases it structurally cannot reach. Note also that with the `- 10.0` tolerance, a low-count wallet may score up to 10 points higher than a high-count one and the test still passes, which is the opposite of the documented property.

### [low] (test)

The hard-coded gap thresholds (gap < 10, gap_loss > 10) are calibrated to the current PF band deltas (+2/-1/-3/-6/-25), but the actual score deltas also depend on unrelated components (win-rate/activity bonuses, drawdown, momentum, penalty-confidence scaling). Any formula change elsewhere can make these fail even when PF graduation is still correct, and any change that shifts both compared scores equally passes while the intended band difference silently drifts. Prefer asserting only the relative ordering of the band values, or derive thresholds directly from the documented bands.

## scripts/cache_invalidation.py (8 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Clearing a freshly constructed instance does not touch the caches of running components. `ActivityBasedCache`, `HeliusCachingWrapper`, `LiquidityProvider`, and `FeatureEnricher` all store state in per-instance attributes (e.g., `self._cache` in activity_cache.py:137 and liquidity.py:155). Instantiating new objects here creates empty caches and `clear()` only empties those new empty instances — the live caches held by the already-running scout process are unaffected, so this invalidation is ineffective by design. Invalidate through an API/signal on the running process, or persist caches in shared storage this script can actually clear.

---

### [high] (bug)

`AdvancedCache` has no instance method `reset_cache()` — the only `reset_cache` defined in advanced_cache.py (line 785) is a module-level function that resets the global `_cache` singleton. This call raises `AttributeError`, which is silently swallowed into `results['errors']`, so the AdvancedCache is never actually cleared. Call the module-level `reset_cache()` from `scout.core.advanced_cache` instead.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`HeliusCachingWrapper.__init__` accepts `cache_config: Optional[CacheConfig]`, not an API key. Passing `self.helius_api_key` as the first positional argument makes `ActivityBasedCache` treat the key string as its `CacheConfig` (activity_cache.py:133 `self._config = config or CacheConfig()`), which corrupts config access later. Construct it with no arguments (`HeliusCachingWrapper()`).

---

### [medium] (bug)

`LiquidityProvider.__init__`'s first parameter is `jupiter_api_url`, not an API key. Passing `self.helius_api_key` here wires the key string into `JupiterLiquidityClient(jupiter_api_url)` (liquidity.py:138) and anywhere else expecting a URL. Use `LiquidityProvider()` (or keyword arguments) instead.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`main()` never propagates failures: even when caches fail to clear (errors are recorded and only printed), the script always prints this success message and exits 0, so automated callers cannot detect that cache invalidation failed. Track a failure flag and call `sys.exit(1)` when `scout_results['errors']` is non-empty or any operator attempt has a non-success status.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The scout package lives at the repo root (`scout/`), not under `scripts/`. `os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), 'scout')` resolves to `scripts/scout`, which does not exist. When run as `python scripts/cache_invalidation.py`, `sys.path[0]` is `scripts/` and the repo root is not on the path, so `import scout.core.caching` fails. Use the script's parent directory instead: `os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(__file__))`.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`clear_scout_caches` is declared `async` but contains no `await` — all work is blocking synchronous calls. As written it provides no concurrency benefit and stalls the event loop while running. Make it a plain synchronous method and call it without `await`, keeping `clear_operator_cache_via_api` as the only async path.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` to avoid the deprecation warning and timezone ambiguity.

## scripts/reset-trading-state.sh (6 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

The script advertises truncating `positions` (confirmation prompt: "Truncate all history tables (trades, positions, dlq, etc.)") and even verifies the positions count in Step 8, but the TRUNCATE list never explicitly includes `positions`. It will only be cleared if `trades` has an FK relationship that triggers CASCADE; otherwise stale position rows survive and the verification step will reveal a non-zero count. Add an explicit truncate for `positions` instead of relying on CASCADE behavior.

```suggestion
TRUNCATE TABLE trades RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;
TRUNCATE TABLE positions RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;
```

---

### [high] (bug)

COPY failures are swallowed by `|| true` while `2>/dev/null` discards the error message. If a preserved table is missing, the DB is unreachable, or the backup is interrupted, the script silently writes a `-- Table:` header with no data, then reports "Backup saved" and proceeds to destroy the data. There is also no post-backup check that the file is non-empty/valid. Worse, the interleaved `-- Table:` comments + `COPY TO STDOUT` plain-text output is not directly restorable by piping the whole file back into psql. Fail loudly on backup error (or at minimum report per-table failures) and verify the backup before truncating.

```suggestion
    if ! docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose-haproxy.yml exec -T postgres psql -U chimera -d chimera -c "COPY $t TO STDOUT" >> "$BACKUP_FILE" 2>&1; then
        echo "ERROR: backup of table $t failed; aborting before destructive steps" >&2
        exit 1
    fi
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Both UPDATE statements only touch `id = 1`. If the `circuit_breaker_state` / `kill_switch_state` rows with id=1 do not exist (e.g., fresh schema or different PK values), the stale state is NOT reset, yet the script still prints success. If multiple rows exist, only id=1 is reset. Prefer an upsert (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE`) or verify the number of affected rows before claiming success.

```suggestion
INSERT INTO circuit_breaker_state (id, state, tripped_at, trip_reason)
VALUES (1, 'ACTIVE', NULL, NULL)
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET state = 'ACTIVE', tripped_at = NULL, trip_reason = NULL;
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Only five hardcoded test database names are dropped; any other orphaned `test_*` databases (e.g., from parallel test runs in the future) will never be cleaned. Additionally, since the `&&`-chained `psql` runs are the script's active command under `set -e`, a `DROP DATABASE` that fails because the DB has active connections will abort the entire reset at Step 4, leaving the operator stopped and tables already truncated. Consider discovering candidates dynamically (e.g., list `pg_database` entries matching `test_%`) and terminating backends before dropping.

```suggestion
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose-haproxy.yml exec -T postgres bash -c \
    "psql -U chimera -Atc \"SELECT 'DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS ' || quote_ident(datname) || ' WITH (FORCE);' FROM pg_database WHERE datname LIKE 'test_%'\" | psql -U chimera"
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`FLUSHDB` only clears the currently selected Redis logical database (default 0). If the application uses multiple Redis databases, stale cache entries in the other DBs survive the reset. Since the intent is a complete cache flush, use `FLUSHALL` or explicitly flush every configured database index.

```suggestion
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose-haproxy.yml exec -T redis redis-cli FLUSHALL > /dev/null
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The script relies on relative paths (`backups/`, `data/logs/...`, `data/parse_failures`) and relative compose file paths, so it only behaves correctly when run from the repo root. Invoked from any other directory, the backup file is written to the wrong location and the stale-data cleanup (`rm` of `data/...`) silently targets the wrong directory. Normalize the working directory at the top of the script to make it location-independent.

```suggestion
cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.."
mkdir -p backups
```

---

## setup-1000-virtual-capital.sh (9 findings, 0 critical, 4 high)

### [high] (bug)

The `sed` replacement drops the leading whitespace of matched lines: `s/^[[:space:]]*${field_name}:.*/${field_name}: ${new_value}/` matches indented keys but rewrites them at column 0. In `operator/config.yaml`, `total_capital_sol`, `max_size_sol`, `min_size_sol`, and `base_size_sol` are nested two spaces under `position_sizing:` (and `max_loss_24h_usd` under `circuit_breakers:`). After this script runs, these keys are promoted to the YAML top level, so the operator silently keeps its defaults and the $1000 position sizing never takes effect — the script still prints "Updated …". Preserve the original indentation, e.g. capture it with `\([[:space:]]*\)` and re-emit it in the replacement.

```suggestion
    sed -i.bak "s/^\([[:space:]]*\)${field_name}:[[:space:]]*.*/\1${field_name}: ${new_value}/" "$config_file"
```

---

### [high] (bug)

This function returns 1 when the field is missing and the user answers "continue", but it is invoked as a bare command (e.g. `validate_and_update_config "total_capital_sol" ...`) while `set -e` is active. A non-zero return from a bare command aborts the whole script, so the "Continue anyway? (y/n)" prompt can never actually continue — answering 'y' immediately terminates the setup. Return 0 after the user confirms, or call the function guarded with `|| true` so the missing-field case can be tolerated as intended.

```suggestion
        if [[ ! $REPLY =~ ^[Yy]$ ]]; then
            log_error "Configuration update cancelled"
            exit 1
        fi
        return 0
```

---

### [high] (security)

The static bearer token `dev-admin-key` is not just a placeholder — `operator/config.yaml` (security.api_keys) configures this exact string as an admin API key, and the operator binds to `0.0.0.0:8080`. Anyone with repo access (or who can reach a deployed operator) knows a working admin credential, enabling roster merges and other admin operations without authorization. Use a per-install randomly generated key read from the environment instead of committing the real admin credential in a script.

---

### [high] (bug)

Without `set -o pipefail`, the exit status of this `docker exec ... | tee` pipeline is `tee`'s (always 0 on success), so a failed or skipped Scout run (e.g. missing `chimera-scout` container, crash inside Scout) is reported as success. The script then proceeds to POST a roster merge with an empty/stale `roster_new.db`, potentially wiping or polluting the operator's wallet roster. Check `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` (or add `set -o pipefail`) and gate the merge on actual Scout success.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Environment updates are not idempotent: if the template/local file already contains `PAPER_TRADE_MODE=false` (the devnet/prod templates do), this appends a second `PAPER_TRADE_MODE=true`, leaving conflicting duplicates whose effective value depends on the loader. Likewise `VIRTUAL_CAPITAL_USD`/`VIRTUAL_CAPITAL_SOL` are only appended when absent, so re-running the script with a different capital amount leaves the stale old values in `docker/env.mainnet-paper.local`. Replace existing values with `sed` instead of blind append.

---

### [medium] (bug)

If the operator never becomes healthy within 60s, the script only prints a warning and then continues through Scout and prints "Setup Complete" with the operator URL, misleading users into believing the system is ready. Track whether the health check succeeded and exit non-zero (or skip the remaining steps) on timeout.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`$$` expands to the shell PID, not a literal dollar sign, so every output line using `$${...}` / `~$$(...)` is malformed: `$${VIRTUAL_CAPITAL_USD}` prints `<PID>{VIRTUAL_CAPITAL_USD}` and the `~$$(echo "scale=0; ..." | bc)` command substitutions never execute (they print literal text). This affects the summary lines at "Virtual Capital", "Total Capital", "Max/Min/Base Position", "Daily Loss Limit", and the final summary (e.g. `~$$(echo ... | bc)` shows a literal `(echo ... | bc)` instead of a USD amount). Use `\$` / `\${...}` to print a dollar sign.

```suggestion
echo "  • Virtual Capital: \$${VIRTUAL_CAPITAL_USD} USD"
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Integer division `$((1000 / 150))` yields 6 SOL, i.e. $900 at the assumed $150/SOL, so the configured `total_capital_sol` (and every derived position size) is ~10% short of the advertised $1000. Also, the comment says the price "will be updated from RPC" but the script never does — SOL_PRICE_USD stays hardcoded at 150. Use `bc` for the conversion (and optionally fetch a live price) so the configured capital matches the intended $1000.

```suggestion
VIRTUAL_CAPITAL_SOL=$(echo "scale=2; $VIRTUAL_CAPITAL_USD / $SOL_PRICE_USD" | bc)
```

---

### [low] (bug)

This pipeline (and the Scout pipeline above) runs without `set -o pipefail`, and `grep ... || true` further swallows the exit status. A failed `docker-compose.sh build` produces no "ERROR" line and returns success, so the script proceeds to `start` and may boot a stale/absent image while printing progress as if the build succeeded. Consider checking the build command's real exit status (e.g. via `${PIPESTATUS[0]}`) before starting services.

## test-auth.sh (6 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

With `set -e` active, `((SUCCESS++))` evaluates to the *old* value of SUCCESS — 0 on the first successful request — and the arithmetic command returns exit status 1 when the expression evaluates to 0. This aborts the script on the very first counted request (and `((FAILED++))` has the same problem), so the loop never completes and the load-test summary / signal-quality tests never run. Use `SUCCESS=$((SUCCESS + 1))` (or `((++SUCCESS))` / `((SUCCESS += 1))`) so the expression is non-zero after incrementing.

```suggestion
    if [ "$STATUS" = "200" ] || [ "$STATUS" = "202" ]; then
        SUCCESS=$((SUCCESS + 1))
        echo -n "."
    else
        FAILED=$((FAILED + 1))
        echo -n "F"
    fi
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

This is not a parallel load test: each `curl` runs to completion before the next iteration starts, so the requests are strictly sequential. It therefore cannot exercise the circuit breaker / rate limiter under real concurrency. Launch the curls in background jobs and `wait` for them (or use `xargs -P`/`seq | parallel`). Note also that all 10 requests reuse the identical payload, so if the server deduplicates webhooks the effective load will be reduced further.

```suggestion
log_section "Load Testing - Multiple Webhooks"
log_info "Sending 10 webhook signals in parallel..."

PIDS=()
for i in {1..10}; do
    TS=$((TIMESTAMP + i))
    SIG=$(generate_signature "$TS" "$PAYLOAD")
    curl -s -o "/tmp/webhook_result_$i" -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST "${API_URL}/api/v1/webhook" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -H "X-Signature: $SIG" \
        -H "X-Timestamp: $TS" \
        -d "$PAYLOAD" &
    PIDS+=($!)
done
wait "${PIDS[@]}"
```

---

### [medium] (security)

If `docker exec` fails (container not running, env var missing, docker unavailable), the script silently falls back to a well-known hardcoded secret that is committed in source. Tests then run against potentially non-production credentials, and — worse — if the server is still configured with that default secret, a production misconfiguration is masked because all signatures validate with a publicly known value. Fail fast instead of falling back so the misconfiguration is surfaced.

```suggestion
WEBHOOK_SECRET=$(docker exec chimera-operator printenv CHIMERA_SECURITY__WEBHOOK_SECRET 2>/dev/null)
if [ -z "$WEBHOOK_SECRET" ]; then
    echo "[FAIL] Could not read CHIMERA_SECURITY__WEBHOOK_SECRET from chimera-operator container" >&2
    exit 1
fi
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The medium-quality signal's timestamp is derived from the previous request's base time (`TIMESTAMP + 1`) rather than the current clock. If the high-quality request and its post-processing took more than a second of wall-clock time, the synthesized timestamp lags behind real time and the server's HMAC timestamp-skew check may reject it as stale. Refresh the timestamp from `date +%s` immediately before each request instead of reusing/re-advancing the previous one.

```suggestion
# Medium quality signal
TIMESTAMP=$(date +%s)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Under `set -e`, a transport-level failure (connection refused, DNS failure, timeout) makes `curl` return a non-zero exit status inside the command substitution, which aborts the entire script immediately. HTTP-level failures (4xx/5xx) are handled via `-w "%{http_code}"`, but network failures bypass the `FAILED` accounting entirely and the summary line is never printed. Capture the curl exit code separately and treat it as a failed request (e.g., wrap with `|| true` and derive the status from the response).

---

### [low] (bug)

If the health endpoint is unreachable, `python3` is not installed, or the JSON body doesn't contain a "circuit_breaker" key, this `grep` (or the earlier pipeline under `set -e`) returns non-zero and the script aborts before printing the final section — the same `set -e` pitfall seen elsewhere in this script. Guard the pipeline with `grep ... || true` (and handle an empty `$HEALTH`).

```suggestion
log_section "Current System Status"
HEALTH=$(curl -s "${API_URL}/api/v1/health" | python3 -m json.tool 2>/dev/null || true)
echo "$HEALTH" | grep -A 3 '"circuit_breaker"' || true
```

## test-detailed.sh (5 findings)

### [medium] (security)

Silent fallback to a hardcoded, publicly-known dev secret when `docker exec` fails. If the operator container is unavailable or the secret differs on the server, requests will be signed with the wrong key and the webhook test will silently return 401/Invalid signature — masking the real configuration failure and making the test pass/fail for the wrong reason. It also embeds a credential in source. Fail loudly instead: read from the environment first and abort with a diagnostic if it can't be obtained.

```suggestion
WEBHOOK_SECRET=${CHIMERA_SECURITY__WEBHOOK_SECRET:-}
if [ -z "$WEBHOOK_SECRET" ]; then
    WEBHOOK_SECRET=$(docker exec chimera-operator printenv CHIMERA_SECURITY__WEBHOOK_SECRET 2>/dev/null || true)
fi
if [ -z "$WEBHOOK_SECRET" ]; then
    echo "ERROR: CHIMERA_SECURITY__WEBHOOK_SECRET unavailable (docker exec failed)" >&2
    exit 1
fi
```

---

### [medium] (test)

The script claims to test circuit-breaker reset but sends an unauthenticated POST and discards the result (piped to `head -3`). The server-side handler (`reset_circuit_breaker` in operator/src/handlers/api.rs) requires the admin role via AuthExtension, so this request will always be rejected before reaching the handler — the test never exercises the reset behavior and never asserts the expected 401/403. Either supply admin credentials from the environment and assert a success response, or explicitly assert that the endpoint rejects unauthenticated requests with 401/403.

```suggestion
HTTP_CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -X POST "${API_URL}/api/v1/config/circuit-breaker/reset" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json")
echo "Unauthenticated reset status: $HTTP_CODE"
[ "$HTTP_CODE" = "401" ] || [ "$HTTP_CODE" = "403" ] || { echo "Unexpected status: $HTTP_CODE" >&2; exit 1; }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Under `set -e`, this piped command aborts the entire script whenever Prometheus is unreachable (curl/`python3 -m json.tool` fails on empty/non-JSON output) or the metric has no data (`grep` returns 1 on no match). The same applies to the RPC health (line 43), circuit-breaker state (line 46), label-values query (line 60), and the Grafana query (line 50). For a diagnostic script this is especially harmful: it dies mid-run with no explanation. Guard these probes with `|| true`/fallback echoes or capture exit codes explicitly.

```suggestion
curl -s "http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=chimera_queue_depth" | python3 -m json.tool 2>/dev/null | grep -A 2 '"value"' || echo "Queue depth metric unavailable"
```

---

### [medium] (security)

Hardcoded Grafana default credentials `admin:admin` in the script. This embeds a known default credential in source and breaks in any environment where Grafana is configured differently. Source both user and password from environment variables (with the default only as an explicit local fallback). Additionally, if Grafana is unreachable, `python3 -m json.tool`'s failure makes the whole `DASHBOARD_UID=$(...)` assignment fail under `set -e`, aborting the script — same class of issue as the Prometheus probes.

```suggestion
GRAFANA_USER="${GRAFANA_USER:-admin}"
GRAFANA_PASSWORD="${GRAFANA_PASSWORD:-}"
DASHBOARD_UID=$(curl -s "http://localhost:3002/api/search?query=Chimera" -u "$GRAFANA_USER:$GRAFANA_PASSWORD" | python3 -c "import sys, json; data=json.load(sys.stdin); print(data[0]['uid'] if data else 'not found')" 2>/dev/null || echo "not found")
```

---

### [low] (test)

The webhook result is only printed, never asserted. If the signature is rejected, the server is down, or the endpoint returns 4xx/5xx, the script still exits 0 and the run looks successful. Since this is the primary thing being tested, assert on the HTTP status (or at least exit nonzero on non-2xx) so a rejected webhook fails the script.

```suggestion
echo "Status: $STATUS"
[ "$STATUS" = "200" ] || { echo "Webhook test FAILED (expected 200, got '$STATUS')" >&2; exit 1; }
```

## test-devnet.sh (14 findings, 0 critical, 5 high)

### [high] (bug)

The script only uses `set -e` and never sets `set -o pipefail`. Every pipeline that ends in `tee` (lines in `build_images`, `run_unit_tests`, `run_integration_tests`, `run_scout_tests`) returns `tee`'s exit status, which is always 0, so failed builds/tests are reported as successes. Add `set -euo pipefail` here so the whole script inherits correct pipeline semantics.

```suggestion
set -euo pipefail
```

---

### [high] (bug)

With `set -e` active when this function runs, a failed health check makes this command substitution fail and the script aborts immediately — the `if [ $? -eq 0 ]` branch below is never reached, so `log_error`/`return 1` and the FAILED counter are skipped. Capture the result in an `if` instead.

```suggestion
if ! response=$(curl -sf http://localhost:8080/api/v1/health 2>&1); then
    log_error "Health endpoint failed: $response"
    return 1
fi
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Same `set -e` hazard as in `test_health`: if the metrics endpoint is unreachable, the failing command substitution terminates the script before the `if [ $? -eq 0 ]` error handling runs, so the `log_error` message and FAILED counter are lost. Guard the assignment (e.g., `if response=$(curl -sf ...); then ... else ...`) or add `|| true` before checking `$?`.

---

### [high] (bug)

`test_database` runs under `set -e`: if `sqlite3` fails (corrupt/locked DB), the command substitution aborts the script before the `if [ $? -eq 0 ]` check, so the `log_error "Database query failed"` path never executes. Guard the substitution, e.g. `if ! table_count=$(sqlite3 ...); then log_error ...; return 1; fi`.

```suggestion
if ! table_count=$(sqlite3 "$PROJECT_ROOT/data/chimera.db" "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table';" 2>&1); then
    log_error "Database query failed"
    return 1
fi
```

---

### [high] (bug)

Without `set -o pipefail`, this pipeline's exit status comes from `tee` (always 0). A failed `docker build` is therefore reported as `log_success` and the suite proceeds against stale or missing images, making all subsequent tests meaningless. Fix the root cause with `set -o pipefail` at the top, or check `PIPESTATUS[0]` here.

```suggestion
bash "$DOCKER_SCRIPT" build "$PROFILE" 2>&1 | tee /tmp/chimera-build.log
if [ ${PIPESTATUS[0]} -eq 0 ]; then
    log_success "Docker images built successfully"
else
    log_error "Docker build failed. Check logs above."
    exit 1
fi
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

This function only behaves as intended because the caller happens to wrap it under `set +e`. If `curl` fails while `set -e` is active (e.g., this function is reused elsewhere), the script aborts before the `log_warning` branch. Make the function self-contained by guarding the assignment instead of relying on the caller's errexit state.

```suggestion
if ! response=$(curl -sf http://localhost:3000 2>&1); then
    log_warning "Web dashboard not accessible: $response"
    log_info "This may be normal if the web service is still starting"
    return 0
fi
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Because `pipefail` is not set, this pipeline reports `tee`'s exit status: failing unit tests are logged as `log_success "Unit tests passed"`. Use `set -o pipefail` (top of file) or test `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` so real failures increment FAILED.

```suggestion
if cargo test --lib 2>&1 | tee /tmp/chimera-unit-tests.log && [ ${PIPESTATUS[0]} -eq 0 ]; then
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Same pipefail masking as `run_unit_tests`: a failing integration test run is swallowed by `tee` and reported as success. This matters even more here because failures are downgraded to warnings — a fully failed suite can print "Integration tests passed".

```suggestion
if cargo test --test '*' -- --test-threads=1 2>&1 | tee /tmp/chimera-integration-tests.log && [ ${PIPESTATUS[0]} -eq 0 ]; then
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Same pipefail issue in the pytest pipeline: a failing scout test run is masked by `tee` and reported as `log_success "Scout tests passed"`. Check `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` or enable `set -o pipefail`.

```suggestion
if python3 -m pytest tests/ -v 2>&1 | tee /tmp/chimera-scout-tests.log && [ ${PIPESTATUS[0]} -eq 0 ]; then
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`grep -q "Up"` passes as long as *any one* container line contains "Up" — including containers shown as "Up (unhealthy)" — so a partially failed stack can still be reported as healthy. Verify each expected service individually (e.g., check every service line from `docker-compose.sh status` is in the Up state and none is Restarting/Exited/unhealthy).

```suggestion
local status_output
status_output=$(bash "$DOCKER_SCRIPT" status "$PROFILE")
if echo "$status_output" | grep -qE 'operator.*Up' && echo "$status_output" | grep -qE 'web.*Up' && ! echo "$status_output" | grep -qE 'Exit|Restarting|unhealthy'; then
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

These tests are invoked while `set +e` is active, so if `cd "$PROJECT_ROOT/operator"` fails (directory missing/moved), the script silently continues and runs `cargo test` from the wrong directory, producing misleading pass/fail results. Guard the cd (or run each test in a subshell, e.g. `(cd "$PROJECT_ROOT/operator" && cargo test --lib)`). The same unguarded `cd` pattern exists in `run_integration_tests` and `run_scout_tests`.

```suggestion
    log_info "Running operator unit tests..."
    cd "$PROJECT_ROOT/operator" || { log_error "operator directory not found"; return 1; }
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Same unguarded `cd` problem as `run_unit_tests`: under `set +e`, a failed cd leaves the shell in the wrong directory and `pytest` runs against the wrong tree. Guard it or run in a subshell.

```suggestion
    log_info "Running scout tests..."
    cd "$PROJECT_ROOT/scout" || { log_error "scout directory not found"; return 1; }
```

---

### [medium] (security)

This hardcodes a well-known webhook HMAC secret as the fallback and the test then relies on the service accepting it. If the deployed service actually defaults to this value, anyone who reads the repo can forge valid webhook requests. Generate a random per-run secret and inject it into the stack (e.g., export `CHIMERA_SECURITY__WEBHOOK_SECRET` and pass it to docker-compose) rather than assuming a shared static default.

```suggestion
TEST_WEBHOOK_SECRET="${CHIMERA_SECURITY__WEBHOOK_SECRET:-$(openssl rand -hex 32)}"
```

---

### [low] (bug)

When the response contains no `chimera_` metrics, `grep -c` prints "0" and exits 1, so the `|| echo "0"` runs and prints a second "0". `metric_count` then contains "0\n0", producing a malformed log line. Use `|| true` and default to empty/0 only if needed.

```suggestion
local metric_count
metric_count=$(echo "$response" | grep -c "^chimera_" || true)
```
