## test-paper-trading.sh (7 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

Under `set -e`, `((PASSED++))` returns exit status 1 while PASSED is 0 (the arithmetic expression evaluates to 0), and the same applies to `((FAILED++))`, `((WARNINGS++))` here and `((success++))`/`((failed++))` in test_load. This only avoids aborting today because every test function is invoked with `|| true` (which disables `set -e` for the whole function body in bash) — if the wrappers are removed or one of these log helpers is ever called from a non-ignored context, the script terminates right after the first PASS/FAIL/WARN and the summary never prints. Prefer arithmetic assignment so the command status is always 0.

```suggestion
    PASSED=$((PASSED + 1))
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Prometheus query responses always contain the `"result"` key, so `grep -q "result"` also matches `"result":[]` (an empty result array). A metric that has never been recorded — or a broken/missing target — is therefore reported as available, giving a false pass. Check that the result array is non-empty instead.

```suggestion
        if echo "$result" | grep -q '"result":\[{'; then
            log_success "Metric ${metric} available"
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

This function calls log_success unconditionally, even when both values failed to parse and defaulted to 'N/A' (Prometheus unreachable, target down, or metric missing). A completely broken metrics pipeline is reported as 'Metrics are being collected'. Only log success when queue depth and active positions are non-empty numbers, otherwise log a warning/error.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The test claims '10 concurrent webhooks' but the loop sends requests strictly sequentially, so server-side concurrency is never exercised. It also only inspects the HTTP status code: response bodies, per-request acceptance/ordering, and whether any paper position/trade was actually created are never validated, so the load test can pass while the trading pipeline is broken. Consider dispatching requests in parallel (e.g. background jobs with `wait` or `xargs -P`) and asserting on the resulting paper state.

---

### [medium] (test)

There is no end-to-end assertion that an accepted webhook actually produced a paper position/trade. Tests 2, 3, 8 and 9 only check endpoint acceptance and metric presence, so if the core paper-trading logic (order simulation, position bookkeeping) is broken the script still reports success. After sending webhook signals, query /api/v1/positions and /api/v1/trades and assert that a new paper trade/position appeared.

---

### [medium] (security)

Hardcoded Grafana default credentials `admin:admin` are embedded in the script and also exposed on the command line (visible via `ps`). If the Grafana password was changed in the deployed stack the check silently produces a wrong result, and committing default credentials into a shared script is a security concern. Read credentials from environment variables (e.g. GRAFANA_USER/GRAFANA_PASSWORD) and fail with a clear message when they are not set.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The curl calls (health, webhook, Prometheus, Grafana, dashboard) have no `--connect-timeout`/`--max-time`. If a service accepts a connection but hangs, or a firewall silently drops packets, the smoke test can block indefinitely and stall CI/local runs. Add a bounded timeout to each curl invocation, e.g. `--max-time 10 --connect-timeout 5`.

---

## tests/load/parallel_execution_bench.js (6 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

This load profile fires far more than the documented "100 signals over 60 seconds": up to 100 VUs each run an iteration every ~0.5s (plus request time), producing roughly 200 req/s at peak — thousands of signals per run. As a result `'signals_accepted': ['count>80']` is trivially satisfied and the test cannot validate the claimed 4x throughput / 100-signals-in-60s outcome. Model the test as a fixed number of iterations (e.g., `exec: 'shared-iterations'` with 100 iters over 60s) or assert a per-minute throughput rate instead of a raw count.

---

### [high] (test)

When the webhook rejects the request (non-200/202), this check returns `true` unconditionally, so malformed error responses are never validated and failures are masked. Restrict the body-shape assertion to accepted responses but also assert that rejected responses parse as JSON (or assert they do NOT contain trade_uuid/status), so response validation cannot silently pass.

---

### [high] (security)

A fallback webhook secret is committed in source and reused by every run that doesn't set WEBHOOK_SECRET. If the server accepts this default value, anyone can forge valid signatures and bypass authentication on the webhook endpoint. Fail fast when WEBHOOK_SECRET is missing (e.g., `if (!__ENV.WEBHOOK_SECRET) throw new Error(...)`) and remove the hardcoded default.

---

### [medium] (test)

The header comments claim this test verifies priority ordering under load (EXIT > SHIELD > SPEAR), but the code only samples strategies randomly and contains no ordering assertions or per-strategy measurements. Add per-strategy metrics (e.g., Trend per strategy or queue position) and assert EXIT is processed before SHIELD/SPEAR under load, or remove the claim from the test description.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`__ENV.PARALLEL_ENABLED || 'true'` makes setting `PARALLEL_ENABLED=false` produce the string 'false', which is still truthy — the flag can never be falsy. Moreover, the value is only echoed into the summary; it never toggles or validates parallel behavior. Parse it as a boolean (`__ENV.PARALLEL_ENABLED === 'true'`) and gate the throughput/parallel assertions on it, or drop the flag entirely.

---

### [low] (documentation)

Documentation/threshold mismatch: the header claims "Latency: p95 < 12s per signal" and "No 503/429 errors from RPC rate limiting", but the actual threshold is `p(95)<5000` (5s) and only 503 is asserted (429 is never checked). Align the documented expectations with the real thresholds/checks so the test results are interpreted correctly.

---

## tests/load/production_wallet_simulation.js (7 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

`require('k6/crypto')` is executed inside the VU function. k6 scripts are ES-module based and do not support CommonJS `require`, so this throws `ReferenceError: require is not defined` on the very first iteration and the whole test fails. Import the module once at the top of the file (`import { crypto } from 'k6/crypto';`) and keep only the HMAC computation here.

```suggestion
    const hasher = crypto.createHMAC('sha256', secret || __ENV.WEBHOOK_SECRET || 'test-secret');
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`wallet_diversity` is a `Trend`, but numeric wallet-type indices are recorded into it. A Trend only stores aggregated numeric samples (avg/min/med/p(95)...), so it cannot represent diversity. Worse, in `handleSummary`, `new Set(data.metrics.wallet_diversity.values).size` operates on the aggregated-stats object (a single object, not raw samples), so the 'unique types' output is always 1/0, not the true count. Use tagged metrics per wallet type instead, e.g. `walletTypeDistribution.add(1, { wallet_type: walletType })` and count the distinct keys in the summary.

```suggestion
    walletTypeDistribution.add(1, { wallet_type: walletType });
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`handleSummary` performs no `return`. When `handleSummary` is exported it completely replaces k6's default end-of-test report, so the configured thresholds (`http_req_duration`, `http_req_failed`, `production_signal_rate`, `checks`) will never be printed or evaluated in the summary output. Return an object mapping filenames to content (e.g. `{ stdout: textSummary(data) }` or a JSON/string summary). Note also that `data.metrics.wallet_diversity.values` is an aggregated object here, not raw samples.

```suggestion
    console.log('Wallet diversity (unique types):', Object.keys(data.metrics.wallet_type_distribution.values).length);

    return {
        stdout: JSON.stringify(data.metrics, null, 2),
    };
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

`PRODUCTION_SIGNALS_FILE` is opened in `setup()` but the loaded `signals` content is never parsed or consumed anywhere in the script — it is dead code that misleads users into thinking production patterns are being loaded. Either remove it or actually parse the file and feed the patterns into `generateProductionSignal`.

---

### [medium] (bug)

These are arrival-rate executors, so k6 already controls iteration cadence; the extra `sleep()` (1–4 s) per iteration keeps VUs occupied and raises the concurrency required to hit the target rate. With `preAllocatedVUs` and no `maxVUs` (which defaults to `preAllocatedVUs`), the pool is exhausted and target rates won't be reached — e.g. steady_state needs ~25/s × ~2.5 s ≈ 60+ concurrent VUs vs the 50 allocated; market_crash needs even more at 100/s. Either raise `preAllocatedVUs`/set `maxVUs` or drop the sleep in arrival-rate scenarios.

```suggestion
            rate: 25, // 25 signals/sec (~2000/day per active wallet)
            timeUnit: '1s',
            duration: '10m',
            preAllocatedVUs: 100,
            maxVUs: 300,
            gracefulStop: '30s',
```

---

### [low] (style)

Nested ternary expressions are not allowed by the project style rules and hurt readability. Refactor the action selection into plain if/else logic.

```suggestion
    let action = 'SELL';
    if (strategy !== 'EXIT' && isBuy) {
        action = 'BUY';
    }
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The second argument passed to `new Counter(...)` is not a supported k6 metric constructor parameter — tag names must be supplied at `add()` time. `['strategy']`/`['action']` are silently ignored, which is misleading. Remove them; tags are already passed on `add(1, { strategy: ... })` / `add(1, { action: ... })`.

```suggestion
const strategyDistribution = new Counter('strategy_distribution');
const signalTypeDistribution = new Counter('signal_type_distribution');
```

---

## tests/load/webhook_flood.js (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

The thresholds reference `dropped_signals` and `accepted_signals`, but the registered metrics are `signals_dropped` and `signals_accepted` (Counters, line 44-45). k6 will reject/ignore these unknown metrics, so the load-shedding assertions silently never run. Additionally, a Counter's `rate` value is a per-second increment count, not a percentage of dropped requests — it cannot express "less than 20% dropped". The file already defines an `acceptance_rate` Rate metric (line 47) that measures the accepted fraction; use it instead.

```suggestion
    'acceptance_rate': ['rate>0.80'], // At least 80% of requests should be accepted
```

---

### [high] (bug)

k6's built-in `http_req_failed` counts every 4xx/5xx response — including the 503/429 responses this test deliberately generates during load shedding — as a failed request. Requiring `rate<0.05` while simultaneously planning to drop up to 20% of requests at peak load (see `dropped_signals`/stages) is contradictory: the run will fail its own threshold in the exact scenario it is designed to exercise. Raise the threshold to accommodate expected drops, or tag 503/429 responses (e.g., via `tags: {shed: 'true'}`) and exclude them from the failure threshold.

```suggestion
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.25'], // Allows for ~20% intentional 503/429 load-shedding drops
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

In k6, `stages[].target` sets the number of concurrent virtual users, NOT requests per second. The actual RPS is `VUs / iteration_duration` and therefore depends on the HTTP round-trip time plus the `sleep(0.01)` — so the test may never actually reach (or may greatly exceed) the 100 req/s queue-drop threshold this file is meant to validate, and the stage comments are misleading. Use the `constant-arrival-rate` executor in `scenarios` to drive a controlled RPS, or keep VU ramping but update the comments and verify RPS against the built-in `http_reqs` metric.

```suggestion
  scenarios: {
    load: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 100, // requests per second
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '3m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,
      maxVUs: 200,
    },
  },
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The two status checks are mutually exclusive: an accepted response (200/202) fails the 'dropped' check and a dropped response (503/429) fails the 'accepted' check, while legitimate rejects (400/401/403) fail both. Since `check()` runs every assertion for every request, this guarantees a large permanent check-failure count in every run regardless of actual server behavior, obscuring real failures. Combine them into a single 'expected status set' check, or assert status conditionally per category.

```suggestion
  check(res, {
    'status is in expected set (accepted/dropped/rejected)': (r) =>
      [200, 202, 400, 401, 403, 429, 503].includes(r.status),
```

## tools/attack-detection.py (13 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

The `command_injection` pattern matches any bare `&`, `|`, `;`, or `` ` `` anywhere in the URL. Since `&` is the standard query-string separator (e.g. `/api/v1/users?page=1&limit=20`), ordinary benign requests are flagged as **critical** command injection — constant false critical alerts that will flood the threat store/history and alerting. Narrow the pattern so shell metacharacters are only matched in decoded parameter values with actual command context (e.g., require a command token next to the metacharacter), and don't match the raw URL text.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The `ldap_injection` pattern matches any `(`, `|`, or `&` character, so any URL containing parentheses or `&`-separated query parameters is flagged as LDAP injection. Likewise the `sql_injection` pattern fires on any `select|union|delete|...` keyword followed by whitespace anywhere in the path/query. Both produce a very high false-positive rate on normal traffic. Scope the regexes to decoded parameter values and require actual injection signatures (e.g., quote/escape the pattern, or combine keyword + metacharacter sequences).

---

### [medium] (bug)

`attack_windows` (keyed per source IP for brute-force/webhook tracking and per endpoint for DDoS tracking) and `baselines` (keyed per endpoint) are never pruned — only the timestamp lists inside them are trimmed. Every distinct IP/endpoint ever seen leaves a permanent dict entry, so a long-running service grows memory without bound. Prune keys whose windows are empty (e.g., delete the key when the filtered list becomes empty, or run periodic cleanup).

---

### [medium] (bug)

`_register_threat` increments the `active_threats` gauge, but nothing ever decrements it: the 1-hour expiry cleanup in `/threats/active` removes threats from `active_threats_store` without calling `.dec()`, and that cleanup only runs when the endpoint is polled. The gauge therefore over-reports active threats indefinitely (only `/threats/clear` resets it). Decrement the gauge for each threat removed during expiry cleanup.

---

### [medium] (performance)

`redis_client.ping()` is a synchronous socket call inside an `async def` handler. If Redis is slow or unreachable (connection timeout is 5s), the whole event loop blocks and every request stalls. Use an async Redis client (`redis.asyncio.Redis`) or offload the call to an executor, e.g. `await asyncio.to_thread(redis_client.ping)`.

```suggestion
        if redis_client:
            await asyncio.to_thread(redis_client.ping)
        return {"status": "healthy", "detector_active": attack_detector.processing}
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

Using `source_ip` as a Prometheus label on counters (`brute_force_attempts_total`, `injection_attempts_total`, and `attacks_detected_total`) creates unbounded label cardinality — every distinct attacker IP adds a new time series, degrading TSDB memory and query performance on a long-running internet-facing service. Drop the raw-IP label or aggregate it (e.g., by ASN/network prefix).

---

### [low] (bug)

`processing` is initialized to `False` and only ever assigned `False` (in `shutdown_event`); it is never set to `True`, so `/health` permanently reports `detector_active: false` even while the service is actively processing events. Set it to `True` at startup (e.g., in `startup_event`).


## tools/check-postgres-health.sh (5 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

All `psql` checks below run inside the container without `-h`/`-p`, so they ignore the configured `POSTGRES_HOST`/`POSTGRES_PORT` and connect via the local socket / default port 5432. This is inconsistent with the `pg_isready` check above: when `POSTGRES_PORT` is non-default (or a different instance is listening on 5432), `pg_isready` can pass while the `psql` checks hit the wrong endpoint or fail, producing false failures. Pass `-h "$POSTGRES_HOST" -p "$POSTGRES_PORT"` to every `psql` invocation (or drop them from `pg_isready`) so both checks target the same endpoint.

```suggestion
if docker-compose exec postgres psql -h "$POSTGRES_HOST" -p "$POSTGRES_PORT" -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c "SELECT 1;" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

With `set -e` at the top, any failed `docker-compose exec postgres psql ...` (nonzero exit) makes this command substitution assignment fail and the script exits immediately. The subsequent `if [ -n "$CONNECTION_COUNT" ]` fallback branches (e.g. "⚠ Could not retrieve connection count") are therefore unreachable — the script just aborts with a raw exit code instead of reporting the intended warning. The same applies to `MAX_CONNECTIONS`, `DB_SIZE`, `TABLE_COUNT`, `LONG_RUNNING`, and `REPLICATION_ENABLED`. Append `|| true` (or `|| VAR=""`) so the fallback logic actually runs.

```suggestion
CONNECTION_COUNT=$(docker-compose exec postgres psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -t -c "SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity;" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ') || true
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`max_wal_senders` is non-zero by default (10), so this will almost always report "Replication configured" even when no replication is set up at all — it says nothing about whether replication is configured or active. Check actual replication state (e.g. `pg_stat_replication` / `pg_is_in_recovery`) instead. Additionally, if the query fails, `REPLICATION_ENABLED` is empty and `[ "" -gt 0 ]` is an invalid integer comparison; guard the empty case first.

```suggestion
if [ -n "$REPLICATION_ENABLED" ] && [ "$REPLICATION_ENABLED" -gt 0 ]; then
```

---

### [medium] (security)

`POSTGRES_DB` is interpolated unescaped into the SQL string. A value containing a single quote (or other SQL metacharacters) breaks the query or can inject arbitrary SQL, and the result is echoed back into the report. Since the value comes from the environment, avoid interpolating it entirely by using `pg_database_size(current_database())`.

```suggestion
DB_SIZE=$(docker-compose exec postgres psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -t -c "SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size(current_database()));" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ')
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Portability/robustness: the script hardcodes the legacy `docker-compose` CLI (fails where only `docker compose` v2 exists), a container name pattern `chimera-postgres.*Up` (brittle if the compose project name or service name differs, and an unhealthy-but-"Up" container still passes), and `docker-compose exec` without `-T`, which can fail with "the input device is not a TTY" when run from cron/CI. Consider abstracting the compose command (e.g. `COMPOSE="${COMPOSE:-docker compose}"`), matching by service name, and adding `-T` for non-interactive execution.

## tools/check-redis-health.sh (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

With `set -e` at the top of the script, this assignment (and the other non-pipelined substitutions: `STATS_INFO`, `PERSISTENCE_INFO`, `CLIENT_INFO`) causes immediate script termination when `docker-compose exec`/`redis-cli` returns non-zero, because the exit status of the assignment is the exit status of the substitution. As a result the `else echo "⚠ Could not retrieve memory info"` warning branch below is unreachable dead code, and stderr is suppressed by `2>/dev/null` so the failure reason is invisible. Note the inconsistency: pipelined substitutions (e.g. `KEY_COUNT`, `REDIS_VERSION`) end with `tr`, whose exit status (0) masks the failure, so those warning branches *are* reachable. Append `|| true` (or move the substitution into the `if` condition) so degraded metrics are reported as warnings instead of aborting the health check.

```suggestion
MEMORY_INFO=$(docker-compose exec redis redis-cli -h "$REDIS_HOST" -p "$REDIS_PORT" INFO memory 2>/dev/null) || true
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`docker-compose exec` allocates a TTY by default. When this script is run from cron, CI, or any other non-interactive shell, the exec fails with "the input device is not a TTY" and the health check can never pass — the first exec at line 20 already aborts the script. Add the `-T` flag to every `docker-compose exec` invocation (lines 20-117) to force non-interactive mode.

```suggestion
KEY_COUNT=$(docker-compose exec -T redis redis-cli -h "$REDIS_HOST" -p "$REDIS_PORT" DBSIZE 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r')
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

No timeout is applied to any `docker-compose exec`/`redis-cli` call in this script. `redis-cli` has no default socket timeout, and `docker-compose exec` itself can hang if the container is hung or paused or the network black-holes. A health check that is supposed to act as a monitoring watchdog can therefore block indefinitely on the first `redis-cli` call. Wrap each invocation in `timeout` (e.g. `timeout 10 docker-compose exec ...`) and/or pass `--connect-timeout`/`--timeout` to `redis-cli`; apply the same wrapping to all other exec calls below.

```suggestion
if timeout 10 docker-compose exec redis redis-cli -h "$REDIS_HOST" -p "$REDIS_PORT" --connect-timeout 5 ping | grep -q PONG; then
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The container detection `grep -q "chimera-redis.*Up"` is brittle: the container name depends on the compose project name (defaults to the directory name or `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME`), and the format differs between Docker Compose v1 (`chimera_redis_1`, underscores — this regex won't match) and v2 (`chimera-redis-1`, hyphens). A simple rename or compose version change causes a false negative that reports a healthy Redis as down. The `Up` substring also matches unhealthy states like `Up (unhealthy)`. Filter using compose itself instead of parsing the ps table, and note the standalone `docker-compose` binary is deprecated in favor of the `docker compose` plugin.

```suggestion
if [ -z "$(docker-compose ps -q redis)" ]; then
```

---

### [low] (performance)

The script spawns a separate `docker-compose exec redis redis-cli` process for every metric (ping, INFO memory, DBSIZE, INFO server ×2, INFO stats, INFO persistence, INFO clients) — 6+ container execs per run. Each exec adds API and process-startup overhead, which matters if this check runs frequently from a monitoring loop. Consider issuing a single `redis-cli INFO all` call (plus DBSIZE) and parsing all sections locally from the captured output.

---

## tools/docker-migrate.sh (10 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (bug)

The migration reads a live SQLite database without stopping or pausing the application containers. Any writes that occur while `cp` snapshots the file or while `migrate_sqlite_to_postgres.py` reads it can produce a torn backup and a migrated dataset that diverges from what the application is actually using (rows written mid-migration can be missed). Stop the operator/scout services (or otherwise quiesce writes) before taking the snapshot and running the migration, and document that requirement.

---

### [high] (bug)

`cp` of a live SQLite file is not a safe backup: the copy is not atomic and does not capture a consistent snapshot while the database is being written (journal/WAL state is not coordinated), so the backup can be corrupt or incomplete. Use SQLite-aware backup, e.g. `sqlite3 "$SQLITE_PATH" ".backup '${SQLITE_PATH}.backup.<ts>'"` or `VACUUM INTO`, which yields a consistent copy even with concurrent writers.

```suggestion
if [ -f "$SQLITE_PATH" ]; then
    sqlite3 "$SQLITE_PATH" ".backup '${SQLITE_PATH}.backup.$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)'"
```

---

### [high] (bug)

PostgreSQL availability is never enforced: the `pg_dump` failure is swallowed (`2>/dev/null ... || echo`) with a misleading "database may not exist yet" message, and nothing starts or waits for the `postgres` service. If it is down or the database/user does not exist, the migration/verify steps fail later with a confusing connection error after backups have already been taken. Add `docker-compose up -d postgres` plus a readiness wait (e.g., `pg_isready` from inside the container) before the backup/migration steps.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`DRY_RUN` is only consulted after the backup (file copies) and, potentially, `docker-compose up -d scout` + `sleep 5` have already run, yet the script later prints "DRY RUN COMPLETE. No changes made." These are real side effects (backup files created, a container started), so the dry-run contract is misleading. Move the backup/container-start steps inside the non-dry-run branch, or at least report in the dry-run output that backups were created and scout may have been (re)started.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The script claims "Updating database mode to dual-write..." and "System now in DUAL-WRITE mode", but it only prints instructions — it never writes `CHIMERA_DB_MODE` to an environment file, never restarts services, and never changes the actual runtime configuration. Users can easily believe dual-write is active when it is not. Either apply the change (update the env file and restart `operator`/`scout`), or reword the output to "Manual action required" to avoid a false sense of completion.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`DRY_RUN` is compared with an exact `= "true"` string, so values like `TRUE`, `True`, `1`, or `yes` silently fall through to a real migration — dangerous for an operation that writes to production databases. Normalize the value (e.g., lowercase it) and accept common truthy inputs.

```suggestion
if [ "$(echo "$DRY_RUN" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')" = "true" ]; then
```

---

### [medium] (security)

`echo "PostgreSQL URL: $POSTGRES_URL"` prints the full connection URL, including the credentials (`postgresql://chimera:changeme@...`), to the console/logs. Mask the password when logging, e.g. print only the host/database part or replace the password portion with `***`.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

`grep -q "chimera-scout.*Up"` only matches if the Compose project is literally named `chimera`; with any other project name the pattern never matches, so the script can wrongly start a second scout instance or misreport status. Use the Compose API instead, e.g. `docker-compose ps -q scout | grep -q .` to check whether the scout service has a running container.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`tools/migrate_sqlite_to_postgres.py` is resolved relative to whatever the container's working directory happens to be; if the scout image's `WORKDIR` differs, the `python3` invocation fails. Use an absolute container path or `docker-compose exec -w` to pin the working directory.

---

### [low] (bug)

A fixed `sleep 5` is not a reliable readiness wait: if the scout container takes longer to come up (or the image must be pulled), the subsequent `docker-compose exec` fails with a connection error. Poll for readiness (e.g., loop until `docker-compose ps -q scout` returns a running container) instead of a blind sleep.

`datetime.now()` returns a naive local-time datetime, but `.isoformat() + "Z"` falsely marks it as UTC. Two correctness issues: (1) for day=0 (today), `replace(hour=9..18)` can produce timestamps in the future relative to the current time, so the dataset contains trades that haven't happened yet; (2) local time is mislabeled as UTC, skewing any time-based analysis. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` for the base time and avoid emitting timestamps after `now` (e.g., use UTC and clamp today's hours to the current hour).

```suggestion

...
timestamp = day_time.replace(hour=hour, minute=minute, second=second)
```

Because this conversion happens inside a broad `try/except Exception` that wraps the entire read loop, a single bad row aborts the whole import and discards all rows already converted (the function returns [] and the partial data is lost). Wrap the per-row conversion in its own try/except and `continue` on malformed rows.

## tools/download-huggingface-data.py (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

`row.get('amount', ...)` does not fall back when the `amount` column exists but its cell is blank: `csv.DictReader` yields `''` for empty cells, so `float('')` raises ValueError and the whole row is silently dropped by the `except ... continue`, shrinking the signal set even though `quantity`/`volume` are available. The same applies to `price_usd`/`token_address` defaults. Treat empty strings as missing (e.g. `row.get('amount') or row.get('quantity') or ...`) before converting to float.

```suggestion
                        amount = float(row.get('amount') or row.get('quantity') or row.get('volume') or 0.1)
                        "action": "buy" if amount > 0 else "sell",
                        "amount_sol": abs(amount),
```

### [medium] (bug)

Timestamp normalization is unsafe for real CSV values: `csv.DictReader` returns `''` for blank cells, so `row.get('timestamp', ...)` returns `''` (the default is only used when the key is absent) and the result becomes the malformed `'T00:00:00Z'` after the append. Unix-epoch values (e.g. `1700000000`) and space-separated datetimes (`2023-01-01 00:00:00`) also get `'T00:00:00Z'` blindly appended, producing invalid timestamps that are then saved into signals and fed into the `min(timestamps)`/`max(timestamps)` time-range report. Normalize based on the actual value: skip blank strings, convert numeric epochs with `datetime.fromtimestamp`, and only append `Z` to date-only strings.

```suggestion
                    raw_ts = row.get('timestamp') or row.get('time') or row.get('date') or datetime.now().isoformat()
                    if 'T' in raw_ts:
                        timestamp = raw_ts
                    elif raw_ts.isdigit():
                        timestamp = datetime.fromtimestamp(int(raw_ts), tz=timezone.utc).isoformat()
                    else:
                        timestamp = raw_ts.replace(' ', 'T') + 'Z'
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The `strategy` classification uses only `row.get('amount', 1)` while `action`/`amount_sol` fall back to `quantity`/`volume`. Rows that lack an `amount` column (or have a blank one) are therefore always classified `spear` even when their `quantity`/`volume` indicates a small shield-size trade, producing internally inconsistent signals. Additionally, since the comparison is `float(...) < 1.0`, any negative amount is always `shield` regardless of magnitude. Compute one normalized amount and reuse it for all three fields, e.g. `strategy: "shield" if abs(amount) < 1.0 else "spear"`.

```suggestion
                        "strategy": "shield" if abs(amount) < 1.0 else "spear",
```

## tools/download-vybe-data.py (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

Trade side and strategy are derived from the sign and magnitude of `amount`, but DEX trade APIs typically return unsigned quantities with a separate side/direction field (and amounts may be in token units rather than SOL). If the Vybe response is unsigned or uses token units, every trade is systematically mislabeled (unsigned amounts are always > 0 → always "buy") and the arbitrary 1.0 spear/shield threshold is meaningless. Verify the actual response schema and prefer the API's explicit direction field if present; otherwise validate sign/units before deriving action and strategy.

---

### [high] (bug)

Missing trade fields are silently replaced with fabricated defaults (current wall-clock time, "unknown" wallet, WSOL mint, $1.00 price, empty signature) and then persisted as if they were real historical signals. Malformed or partial API records therefore contaminate the evaluation dataset with plausible-looking fake data. Skip (and log) records that lack required fields instead of fabricating values, and treat the `1` default for `amount` the same way since it also fabricates a buy/shield signal.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`download_vybe_historical_trades()` returns None for every failure mode (network error, 404 endpoint change, auth required, empty success, generic exception), but `main()` unconditionally prints "Vybe Network API requires authentication" and directs the user to sign up for an API key whenever signals is None. That sends users to the wrong workaround when the actual cause was, e.g., a network outage or a changed endpoint (the function already printed the true error above). Have the function return a reason/error code, or let main() distinguish the failure cause before printing the auth guidance.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`signal['timestamp']` is sliced as a string unconditionally, but the API may return a numeric epoch timestamp, or an explicit None (`.get("timestamp", ...)` returns None when the key exists with a null value). In those cases `signal['timestamp'][:19]` raises TypeError and crashes the script at the end of a successful download. Normalize the timestamp (e.g., convert numeric/None to an ISO string) before slicing; `signal['token_address'][:8]` has the same hazard if a non-string value arrives.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`csv` and `timedelta` are imported but never used anywhere in this module. Remove them to eliminate dead code and avoid confusing future maintainers.

## tools/fetch-dex-activity.py (7 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (security)

Hardcoded live Helius API key committed in source and embedded directly in the request URL. Anyone with access to this file can consume the account's API quota and incur cost, and the key cannot be rotated without a code change. Read it from an environment variable (e.g. os.environ["HELIUS_API_KEY"]) and fail fast if it is not set.

```suggestion
import os
HELIUS_API_KEY = os.environ.get("HELIUS_API_KEY", "")
if not HELIUS_API_KEY:
    raise SystemExit("HELIUS_API_KEY environment variable must be set")
BASE_URL = f"https://mainnet.helius-rpc.com/?api-key={HELIUS_API_KEY}"
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The signals are mostly fabricated rather than observed: the buy/sell label is inferred merely from comparing pre/post token balance list lengths (which is not a valid indicator of trade direction), amount_sol is a random uniform draw, and token_address is picked at random from POPULAR_TOKENS. The output file is labeled as "real trading signals", which is misleading — downstream consumers will treat randomly generated values as ground-truth DEX activity. Derive the amounts/tokens from the actual postTokenBalances/tokenAmount deltas in the transaction meta, and only label a transaction as buy/sell when balance deltas actually confirm the direction.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The days_back parameter is never used: the function prints "Time range: Last {days_back} days" but no transaction is ever filtered by blockTime, so the collected data does not honor the claimed window. Filter parsed transactions to blockTime >= (now - days_back) before appending a signal.

```suggestion
def collect_real_dex_activity(days_back=10, target_signals=1500):
    cutoff_ts = (datetime.now() - timedelta(days=days_back)).timestamp()
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The loop can never reach target_signals=1500: each attempt fetches at most 50 transactions and each transaction yields at most one signal, so the maximum possible is 50 * max_attempts (20) = 1000 signals — always terminating on the attempts cap while the user is told the run succeeded in collecting signals. Raise max_attempts to at least ceil(target_signals / limit) or iterate until the target is met (bounded by a sane timeout).

---

### [medium] (bug)

getBigTransactions is called repeatedly without any pagination or signature tracking, so successive attempts re-fetch and re-process the same recent transactions. The same transaction can therefore be saved multiple times as separate "signals", inflating the dataset with duplicates. Track already-seen signatures and skip them, or add pagination/position tracking between attempts.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

DEX_PROGRAMS is declared but never referenced anywhere in the file, yet the script's stated purpose is to collect "actual DEX program activity rather than specific wallets". Without filtering by these program IDs (e.g. checking accountKeys/log messages against them), the processed transactions are not guaranteed to be DEX trades at all. Either apply the filter or remove the dead constant.

---

### [low] (bug)

datetime.fromtimestamp() returns local time but the appended "Z" labels it as UTC, producing timestamps that are off by the machine's UTC offset. Use datetime.fromtimestamp(..., tz=timezone.utc) so the recorded timestamp matches its timezone marker.

```suggestion
    timestamp = datetime.fromtimestamp(tx.get("blockTime", time.time()), tz=timezone.utc).isoformat()
```

## tools/gen_schema.py (8 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

The ON CONFLICT conflict target is taken from the first key of the seed row dict, which is not guaranteed to be the table's primary key (or even a unique column). If a seed row is written with columns in a different order (or the PK is omitted), PostgreSQL rejects the statement with "there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification". Today this only works because circuit_breaker_state.yaml happens to list `id` first. Derive the conflict target from the schema definition (columns with `pk: true`), or fall back to the table's actual PK instead of assuming the first seed column.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The trigger function name is hardcoded as `update_<column>_column`, but `generate_pg_functions()` only defines `update_updated_at_column` and `update_last_updated_column`. Any trigger on a different column (e.g. a future `modified_at` column) will generate a CREATE TRIGGER referencing a function that does not exist, causing the migration to fail at runtime. Either generate the function bodies alongside the triggers, or validate that the referenced function is defined.

---

### [medium] (bug)

For the scout PostgreSQL output (`scout_tables_only=True`), `generate_pg_functions()` is skipped entirely, yet `generate_triggers()` still emits `CREATE TRIGGER ... EXECUTE FUNCTION ...` statements for any trigger defined on a scout table. The scout schema file would then reference trigger functions that are never defined in it (they exist only in the operator migration). Currently no scout table declares triggers, but this is a latent breakage the moment one is added. Emit the function definitions for scout output as well, or skip trigger generation consistently with the missing functions.

---

### [medium] (bug)

String literal defaults are wrapped in single quotes with no escaping of embedded quotes or backslashes. A default such as `default: "O'Brien"` produces `DEFAULT 'O'Brien'` — broken SQL. Escape `'` as `''` (and backslashes for PG) before quoting, e.g. `default.replace("'", "''")`.

---

### [medium] (bug)

Seed string values are re-quoted without escaping embedded apostrophes (`.strip("'")` only removes surrounding quotes). A seed value containing `'` (e.g. a wallet note or error message) yields invalid SQL. Escape `'` as `''` when formatting the literal.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The table description is interpolated into a single-quoted `COMMENT ON TABLE` string (and a `--` comment line) with no escaping. A description containing an apostrophe or newline produces a broken comment statement. Escape the description (e.g. replace `'` with `''`) before emitting it.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Every migration silently includes only the tables hardcoded in `operator_tables`/`scout_tables`; any YAML schema not present in either list is dropped from all four generated files with no warning. Right now all 33 YAML tables happen to be covered, but adding a new table to `database/schema_yaml/` without also editing these lists causes silent schema drift (tables missing from deployed schemas). Consider deriving the lists from the YAML directory, or validating that every loaded schema is assigned to exactly one list and failing loudly otherwise.

---

### [low] (other)

This loop is dead code: every branch `continue`s and no statement ever executes. Column-level `check` constraints are already emitted inline by `generate_column_def`, so this block can be removed entirely (or replaced with the real table-level check-constraint handling it appears to intend).

## tools/geoip-lookup.py (9 findings, 1 critical, 3 high)

### [critical] (bug)

`/geoip/{ip_address}` is registered BEFORE this route, and FastAPI/Starlette matches routes in registration order. A GET to `/geoip/batch` will be captured by the dynamic route with `ip_address="batch"` (which then fails the `len < 7` validation → 400), so this batch endpoint is unreachable. Move the static `/geoip/batch` route above `/geoip/{ip_address}` or use a distinct path such as `/geoip/batch/lookup` that cannot collide with the single-segment dynamic route.

---

### [high] (performance)

`redis_client` is the synchronous `redis.Redis` client, and `get()/setex()/info()/dbsize()/keys()/delete()` are all blocking network I/O called directly inside `async def` handlers/helpers. Every call stalls the shared event loop, so one slow Redis round-trip delays all concurrent requests. Use `redis.asyncio.Redis`, or wrap each call with `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`.

```suggestion
        cache_key = f"geoip:{ip_address}"
        cached_data = await asyncio.to_thread(redis_client.get, cache_key)
```

---

### [high] (performance)

`geoip2.database.Reader.city()/country()/asn()` perform synchronous (mmap/file-backed) reads inside `async def lookup_*` functions. On a busy event loop this blocks all request handling. Run the lookups in an executor via `await asyncio.to_thread(city_reader.city, ip_address)`, or make the handlers synchronous (FastAPI runs sync handlers in a threadpool).

```suggestion
        response = await asyncio.to_thread(city_reader.city, ip_address)
```

---

### [high] (bug)

On transient failures, `lookup_country`/`lookup_asn` return `"error"` placeholder strings (e.g. `country_code="error"`), and `perform_geoip_lookup` unconditionally stores that result via `set_cached_geoip` with `CACHE_TTL` (1 hour). This poisons the Redis cache with invalid data for the whole TTL, serving garbage to every subsequent request. Skip caching when the result contains `"error"` sentinels (or treat those as 5xx without caching), and only cache genuine `"unknown"`/`AddressNotFoundError` results if intended.

---

### [medium] (bug)

These metrics are declared but never fed: `geoip_lookup_duration.observe()` is never called (the computed `lookup_time` is only stored in the payload), `geoip_cache_hits` is never `.set()`/`.inc()`, and `geoip_database_age` is hard-coded to `.set(0)` at startup instead of reading the mmdb build epoch. Prometheus dashboards for latency, cache ratio, and DB freshness will show no real data. Wire up `observe()`/`set()`/`inc()` at the appropriate call sites, or remove the dead metrics.

---

### [low] (bug)

On a cache hit, `get_cached_geoip` returns the stored dict whose `cache_status` field is always `"miss"` and whose `lookup_time` comes from the original lookup. The API therefore reports `cache_status="miss"` even when served from cache, making the field misleading. Refresh `cache_status`/`lookup_time` on the hit path before returning.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`asyncio` is imported but never used anywhere in this module. If you adopt the `asyncio.to_thread` approach for the blocking Redis/GeoIP calls above, this import becomes useful; otherwise remove it.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`POLICY_CACHE_TTL` is read from the environment but never referenced anywhere — policy evaluations always go through the regular GeoIP cache with `CACHE_TTL`. Either implement policy-level caching using this TTL or remove the dead configuration.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`Instrumentator(app)` is instantiated but `.instrument(app)`/`.expose(app)` are never called, so it registers nothing and contributes no default HTTP metrics. Either wire it up (e.g. `instrumentator.instrument(app)` and expose via the existing `/metrics` endpoint) or remove the dead initialization.

## tools/geoip-updater.py (8 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

MaxMind's GeoIP download API authenticates via a `license_key` query parameter, not HTTP Basic auth. Sending Basic credentials with the undocumented username `sid` is not a supported scheme — every request will be rejected with HTTP 401, so the script can never download any database. Build the URL as `{DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL}?edition_id=...&suffix=tar.gz&license_key=...` and drop the `auth=` argument (the same applies to the `.sha256` sidecar referenced in the checksum finding).

```suggestion
        download_url = f"{DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL}?edition_id={edition_id}&suffix=tar.gz&license_key={MAXMIND_LICENSE_KEY}"

        logger.info(f"Downloading {db_name} database from MaxMind...")

        # Download with authentication
        response = requests.get(
            download_url,
            stream=True,
            timeout=300  # 5 minute timeout
        )
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The new database is moved over the live file inside `download_database` before any verification happens. When `verify_database_integrity` later fails, the `.backup` created just before the move is never restored — a corrupt MMDB stays live in `/geoip` while the known-good copy sits unused. Verify the downloaded file *before* replacing the live copy (or restore the backup on the failure branch) so a failed update leaves the previous database intact.

---

### [medium] (security)

The module docstring promises "Verifies checksums for security" and `hashlib` is imported, but no checksum is ever fetched or compared — MaxMind publishes a `.tar.gz.sha256` sidecar for every edition, and the streamed archive is trusted as-is. A tampered or corrupt download therefore silently replaces the live database with no integrity check. Fetch the `.sha256` sidecar (using the same `license_key` authentication) and verify the digest before extracting; this also eliminates the currently-dead `hashlib` import.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The success `return` inside the tar-member loop exits before `os.unlink(temp_path)` is reached, so every successful cron run leaks the downloaded `.tar.gz` in the temp directory. Exceptions thrown during download/extract also skip the cleanup (the outer `except` returns without unlinking). Wrap the download/extract in `try/finally` (or otherwise guarantee cleanup) so the temp file is always removed on every exit path.

```suggestion
                    logger.info(f"Updated {db_name} database successfully")
                    os.unlink(temp_path)
                    return True, final_path
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

`force` is accepted by argparse (documented as "Force update even if recent") and passed into `update_databases`, but the parameter is never read and no recency/skip-if-recent logic exists at all — the flag is a complete no-op. Either implement the check-and-skip behavior keyed off `force`, or remove the parameter and the `--force` flag so the advertised behavior isn't misleading.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The bare `except: pass` swallows everything, including `KeyboardInterrupt`/`SystemExit`, and silently discards test-lookup failures. As written, a structurally parseable but corrupt database would still pass "integrity" verification. Narrow the catch to the expected exceptions (e.g. `geoip2.errors.AddressNotFoundError` for a missing record) and log the failure, or at minimum use `except Exception:` and record the error.

---

### [medium] (bug)

The docstring claims databases are "updated atomically", but the new file is extracted under `tempfile.gettempdir()` and then `shutil.move`d to `GEOIP_DB_DIR`. When /tmp and /geoip live on different filesystems (common when /geoip is a mounted volume), `shutil.move` falls back to copy+delete and is not atomic — a crash mid-copy leaves a truncated file at the live path. Download/extract to a temp name inside `GEOIP_DB_DIR` (same filesystem) and use `os.replace` for the final swap to get the promised atomicity.

---

### [low] (security)

`tar.extract` uses archive-supplied member names without any validation. Combined with the missing checksum verification above, a tampered archive containing entries like `../../...` could write files outside the intended directory (path traversal). Validate that each member name is absolute-path-free and contains no `..` segments before extraction (or use Python 3.12+'s `filter='data'`) — defense-in-depth even though archives normally come from MaxMind.

---

## tools/migrate_sqlite_to_postgres.py (9 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

`self.pg_conn` is assigned the typing alias object `Optional[psycopg2.extensions.connection]` instead of `None`. This object is truthy, so if `connect()` fails before assigning a real connection (missing SQLite file or a `psycopg2.connect` error), `finally: runner.close()` in `main()` will call `.close()` on the typing object and raise `AttributeError`, masking the original failure. Initialize to `None` and use a type annotation instead.

```suggestion
self.pg_conn: Optional[psycopg2.extensions.connection] = None
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The return value of `runner.validate()` is discarded and `DataValidator.errors` is never merged into `stats['errors']`. Consequently, row-count mismatches still yield a report with status 'success' and exit code 0 — a silent data-integrity failure. Capture the result and propagate validation errors into the report/exit code.

```suggestion
        valid = runner.validate()
        if not valid:
            runner.stats["errors"].append("Validation failed: row counts differ between SQLite and PostgreSQL")
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`validate_checksums()` is never called from `validate()`, so this method is dead code. Even if it were called, stock SQLite has no `MD5()` function, so the SQLite query always raises (swallowed by the `except`, which then returns `True` — meaning checksum errors are always 'passed'). It also hardcodes the `id` column while ignoring the `key_column` parameter, and SQLite's `GROUP_CONCAT` ordering is not guaranteed to match PostgreSQL's `ORDER BY id`. Implement a Python-side checksum (e.g. `hashlib.md5` over all rows in a deterministic order) and invoke it from `validate()`, or remove the method.

---

### [medium] (bug)

This validation list omits `circuit_breaker_state`, `kill_switch_state`, `admin_wallets`, and `schema_migrations` — all tables that `migrate_all()` actually processes — so their row counts are never validated. Additionally, the broad `except` logs 'Could not validate table' and continues, so a table missing from PostgreSQL entirely would not fail validation. Add the missing tables (and consider treating missing tables as validation errors).

```suggestion
        tables = [
            "trades",
            "positions",
            "wallets",
            "dead_letter_queue",
            "circuit_breaker_state",
            "kill_switch_state",
            "admin_wallets",
            "schema_migrations",
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`column_mapping` renames the local `columns` list, but that list is never used: the INSERT is built from `row_dict.keys()` (the original SQLite column names) and `value_transforms` is keyed by the original names too. If either option is ever exercised (all call sites currently pass `None`), the generated INSERT will reference unmapped column names and fail or corrupt data. Apply the mapping to `row_dict` before building the insert, or explicitly document that `column_mapping` is unsupported.

```suggestion
            if column_mapping:
                row_dict = {column_mapping.get(k, k): v for k, v in row_dict.items()}
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The module docstring advertises rollback support, but the connection is set to AUTOCOMMIT and inserts use `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, so a mid-migration failure leaves partial data with no way to roll back. Wrap the migration in a single transaction (drop AUTOCOMMIT, commit at the end, rollback on error), or at minimum TRUNCATE the target tables on restart so a re-run is idempotent.

```suggestion
        # Wrap migration in a single transaction so a failure can be rolled back
        self.pg_conn.set_isolation_level(ISOLATION_LEVEL_DEFAULT)
```

---

### [low] (bug)

The file opened as pg_dump's stdout is never closed, leaking a file descriptor, and `result` is unused. On failure, the partial backup file is also left on disk. Use a context manager around the subprocess call. Consider treating a failed backup as fatal, since the documented rollback relies on it.

```suggestion
            with open(backup_path, "w") as backup_file:
                result = subprocess.run(
                    ["pg_dump", self.config.postgres_url],
                    stdout=backup_file,
                    check=True,
                )
```

---

### [low] (bug)

In dry-run mode, per-table migration exceptions are swallowed and the run continues, but `main()` still logs 'Migration completed successfully!' and exits 0 even when `stats['errors']` is non-empty (the report itself is correctly 'partial_failure'). Make the final log message and exit code reflect the recorded failures.

### [low] (maintainability)

`os` is imported only inside the `__main__` guard. It works when the file is run as a script, but if this module is imported elsewhere and `main()` is invoked, `os.environ` in `main()` will raise `NameError`. Move `import os` to the top-level imports.

## tools/monitor-rpc-latency.py (6 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

Prometheus histogram bucket lines are cumulative counters (number of samples with latency ≤ le), not percentile latencies. Storing the cumulative count from the `le="5"`/`le="50"`/`le="100"` buckets into p50/p95/p99 and rendering them as `...ms` produces misleading output — e.g. "p95" becomes the number of samples ≤50ms, not a 95th-percentile latency. p50/p99 are also never rendered anywhere. Compute real percentiles from the histogram (total `_count` plus interpolation across `le` buckets) or drop these fields entirely.

```suggestion
            import re
            bucket_counts = {}
            total_count = 0.0
            for line in metrics_text.split('\n'):
                m = re.match(r'^chimera_rpc_latency_ms_bucket\{le="([^"]+)"\}\s+([0-9.eE+-]+)$', line)
                if m:
                    bucket_counts[float(m.group(1))] = float(m.group(2))
                elif line.startswith('chimera_rpc_latency_ms_count'):
                    total_count = float(line.split()[-1])
                elif line.startswith('chimera_rpc_health'):
                    metrics["health"] = float(line.split()[-1])
            if total_count:
                for key, p in (("p50", 0.50), ("p95", 0.95), ("p99", 0.99)):
                    target = total_count * p
                    for le in sorted(bucket_counts):
                        if bucket_counts[le] >= target:
                            metrics[key] = le
                            break
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The ordering of --warning vs --critical is never validated. If a user passes --warning >= --critical (e.g. warning=60, critical=50), `get_status_symbol` checks `latency < warning` first, so latencies between critical and warning are shown GREEN/YELLOW while the alert logic (`latency_ms >= args.critical`) still fires — the display silently disagrees with the alert and never shows red. Validate `warning < critical` at startup and abort otherwise.

```suggestion
    args = parser.parse_args()

    if args.warning >= args.critical:
        parser.error(
            f"--warning ({args.warning}ms) must be less than --critical ({args.critical}ms)"
        )

    print_header(args.warning, args.critical)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Truthiness check on `rpc_latency_ms` hides a valid 0.0ms RPC latency (0.0 is falsy), so the health endpoint reporting zero latency makes the "RPC: ..." segment disappear from the status line. Use `is not None` so 0.0 is displayed.

```suggestion
        if check_data.get("rpc_latency_ms") is not None:
            status_line += f" | RPC: {check_data['rpc_latency_ms']:.1f}ms"
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

print_header always prints the module constant CHECK_INTERVAL_SECONDS even when the user overrides --interval, so the header can misreport the actual polling interval. Thread the parsed value through (e.g. `print_header(args.warning, args.critical, args.interval)`).

```suggestion
def print_header(warning_ms: float, critical_ms: float, interval_seconds: int):
    """Print the monitoring header."""
    print(f"\n{'='*70}")
    print(f"RPC Latency Monitor")
    print(f"{'='*70}")
    print(f"WARNING Threshold: {warning_ms}ms")
    print(f"CRITICAL Threshold: {critical_ms}ms")
    print(f"Check Interval: {interval_seconds} seconds")
```

### [low] (bug)

Same truthiness issue as the RPC latency field: a fallback_duration of 0.0s (a valid and meaningful value) is silently omitted because 0.0 is falsy. Compare with `is not None` instead.

```suggestion

            fd = check_data["fallback_duration"]
            status_line += f" | Fallback: {fd}s"
```

### [low] (maintainability)

`rpc_healthy` is extracted into the returned dict but never read by any caller (print_status_row only uses rpc_latency_ms, queue_depth, circuit_breaker, fallback_duration). ## tools/monitoring-tester.py (7 findings, 0 critical, 3 high)

### [high] (security)

Gateway credentials with default password 'changeme_asap' are hardcoded in the source. If these match the deployed gateway, the suite is validating against default credentials that should not exist in production (a security risk); if they don't match, every auth/RBAC test silently produces misleading failures. Likewise, the per-role allow/deny expectations in test_role_based_access (e.g., viewer denied on Prometheus targets but allowed on Grafana dashboards) are baked in, so the suite's validity depends entirely on the deployed gateway matching these exact defaults. Recommend reading credentials from environment variables/config and making the RBAC matrix configurable.

---

### [high] (security)

verify_ssl defaults to False, so every request in the suite skips TLS certificate validation by default (and each request also emits an InsecureRequestWarning). For a tool whose stated goal includes validating SSL/TLS connectivity and certificate correctness, certificate misconfiguration will never be detected unless the user explicitly passes --verify-ssl. Default to True (or require an explicit --insecure flag) so a secure default is the norm.

```suggestion
    def __init__(self, base_url: str = "https://localhost", verify_ssl: bool = True):
```

---

### [high] (bug)

The SSL/TLS test defeats its own purpose in two ways: (1) the request uses verify=self.verify_ssl which defaults to False, so the certificate is never actually validated even on the success path — the 'SSL/TLS connection successful' PASS only proves TCP+HTTP worked; (2) any exception (TLS handshake failure, connection reset, gateway down) is downgraded to WARN as 'SSL test inconclusive', so a genuinely broken TLS endpoint never surfaces as FAIL. Force certificate verification for this test (or inspect the presented cert chain) and report TLS/connection failures as FAIL, not WARN.

---

### [medium] (bug)

When an endpoint returns a non-200 status, the inner loop breaks and that endpoint is silently dropped — nothing is logged and it contributes nothing to `latencies`. Only endpoints with at least one successful sample are measured, so a downed Prometheus/Grafana/AlertManager is masked and the overall benchmark can still report PASS ('Excellent average latency'). Log failed endpoints as FAIL and include them in the overall performance assessment instead of discarding them.

### [medium] (bug)

Every exception path (connection refused, TLS failure, gateway down) is attributed to 'GeoIP may not be configured' and downgraded to WARN, which can hide a real outage during the geographic test. Only evidence of GeoIP being absent (e.g., a specific status code indicating the geo plugin isn't configured) should be WARN; connectivity errors should be FAIL. Also note the test simulates countries purely via client-supplied X-Forwarded-For/X-Real-IP headers — if HAProxy trusts these headers instead of overwriting them, the geographic restriction can be trivially bypassed in production and this test will not catch it.

## tools/register_helius_webhooks.py (5 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

The `--list` branch does not `return` after printing existing webhooks, so execution falls through to the registration path below. When the database contains ACTIVE wallets, a plain `--list` invocation will silently register a new webhook — a destructive side effect the user never asked for. Add `return` after the `if args.list:` block (the other modes — `--test`, `--delete`, `--delete-all` — all return correctly).

```suggestion
    # List existing webhooks
    if args.list:
        print("\n📋 Existing Webhooks:")
        webhooks = get_existing_webhooks()

        if not webhooks:
            print("No existing webhooks found")
        else:
            for webhook in webhooks:
                print(f"  ID: {webhook.get('webhookID', 'N/A')}")
                print(f"  URL: {webhook.get('webhookURL', 'N/A')}")
                print(f"  Type: {webhook.get('webhookType', 'N/A')}")
                print(f"  Accounts: {', '.join(webhook.get('accountKeys', []))}")
                print()
        return
```

### [medium] (security)

The Helius API key is printed to stdout (and thus captured in any log/CI output). `HELIUS_API_KEY[:10]` leaks the key prefix, and if the key is 10 characters or shorter the entire secret is printed. Additionally, when `HELIUS_API_KEY` is unset the tool still proceeds with an empty key and prints a misleading `...`. Mask it or only report whether it is configured, and bail out early if it is missing.

```suggestion
    if not HELIUS_API_KEY:
        print("Helius API Key: NOT SET (export HELIUS_API_KEY)")
        return
    print("Helius API Key: configured")
    print("=" * 70)
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`str.isalnum()` is not a valid Solana address check: it accepts characters outside the base58 alphabet (`0`, `O`, `I`, `l` are excluded from base58, while digits/letters like `1` are included), and it also accepts Unicode alphanumerics (e.g. `é`, fullwidth digits). Invalid addresses can therefore be forwarded to Helius and cause registration failures or monitor the wrong account. Validate against the base58 charset (ideally decode and check the 32-byte length with a base58 library).

```suggestion
    # Basic validation: Solana addresses are base58 encoded, typically 32-44 characters
    base58_chars = set("123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz")
    return (
        isinstance(address, str)
        and 32 <= len(address) <= 44
        and all(c in base58_chars for c in address)
    )
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The HTTP calls to Helius (`register_webhook`, `get_existing_webhooks`, `delete_webhook`) pass no `timeout`, so a stalled connection or unresponsive Helius endpoint can hang the CLI indefinitely. Add a reasonable `timeout` (e.g. 10–30s) to every request, including the two other call sites at `requests.get(url)` in `get_existing_webhooks` and `requests.delete(url)` in `delete_webhook`.

```suggestion
        response = requests.post(url, json=webhook_config, timeout=30)
```

## tools/security-log-parser.py (9 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

The command-injection regex `(;|\||&)` flags any literal `&`, `;`, or `|` as a CRITICAL command-injection attempt. Since `&` is the standard query-string parameter separator (and `;`/`|` appear in legitimate URLs, e.g. filter parameters or encoded data), ordinary requests such as `/search?a=1&b=2` are misreported as critical attacks. This pollutes `attack_detected_total`, produces noisy warnings, and can trigger false security alerts. Restrict the pattern to shell metacharacters actually followed by shell commands/tokens instead of matching bare separators.

```suggestion
    "command_injection": re.compile(r"(?:[;&|]\s*)(?:cat|id|whoami|rm|wget|curl|nc|bash|sh|cmd|powershell|exec|system)\b", re.IGNORECASE),
```

---

### [high] (security)

This endpoint accepts arbitrary JSON from any unauthenticated client and feeds it directly into `_categorize_event`, which mutates Prometheus counters and inserts entries into `active_threats_store` (an unbounded dict that is only pruned when `/threats/active` is polled). Because the service binds to 0.0.0.0 with no auth anywhere, any attacker can forge security events to corrupt metrics/alerting and grow the in-memory store until memory is exhausted (DoS). Require an API key/header, bind this endpoint to localhost, or disable it in production.

```suggestion
@app.post("/parse-log", response_model=SecurityEventResponse)
async def parse_log_line(log_line: str, api_key: str = Header(None)):
    if api_key != os.getenv("PARSER_API_KEY", ""):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Unauthorized")
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`active_threats` gauge is only ever `.inc()`ed here and never decremented. `/threats/active` prunes entries older than 24h from `active_threats_store` (and even clears/replaces the store) but never calls `.dec()` on the gauge, so the gauge stays permanently inflated after cleanup and grows monotonically with every reprocessed event. Note that the local variable `active_threats = {}` inside `get_active_threats` shadows the module-level gauge, so the gauge is unreachable in that function at all (the comment "Update gauge for each threat type" computes `threat_counts` but never touches the gauge). Decrement the gauge for each pruned threat (and rename the local dict), or recompute the gauge from the store. Also consider pruning on a background TTL schedule so the store doesn't grow unboundedly when the endpoint isn't polled.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`last_position` is kept only in memory. On service restart it resets to 0, so the whole log file is reprocessed from the beginning and every counter/gauge is double-counted. After a log rotation/truncation, the new file is usually smaller than `last_position`; `seek()` past EOF then silently yields no lines, so all events written after rotation are missed until the offset is eventually exceeded. Guard against file truncation/rotation by comparing the current file size (or inode) with `last_position` and resetting it when the file shrinks or is recreated.

```suggestion
                        current_size = os.path.getsize(HA_PROXY_LOG_PATH)
                        if current_size < self.last_position:
                            self.last_position = 0
                        f.seek(self.last_position)
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

`open()` and the blocking `for line in f` loop run synchronously inside the async background task, directly on the event loop shared with the API. When a large chunk of log lines needs to be read (especially right after startup, when the whole file is read), all HTTP handlers (`/health`, `/metrics`, `/parse-log`) and Prometheus scrapes are stalled until the read completes. Run the blocking read in an executor (e.g. `asyncio.to_thread`) or use `aiofiles`.

```suggestion
                def _read_new_lines():
                    with open(HA_PROXY_LOG_PATH, 'r') as f:
                        f.seek(self.last_position)
                        lines = [ln.strip() for ln in f]
                        return lines, f.tell()
                new_lines, new_position = await asyncio.to_thread(_read_new_lines)
                self.last_position = new_position
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The task returned by `asyncio.create_task()` is never stored. As documented by asyncio, a task with no strong reference may be garbage-collected mid-execution, silently stopping the log-processing loop; any exception escaping the task is also swallowed. Keep a reference on the processor (e.g. `log_processor.task = asyncio.create_task(...)`) and cancel it in `/stop-processing` and shutdown. Also, a stop followed by an immediate start can briefly run two loops over the same file because the old task may still be draining its final sleep, causing duplicate processing.

```suggestion
    # Start background log processing
    log_processor.processing = True
    log_processor.task = asyncio.create_task(log_processor.process_logs())
```

---

### [medium] (performance)

`security_events_total` (and several other counters here) are labeled with `source_ip` (and `geo_country`), which is effectively unbounded cardinality: every distinct source IP creates a new Prometheus time series that never goes away. At security-event volume this can exhaust memory on both the exporter process and the Prometheus server. Aggregate by IP only where necessary (e.g. a separate top-N endpoint) or keep IP out of metric labels.

---

### [low] (bug)

Bare `except:` catches everything, including `KeyboardInterrupt`/`SystemExit`, and silently drops entries whose timestamp can't be parsed without any log. Narrow it to the parsing failures that are actually expected (e.g. `ValueError`, `TypeError` from `datetime.fromisoformat` on empty/malformed timestamps).

```suggestion
            except (ValueError, TypeError):
                pass
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

Dead code: `threat_countries` and `threat_history` are declared but never referenced anywhere, and the `Tuple` and `BackgroundTasks` imports are unused. Remove them to avoid confusion.

## tools/test-helius-webhook.sh (7 findings, 0 critical, 1 high)

### [high] (bug)

test_hmac returns success (0) for every possible HTTP status: 2xx, 401, and all unexpected statuses. Because every branch returns 0, this test can never fail, and it will report a pass even if the endpoint performs no HMAC validation at all. The 401 note is also misleading — 401 only proves the request was rejected; with a hard-coded secret that doesn't match the server's, 401 is expected and proves nothing. Only a genuine 2xx should be treated as success; everything else should return non-zero.

```suggestion
    if [[ "$http_code" =~ ^2 ]]; then
        echo -e "${GREEN}✅ HMAC test passed (HTTP $http_code)${NC}"
        echo "Response: $body"
        return 0
    else
        echo -e "${RED}❌ HMAC test failed (HTTP $http_code)${NC}"
        echo "Response: $body"
        return 1
    fi
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

test_helius_payload always prints a green success message regardless of the HTTP status code, so a 400/500 rejection of the simulated Helius payload is reported as a pass. This masks webhook schema or integration failures. Branch on the status code like test_endpoint does and return non-zero on failure.

```suggestion
    if [[ "$http_code" =~ ^2 ]]; then
        echo -e "${GREEN}✅ Helius payload accepted (HTTP $http_code)${NC}"
        echo "Response: $body"
        return 0
    else
        echo -e "${RED}❌ Helius payload rejected (HTTP $http_code)${NC}"
        echo "Response: $body"
        return 1
    fi
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

None of the three curl invocations (test_endpoint, test_hmac, test_helius_payload) specify --connect-timeout/--max-time. If the target host is unreachable and packets are silently dropped, the script hangs indefinitely instead of failing quickly. Add e.g. --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 15 to every curl call.

```suggestion
    response=$(curl -s --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 15 -w "\n%{http_code}" -X "$method" "$url" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d "$data" 2>&1) || {
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

The HMAC signature is always computed with the hard-coded default 'test_secret', so the test can never validate the real shared-secret flow: unless the server happens to use this literal default, the request always returns 401 (which the script even celebrates as 'HMAC validation is working'). Require the real secret via an argument or the HELIUS_WEBHOOK_SECRET environment variable and fail if it is unset. Also verify the signed message format (${timestamp}.${payload}) matches the server's scheme, otherwise the test is meaningless even with the correct secret.

```suggestion
    local url="$1"
    local secret="${HELIUS_WEBHOOK_SECRET:?HELIUS_WEBHOOK_SECRET must be set to the real webhook secret}"
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

HEALTH_URL is derived by blind string substitution. If a caller passes a webhook URL that does not contain the literal '/monitoring/helius-webhook' segment (e.g. a dev/staging path or a trailing-slash variant), the substitution silently leaves the URL unchanged and the 'health check' then requests the webhook endpoint instead, making the first test fail confusingly. Guard the substitution and fall back to appending /health.

```suggestion
WEBHOOK_URL="${1:-https://chimera.example.com/api/v1/monitoring/helius-webhook}"
HEALTH_URL="${WEBHOOK_URL/\/monitoring\/helius-webhook/\/health}"
if [[ "$HEALTH_URL" == "$WEBHOOK_URL" ]]; then
    HEALTH_URL="${WEBHOOK_URL%/}/health"
fi
```

---

### [low] (bug)

The health check is issued as a GET but curl is always invoked with -d (here an empty string) plus a JSON Content-Type header. With -X GET, curl still transmits a request body, and stricter servers may reject a GET-with-body with 400, causing a false negative on the first test. Consider only adding -d when data is non-empty (and only for POST/PUT).

---

### [low] (maintainability)

'head -n -1' is a GNU head extension; on macOS/BSD head it errors with 'illegal line count', breaking body extraction for the whole script. Use a portable alternative such as sed '$d' to drop the trailing HTTP code line.

```suggestion
    http_code=$(echo "$response" | tail -1)
    body=$(echo "$response" | sed '$d')
```

## web/.eslintrc.json (3 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

`env.es2021` registers globals only up to ES2021, while `ecmaVersion: "latest"` parses the newest syntax. This mismatch means code using ES2022+ globals (e.g. `structuredClone`, `Object.hasOwn`, `Array.prototype.findLast`) will parse fine but trigger `no-undef` errors (enabled by `eslint:recommended`) because those globals aren't declared in any env. Align both settings to the same ES version (e.g. add `es2022`/`es2023` env or drop `es2021` if `latest` is intended).

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`varsIgnorePattern: "^error"` suppresses `no-unused-vars` for *any* identifier beginning with "error" (e.g. `errorMessage`, `errorCode`), which is broader than the likely intent of ignoring a `catch (error)` binding. At the same time, `caughtErrorsIgnorePattern: "^error"` does not match the very common `catch (err)` identifier, so unused caught errors named `err` will still be reported. Consider a single explicit convention (e.g. `^_` prefix for ignored bindings) and align both patterns, or document why only `error`-prefixed names should be exempted.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

In legacy `.eslintrc` config, `ignorePatterns` uses gitignore-style glob semantics, so `*.config.js` / `*.config.ts` match at any directory depth — any file ending in `.config.js`/`.config.ts` anywhere in the repo (including nested sub-projects or test fixtures) will be excluded from linting. If only the root-level build configs were meant to be skipped, anchor the patterns (e.g. `/vite.config.ts`, `/*.config.ts`).

## web/index.html (3 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

Hardcoded `<base href="/">` assumes the app is always served from the domain root. When deployed under a subpath (e.g. `/trading/`), absolute URLs like `/src/main.tsx`, `/chimera.svg`, and client-side router paths resolve against the root and break. Prefer configuring Vite's `base` option and letting Vite rewrite asset URLs; if the tag must stay, use Vite's `%BASE_URL%` placeholder so it matches the configured base.

```suggestion
<base href="%BASE_URL%" />
```

### [low] (performance)

The Google Fonts stylesheet is a render-blocking external dependency loaded synchronously in `<head>`: if fonts.googleapis.com is slow or unavailable, first paint is delayed for a trading dashboard where latency matters, and every page load sends a request to a third-party host (privacy/availability dependency). Consider self-hosting the fonts or loading the CSS asynchronously (e.g. the `media="print" onload` swap pattern) while keeping `display=swap`.

### [low] (maintainability)

Hardcoding `class="dark"` on `<html>` forces dark mode before hydration and overrides any system/saved preference. If the app reads a stored/system theme on hydration, users get a theme flash (FOUC) or an inconsistent theme until the app takes over. Apply the theme with a small inline pre-hydration script (reading localStorage/system preference) or keep this static class in sync with the app's theme initialization logic.

The dev server port/host is hardcoded in multiple places that must stay in sync: `baseURL` here, `webServer.url` below, and the Vite config itself. If the dev server port or host changes (e.g., different CI environment, port conflict), these will silently diverge and cause confusing failures. Consider validating the server serves the expected app (health/version endpoint) before reuse, or default to starting a fresh server.

If parallelism is not actually wanted in CI, this is misleading; consider making the worker count configurable or removing the CI cap so the config matches its stated intent.

With `retries: 0` locally (and retries only on CI), `trace: 'on-first-retry'` means traces are never captured for local failures, which makes debugging local test failures harder (you only get screenshots). Consider `trace: 'retain-on-failure'` or `'on'` for local runs so traces are available on the first failure.

`isLoading` is derived purely from data presence (`!portfolioRisk || !positionsData`), so it cannot distinguish an in-flight request from a failed one. If `usePortfolioRisk()` errors, `portfolioRisk` stays undefined and the UI will be stuck in a loading state indefinitely; likewise once data is loaded a background refetch won't reflect loading. This fallback silently mixes two incompatible quantities: `wallet_balance_sol` is the actual available balance (capital + realized PnL − active exposure), while `total_capital_sol` is the configured capital cap. When `wallet_balance_sol` is missing/null, NAV becomes "capital cap + unrealized PnL", which is not the real NAV and can be materially wrong without any warning. export async function retryDeadLetterItem(tradeUuid: string): Promise<RetryResponse> {
