```suggestion
    const { data } = await apiClient.post<RetryResponse>(
      `/incidents/dead-letter/${tradeUuid}/retry`
    )
    return data
  } catch (error) {
    // Map raw API/network errors to a user-friendly message before rethrowing
    throw new Error(
      error instanceof Error ? `Retry failed: ${error.message}` : 'Retry failed. Please try again.'
    )
  }
}
```

## web/src/api/performance.ts (10 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (bug)

The `meta.onError` callbacks in this file (and the identical pattern in all other hooks here) never execute. In TanStack Query v5, `meta` is passive metadata — it is not invoked as a callback, and `QueryClient` in main.tsx is created with no `queryCache`/`onError` handler that dispatches `query.meta?.onError`. As a result the console.error/toast.error error handling for all five hooks is dead code: RPC latency and database performance failures (marked "critical" here) will never show their toast, and errors are silently swallowed. Wire a global QueryCache with an onError handler that calls `query.meta?.onError?.(error)`, or move error handling to the consuming components (they already receive `error` from useQuery).

### [high] (bug)

`timeRange` is only used in the queryKey and is never sent to the API, so changing the TimeRangePicker value refetches the exact same data — the range selector has no effect on cost analysis. Pass the range as a request param like useTradeLatency does (`params: timeRange ? { range: timeRange } : undefined`).

The UI will render fabricated/misleading cost breakdowns. ### [medium] (bug)

`reset_at` is fabricated as `Date.now() + window_seconds` and regenerated on every 5-second poll, so the countdown never approaches an actual server reset and operators are misled. Also `remaining` is unclamped and can go negative when `current_rate > limit`. Prefer server-provided reset/limit fields if available (or drop the fabricated `reset_at`), and clamp remaining with `Math.max(0, ...)`.

```suggestion
          remaining: Math.max(0, (limit.limit || 100) - (limit.current_rate || 0)),
          reset_at: limit.reset_at ? new Date(limit.reset_at).toISOString() : undefined,
```

### [medium] (bug)

`sample_size` is a count (number of samples), not a rate; mapping it to `request_rate` produces semantically incorrect metrics in the UI (e.g. a 60-sample batch over an hour would be shown as 60 RPS). `response.data` is dereferenced without a null guard in every transform in this file (`data.endpoints`, `data.query_latency`, etc.). If the endpoint returns an empty body (204/no content), this throws at runtime instead of falling back to the `?? 0` defaults on nested fields. Guard with `const data = response.data ?? {}` in all three transform hooks (RPC, database, request-rate).



```suggestion
          })
```

The `'dashboard:update'` event name is a hardcoded magic string used in both `addEventListener` and `removeEventListener`. A typo or mismatch with the dispatcher's event name silently breaks all WebSocket updates with no error. Extract it to a single shared exported constant and reuse it in both places (and in the dispatcher code).

```suggestion
      window.removeEventListener(DASHBOARD_UPDATE_EVENT, handleDashboardEvent as EventListener)
```

The `as any` casts on both the event name and the handler completely bypass TypeScript's event type checking, hiding any mismatch between the dispatcher's `detail` payload and the declared `DashboardWebSocketMessage` interface. Type the handler explicitly (e.g. `as EventListener`) and keep the typed `handleDashboardEvent` signature so payload drift is caught at compile time.

```suggestion

```

`refreshAllData` only explicitly invalidates `['risk']` and `['signals']`. It currently also refreshes the `['risk','portfolio']`, `['signals','consensus']` and `['signals','quality']` queries only because `invalidateQueries` does implicit prefix matching. This reliance is fragile and the intent is not self-documenting — list the concrete query keys the hook manages so coverage is explicit and robust.

```suggestion
    queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['signals'] })
    queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['risk', 'portfolio'] })
    queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['signals', 'consensus'] })
    queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['signals', 'quality'] })
```

## web/src/index.css (6 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

`.text-profit`/`.text-loss` are redundant and shadow Tailwind-generated utilities. Because `profit` (`#00FF88`) and `loss` (`#FF4444`) are already defined in `web/tailwind.config.js` theme colors, Tailwind auto-generates `text-profit` and `text-loss`. This custom block (declared after `@tailwind utilities`) overrides the generated ones with hard-coded arbitrary hex values, so if the theme tokens change, the class silently diverges from `bg-profit`/`border-profit` etc. Recommend deleting these two custom classes and relying on the generated utilities.

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Hard-coded `rgba(0, 255, 136, 0.5)` duplicates the `profit` theme token (`#00FF88`) already applied via `@apply bg-profit`. If the theme's profit color is changed, the dot color and its glow will drift out of sync. Consider deriving the glow from the same token, e.g. `box-shadow: 0 0 8px color-mix(in srgb, theme(colors.profit) 50%, transparent);` (same applies to `.status-dot-degraded`/`.status-dot-unhealthy` glows).

```suggestion
  .status-dot-healthy {
    @apply bg-profit;
    box-shadow: 0 0 8px color-mix(in srgb, theme(colors.profit) 50%, transparent);
  }
```

---

### [medium] (maintainability)

Only WebKit pseudo-elements (`::-webkit-scrollbar-*`) are styled here; Firefox and other engines will render default (light) scrollbars in this dark theme, producing an inconsistent appearance. Add the standard `scrollbar-width`/`scrollbar-color` properties (supported by Firefox) using the same `background`/`border`/`surface-light` tokens so scrollbars match across browsers.

```suggestion
  html {
    scrollbar-width: thin;
    scrollbar-color: theme(colors.border) theme(colors.background);
  }
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The glow color `rgba(0, 212, 255, 0.3)` is a hard-coded duplicate of the `shield` theme token (`#00D4FF`); likewise `.glow-spear` duplicates the `spear` token (`#FF8800`). These will silently drift if the theme palette changes. Derive from theme tokens (e.g. `color-mix(in srgb, theme(colors.shield) 30%, transparent)`) to keep glows consistent with the rest of the UI.

```suggestion
  .glow-shield {
    box-shadow: 0 0 20px color-mix(in srgb, theme(colors.shield) 30%, transparent);
  }
```

---

### [low] (bug)

`env(safe-area-inset-bottom)` is unsupported on older iOS Safari (< 11.2), which only understands the deprecated `constant()` function, so the safe-area padding will silently be missing there. Add a `constant()` fallback before the `env()` declaration.

```suggestion
  .safe-area-bottom {
    padding-bottom: constant(safe-area-inset-bottom);
    padding-bottom: env(safe-area-inset-bottom);
  }
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`font-family: 'JetBrains Mono', monospace;` duplicates the theme's `fontFamily.mono` definition in `web/tailwind.config.js`. Use `@apply font-mono` so the custom class stays in sync if the configured mono font stack changes.

```suggestion
  .font-mono-numbers {
    @apply font-mono;
    font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums;

```

## web/src/lib/format.ts (4 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

`decimals` is caller-controlled and never validated. `String.prototype.repeat` and `Number.prototype.toFixed` both throw `RangeError` for out-of-range values: negative or `Infinity` decimals crash `repeat`, and values outside [0, 100] crash `toFixed` (e.g. `safeToFixed(x, -1)`, `safeToFixed(x, 101)`). Non-integer/NaN decimals don't crash but silently produce unexpected output. Normalize `decimals` once at the top and reuse it:

```suggestion
export function safeToFixed(value: unknown, decimals: number = 2): string {
  // toFixed only supports [0, 100]; repeat throws for negative/Infinity, so clamp first.
  const d = Number.isFinite(decimals) ? Math.min(100, Math.max(0, Math.trunc(decimals))) : 2
  if (value === null || value === undefined || value === '') {
    return '0.' + '0'.repeat(d)
  }
  const num = typeof value === 'number' ? value : Number(value)
  if (isNaN(num) || !Number.isFinite(num)) {
    return '0.' + '0'.repeat(d)
  }
  return num.toFixed(d)
}
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`isNaN()` does not catch non-finite results: `Number('Infinity')` and `Number('1e999')` return `Infinity`, which passes `isNaN` (Infinity is not NaN). As a result `toNum('Infinity')` returns `Infinity` and `safeToFixed('Infinity')` renders the string `'Infinity'` instead of a numeric fallback. Use `Number.isFinite()` to reject non-finite values:

```suggestion
export function toNum(value: unknown): number {
  if (value === null || value === undefined || value === '') return 0
  if (typeof value !== 'number' && typeof value !== 'string') return 0
  const n = typeof value === 'number' ? value : Number(value)
  return Number.isFinite(n) ? n : 0
}
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

`Number(value)` throws a `TypeError` for a `Symbol`. Since the parameter is typed `unknown` and these helpers are meant to defensively handle arbitrary API data, callers can pass an unsupported type and crash the app. Guard the type before converting (or wrap in try/catch) so the helper genuinely never throws. The same fix should be applied in `toNum` for consistency.

```suggestion
  if (typeof value !== 'number' && typeof value !== 'string') {
    return '0.' + '0'.repeat(decimals)
  }
  const num = typeof value === 'number' ? value : Number(value)
  if (isNaN(num) || !Number.isFinite(num)) {
```

---

### [low] (other)

Converting high-precision decimal strings (e.g. `'0.12345678901234567890'`) to a JS `number` rounds to ~15-17 significant digits before `toFixed`, so the result can differ from exact decimal rounding of the original string. This is acceptable for display-only formatting, but the header advertises these helpers for "comparing" — comparing the coerced numbers can yield incorrect equality results. If comparison accuracy matters, compare the original strings or use a decimal library.

## web/src/lib/version.ts (2 findings)

### [medium] (security)

Importing the entire root package.json into client code pulls all package metadata (name, scripts, dependencies, devDependencies, repository, engines, etc.) into the web bundle's module graph. In dev mode Vite serves the full JSON to the browser, exposing dependency names/versions publicly, and the production bundle only avoids shipping it if the bundler successfully tree-shakes the unused named exports (fragile and bundler-dependent). Prefer a dedicated minimal file (e.g. `web/src/lib/version.json` containing only `{"version": "..."}` or build-time injection via Vite `define`/`import.meta.env`) so only the version string ever reaches the client.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`version` is untyped and has no fallback: if the `version` field is ever removed from package.json, this silently renders as `vundefined`. Consider a defensive fallback (e.g. `version ?? '0.0.0'`) or type the constant explicitly to make the contract clear.

---

## web/src/stores/authStore.ts (5 findings, 0 critical, 2 high)

### [high] (security)

`login()` never resets `refreshToken`. If a user is logged in without an explicit `logout()` (e.g., switching accounts from a login page), the previous session's `refreshToken` remains in the store and could be used to obtain access tokens for the old account, or be persisted across sessions. Clear `refreshToken` on login (it is set later via `updateTokens`).

```suggestion
        set({
          user,
          isAuthenticated: true,
          tokenExpiresAt: expiresAt,
          refreshToken: null,
          lastActivity: now,
        })
```

---

### [high] (bug)

`partialize` persists `isAuthenticated: true` and a `user` object stripped of its `token` (the `as AuthUser` cast hides that `token` is dropped), but omits `tokenExpiresAt` and `refreshToken`. After a page reload the store is rehydrated with `isAuthenticated === true` while `tokenExpiresAt` is `null`, so `isTokenExpired()` immediately returns `true` and `user.token` is `undefined` — the UI shows an authenticated user that cannot actually authenticate or refresh. Either persist `tokenExpiresAt`/`refreshToken` alongside `isAuthenticated`, or reset auth state (e.g., in `onRehydrateStorage`) when the token can't be restored.

---

### [medium] (bug)

`updateTokens()` can leave the store in an inconsistent half-updated state: when `user` is `null` it still writes `tokenExpiresAt` and `refreshToken` while leaving `isAuthenticated` as-is, and it never sets `isAuthenticated: true`. It also does not refresh `lastActivity`, so a successful token refresh does not reset the 30-minute inactivity timer, causing active users to be logged out mid-session. Guard against the null-user case (fail the refresh / logout) and decide whether refresh activity should extend the session.

---

### [low] (bug)

`isSessionExpired()` returns `false` whenever `lastActivity` is missing. While this is convenient before login, a rehydrated or legacy session whose `lastActivity` was never recorded will never be considered expired, keeping a stale session alive indefinitely. When authenticated, a missing `lastActivity` should be treated as expired (or defaulted to the rehydrate time) so old sessions cannot bypass the inactivity timeout.

---

### [low] (maintainability)

`_hasHydrated` is declared in `AuthState` and initialized but never updated or read anywhere, and `onRehydrateStorage` is a no-op even though its comment claims `_hasHydrated` was removed. This is dead code — remove both the interface field, the initializer, and the no-op callback (or actually implement hydration tracking if it is still needed elsewhere).

---

## web/src/types/index.ts (7 findings)

### [medium] (bug)

wqs_score is typed `number | null` only, but sibling numeric columns (roi_7d, max_drawdown_30d, avg_trade_size_sol) are `number | string` because the API serializes Postgres NUMERIC as strings (as noted in the comment above). If wqs_score is a NUMERIC column it will arrive as a string and silently break arithmetic/formatting downstream. Align the type for parity.

```suggestion
  wqs_score: number | string | null
```

---

### [medium] (bug)

Same serialization-parity concern as wqs_score: win_rate is presumably a derived/NUMERIC column but is typed `number | null`, while sibling numeric fields in this interface use `number | string`. If the API returns it as a string, numeric consumers (percent formatting, sorting) will behave unexpectedly. Consider `number | string | null`.

```suggestion
  win_rate: number | string | null
```

Field-name convention is inconsistent: ConfigResponse uses `cool_down_minutes` while HealthResponse uses `cooldown_remaining_secs` for the same breaker-cooldown concept. Besides the unit (minutes vs secs), the divergent spelling (`cool_down` vs `cooldown`) invites field-name mismatch bugs in frontend code. Standardize on one spelling and encode the unit in the name.

These config sections are declared optional (`monitoring`, `profit_management`, `position_sizing`, `mev_protection`, `token_safety`, `notifications`, `queue`), so any consumer destructuring ConfigResponse without defaults or null-checks will hit runtime errors (undefined access). Ensure all UI consumers guard these sections, or document that the backend always returns them even in degraded responses.

### [low] (maintainability)

circuit_breaker.state is a plain `string`, unlike the enumerated unions used elsewhere in this file (e.g., HealthResponse.status). Silent typos in comparisons and unhandled new states won't be caught at compile time. Narrow it to a union matching the backend (e.g., 'CLOSED' | 'OPEN' | 'HALF_OPEN' | 'TRIPPED').

### [low] (maintainability)

rpc_status.primary and rpc_status.active are plain strings while the rest of the file uses narrowed unions. If these denote discrete provider states/names, a typo in a comparison (e.g., `=== 'fallback'`) would silently fail. Consider a union type for active/primary or at least a comment documenting the possible values.

### [low] (maintainability)

Trade.status mixes execution states (PENDING/QUEUED/EXECUTING/RETRY/DEAD_LETTER) with position lifecycle states (ACTIVE/EXITING/CLOSED). UI code must exhaustively handle all nine values, and these must match the backend's actual status strings. Also note Trade.strategy includes 'EXIT' while Position.strategy only allows 'SHIELD' | 'SPEAR' — confirm the backend semantics so comparisons/switch statements stay in sync.

## web/vite.config.ts (2 findings)

### [medium] (maintainability)

The dev-server port and backend proxy targets are hardcoded (3000, http://localhost:8080, ws://localhost:8080). This ties the config to a single local backend and breaks non-local environments (CI, staging, devcontainers, or a backend on a different host) unless source is edited. Make them configurable via environment variables (e.g. `process.env.PORT`, `process.env.VITE_API_TARGET`, `process.env.VITE_WS_TARGET`, or `loadEnv(mode, ...)` inside a `defineConfig(({ mode }) => ...)` function) with localhost defaults.

```suggestion
  server: {
    port: Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000,
    proxy: {
      '/api': {
        target: process.env.VITE_API_TARGET || 'http://localhost:8080',
        changeOrigin: true,
      },
      '/ws': {
        target: process.env.VITE_WS_TARGET || 'ws://localhost:8080',
        ws: true,
      },
    },
  },
```

---

### [low] (maintainability)

The project is ESM (`"type": "module"` in package.json), where `__dirname` is not natively defined. It happens to work here because Vite's config loader bundles the config and injects a `__dirname` shim, but that relies on Vite's internal bundling behavior. For robustness/portability (e.g. if the config is ever loaded directly as Node ESM), prefer deriving the path from `import.meta.url`, e.g. `path.resolve(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url), '../src')` or `fileURLToPath(new URL('./src', import.meta.url))`.
